text: One mature afternoon during August, a slender, lofty young woman, who was “half-past sixteen,” featuring grave gray eyes alongside locks her acquaintances labeled auburn, had taken a seat upon the wide red sandstone doorstep belonging to a farmhouse on St. Brendan’s Island, resolutely determined to translate a specific number of Virgil’s lines.

However, a day in August during the afternoon, featuring azure mists wrapping the gathered crops on the hills, small breezes murmuring softly among the poplars, and a shimmering brilliance of crimson poppies blazing brightly in contrast to the deep thicket of small fir trees within a nook of the cherry orchard, suited dreaming far better than extinct tongues. Unregarded, the Virgil presently slid down to the grass, and Nell, resting her chin upon her joined hands, while her gaze rested on the magnificent pile of soft clouds gathering directly above Mr. J. A. Pettifer’s residence resembling a vast pale peak, found herself distant in a delightful realm in which a particular schoolmaster was achieving an extraordinary labor, moulding the fates of prospective leaders, and encouraging young intellects and souls toward noble and grand aspirations.

Undeniably, if one reduced things to stern reality . . . a process, it has to be acknowledged, Nell rarely engaged in before it became necessary . . . the existence of much potential for famous people within Brierley school appeared improbable; yet the outcome remained uncertain when an instructor exerted her sway toward the right. Nell possessed particular optimistic visions regarding the achievements a educator could realize if she simply approached the matter correctly; and she was right in the middle of an enchanting picture, four decades in the future, wherein a celebrated figure . . . the precise nature of his renown was preserved in a handy ambiguity, though Nell felt it would be quite lovely for him to be a university president or a Canadian prime minister . . . bent deeply above her withered hand and declared to her that she was the one who had initially ignited his drive, and that the entirety of his life's achievements stemmed from the instruction she had imparted decades prior at Brierley school. This enjoyable reverie was abruptly broken by a exceedingly disagreeable disturbance.

A modest small Jersey cow hastened down the path, and five seconds after, Mr. Pettifer made his appearance . . . provided that “arrived” is not an excessively gentle word for expressing the way he burst into the yard.

He leaped above the fence rather than taking the time to unlatch the gate, furiously approaching a surprised Nell, who had gotten up and was observing him with a degree of confusion. The man, Mr. Pettifer, was the new neighbor living directly to their right, and she had never been introduced to him previously, despite having caught sight of him on one or two occasions.

Prior to Nell returning from Regent’s in early April, the Abernethy place's western neighbor, Mr. Robert Bell, had disposed of his farm and relocated to Port Marlow. A individual named Mr. J. A. Pettifer purchased his property, and nothing beyond his name and his status as a New Brunswick man was recognized concerning him. Nevertheless, within a month of arriving in Brierley, he had acquired the fame of being an eccentric individual . . . “a crank,” declared Mrs. Agatha Sowerby. Mrs. Agatha was a candid woman, as those among you who might have previously met her will recall. Mr. Pettifer was undoubtedly distinct from the rest of humanity . . . and that defines the fundamental trait of a crank, as all people are aware.

To begin with, he maintained his own home and had openly declared that no foolish women were desired near his premises. The women of Brierley avenged themselves through the macabre stories they told regarding his culinary and domestic skills. He had employed young John Henry Carter of Pale Sands, and it was John Henry who initiated the rumors. To begin with, fixed meal times were nonexistent in the Pettifer household. Mr. Pettifer “got a bite” whenever hunger struck him, and should John Henry happen to be present then, he received a portion, but should he be absent, waiting for Mr. Pettifer’s subsequent bout of hunger was his only option. John Henry sadly declared that he would have succumbed to starvation had he not returned home on Sundays to get a proper fill, and had his mother not consistently provided him with a basket of “grub” to carry back on Monday mornings.

Regarding the chore of dishwashing, Mr. Pettifer never even pretended to perform it except when a wet Sunday occurred. On those occasions, he set to work and cleaned every one of them together inside the rainwater hogshead, after which he allowed them to dry by draining.

Furthermore, Mr. Pettifer was “stingy.” Upon being requested to chip in for the Rev. Mr. Wace’s earnings, he replied that he would hold off to observe how many dollars’ worth of benefit he derived from his sermons initially . . . he was disinclined to purchase a pig in a poke. Furthermore, when Mrs. Sowerby paid a visit to request a donation for missions . . . and by the way to catch a glimpse of the interior of the home . . . he informed her that a greater number of pagans existed among the elderly female busybodies in Brierley than in any other location he was aware of, and he would gladly give money toward a mission aimed at converting them to Christianity if she would take it on. Mrs. Agatha departed and remarked that it was a blessing poor Mrs. Robert Bell was resting peacefully in her tomb, because witnessing the condition of her dwelling, which she once held in such high esteem, would have crushed her spirit.

“Well, the kitchen floor was scrubbed by her every other day,” Mrs. Sowerby said to Thirza Abernethy with indignation, “and if its present state were visible to you! As I crossed it, gathering up my skirts was necessary.”

Lastly, Mr. Pettifer possessed a parrot named Nutmeg. No one in Brierley had previously owned a parrot; as a result, the act was regarded as hardly proper. And what a bird it was! According to John Henry Carter, there had never existed a more wicked creature. Its cursing was awful. Mrs. Carter would have removed John Henry immediately had she been certain of finding him another job. Furthermore, Nutmeg had chomp-bitten a chunk directly from the rear of John Henry’s neck on an occasion when he bent over excessively close to its cage. Mrs. Carter displayed the scar to all when the unfortunate John Henry visited home on Sundays.

Every one of these thoughts raced through Nell’s mind while Mr. Pettifer, seemingly entirely rendered mute by anger, remained standing in front of her. Even at his most pleasant, Mr. Pettifer would not have been judged a good-looking man; he was low in stature, heavy-set, and lacking hair; and at present, with his circular countenance turned violet from fury and his bulging azure eyes nearly protruding from his skull, Nell considered him truly the most repulsive individual she had ever beheld.
Suddenly Mr. Pettifer regained the ability to speak.

“I will not tolerate this,” he gasped out, “not for one more day, do you understand, miss. Good heavens, this makes three times, miss . . . three separate occasions! Patience isn't a virtue anymore, miss. On the previous occasion, I gave your aunt a warning that it must not happen again . . . yet she permitted it . . . she committed it . . . what is her reason for doing so, that is the question I require an answer to. That is the purpose of my visit, miss.”

“Are you going to clarify the problem?” Nell inquired, using her utmost formal tone. Lately, she had devoted much effort to rehearsing this demeanor so it would function smoothly once the school term commenced; nevertheless, it seemed to produce no impact whatsoever upon the furious J. A. Pettifer.

“Is it trouble? May my soul be blessed, I would certainly imagine there is sufficient trouble. Miss, the problem lies in the fact that I discovered your aunt’s Jersey cow inside my oats once more, under thirty minutes back. Pay attention, as this makes three times. I caught her there on Tuesday of last week and I caught her there the day before today. I traveled to this place and informed your aunt to ensure it did not happen another time. She permitted it to happen another time. Miss, where can your aunt be found? I merely wish to locate her for a brief moment and speak bluntly to her . . . speak as J. A. Pettifer bluntly speaks, miss.”

“Should you be referring to Miss Thirza Abernethy, my aunt she is not, and her departure to East Welby was to visit a far-off relation of hers who is exceedingly sick,” stated Nell, her loftiness growing appropriately alongside each utterance. “It causes me much regret that my oats should have been trespassed upon by my cow . . . my cow she is, rather than Miss Abernethy’s . . . three years back, when she was a small calf after he purchased her from Mr. Bell, Obed presented her to me.”

“Apologies, young lady! Expressing regret will not fix what happened. You ought to walk over and view the destruction that creature caused among my oats . . . crushed them completely from the middle to the edges, young lady.”

“I am very sorry,” reiterated Nell resolutely, “but maybe Dolly would not have entered had you maintained your fences more effectively. The section of the boundary fence dividing your oatfield from our pasture belongs to you, and I observed just a few days ago that its state was quite poor.”

“There is nothing wrong with my fence,” Mr. Pettifer retorted, his fury escalating at this offensive maneuver into his own territory. “A demonic cow of that sort could not be contained even by the prison fence. Furthermore, you ginger-haired slip of a thing, if that cow belongs to you, as you claim, your time would be far better spent keeping her away from the grain of others instead of lounging about reading yellow-backed books,” . . . casting a contemptuous look at the blameless tan Virgil near the feet of Nell.
A thing other than Nell’s hair was red right then . . . a feature that had forever been a sensitive subject for her.
“I’d prefer to possess red hair instead of being completely hairless, apart from a small strip encircling my ears,” she snapped.

The strike struck home, because Mr. Pettifer was actually extremely touchy regarding his hairless scalp. His fury gagged him once more and left him able only to stare wordlessly at Nell, who regained her composure and pressed her upper hand.

“Because I possess an imagination, I am able to excuse you, Mr. Pettifer. It is simple for me to picture how extremely aggravating discovering a cow among your oats must be, and the remarks you made will not cause me to hold a grudge against you. That Dolly will not ever force her way into your oats again is something I promise you. On that matter, I pledge my word of honor.”

“Well, take care that she does not,” murmured Mr. Pettifer with a rather hushed voice; nevertheless, he marched away in quite a rage, and Nell listened to his self-directed muttering until he moved beyond her hearing.
With a deeply troubled spirit, Nell strode across the yard and locked the mischievous Jersey inside the milking pen.

“Unless she pulls down the fence, getting out of there is impossible for her,” she mused. “At present, she appears quite calm. It is likely that those oats have made her feel ill. Selling her to Mr. Shearer when he expressed interest last week would have been better, I wish I had done so, yet I considered it preferable to hold off until the stock auction took place and dispose of the lot as one. The claim that Mr. Pettifer is a crank seems to be accurate. He definitely shares no kindred spirit with anyone.”
Nell constantly kept an alert watch to spot matching souls.
Thirza Abernethy pulled into the yard just as Nell emerged from the house, prompting the latter to rush inside and prepare tea. As they sat at the tea table, the issue was discussed between them.

“I will be happy once the sale is finished,” Thirza remarked. “Holding such a large amount of livestock around the property with only that untrustworthy Martin to care for them creates too great a burden. He has failed to return so far, despite promising he would definitely return yesterday evening if I granted him the day to attend the funeral of his aunt. I certainly have no idea how many aunts belong to him. Since he was employed here twelve months back, that makes four who have passed away. Once the harvest is gathered and Mr. Pembroke assumes control of the farm, I will be deeply grateful. Until Martin arrives, we must confine Dolly to the enclosure, because she needs to be placed in the rear field and those boundaries require repair. Truly, it amounts to a universe of grief, just as Agatha states. Over there, poor Mary Farrow is on her deathbed, and whatever will happen to her pair of youngsters is beyond my understanding. A brother of hers resides in British Columbia and she has sent a letter to him regarding them, though no response from him has reached her yet.”
“What manner of children are they? What ages have they reached?”
“Six minutes after . . . a pair of twins.”
“Oh, ever since the time Mrs. Rudge gave birth to so many, I’ve had a particular fascination with twins,” Nell said enthusiastically. “Are they good-looking?”

“Gracious, it was impossible to see . . . their filth was so great. Robin was outside creating mud pies when Lucy stepped out to bring him back inside. Robin shoved her face-down into the largest pie, and after she wept, he climbed in too and rolled around to demonstrate that no tears were necessary. Mary mentioned that Lucy actually behaved quite well, whereas Robin possessed a mischievous nature. It could be argued he was never raised properly. Shortly after his birth, his father passed away, and Mary’s poor health has persisted virtually from that moment on.”

“Children who are raised without guidance always make me feel pity,” Nell remarked with gravity. “As you are aware, I possessed none until you began taking care of me. It is my hope that they will be cared for by their uncle. Precisely how is Mrs. Farrow related to you?”
“Mary? Absolutely none. It was her spouse . . . he was related to us as a third cousin. Mrs. Sowerby is walking across the yard now. I figured she would come up to get news concerning Mary.”
“Please do not inform her regarding Mr. Pettifer and the cow,” begged Nell.
Thirza gave her word, although there was really no need for it, because Mrs. Sowerby had barely settled into her seat when she remarked,
“While I was returning from Delford today, Mr. Pettifer was seen by me driving your Jersey from his oats. It appeared to me that he was quite furious. Was a big fuss made by him?”
Nell and Thirza secretly traded entertained grins. Scarcely anything in Brierley ever went unnoticed by Mrs. Sowerby. Just that morning Nell had remarked,

“Should you retire to your personal chamber when night turns to twelve, turn the key in the lock, lower the window shade, and let out a sneeze, the following day Mrs. Sowerby would inquire about the state of your cold!”
“I think he did,” Thirza confessed. “I wasn’t there. He told Nell what he thought of her.”
“I believe he is an extremely unpleasant individual,” declared Nell, indignantly throwing back her reddish head.

“You have never spoken a more accurate word,” Mrs. Agatha stated with gravity. “I was certain that difficulty would arise the moment Robert Bell disposed of his property to an individual from New Brunswick, indeed I was. I cannot imagine what Brierley is turning into, given that such a multitude of unfamiliar folks is flooding inside it. Before long, resting peacefully in our beds will no longer be secure.”
“Why, what different visitors are arriving here?” Thirza asked.

“Are you unaware? To begin with, there is a Trask family. The former home of Peter Mott has been leased by them. That man was engaged by Peter to operate his mill. Coming from down east, they are complete unknowns to everyone. Additionally, the Timothy Cotton family, who are lazy, plan to relocate from Pale Sands, becoming nothing less than a strain on the community. He suffers from consumption . . . whenever he is not committing theft . . . while his wife is a spiritless woman incapable of performing any task. Sitting down is how she does her dishes. An orphaned nephew of her husband, Anthony Tulk, has been taken in by Mrs. Laurence Tulk. He will be attending your school, Nell, which means you should anticipate difficulty, mark my words. Furthermore, an additional new student will be yours. Arriving from the States, Cedric Stanhope will reside with his grandmother. Thirza, do you recall his father . . . Stephen Stanhope, the one who abandoned Rosalind Penrose over in Welby?”
“I am not of the opinion that she was jilted by him. A quarrel took place . . . it seems to me that both parties shared the fault.”

“At any rate, he never wed her, and rumor has it she has been extremely odd ever since . . . residing entirely alone in that small stone dwelling named Echo Cottage. Stephen departed for the States, entered into a enterprise with his uncle, and took a Yankee as his wife. He has not returned home a single time, even though his mother has traveled up to visit him on one or two occasions. His wife passed away two years ago, and he is dispatching the boy back home to his mother for a time. He is ten years of age, and I am uncertain whether he will prove to be a very pleasant student. It is impossible to know what to expect from those Yankees.”

Mrs Sowerby viewed everyone who possessed the bad luck of being born or raised anywhere other than St. Brendan’s Island with an unequivocal can-any-good-thing-come-out-of-Nazareth attitude. It was possible, naturally, that they were decent individuals; nevertheless, one was wiser to remain skeptical. A particular bias against “Yankees” was harbored by her. A Boston boss for whom her husband had formerly labored had defrauded him of ten dollars, and no angels, principalities, or powers possessed the ability to persuade Mrs. Agatha that the entire United States did not bear the blame for this.

“A bit of fresh blood will do Brierley school no harm,” Thirza remarked drily, “and provided this youth resembles his father, he will do fine. Steve Stanhope was the finest boy ever brought up around here, even if certain folks considered him arrogant. I imagine Mrs. Stanhope will be delighted to take the youngster in. Ever since her husband passed away, she has been terribly lonely.”

“Well, the boy might be fine, but he will not resemble Brierley children,” stated Mrs. Agatha, as though that settled the issue. The views held by Mrs. Agatha regarding any individual, location, or item were invariably durable. “What is this rumor about you beginning a Village Improvement Society, Nell?”

“I was merely discussing it with a few of the girls and boys during the recent Debating Club,” Nell stated, her face reddening. “They believed it would be quite pleasant . . . as do Mr. and Mrs. Wace. Many villages possess them these days.”
“Indeed, a world of trouble awaits you if you proceed. It would be wiser to drop the matter, Nell, truly. Nobody enjoys being made better.”

“Oh, we do not intend to attempt the betterment of the populace. It is Brierley on its own. A great deal could be performed to render it more attractive. To give an example, would it not be a change for the better if Mr. Levi Gammon could be persuaded by us to demolish that terrible aged dwelling situated on his upper farm?”

“It certainly would,” Mrs. Agatha conceded. “For years, the settlement has had its view spoiled by that old ruin. However, if your group of Improvers manages to persuade Levi Gammon into performing an unpaid act for the community, I hope to witness the sight and sound of it myself, that’s what. I am not trying to dishearten you, Nell, because your notion might hold value, even if you likely derived it from a trashy American periodical; nevertheless, managing your school will keep you completely occupied, so my friendly counsel is to leave these improvements alone, that’s what. Even so, I realize you will proceed once your determination is fixed. You have constantly been someone who manages to complete a task one way or another.”

The definite contours of Nell’s lips indicated that Mrs. Agatha was quite accurate in her judgment. Nell had set her heart on creating the Improvement Society. Hugh Carrow, who would be instructing in Pale Sands yet was bound to return home every Friday evening until Monday morning, showed great enthusiasm for the project; furthermore, the majority of the other people were ready to join any endeavor that involved periodic gatherings and thus a bit of “fun.” Regarding the nature of these “improvements,” no one possessed a very distinct concept apart from Nell and Hugh. The pair had discussed and mapped them out to such an extent that a perfect Brierley lived within their imaginations, even if it was found nowhere else.
Mrs. Agatha possessed a further piece of information.
“A Honora Hollis has been assigned the Delford school. Nell, weren’t you at Regent’s alongside a girl by that name?”

“Indeed, yes. Honora instructing at Delford! How utterly delightful!” cried Nell, her grey eyes brightening so much that they resembled stars in the night sky, making Mrs. Sowerby ponder once more if she would ever resolve to her own contentment whether Nell Harcourt was actually a lovely girl or if she was not.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: The following afternoon, Nell made a trip by car to Delford to go shopping, accompanied by Isolde Pembroke. Being an official member of the Improvement Society, Isolde joined the other girl in speaking of almost nothing besides it during the entire journey to Delford and their return.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “As soon as we begin, our topmost priority should be giving that hall a coat of paint,” Isolde remarked while they passed the Brierley hall, an unsettled structure looking quite run-down in a tree-filled dale, encircled everywhere by looming spruce trees. “The sight of it is shameful, so we need to deal with it prior to attempting to make Mr. Levi Boulder demolish his home. Father believes our efforts there are doomed to fail . . . Levi Gammon lacks the generosity to devote the necessary time.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Maybe he will allow the boys to dismantle it if they give their word to carry the planks away and chop them into kindling for him,” Nell remarked with optimism. “It is necessary that we do as much as possible and be satisfied to advance gradually in the beginning. Expecting to make all things better right away is impossible. Naturally, our initial step must be to cultivate public opinion.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: While Isolde lacked a clear understanding of what educating public sentiment entailed, it sounded grand, and the prospect of joining an organization with such a purpose filled her with a sense of pride.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “I hit upon a plan yesterday evening that we might carry out, Nell. Are you aware of that triangular plot of land located where the roads coming from Delford, Stonebridge, and Pale Sands intersect? Young spruce have completely covered it; however, would it not be pleasant if they were entirely removed, leaving only the two or three birch trees growing there?”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “How wonderful,” Nell concurred cheerfully. “Also, ensure a country-style bench is placed beneath the birch trees. Then, upon the arrival of spring, a plot for blossoms must be fashioned right in the center so we can set out geraniums.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Yes; but we must figure out a method to make old Mrs. Hiram Mott prevent her cow from roaming the road, otherwise it will consume all our geraniums,” Isolde chuckled. “I am starting to comprehend your concept of cultivating public opinion, Nell. Look at the former Gammon place over there. Have you ever beheld such a dilapidated structure? Plus, it sits immediately adjacent to the road. A neglected home missing its windowpanes continually reminds me of a corpse whose eyes have been pecked out.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “I believe that a dilapidated, abandoned dwelling is a deeply mournful view,” Nell remarked in a daydreaming manner. “To my mind, it appears to constantly ponder its former days and grieve over its past happiness. According to Thirza, a big family grew up inside that aged home a long time back, and it used to be a genuinely lovely spot, featuring an exquisite garden and climbing roses covering it entirely. Little boys and girls, along with mirth and music, filled it completely; yet today it stands vacant, visited by no occupant except the blowing breeze. Its sense of isolation and grief must be so profound! It may be that every one of them returns when the moon shines . . . the spirits of those young boys and girls from days gone by, as well as the roses and the music . . . so that briefly, the ancient dwelling is able to imagine itself youthful and glad once more.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: Isolde shook her head.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “I do not picture things of that nature regarding locations anymore, Nell. Have you forgotten how angry mother and Thirza got when we pictured ghosts inside the Whispering Wood? Even now I am unable to walk past that shrub at night with ease; and were I to start picturing such matters concerning the old Gammon residence, I would likewise be terrified to walk by it. Furthermore, those youths have not died. Every one of them has reached adulthood and is thriving . . . with one working as a butcher. And in any case, blossoms and melodies could not possess ghosts.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: A quiet sigh was stifled by Nell. Isolde was dearly loved by her, and they had constantly been solid companions. However, she had discovered long before that she was required to travel unaccompanied whenever she roamed into the domain of imagination. The road leading there was an entranced trail upon which she could not be pursued by even those closest to her heart.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: A rainstorm with thunder arose during the time the girls spent at Delford; nevertheless, it was brief, and there was great pleasure in the journey back, passing along roads where the tree branches held gleaming drops of rain and through small wooded hollows where aromatic scents arose from the soaked ferns. Yet, at the exact moment they made the turn onto the Abernethy road, a sight met Nell’s eyes that ruined the scenic charm of her surroundings.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: Off to their right, Mr. Pettifer’s wide, grey-green expanse of late oats stretched out, soaked and thick; and right in the center of it, submerged up to her smooth flanks in the rich crop, and placidly blinking at them across the surrounding stalks, stood a Jersey cow!

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: Releasing her hold on the reins, Nell rose to her feet with a firm setting of her mouth that spelled trouble for the thieving beast. Without uttering a single word, she agilely clambered down past the wheels and darted over the fence ere Isolde grasped the situation.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Nell, return,” screamed the second woman, the moment she regained the ability to speak. “In that damp wheat, your gown will be ruined . . . destroyed. My words aren't reaching her! Oh well, extracting that bovine on her own is impossible for her. Naturally, I have to go render assistance.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: Nell was rushing through the grain as if she were insane. Isolde leaped down with agility, fastened the horse firmly to a post, flipped the hem of her lovely gingham gown above her shoulders, climbed onto the fence, and began chasing after her agitated companion. She was able to run at a higher speed than Nell, who was restricted by her heavy and soaked skirt, and she quickly caught up with her. In their wake, they left a track that would cause Mr. Pettifer immense grief whenever he happened to spot it.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Nell, please stop, for goodness’ sake,” gasped exhausted Isolde. “I have no breath left, and your clothes are completely soaked.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “I have . . . to move . . . that cow . . . away . . . prior to . . . Mr. Pettifer . . . spotting her,” wheezed Nell. “It doesn’t . . . matter . . . if I . . . drown . . . provided we . . . are able . . . to just . . . accomplish that.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: Yet the Jersey cow seemed to find no valid cause to be hurried away from her rich feeding spot. Hardly had the pair of out-of-breath girls approached her when she spun around and sprinted straight toward the far corner of the pasture.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Intercept her,” Isolde heard Nell screech, urging, “run, Isolde, run.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: Isolde certainly took off at a run. Nell attempted to do the same, while that malicious Jersey tore about the pasture as though a demon controlled her. In her own mind, Isolde believed the cow actually was. A good ten minutes passed before they managed to block her path and force her through the opening in the corner that led onto the Abernethy lane.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: It cannot be disputed that, at that exact instant, Nell possessed a disposition that was far from sweet. Furthermore, her mood was not calmed in any way by the sight of a carriage stopped right beside the lane, which carried Mr. Shearer of Delford along with his son, each displaying a wide grin.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “I suppose it would have been wiser for you to sell me that cow when I was looking to purchase her last week, Nell,” Mr. Shearer laughed softly.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “If you desire her, I will sell her to you right away,” declared her disheveled and flushed master. “She can be yours at this precise moment.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Agreed. I am going to pay you twenty for her like my previous offer, and Saul right beside me is able to take her immediately to Delford. The rest of the shipment tonight will include her when going to town. A Jersey cow is desired by Mr. Reed of Brighton.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: A short five minutes afterward, Saul Shearer paraded down the road alongside the Jersey cow, whereas impulsive Nell traveled down the lane to Grey Shutters carrying her twenty dollars.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “What is Thirza going to say?” Isolde inquired.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Oh, she will not mind. Dolly belonged to me personally, and her sale at the auction would probably not yield over twenty dollars. But goodness me, should Mr. Pettifer spot that grain, he is going to realize she got in a second time, right after I solemnly promised him I would prevent it! Indeed, this experience showed me I should not make solemn promises concerning cows. Any cow capable of clearing or smashing the fence around our milk-pen is not trustworthy in any place.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: Thirza’s trip down to Mrs. Sowerby’s ended with her learning every detail regarding the sale and transfer of Dolly, because the majority of the deal had been witnessed by Mrs. Sowerby from her window, with her inferring the remaining parts.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Although you handle affairs in a terribly impulsive manner, Nell, I guess her departure is for the best. Nevertheless, I fail to understand how she escaped the pen. Some of the boards must have been kicked loose by her.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “It did not occur to me to search,” Nell remarked, “however I am going to check right away. Martin has still not returned. Maybe additional aunts of his have passed away. In my mind, it resembles the situation with Mr. Peter Mott and the octogenarians. A few nights ago, Mrs. Mott was perusing a paper and remarked to Mr. Mott, ‘It says in this place that yet another octogenarian has passed away recently. Peter, what constitutes an octogenarian?’ And Mr. Mott replied that he was uncertain, though they had to be extremely frail beings, because the only time anyone ever spoke of them was when they were passing away. Martin’s aunts are just like that.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Martin is merely identical to all those other Frenchmen,” Thirza remarked with revulsion. “They cannot be relied upon for even one day.” As Thirza inspected the items Nell bought in Delford, a piercing scream echoed from the barnyard. Within a minute, Nell burst into the kitchen, clutching her hands in distress.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Nell Harcourt, what is wrong this time?”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Oh, Thirza, what am I going to do? It is awful. And I am entirely to blame. Oh, is there any chance I will learn to pause and think a bit prior to acting recklessly? I was always warned by Mrs. Sowerby that I’d commit some terrible act eventually, and now it has happened!”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “What have you done, Nell? You really are the most infuriating girl!”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Mr. Pettifer’s Jersey cow . . . which Mr. Bell sold to him previously . . . has been purchased by Mr. Shearer! Right now, Dolly stands outside within the milking pen.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Nell Harcourt, are you dreaming?”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “How I want that to be true. No dreaming is involved, even if it closely resembles a bad dream. Furthermore, the cow belonging to Mr. Pettifer has reached Port Marlow already. Oh, Thirza, my belief was that I had stopped causing trouble for myself, yet now I find myself in the most dreadful trouble of my entire existence. What course is open to me?”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Do? There is no action to take, child, other than going to speak with Mr. Pettifer regarding the matter. Should he refuse the cash, we are able to propose swapping our Jersey with him instead. Our cow matches his in quality.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “However, I’m certain he’ll be extremely annoyed and unpleasant regarding it,” Nell lamented.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “I imagine that he will. A short-tempered kind of fellow appears to be what he is. If it pleases you, I will make my way over and clarify matters to him.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Certainly not, my stinginess does not go that far,” Nell cried out. “Because the blame lies entirely with me, I will definitely not permit you to be punished in my place. Going myself is what I will do, and I will do it immediately. Since the humiliation will be dreadful, getting it finished quickly is preferable.”

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: Unhappy Nell retrieved her twenty dollars along with her hat, and as she was leaving, her eyes chanced to fall through the pantry’s unclosed door. Resting upon the table was a nut cake that she had made earlier that day . . . an especially delicious creation coated in pink frosting and decorated with walnuts. Nell’s plan was to serve it on Friday night, when the young people of Brierley were scheduled to gather at Grey Shutters for the purpose of founding the Improvement Society. Yet how did they measure up to Mr. Pettifer, who had every right to be angry? Nell reasoned that such a cake should melt the heart of any man, particularly someone forced to prepare his own meals, so she quickly placed it inside a box. It would serve as a peace offering when she presented it to Mr. Pettifer.

chapter_title: II Selling in Haste and Repenting at Leisure
text: “Provided he grants me the opportunity to speak whatsoever,” she reflected with regret while scaling the lane fence and beginning her route across the fields, which gleamed gold beneath the gentle glow of the hazy August dusk. “I truly comprehend at present the sensations of those being escorted to their death.”
A thick grove of spruce backed the whitewashed, low-eaved, old-fashioned structure that was Mr. Pettifer’s house.

In his shirt sleeves, Mr. Pettifer himself sat upon his vine-shaded veranda, taking pleasure in his pipe for the evening. As soon as he recognized the person approaching along the path, he leaped abruptly to his feet, darted inside the house, and closed the door. Although this was simply the awkward consequence of his astonishment, combined with a significant amount of shame regarding his fit of anger from the previous day, it almost completely robbed Nell of what little courage she had left in her heart.
“If his temper is this bad already, how will he react upon learning my actions,” she pondered in despair while knocking on the door.

However, Mr. Pettifer, displaying a sheepish smile, unfastened it and asked her to come inside using a voice that was rather anxious, yet completely gentle and amiable. Having put away his pipe and put on his jacket, he most courteously tendered Nell a seat covered in dust, and her greeting might have transpired agreeably enough were it not for the betrayer in the form of a parrot, who was gazing out from between the bars of his cage with malevolent yellow eyes. The moment Nell took her seat, Nutmeg cried,
“Goodness gracious, why is that red-haired slip of a girl heading over this way?”
Determining whether Mr. Pettifer’s or Nell’s face displayed the deeper shade of red would prove difficult.

“Ignore that parrot,” Mr. Pettifer requested, glaring angrily at Nutmeg. “He . . . he utters foolishness constantly. My brother, a seafaring man, gave him to me. A sailor's speech isn't always particularly refined, and birds like parrots copy things easily.”

“I ought to imagine so,” replied wretched Nell, her recollection of her mission suppressing her anger. It was clear that she was in no position to insult Mr. Pettifer given the situation. Once you had abruptly disposed of a person's Jersey cow without their awareness or permission, you had to accept his parrot echoing unflattering remarks. Even so, the “redheaded snippet” failed to display the complete submissiveness she might have shown under different conditions.
“I’ve come to admit something to you, Mr. Pettifer,” she said with determination. “It’s . . . it’s regarding . . . that Jersey cow.”

“Bless my soul,” Mr. Pettifer nervously cried out, “did she go and force her way into my oats once more? Oh well, forget it . . . forget it if she did. It makes no difference . . . none whatever, I . . . I acted too hastily yesterday, that’s the truth. Forget it if she did.”
“Oh, if that were the only issue,” Nell sighed. “However, it is ten times more terrible. I do not . . .”
“May God bless my soul, are you trying to tell me that she has wandered into the wheat I own?”
“No . . . no . . . it isn't the wheat. But . . .”
“So it must be the cabbages! Has she gotten into the cabbages I was growing for the Exhibition, then?”

“The cabbages aren't the issue, Mr. Pettifer. I will disclose all . . . my purpose here was precisely that—however, I ask that you refrain from cutting in. My nerves are unsettled by it. Allow me to simply relate what happened without speaking a word until I have finished—after which you will surely have a lot to say,” was the ending Nell delivered, though merely in her mind.

“I won’t say another word,” said Mr. Pettifer, and he kept his promise. Nutmeg, however, was under no agreement to remain quiet and continued to blurt out, “Redheaded snippet” every now and then, driving Nell almost out of her mind.

“Yesterday, I locked my Jersey cow in our pen. I traveled to Delford this morning, and upon my return, I noticed a Jersey cow inside your oat field. Isolde and I drove her out, and it was unbelievably difficult. I was terribly soaked, exhausted, and annoyed—and right then, Mr. Shearer drove past and proposed purchasing the cow. Right then and there, I sold her to him for twenty dollars. My actions were improper. Naturally, I ought to have paused and discussed it with Thirza. However, I have a terrible habit of acting impulsively—anyone acquainted with me can confirm that. Mr. Shearer immediately led the cow off so she could be loaded onto the afternoon train.”
“Redheaded snippet,” Nutmeg repeated, her voice dripping with deep disdain.

Then Mr. Pettifer stood up and, displaying a look that would have terrified any bird except a parrot, moved Nutmeg’s cage into a neighboring room and closed the door. Nutmeg screamed, used foul language, and generally behaved in a manner consistent with his reputation, but upon realizing he was alone, reverted to a moody silence.
“Pardon me and continue,” Mr. Pettifer said as he resumed his seat. “That bird was never taught any manners by my brother the sailor.”

“I returned to my house, and once I had finished my tea, I walked out toward the milking pen. Mr. Pettifer,” . . . Nell bent her body forward, interlacing her fingers in her accustomed youthful manner, as her large gray eyes stared pleadingly directly at Mr. Pettifer’s uncomfortable face . . . “I discovered that my cow was still locked inside the pen. The cow I had sold to Mr. Shearer belonged to you.”
“Bless my soul,” cried Mr. Pettifer, utterly astonished by this unexpected ending. “What a very extraordinary thing!”

“Oh, my causing trouble for myself and everyone else is not at all surprising,” Nell stated in a sorrowful manner. “That is what I am known for. One would think I would have outgrown such behavior at my age . . . I turn seventeen this coming March . . . yet it appears I still have not. Mr. Pettifer, can I dare to ask for your forgiveness? Returning your cow is no longer possible, I fear, but this money will pay for her . . . or if you prefer, you may take mine as a replacement. My cow is an excellent one. And my regret over everything that happened is beyond words.”

“Tut, tut,” Mr. Pettifer said smartly, “miss, do not utter a single further word regarding it. It is immaterial . . . utterly immaterial. Misfortunes are bound to occur. On occasion, I am overly impetuous myself, miss . . . much too impetuous. However, I am unable to refrain from voicing my exact thoughts, and people are required to accept me as I am. Now, had that cow gotten into my cabbages . . . yet do not dwell on it, she did not, hence everything is fine. Because you wish to dispose of her, I believe I would prefer taking your cow in trade.”
“Ah, my gratitude, Mr. Pettifer. It brings me great joy that you feel no annoyance, as I feared it would upset you.”

“And I imagine you were terrified to come over here and inform me, given the scene I caused yesterday, right? However, you must not pay me any attention, as I am merely a terribly candid old man . . . extremely prone to stating what is real, even when it happens to be somewhat direct.”
“Mrs. Sowerby is too,” Nell remarked, blurting it out before she could stop herself.
“Who? Mrs. Sowerby? Do not tell me that I resemble that ancient chatterbox,” Mr. Pettifer said in an annoyed manner. “I am not . . . not in the least. What is inside that box?”

“A cake,” Nell stated playfulnessly. Her mood rose as light as a feather due to her relief regarding the unpredicted friendliness of Mr. Pettifer. “I brought it over for you . . . I thought perhaps you didn’t have cake very often.”
“I do not, indeed, and I am extremely pleased with it, as well. You have my gratitude. The surface appears nice. My expectation is that it remains just as nice underneath.”

“It is,” Nell remarked, filled with cheerful certainty. “In the past, I have baked cakes that were not, which Mrs. Wace could confirm for you, yet this particular one is perfectly fine. Although I baked it for the Improvement Society, I am able to bake them another one.”
“Listen to my suggestion, young lady, you need to assist me in consuming it. After I set the kettle to boil, a cup of tea will be enjoyed by both of us. Is that acceptable to you?”
“Would you allow me to prepare the tea?” Nell asked uncertainly.
A laugh came softly from Mr. Pettifer.

“It appears you lack faith in my tea-making skills. You are mistaken . . . the pot of tea I can make is as fine as any you have ever tasted. However, you may proceed on your own. Luckily, Sunday brought rain, meaning clean dishes are available in abundance.”

Leaping up nimbly, Nell got to work. Prior to putting the tea to steep, she rinsed the teapot through a number of waters. Next she swept the stove and laid the table, fetching the dishes from inside the pantry. Although the condition of that pantry appalled Nell, she prudently kept quiet. Mr. Pettifer directed her to the place where the bread and butter and a tin of peaches were kept. Nell decorated the table using a flower arrangement gathered from the garden and ignored the spots on the tablecloth. Before long, the tea had brewed, and Nell was seated across from Mr. Pettifer at his personal table, serving his tea, and conversing openly with him regarding her school, companions, and intentions. The reality of her experience seemed almost unbelievable to her.

Nutmeg was returned by Mr. Pettifer, who declared that the unfortunate bird would become lonely; whereupon Nell, convinced that she was able to pardon all people and all things, extended a walnut to him. Nevertheless, Nutmeg suffered from deeply wounded emotions and spurned every attempt at reconciliation. Perched disconsolately, he puffed out his plumage to such a degree that he resembled nothing more than a sphere of gold and green.
“Why do you call him Nutmeg?” inquired Nell, who favored fitting names and believed Nutmeg did not suit such magnificent feathers in the least.

“It was my brother, the sailor, who gave him his name, perhaps as an allusion to the way he behaves. Nevertheless, I hold that bird in high regard . . . you would hardly believe how deeply attached to him I am. Naturally, he is not without his flaws, and in various ways, he has proved quite expensive for me. A few individuals dislike the fact that he curses, yet the habit is impossible to cure, despite my own efforts and those of others. Certain people harbor a dislike for parrots, which seems foolish, doesn't it? As for me, I am fond of them, and Nutmeg provides me with a great deal of companionship. Not a single thing on this earth could persuade me to part with him . . . absolutely nothing, miss.”

Mr. Pettifer hurled the final sentence toward Nell with such explosive force that he might have thought she possessed a secret intention to convince him to relinquish Nutmeg. Nell, nonetheless, was starting to grow fond of the peculiar, anxious, restless small man, and prior to the conclusion of the meal, they had become rather good friends. Mr. Pettifer learned of the Improvement Society and felt inclined to view it favorably.
“That is correct. Proceed. Ample space exists for progress within this colony . . . as well as among its inhabitants.”

“Oh, I don’t know,” Nell snapped back. In her own mind, or when speaking with her closest friends, she could concede that Brierley and the folks living there possessed a few minor flaws that could be readily fixed. However, listening to a virtual stranger such as Mr. Pettifer express that view was a completely different matter. “I think Brierley is a lovely place; and the people in it are very nice, too.”

“It seems you possess a bit of a temper,” remarked Mr. Pettifer, observing the red cheeks and angry eyes across from him. “I suppose that accompanies hair of your shade. Brierley is quite a nice location or I would not have settled here; however, I assume even you will agree it possesses a few shortcomings?”

“I prefer it all the more because of them,” answered faithful Nell. “I do not care for places or folk that do not possess any flaws. It seems to me that an entirely flawless individual would be extremely dull. Mrs. Milton White mentions that she has not encountered a flawless individual herself, though she has listened to plenty regarding one . . . the initial wife of her husband. Is it not your opinion that living as the spouse of a man whose initial wife possessed no flaws would be quite unpleasant?”
“To be wedded to the flawless wife would prove even more unpleasant,” Mr. Pettifer announced, displaying an abrupt and unexplainable intensity.

After they finished tea, Nell made a point of doing the dishes, even though Mr. Pettifer gave her his word that the house contained sufficient crockery to last for weeks to come. She would have been delighted to sweep the floor as well, but because no broom could be seen, she refrained from asking about its location out of concern that one did not exist.

“You could come over and speak with me now and then,” proposed Mr. Pettifer as she was departing. “The distance isn't great and people should show neighborliness. I feel a bit intrigued by that society of yours. It appears to me that it will offer some amusement. Which person will you approach first?”
“It is only places we mean to improve . . . we are not going to meddle with people,” Nell stated, adopting a dignified tone. That Mr. Pettifer was mocking the endeavor was her sneaking suspicion.
After her departure, Mr. Pettifer observed her through the windowpane . . . a supple, youthful figure, stepping buoyantly over the meadows amid the evening twilight.

“I’m a crabbed, lonesome, crusty old chap,” he spoken out loud, “but I feel young again because of something about that little girl . . . and having that sensation repeated once in a while is something I’d like, since it’s so pleasant.”
“Redheaded snippet,” rasped Nutmeg in a taunting manner.
Mr. Pettifer brandished his fist toward the parrot.
“You stubborn creature,” he grumbled, “I nearly wish I had broken your neck back when my brother the sailor carried you to our house. Are you ever going to stop causing me difficulties?”
Nell rushed back to her house cheerfully and described her experiences to Thirza, who had felt quite anxious because she had been away for so long and was just about to go search for her.

“Taking everything into account, this world is actually rather nice, wouldn’t you say, Thirza?” Nell cheerfully remarked. “A few days ago, Mrs. Sowerby was grumbling about how disappointing the world is. According to her, any pleasant anticipation inevitably ends in some degree of letdown . . . maybe she has a point. Even so, there is a positive aspect as well. Dismal anticipations also fail to materialize as terribly as expected . . . almost invariably, the reality proves far superior to one's fears. My trip to Mr. Pettifer’s house this evening was something I anticipated with utter dread; yet he proved to be rather gentle, making the visit almost enjoyable. Provided we show each other great tolerance, I believe genuine friendship lies ahead for us, and the entire situation has resolved most favorably. Even so, Thirza, I am positive that I will never dispose of a cow again without first confirming her rightful owner. Furthermore, parrots are not to my liking!”

As the sun was setting one evening, Odette Pullen, Hugh Carrow, and Nell Harcourt stayed a while beside a fence beneath softly rustling spruce branches, at the junction where a trail through the trees named the Aspen Path met the primary thoroughfare. Having gone up to pass the afternoon hours in Nell's company, Odette was being accompanied a portion of her journey back by Nell; the pair encountered Hugh at the fence, and the three of them were presently conversing regarding the momentous next day; this was because that upcoming day marked the first of September, bringing the commencement of the school term. Stonebridge was where Odette would travel, whereas Pale Sands was Hugh's destination.

“The two of you possess an edge over me,” Nell sighed. “Your future pupils do not know you, whereas I am required to instruct my former classmates, and Mrs. Sowerby mentions her fear that they will fail to respect me the way they would a newcomer, unless I act extremely strict right from the start. However, I am not convinced that an educator ought to be strict. Oh, I feel as though this is such an immense duty!”

“I guess we’ll get on all right,” Odette stated in a relaxed manner. No desires to act as a positive inspiration bothered Odette. Her intentions were to honestly merit her pay, satisfy the board, and have her name placed on the honor roll of the School Inspector. Beyond these, Odette possessed no other goals. “The main thing will be to keep order and a teacher has to be a little cross to do that. If my pupils won’t do as I tell them I shall punish them.”
“How?”
“Naturally, administer a proper thrashing to them.”
“Oh, Odette, you would not,” Nell exclaimed, appalled. “Odette, you could not!”
“I certainly could and would, provided they merited it,” Odette stated with determination.

“I could never strike a youngster,” stated Nell with the same firmness. “I do not support it whatsoever. Miss Thorne never struck a single one of us yet maintained absolute discipline; whereas Mr. Pidgeon was constantly striking and maintained no discipline whatsoever. No, should I be unable to succeed without striking, I will not attempt to instruct a class. Superior methods of discipline exist. I will endeavor to gain my students’ love, which will make them desire to follow my instructions.”
“However, what if they fail to do so?” inquired pragmatic Odette.
“I would not beat them regardless. I am certain that it would not accomplish a thing. Oh, do not beat your students, Odette dear, regardless of their actions.”
“How do you feel about this, Hugh?” asked Odette. “Is it your belief that certain children truly require a spanking from time to time?”
“Is it not your opinion that whipping a youngster . . . any youngster, is a brutal, merciless act?” Nell burst out, her cheeks turning red with intensity.

“Well,” Hugh uttered in a deliberate manner, caught between his genuine beliefs and his desire to satisfy Nell’s expectations, “valid arguments exist for each perspective. My belief is not in the frequent spanking of kids. As you mention, Nell, my opinion is that superior methods of discipline generally exist, making physical correction an ultimate measure. However, looking at the opposite view, just as Odette mentions, my conviction is that a rare youngster exists who remains unresponsive to different approaches and who, to put it briefly, requires a spanking and would benefit from one. My principle will be physical correction used solely when all else fails.”
Attempting to satisfy both parties, Hugh achieved the customary and entirely proper result of satisfying no one. A toss of her head came from Odette.
“I’ll give my pupils a whipping whenever they misbehave. That is the most direct and simple method to persuade them.”
A look of disappointment was cast toward Hugh by Nell.
“I will under no circumstances beat a young one,” she reiterated with determination. “I am convinced it is neither proper nor required.”
“What if a boy gave you attitude when you gave him an order?” Odette asked.

“I’d make him stay after class and speak to him with kindness and firmness,” Nell said. “Goodness exists within each individual if you are able to locate it. Finding and cultivating it is the obligation of an educator. As you are aware, that is what we were instructed by our Regent’s School Management professor. Do you think that by beating a child you could discover any goodness in them? Professor Rennie asserts that guiding the children correctly matters much more than even instructing them in the three R’s.”
“Yet the Inspector tests them in reading, writing, and arithmetic, remember, and he will not present you with a favorable report unless they reach his level,” Odette objected.
“I would prefer that my students affectionally regard me and remember me in future years as a genuine benefactor instead of being listed on the honor roll,” Nell firmly declared.
“If children were to misbehave, would you refrain from punishing them entirely?” Hugh inquired.
“Oh, indeed, I think I must, even though I am certain I will detest doing it. However, you are able to detain them during recess, make them stand on the floor, or assign them lines for writing.”
“I assume you will not discipline the girls by forcing them to sit beside the boys?” Odette asked cunningly.

Hugh and Nell exchanged glances, wearing somewhat silly grins. A long time ago, Nell was forced to sit next to Hugh as a disciplinary measure, and the results of that event had proved gloomy and painful.
“Indeed, future events shall demonstrate the superior method,” Odette remarked wisely when the two of them separated.

Nell returned to Grey Shutters by travelling along Aspen Path, which was dim, whispering, and fragrant with ferns, through Primrose Dell and past Reedmere, where shade and brightness touched beneath the fir trees, and downward along Linger Lane . . . places that she and Isolde had given those names to a long time before. Moving at an unhurried pace, she took pleasure in the sweet air of the woods and fields as well as the starry summer dusk, while giving serious thought to the unfamiliar responsibilities she would assume the next day. Upon arriving at the yard at Grey Shutters, the booming, firm voice of Mrs. Sowerby drifted outward from the unclosed kitchen window.

With a wry face, Nell reflected, “Mrs. Sowerby has arrived to offer me wise counsel regarding tomorrow, but I doubt I will enter. It seems to me that her counsel resembles pepper . . . fine when used sparingly, yet quite fiery when she dispenses it. Rather than that, I will dash across to converse with Mr. Pettifer.”

Ever since the memorable incident involving the Jersey cow, Nell had hurried across to converse with Mr. Pettifer on more than one occasion. Her visits had occurred on a number of nights, establishing a firm friendship between Mr. Pettifer and herself, even if his boasted frankness occasionally tested her patience. Her presence was still met with distrust by Nutmeg, who always sarcastically addressed her as “redheaded snippet.” In an effort to cure him of this behavior, Mr. Pettifer would leap up in excitement each time he spotted Nell approaching, shouting,

“Bless my soul, there is that charming young lady once more,” or a remark of an identical complimentary nature. Nutmeg, however, perceived the ruse and held it in contempt. Nell was destined to remain ignorant of the numerous flatteries Mr. Pettifer bestowed upon her in her absence. He undoubtedly refrained from offering her a single one in her presence.
“Well, I guess you have been out among the trees gathering a store of rods for the next day?” he said to welcome her while Nell walked up the stairs to the porch.

“No, indeed,” Nell replied with indignation. Because she constantly took matters with such earnestness, she made a wonderful target to tease. “There will never be a switch present in my school, Mr. Pettifer. Naturally, a pointer will be necessary for me to possess, yet I will employ it solely for pointing.”

“So you intend to use the strap on them in place of that? Well, I am not certain, yet you might be correct. Although a switch causes a sharper pain initially, there is no denying that the strap leaves a lingering ache.”
“I will use nothing like that. It is not my intention to whip those I teach.”
“Bless my soul,” Mr. Pettifer cried out, truly amazed, “in what way do you plan to maintain discipline then?”
“My rule will be one of affection, Mr. Pettifer.”

“It isn't right,” Mr. Pettifer said, “not right whatsoever, Nell. ‘Spare the rod and spoil the child.’ Back when I attended school, the master flogged me routinely each day on the grounds that if I was not causing trouble at that moment, I was planning it.”
“Since the time you attended school, Mr. Pettifer, techniques have evolved.”
“Yet mankind's essence remains unchanged. Pay attention to what I say, you will not succeed in controlling the youth if you do not have a punishment prepared for them. It cannot be done.”
“Well, I’m going to try my way first,” declared Nell, whose will was quite resolute and who tended to hold on extremely firmly to her ideas.

“I suppose you possess a fair amount of obstinacy,” Mr. Pettifer expressed. “Oh well, time will tell. On some future occasion when your temper is ignited . . . and individuals possessing your shade of hair have a strong tendency to lose their tempers . . . you will cast aside all your delicate ideas and thrash a few of them. In any case, your age makes you unsuitable for teaching . . . much too youthful and immature.”

On the whole, a somewhat gloomy state of mind accompanied Nell as she retired for the night. Her sleep was fitful, and her appearance at the following morning's breakfast was so wan and mournful that Thirza felt frightened and demanded that she drink a cup of burning ginger tea. Nell drank it slowly and without complaint, even though she failed to see how ginger tea could help. If it had been a magical potion capable of bestowing maturity and wisdom, Nell would have gulped down a quart without hesitation.
“Thirza, suppose I do not succeed!”

“You’re unlikely to suffer total failure during a single day, and many additional days lie ahead,” Thirza remarked. “Your problem, Nell, stems from your expectation that you will instruct those kids in every subject and correct every one of their flaws immediately, and should that prove impossible, you will view yourself as a failure.”

As Nell arrived at the school on that morning . . . having traveled the Aspen Path for the very first time in her life oblivious and unseeing to its charm . . . everything was calm and motionless. The former instructor had taught the pupils to be seated upon her coming, and as Nell stepped into the classroom she was met by neat lines of “shining morning faces” and gleaming, curious eyes. Hanging up her hat, she turned toward her students, trusting that she did not appear as terrified and silly as she felt inside and that they would fail to notice how her body shook.

She had remained awake until almost midnight on the previous evening drafting an address that she intended to deliver to her students when school commenced. Having meticulously edited and refined the piece, she subsequently committed it to memory. It was an excellent address containing several truly wonderful concepts, particularly regarding shared assistance and the diligent pursuit of learning. Its sole defect was her present inability to recall any part of it.

Following what felt like a year to her—though it was actually roughly ten seconds—she whispered weakly, “Take your Testaments, please,” and dropped out of breath into her seat behind the noise of desktop lids opening and slamming that came next. As the verses were being read by the children, Nell rallied her trembling thoughts into place and surveyed the assembled small travelers bound for the Grownup Land.

Naturally, the majority of them were already very familiar to her. Although her personal classmates had graduated during the previous year, she had attended school alongside all the others, with the exception of the primer class and ten individuals who were new to Brierley. Nell harbored a covert curiosity regarding these ten that surpassed her interest in those whose potential was already reasonably clear to her. Granted, they could turn out to be every bit as ordinary as the others; nevertheless, it was also possible that a genius was in their midst. The thought was electrifying.

Anthony Tulk was seated alone at a desk in the corner. His small face was dark and gloomy, and he glared at Nell, his black eyes filled with enmity. Right then, Nell resolved to gain the boy’s love and completely defeat the Tulks.

Sitting with Arty Mott in the opposite corner was one more unusual boy . . . a merry-faced little fellow, who had a snub nose, a face covered in freckles, and large, pale blue eyes that were bordered by whitish eyelashes . . . likely the Trask boy; and if there was any truth in a likeness, his sister was seated with Mary Bell across the aisle. Nell pondered the nature of the child's mother, who would allow her to go to school wearing such clothes. A washed-out pink dress made of silk was what she had on, adorned with an abundance of cotton lace, dirty white slippers of kid leather, and stockings of silk. Her sandy-colored hair had been twisted into countlessly tight and unnatural curls, topped by an extravagant pink ribbon bow that exceeded the size of her head. Based on her look, she felt extremely pleased with her appearance.

A faint, small child, whose shoulders were draped in sleek waves of soft, delicate, fawn-hued hair, Nell reasoned, had to be Annetta Bell, a girl whose mother and father used to reside within the Stonebridge school area, yet, because they dragged their home fifty yards to the north of its previous location, currently belonged to Brierley. A trio of sickly-looking little girls jammed together in a single desk were unquestionably Cottons; while there could be no uncertainty that the little belle boasting extended brown ringlets and hazel-colored eyes, who threw flirtatious glances toward Jack Gills from behind her Testament, was Prillie Rogerson, a child whose father had lately taken a second spouse and fetched Prillie back to the area from the residence of her grandmother located in Welby. A lanky, ungainly girl positioned in a rear desk, who appeared to possess an excess of feet and hands, Nell was completely unable to identify, though she subsequently learned that she was called Barbara Shaw and had arrived to reside alongside an aunt residing in Brierley. Nell was likewise destined to learn that whenever Barbara succeeded in navigating the aisle without tripping over her own boots or those belonging to someone else, the Brierley pupils recorded that exceptional occurrence upon the wall of the porch to mark the event.

However, as Nell’s gaze connected with the eyes of the boy sitting at the front desk opposite hers, a strange small tremor passed through her, as though her genius had been discovered. It was clear to her that this had to be Cedric Stanhope and that, on this occasion, Mrs. Agatha Sowerby had accurately predicted his unlikeness to the Brierley children. Beyond that, it hit Nell that he was different from other children in any place, and that a soul delicately related to hers was staring back at her from the extremely dark blue eyes observing her with such fixed attention.

Although aware that Cedric was ten years old, she thought he appeared to be at most eight. In her eyes, his tiny face was the most beautiful she had ever observed on a child . . . displaying features of delicate and exquisite refinement surrounded by a halo of chestnut curls. Full without any pout, his mouth was delicious, with crimson lips that barely touched each other and curved into finely crafted tiny corners that almost formed dimples. A sober, grave, and meditative expression was upon him, as though his spirit possessed much greater age than his body; however, the moment Nell gave him a soft smile, that look disappeared into an abrupt responsive smile that appeared to illuminate his entire being, like an internal lamp suddenly lighting into a flame that irradiated him from head to foot. Best of all, this reaction was involuntary, arising from no outer motive or effort, but merely the outward flash of a concealed personality that was fine, sweet, and rare. Through this swift exchange of smiles, Nell and Cedric became fast friends forever prior to any words passing between them.

The day passed as though it were a dream, and Nell was unable to distinctly remember it later on. It felt nearly as if someone other than herself was doing the teaching. Mechanically, she set copies, worked sums, and heard classes. Quite well-behaved, the children presented only two instances requiring discipline. Morley Pullen received a catching while steering a team of trained crickets down the aisle. Nell made Morley stand upon the platform for an hour and—an act Morley felt far more deeply—took away his crickets. Having placed them inside a box, she liberated them at Primrose Dell as she walked home from school; nevertheless, Morley thought, both at that time and perpetually after, that she carried them to her home to keep for her personal entertainment.

Anthony Tulk was the second offender, emptying the final drops of water contained in his slate bottle onto the back of Aurelia Clay’s neck. Keeping Anthony inside during recess, Nell discussed with him how gentlemen ought to behave, warning him that ladies’ necks were never to have water poured down them by such men. She explained that it was her wish for every one of her boys to become a gentleman. Quite kind and touching though her brief lecture was, Anthony was regrettably left entirely unaffected. Maintaining a silent posture alongside his unchanged sullen look, he listened to her, letting out a contemptuous whistle upon his departure. Nell let out a sigh, but she subsequently raised her own spirits by recalling that earning the regard of a Tulk was not accomplished in a single day, much like the construction of Rome. Indeed, whether certain Tulks possessed any affections capable of being won remained questionable; nevertheless, Nell held higher expectations for Anthony, whose appearance suggested he could be a fairly pleasant boy if his sullen exterior were ever penetrated.

Once school had been let out and the pupils were gone, Nell sank exhaustedly into her seat. A headache plagued her, and a profound sense of disheartening weight came over her. No genuine cause existed for such despair, given that no truly terrible incident had transpired; nonetheless, Nell suffered from deep fatigue and was disposed to think that developing a fondness for pedagogy was beyond her. Furthermore, spending each day engaged in an unappealing occupation for . . . say, four decades, struck her as an appalling prospect. Nell hesitated between weeping immediately on the spot, or postponing her tears until she reached the security of her own white bedroom at home. Prior to reaching a choice, the sound of tapping heels and the rustle of silk sounded across the porch floor, bringing Nell face to face with a woman whose attire brought to mind a comment Mr. Pettifer had lately made regarding a excessively adorned woman he observed within a Port Marlow shop. “She looked like a head-on collision between a fashion plate and a nightmare.”

The late arrival had put on a magnificent pale blue summer silk outfit, which was puffed, frilled, and shirred in every conceivable spot where puffing, frilling, or shirring could be added. Sitting atop her head was an enormous white chiffon hat, adorned with three extended yet somewhat scrawny ostrich feathers. A veil made of pink chiffon, generously dotted with gigantic black spots, draped down like a flounce from the brim of the hat to her shoulders, drifting behind her in a pair of light streamers. She was decked out in as much jewelry as a single petite woman could fit upon herself, and a powerful scent of perfume accompanied her.

“I am Mrs. Trask . . . Mrs. H. B. Trask,” declared this sight, “and the reason I have visited you is regarding an issue Clarice Almira mentioned to me upon returning home for dinner today. It caused me extreme annoyance.”
“I’m sorry,” Nell stammered, attempting without success to recall a single event from that morning involving the Trask children.

“Clarice Almira mentioned to me that you said our name was Trask. However, Miss Harcourt, Trask is the proper way to pronounce our name . . . with the stress placed on the final syllable. I trust you will keep this in mind going forward.”

“I will attempt to,” Nell panted, suppressing a hysterical urge to giggle. “It is very disagreeable to have a person's name misspelled, as I have learned firsthand, and I imagine having it mispronounced is likely still more dreadful.”
“Of course it is. Furthermore, Clarice Almira let me know that you address my son as Jacob.”
“Jacob was the name he gave me,” Nell objected.

“I might have expected that,” Mrs. H. B. Trask said, using a voice suggesting that one could not anticipate thankfulness from youth in these fallen times. “That boy possesses very common preferences, Miss Harcourt. At his birth, my wish was to name him St. Clair . . . it has such an aristocratic ring, doesn't it? His father, however, demanded that he be named Jacob after his uncle. I gave in, since Uncle Jacob happened to be a wealthy old bachelor. And what do you imagine, Miss Harcourt? Once our blameless child reached five years of age, Uncle Jacob went ahead and took a wife, and he currently possesses three sons himself. Have you ever known such a lack of appreciation? As soon as the wedding invitation . . . because he possessed the audacity to mail us an invitation, Miss Harcourt . . . arrived at our home, I said, ‘No more Jacobs for me, thank you.’ Ever since that day, I referred to my son as St. Clair, and I am resolved that St. Clair is what he must be named. His father stubborn-headedly keeps calling him Jacob, while the youth himself displays a completely baffling liking for that coarse name. Nevertheless, he is St. Clair, and St. Clair he will continue to be. You will be good enough to bear this in mind, Miss Harcourt, won't you? Thank you. I informed Clarice Almira of my certainty that this was merely a misinterpretation which a single word would fix. Trask. . . stress the final syllable . . . and St. Clair . . . under no circumstances Jacob. You will keep this in mind? Thank you.”

Once Mrs. H. B. Trask had glided off, Nell secured the door of the school and headed home. Near the base of the hill, she encountered Cedric Stanhope beside the Aspen Path. He presented her with a bunch of the delicate small wild orchids that young ones in Brierley named “rice lillies.”

“I ask you to take these, teacher, which I discovered in the field belonging to Mr. Duckett,” he uttered bashfully, “and I returned so I could offer them to you since I believed you were a lady who would appreciate them, and also because . . .” he raised his large, gorgeous eyes . . . “teacher, I am fond of you.”

“You darling,” said Nell, as she took the scented blooms. Just as though a magical spell had been cast by Cedric’s words, tiredness and gloom left her soul, while a surge of hope, like a fountain dancing, rose within her heart. She walked along the Aspen Path with light steps, accompanied by the sweet perfume of her orchids as if receiving a blessing.
“So, what progress did you make?” Thirza inquired.

“Inquire about that in a month’s time and I might be capable of informing you. At present I am unable to . . . I do not know personally . . . I am excessively close to it. It feels as though my thoughts were completely churned about until they became dense and murky. The single matter I am truly certain of achieving today is my teaching Cliffie Duckett that A is A. Prior to this, he was unaware of it. Is it not an achievement to have set a soul upon a route that might terminate in Shakespeare and Paradise Lost?”
Afterwards, Mrs. Sowerby arrived bringing additional cheer. At her gate, that kind woman had stopped the pupils from school and asked them what they thought of their new instructor.

“And each single one of them stated they liked you splendid, Nell, with the exception of Anthony Tulk. I have to confess he failed to. He stated you ‘weren’t any good, just like all girl teachers.’ There is the Tulk leaven for you. But do not mind.”
“I will not mind,” Nell said softly, “and Anthony Tulk will come to like me eventually. He will certainly be won over by patience and kindness.”

“Indeed, predicting what a Tulk might do is impossible,” Mrs. Agatha remarked guardedly. “More often than not, they act in opposition to expectations, much like dreams. Regarding that Trask woman, I certainly won't be referring to her as Donnelling, you may be certain of that. Trask is her name and always was. In my opinion, the woman is simply insane. She owns a pug dog named Queenie who sits at the dinner table with the rest of the family, consuming its food from a china plate. Were I in her shoes, I would fear divine punishment. Thomas considers Trask himself to be a practical, industrious man, though he believes he lacked good sense when selecting a spouse.”
