text: It was a day in September upon the hills of St. Brendan’s Island; an invigorating breeze blew from the ocean across the sand dunes; a lengthy red road wound amid woods and fields, at times curving around a bend of dense spruces, at times passing through a grove of youthful maples with vast, plume-like expanses of ferns beneath, at times descending into a depression where a stream emerged briefly from the trees before re-entering them, at times reclining in the unshaded sunlight amidst stripes of smoke-blue asters and golden-rod; the atmosphere vibrated with the chirping of countless crickets, those joyful small dependents of the summer slopes; a stout brown pony ambled down the route; a pair of girls sat behind him, brimful with the pure, invaluable happiness of vitality and youth.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Oh, this is a day left over from Eden, isn’t it, Isolde?” . . . and Nell sighed out of pure joy. “Magic fills the air. See the purple shade resting in the basin of the harvest valley, Isolde. And oh, do catch the scent of the dying fir! That aroma rises from the small sunny hollow where Mr. Eben Duckett has been chopping fence poles. To be alive on a day like this is bliss; but smelling dying fir is sheer heaven. Two thirds of that comes from Wordsworth and one third from Nell Harcourt. It hardly seems possible for dying fir to exist in heaven, does it? Yet I feel heaven would lack complete perfection if you failed to catch a breeze of dead fir while walking in its forests. Maybe the scent will exist there apart from death. Yes, I believe it will work that way. That delightful smell has to be the firs’ souls . . . and naturally heaven will consist only of souls.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Trees don’t possess souls,” practical Isolde remarked, “yet the aroma of dead fir is undeniably wonderful. I intend to craft a cushion and stuff it with needles from the firs. You ought to craft one as well, Nell.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “I believe I will . . . and nap inside it. That would surely make me dream of being a woodnymph or a dryad. Right now, though, I am completely satisfied being the Brierley schoolteacher, Nell Harcourt, traveling along a road like this on a day so friendly and sweet.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “The weather is delightful, yet our upcoming duty is far from pleasant,” Isolde let out a sigh. “What possessed you to volunteer for this street, Nell? Nearly every eccentric person in Brierley resides here, and people will likely view us as if we are soliciting handouts for our own benefit. Of all the streets, this is absolutely the most dreadful.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “I selected it for that very reason. Naturally, Hugh and Gideon would have chosen this path had we requested them to do so. However, Isolde, as the person who originally proposed the B.V.I.S., I consider myself accountable for it, so it feels right that I should take on the most unpleasant tasks. My apologies to you for this; nevertheless, you are not required to utter a single word when we reach the difficult spots. The speaking will be handled entirely by me . . . According to Mrs. Sowerby, I am certainly capable of doing so. Mrs. Sowerby remains undecided about whether she should support our project. She leans toward favoring it whenever she recalls Mr. and Mrs. Wace’s endorsement; on the other hand, the American origins of village improvement societies serve as a point against it. Consequently, she wavers between both views, meaning Mrs. Sowerby will judge us favorably only if we succeed. Honora plans to compose an essay for our upcoming Improvement gathering, which I anticipate will be excellent, given how gifted her aunt is at writing and how likely such talent is inherited. Discovering that Mrs. Charlotte E. Varley was aunt to Honora provided me with an unforgettable excitement. It felt truly extraordinary that I held a friendship with the young woman whose aunt authored ‘Edgewood Days’ and ‘The Rosebud Garden.’”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Where is Mrs. Varley’s residence?”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “In Toronto. Also, Honora mentions that she plans to travel to the Island for a visit next summer, and provided it can be managed, Honora intends to organize a way for us to meet her. That appears nearly too wonderful to actually happen—yet it gives you something nice to picture once you get into bed.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: An established reality was the Brierley Village Improvement Society. Serving as president was Hugh Carrow, with Gideon Duckett as vice-president, Nell Harcourt as secretary, and Isolde Pembroke as treasurer. At the residences of its members, the “Improvers,” a nickname given to them right away, were scheduled to gather every two weeks. Although it was acknowledged that accomplishing numerous enhancements this late in the year was unlikely, their intention was to organize the upcoming summer's efforts, gather and analyze suggestions, compose and recite essays, and, to quote Nell, “educate the public sentiment generally.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: Naturally, a degree of opposition existed, alongside a significant amount of mockery, which wounded the Improvers far more deeply. It was rumored that Mr. Elisha Duckett had remarked that calling the association the Courting Club would suit it better. Mrs. Hiram Mott announced that word had reached her that the Improvers intended to till every roadside and plant geraniums along them. A caution was issued by Mr. Levi Gammon to his neighbors, stating the Improvers would demand that all residents demolish their homes and construct new ones following society-sanctioned designs. A message was delivered from Mr. James Tranter expressing his desire for them to pleasantly flatten the church hill. Nell was informed by Eben Duckett of his hope that the Improvers might persuade old Josiah Mott to trim his beard. Mr. Lawrence Bell stated that he was willing to apply whitewash to his barns if that was required to satisfy them, but hanging lace curtains in the cowstable windows was where he drew the line. A question was posed by Mr. Major Tranter to Clifton Mott, a member of the Improvers who transported milk to the cheese factory in Delford, inquiring whether it was a fact that all residents would be required to hand-paint their milk-stands by the following summer and adorn them with embroidered centerpieces.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: Regardless of this . . . or maybe, given how human nature operates, on account of it . . . the Society courageously set to work on the sole upgrade they had any chance of accomplishing that autumn. During their second assembly, located in the Pembroke parlor, Oliver Mott proposed starting a collection of funds to put new shingles and paint on the hall; Julia Bell provided a second to the motion, though she felt uncomfortable and worried that her action was not quite proper for a lady. Hugh presented the motion to a vote, everyone voted in favor of it, and Nell soberly entered it into her minutes. Selecting a committee was the subsequent task, and Tibby Tulk, who was resolved to prevent Julia Bell from taking all the glory, daringly proposed that Miss Odette Pullen serve as the head of the designated committee. After this proposal was likewise properly seconded and passed, Odette repaid the favor when she named Tibby to the committee, together with Hugh, Nell, Isolde, and Gideon Duckett. The members of the committee selected their assigned paths during a confidential meeting. Nell and Isolde received their assignment for the Stonebridge road, Hugh and Gideon were designated for the Pale Sands road, and Odette and Tibby were selected for the Delford road.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Because,” Hugh clarified to Nell, while the pair traversed the Whispering Wood on their way home, “the Tulks reside entirely on that road, and they refuse to contribute a single cent unless a member of their own group solicits them.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: Nell and Isolde set off the following Saturday. Having driven to where the road ended, they worked their way back toward home, visiting the “Andrew girls” before anyone else.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: Isolde remarked, “If Catherine is by herself we might obtain something, but if Eliza is present we will not.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: Eliza was present . . . to a great degree . . . and possessed an appearance even more severe than she normally did. Miss Eliza belonged to that category of individuals who convey the feeling that existence is truly a valley of sorrow, and that grinning, not to mention laughing, constitutes a genuinely blameworthy misuse of nervous force. The Andrew sisters had been known as “girls” for a bit more than fifty years and appeared probable to continue as girls until the conclusion of their journey on earth. Catherine, according to rumor, had not completely abandoned hope, whereas Eliza, a pessimist from birth, had never possessed any. Their home was a tiny brown dwelling constructed in a sunlit spot carved out of Mark Andrew’s beech forest. Eliza grumbled that the heat was dreadful during summer, whereas Catherine was accustomed to remarking that it was delightfully warm during winter.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: Eliza was stitching together pieces of quilt, not out of any necessity, but purely to demonstrate her disapproval of the light, ornamental lace that Catherine was making with her hook. Eliza paid attention while wearing a scowl and Catherine while wearing a grin, as the young women made the purpose of their visit clear. Naturally, every time Catherine’s gaze met Eliza’s, she abandoned her grin out of remorseful embarrassment; nevertheless, it reappeared a short time later.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Were I possessed of funds to squander,” Eliza remarked sternly, “I would ignite them and perhaps enjoy the spectacle of a fire; however, I refuse to grant a single penny to that hall. The community gains nothing from it . . . it serves merely as a gathering spot for youth to misbehave when they ought to be sleeping in their beds at home.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Oh, Eliza, a bit of entertainment is necessary for youth,” Catherine objected.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “The need for it escapes me. When we were young, Catherine Pullen, we did not go gallivanting to halls and such locations. With each passing day, this world deteriorates.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “I believe the situation is improving,” declared Catherine with conviction.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “You believe!” The deepest disdain was evident in Miss Eliza’s tone. “Whatever you believe holds no importance, Catherine Pullen. Facts remain facts.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Well, Eliza, I am always fond of viewing things positively.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “There is no silver lining.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Oh, indeed there is,” exclaimed Nell, who was unable to quietly tolerate such heresy. “Why, there are so very many bright sides, Miss Pullen. It is truly a beautiful world.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “You won’t hold it in such high regard once you’ve spent as much time in it as I have,” Miss Eliza replied testily, “nor will you display such eagerness to make it better. Isolde, how is your mother? Goodness gracious, she has certainly declined recently. She appears extremely exhausted. And Nell, how much time does Thirza have left until she anticipates becoming completely blind?”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Her eyes will not deteriorate further if she exercises extreme caution, according to the doctor,” Nell stammered.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Must we not prepare ourselves for the finest outcome as well?” Nell implored. “That is precisely as probable as the most terrible.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “I have not found that to be true, and my fifty-seven years outweigh your sixteen,” Eliza shot back. “Are you leaving? Well, it is my hope that your new society can prevent Brierley from slipping any lower, though my expectations are small.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: Nell and Isolde gratefully disembarked, before departing as rapidly as the chubby pony was able to travel. When they made their way around the bend beneath the beech wood, a chubby person arrived running across Mr. Pullen’ pasture, gesturing at them with great excitement. The person was Catherine Pullen, and being so short of breath that speaking was nearly impossible for her, she nevertheless pushed two quarters into the hand of Nell.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “This represents what I can offer toward the hall painting,” she panted. “Giving a dollar to you would be my preference, yet taking an additional sum out of my egg savings is something I dare not attempt, as Eliza would discover it if I were to do so. Your society holds a true interest for me, and my belief is that you will accomplish a great deal of good. My nature is that of an optimist. Living alongside Eliza leaves me no choice but to be one. Returning quickly is necessary before my absence is noticed by her . . . she believes I am busy feeding the hens. May you experience good fortune while canvassing, and refrain from feeling discouraged by Eliza's words. Better times are coming to the world . . . they truly are.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: Daniel Blair’s was the subsequent house.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “At present, everything hinges on his wife being there or absent,” Isolde remarked, while they bounced down a track marked with deep ruts. “Should she be present, not one cent will come to us; all the town declares Dan Blair lacks the courage to get a haircut unless she allows it, and to speak mildly, her stinginess is beyond doubt. Her own explanation is that being just must precede being generous. However, according to Mrs. Sowerby, that 'preceding' distance is so great that she never achieves generosity whatsoever.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: During that evening, Thirza was told by Nell about what had happened to them at the Blair place.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “After hitching the horse, we knocked on the kitchen door. No one answered, yet the door was unlocked, and someone could be heard in the pantry, carrying on terribly. Although we were unable to understand the words, Isolde claims she recognizes they were curses based on their tone. I am unable to think that of Mr. Blair, since he is constantly so silent and humble; however, he certainly had strong cause, because Thirza, when the unfortunate man arrived at the door, as red as a beet, with sweat running down his face, he was wearing a large gingham apron belonging to his wife. ‘I can’t get this durned thing off,’ he said, ‘for the strings are tied in a hard knot and I can’t bust ’em, so you’ll have to excuse me, ladies.’ We pleaded with him not to speak of it, then entered and took a seat. Mr. Blair also took a seat; he swiveled the apron around to his rear and rolled it up, yet he appeared so humiliated and anxious that I pitied him, and Isolde stated she worried we had visited at an awkward moment. ‘Oh, not at all,’ said Mr. Blair, attempting to grin . . . you are aware he is continually quite courteous . . . ‘I’m a little busy . . . getting ready to bake a cake as it were. My wife got a telegram today that her sister from Montreal is coming tonight and she’s gone to the train to meet her and left orders for me to make a cake for tea. She writ out the recipe and told me what to do but I’ve clean forgot half the directions already. And it says, ‘flavor according to taste.’ What does that mean? How can you tell? And what if my taste doesn’t happen to be other people’s taste? Would a tablespoon of vanilla be enough for a small layer cake?”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “My sympathy for the unfortunate fellow grew deeper than ever. He appeared to be completely out of his element. Having heard tales of henpecked husbands, I now believed I was looking at one. I was on the verge of stating, ‘Mr. Blair, if you’ll give us a subscription for the hall I’ll mix up your cake for you.’ However, it abruptly occurred to me that driving such a hard bargain with a struggling fellow creature would not be very neighborly. Therefore, I volunteered to mix his cake without demanding anything in return. He eagerly accepted my proposal right away. He explained that although he was accustomed to baking his own bread prior to his marriage, he worried that cake exceeded his abilities, though he dreaded letting his wife down. After he retrieved a second apron for me, Isolde whipped the eggs while I combined the cake ingredients. Mr. Blair scurried around, fetching us the necessary items. Having completely forgotten he was still wearing his apron, it trailed behind him as he dashed about, causing Isolde to remark that the sight would be the death of her. He mentioned that baking the cake would pose no problem . . . he possessed experience with that part . . . and he subsequently requested our sheet and pledged four dollars. Thus, as you can tell, our efforts brought a reward. Nevertheless, had he withheld every penny, I would still maintain that assisting him constituted a genuinely Christian deed.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: The location where Theodore White resided served as the subsequent destination. Nell and Isolde were both visiting for the first time, and their familiarity with Mrs. Theodore was extremely minimal, as she rarely entertained guests. They debated in hushed tones whether to approach the rear entrance or the main entrance. During this quiet discussion, Mrs. Theodore emerged at the front entrance carrying a bundle of newspapers. In a calculated manner, she placed them individually upon the floor of the porch, the steps of the porch, and along the walkway until reaching the exact spot where her bewildered visitors stood.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Would you mind wiping your feet very thoroughly on the grass before stepping onto these papers?” she asked with concern. “I have only just finished sweeping the entire house, so I cannot tolerate any additional dust being brought inside. Ever since yesterday’s rain, the path has been extremely muddy.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Do not presume to laugh,” Nell cautioned softly while they stepped over the newsprint. “Furthermore, Isolde, I beg you to refrain from glancing my way, regardless of her words, lest I prove incapable of remaining serious.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: The documents spread throughout the entrance and went into a neat, immaculate parlor. Nell and Isolde seated themselves cautiously upon the closest chairs and detailed the reason for their visit. Mrs. White listened to them courteously, pausing the conversation a mere two times, first to drive away a daring fly, and second to gather a minute piece of grass that had dropped onto the rug from the dress of Nell. Nell experienced a miserable sense of guilt; nevertheless, Mrs. White pledged two dollars and handed over the cash immediately . . . “to prevent us from having to go back for it,” Isolde remarked after they escaped. Mrs. White had collected the newspapers prior to them unfastening their horse, and while they moved their vehicle out of the driveway, they observed her vigorously sweeping with a broom inside the entrance.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “After what we just saw, I am convinced that the rumors about Mrs. Theodore White being the most orderly person in existence are true,” remarked Isolde, letting out her pent-up amusement the moment she could safely do so.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “It makes me happy that no children were born to her,” Nell remarked with gravity. “Had there been any, their situation would have been terribly awful.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: During the visit to the Spencers’, Mrs. Isabella Tranter caused everyone distress by uttering a spiteful remark regarding every person in Brierley. Mr. Thomas Gammon declined to contribute any funds on the grounds that two decades earlier, when the hall was constructed, it was not erected upon the location he had advised. Mrs. Esther Bell, appearing perfectly healthy, spent thirty minutes describing each of her ailments in detail, and mournfully pledged fifty cents since she claimed she would not be alive to contribute when that time arrived the following year . . . rather, she expected to be buried in her grave.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: Their most unpleasant welcome, nevertheless, happened at Simon Fletcher’s. As they pulled into the yard, a pair of faces was seen by them looking out from the porch window. Yet despite the fact that they knocked and stood by with patience and persistence, not a soul answered the door. A pair of distinctly flustered and angry girls departed in their carriage from Simon Fletcher’s. Nell herself conceded that a sense of discouragement was starting to come over her. Nevertheless, the situation improved following that moment. A number of Mott properties were visited next, at which generous donations were secured by them, and from then until the conclusion they met with success, suffering merely a rare rejection. The final location they visited was at Robert Dickson’s near the pond bridge. They remained for tea at this house, even though home was quite close, to avoid the chance of angering Mrs. Dickson, who possessed the fame of being an extremely “touchy” lady.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: During the time they spent in that place, an visit was paid by elderly Mrs. James White.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “I’ve just come back from Lorenzo’s,” she declared. “Right now, he’s the proudest man in Brierley. Guess what? A brand new boy is there . . . and following seven girls, I can assure you that’s quite an event.” Nell listened intently, and as they drove off she remarked.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “My immediate destination is Lorenzo White’s place.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “However, his residence is along the Pale Sands road, which takes us considerably off our route,” Isolde objected. “Gideon and Hugh are going to solicit his vote.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Next Saturday is when they are going around, which makes it far too late,” Nell stated with conviction. “By that point, the novelty will have vanished. Even though Lorenzo White is terribly stingy, he is willing to contribute to any cause right at this moment. Isolde, this golden chance cannot be allowed to pass.” Nell’s shrewdness was validated by the outcome. In the yard, Mr. White encountered them, radiating joy like the sun on an Easter morning. He offered his eager assent when Nell requested a contribution.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Without a doubt, without a doubt. Simply record my name for one dollar above the largest contribution you have received.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Five dollars is the amount . . . four was what Mr. Daniel Blair left,” Nell said, feeling a bit fearful. Lorenzo, however, did not shrink back.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Five it is . . . and the cash is right here on the spot. Now, my desire is for you to step inside the house. A sight worth taking in awaits in there . . . a thing that very few individuals have laid eyes on up to now. Simply step inside and give your verdict.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “In the event that the infant lacks beauty, what shall be our response?” Isolde inquired in a fearful whisper while they trailed behind the enthusiastic Lorenzo into the residence.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Oh, something else pleasant will surely be said regarding it,” Nell remarked casually. “A baby always brings that out.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: The infant possessed beauty, nevertheless, and Mr. White considered the five dollars well spent for the genuine joy the chubby little arrival brought the girls. Yet that instance marked the single, ultimate, and solitary occasion on which Lorenzo White ever contributed to a cause.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: Exhausted though she felt, Nell exerted herself one last time that evening for the general good, stealing across the meadows to speak with Mr. Pettifer, who sat according to his habit on the veranda, smoking his pipe with Nutmeg at his side. Technically, his residence was situated on the Delford road; nevertheless, Odette and Tibby, who knew him only through dubious rumor, had anxiously pleaded with Nell to solicit his support.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: Mr. Pettifer, nevertheless, utterly declined to contribute a penny, and every one of Nell’s charms proved futile.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “However, it was my impression that our society had your approval, Mr. Pettifer,” she lamented.

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “Indeed I do . . . indeed I do . . . yet my consent fails to reach as deep as my coin, Nell.”

chapter_title: VI All Sorts and Conditions of Men . . . and women
text: “If I were to undergo just a couple more events like those I encountered today, I would become just as pessimistic as Miss Eliza Pullen,” Nell remarked to her image in the mirror of the east gable as she prepared for sleep.

Nell reclined in her chair and let out a sigh on a temperate evening in October. She occupied a seat beside a table that was laden with exercise books and textbooks, yet the pages in front of her, filled with dense writing, seemed to have no relation to school work or studies.
“What is the matter?” asked Hugh, who had reached the unclosed door of the kitchen right when the sigh was uttered.
Nell blushed, shoving her written work from view beneath a few school papers.

“It is not anything too terrible. Following Professor Hamilton's counsel, I attempted to draft a few of my ideas, yet I was unable to make them satisfy me. The moment they are recorded using black ink on white paper, they appear terribly motionless and silly. Whims resemble shadows . . . they are such untamed, leaping entities that you are unable to imprison them. Still, if I persist in my efforts, maybe I will master the trick eventually. As you are aware, my free time is quite limited. When I complete the grading of school assignments and essays, I am not always in the mood to compose something of my own.”
“Nell, your progress at school is going wonderfully. You are liked by all the children,” Hugh said, as he seated himself upon the stone step.

“No, not entirely. Anthony Tulk does not and will not like me. Worse still, he lacks respect for me . . . no, he really does not. He merely regards me with disdain, and I am not ashamed to admit to you that this distresses me terribly. It is not because he is particularly wicked . . . he is merely somewhat cheeky, though no more so than a few of the rest. He rarely defies my commands; yet he complies with a disdainful look of endurance, as though contesting the matter were not worth his time or else he would . . . and this influences the rest negatively. I have attempted all possible means to gain his favor, but I am starting to worry that I never will. I wish to, because he is a fairly clever young boy, even if he is a Tulk, and I might affectionally regard him if he allowed me to.”
“It is likely just the result of what is said in his household.”

“Not entirely. Anthony is a self-reliant young fellow who forms his own opinions regarding matters. He has continually been taught by male instructors in the past and he claims female educators are useless. Anyway, we will observe what can be achieved through patience and gentle care. Tackling obstacles appeals to me, and instructing children is truly quite fascinating labor. Cedric Stanhope compensates for everything that is absent in the rest. That youngster is an absolute treasure, Hugh, as well as a brilliant mind. I am convinced that society will learn about his talents in the future,” Nell finished with a voice full of certainty.

“Teaching is something I enjoy as well,” Hugh remarked. “For a start, it serves as excellent preparation. Really, Nell, during these weeks spent instructing the youth of Pale Sands, I have acquired more knowledge than throughout my entire time as a student. Everything appears to be progressing smoothly for us. Word has reached me that Odette is well-liked by those in Stonebridge; meanwhile, I believe Pale Sands finds your obedient servant reasonably acceptable . . . save for Mr. Andrew Tranter. While returning home yesterday evening, I encountered Mrs. Peter Scobie, who mentioned feeling obligated to let me know that Mr. Tranter was dissatisfied with my approach.”

“Have you ever observed,” Nell asked in a thoughtful tone, “that whenever individuals declare it to be their duty to inform you of something, you can expect an unpleasant revelation? For what reason do they never appear to consider it a duty to relay the nice remarks they hear regarding you? Mrs. H. B. Trask paid another visit to the school yesterday and said she felt it her duty to notify me that Mrs. Gorham Pullen disapproved of my reading fairy tales to the pupils, and that Mr. Rogerson believed Prillie was not progressing quickly enough in arithmetic. Were Prillie to devote less time to flirting with the boys over her slate, she could make better progress. I am fairly certain that Jack Pettigrew solves her class arithmetic problems for her, even if I have failed to catch him in the act.”
“Did you manage to make the optimistic son of Mrs. Trask accept his holy name?”

“Yes,” Nell chuckled, “yet the undertaking was truly hard. In the beginning, he refused to pay the slightest attention when I addressed him as ‘St. Clair’ until I had repeated it two or three times; after which, as the other boys poked him, he would glance upward wearing a terribly offended expression, as though I had referred to him as John or Wilfred and he could not possibly realize I was addressing him. Therefore, I detained him after classes one evening to speak with him gently. I explained that his mother desired me to address him as St. Clair and I was unable to act contrary to her desires. Once everything was fully laid out he understood . . . he is actually quite a sensible little boy . . . and he stated that I had permission to address him as St. Clair, though he would ‘lick the stuffing’ from any boy who attempted to do so. Naturally, I was obliged to scold him once more for employing such awful phrasing. From that time on I address him as St. Clair while the boys address him as Jake, and everything proceeds without trouble. He tells me he intends to become a carpenter, whereas Mrs. Trask instructs me to turn him into a college professor.”

Hugh’s train of thought shifted to another path when college was brought up, and for a while the two of them conversed about their hopes and intentions . . . seriously, solemnly, with optimism, in the manner that young people enjoy conversing, when what lies ahead remains an unexplored trail brimming with amazing potential.
Hugh had at last decided that he would become a doctor.

“It is a wonderful career,” he declared with passion. “Throughout existence, a person must battle against something . . . was it not once stated that man is a combative creature? . . . and my desire is to battle illness and suffering and lack of knowledge . . . which are entirely interconnected. Nell, I desire to contribute my portion of genuine, sincere labor to this earth . . . contribute a tiny bit to the total of human understanding that every noble person has collected since the start of time. Those who existed prior to my time have accomplished a great deal for my benefit, so I desire to demonstrate my appreciation by accomplishing something for those who will exist following my time. In my view, that represents the sole method a person can settle his debts to humanity.”

“My wish is to bring more beauty into the world,” Nell remarked with a dreamy tone. “Increasing people's knowledge isn't quite my goal . . . even if I recognize that as the highest aim . . . rather, I would delight in giving them a more enjoyable experience through my presence . . . in sparking some modest happiness or cheerful feeling that wouldn't have come to pass had I not come into existence.”
“I believe you achieve that goal daily,” Hugh remarked with admiration.

And he spoke the truth. Nell belonged among the children of light by right of birth. Once she had traversed a life, casting a smile or a word over it like a beam of sunlight, the possessor of that life perceived it, at least temporarily, as full of hope, beautiful, and commendable.
At last Hugh stood up with reluctance.
“Well, I need to hurry over to MacPhersons’,” I said. “Elias Purdy returned from Regent’s today to spend Sunday, and he was supposed to carry out a book that Professor Garrick is loaning to me.”
“Furthermore, I need to prepare Thirza’s tea. Since she departed to visit Mrs. Farrow earlier tonight, her return will happen shortly.”

Upon Thirza's return, tea had been prepared by Nell; lively snaps came from the burning fire, a jar containing pale, frosted ferns alongside dark red maple leaves decorated the table, and delicious scents of toast and ham filled the room. Thirza, however, let out a heavy sigh as she dropped into her chair.
“Do your eyes bother you? Is your head aching?” Nell asked with concern.

“No. I’m just exhausted . . . and concerned. It’s regarding Mary and those children . . . Mary has gotten worse . . . she cannot survive much longer. And regarding the twins, I do not know what will happen to them.”
“Is there no news from their uncle?”

“Yes, Mary received a letter from him. He is employed at a lumber camp and ‘shacking it,’ regardless of what that implies. At any rate, he states that taking the children before the spring is an absolute impossibility for him. He anticipates being married at that time and will possess a home where he can bring them; however, he states that she has to find some neighbors who will harbor them during the winter. She states that asking any of them is something she cannot endure. Mary never was on particularly good terms with the East Welby people, and that is the truth. And the upshot of the whole matter, Nell, is that I am certain Mary desires that I take those children . . . she did not state it outright, but her expression conveyed it.”
“Oh!” Nell brought her hands together, filled with intense excitement. “And surely you are going to, Thirza, aren’t you?”

“My decision is not yet made,” Thirza replied somewhat sharply. “Nell, I do not leap into matters with your impetuous style. Being third cousins provides a rather weak basis. Furthermore, taking charge of a pair of six-year-old youngsters will represent a terrible obligation . . . especially since they are twins.”
Thirza held the belief that a pair of twins was simply double the trouble of an individual child.

“Twins are quite fascinating . . . or a single set of them, anyway,” Nell remarked. “Only upon having a second or third set does it become tedious. Furthermore, I believe it would be truly lovely if you possessed an activity to keep you entertained while I am off at school.”

“I don’t suppose it would offer much fun . . . I’d expect it to bring more anxiety and trouble than anything. The danger wouldn’t be as great if their ages matched yours when I brought you in. Lucy wouldn’t concern me as deeply . . . she appears well-behaved and calm. But Robin is a handful.”

Nell possessed a fondness for children, and her heart went out to the Farrow twins. Her memory retained a very vivid picture of her own neglected youth. Knowing that Thirza could only be reached through her uncompromising commitment to what she considered her duty, Nell cleverly aligned her arguments to appeal to this principle.

“Should Robin be misbehaving, that makes it even more necessary for him to receive proper discipline, doesn't it, Thirza? Should we refuse to take them, their destination remains unknown, as do the sorts of conditions that might encompass them. Imagine if they were taken in by Mrs. Farrow’s next door neighbors, the Sprotts. According to Mrs. Sowerby, Henry Sprott utters more profanity than anyone who ever lived, and his children's words are entirely untrustworthy. Would it not be awful if such habits were acquired by the twins? Alternatively, imagine their going to the Wiggins’. As Mrs. Sowerby tells it, Mr. Wiggins converts everything sellable on the property into cash and raises his household using skim milk. You surely would not wish starvation upon your kin, even if your connection is merely that of third cousins, would you? It strikes me, Thirza, as our obligation to accept them.”

“I guess that’s true,” Thirza agreed dejectedly. “I suppose I will inform Mary that I’m going to accept them. There is no reason for you to appear so thrilled, Nell. This is going to result in a large amount of additional labor for you. My eyes prevent me from doing any sewing whatsoever, which means the responsibility of crafting and repairing their garments will fall to you. And sewing is not something you enjoy.”

“I detest it,” Nell remarked placidly, “however, if you are prepared to accept those children out of a feeling of duty, I certainly am able to perform their sewing out of a feeling of duty. It benefits people to be required to execute tasks they dislike . . . within reason.”

Mrs. Agatha Sowerby was positioned by the window of her kitchen, working on a quilt with her knitting needles, in the exact same manner she had been seated a few years before on a particular evening when Obed Abernethy had come driving down the hill bringing along the person Mrs. Agatha described as “his imported orphan.” However, that prior occasion occurred during the spring season; whereas the current time was the end of autumn, with the fields faded to brown and every tree in the forests stripped of leaves. The sun was in the process of going down in a grand display of gold and purple splendor beyond the black forests to the west of Brierley as a buggy pulled by a gentle brown horse traveled down the incline. Mrs. Agatha looked closely and intently toward it.

“Thirza is arriving back from the funeral,” she remarked to her spouse, who was resting on the couch in the kitchen. Thomas Sowerby spent a greater amount of time on the couch lately than was his former habit, though Mrs. Agatha, despite her keenness for observing matters outside her own home, had failed to observe this so far. “And both the twins are with her, . . . indeed, Robin is bent over the dashboard attempting to seize the pony’s tail while Thirza pulls him backward. Lucy sits upon the bench as neat as can be. She constantly appears as though she was recently starched and ironed. Ah well, unfortunate Thirza will certainly have her time completely occupied this winter. Even so, I fail to see how she could have done otherwise than accept them, given the situation, and Nell will assist her. Nell is utterly delighted about the entire affair, and she possesses a truly clever knack with youngsters, I have to admit. Goodness, it feels like only yesterday that poor Obed returned home with Nell herself and everyone mocked the thought of Thirza raising a youngster. Now she has taken in twins. A person is never secure against being astonished until they pass away.”

The rotund pony trotted across the bridge located in Sowerby’s Hollow before continuing down the Grey Shutters lane. Thirza wore a somewhat stern expression. East Welby lay ten miles behind them, and an obsession with endless movement appeared to hold Robin Farrow in its grip. Thirza lacked the ability to compel his stillness, and throughout the entire journey she endured severe anxiety that he might tumble off the wagon's rear to snap his neck, or pitch across the dashboard beneath the pony’s hooves. Desperate at last, she warned that she would give him a thorough whipping once she brought him home. At this, Robin scrambled onto her lap without care for the reins, wrapped his plump arms around her neck, and embraced her fiercely like a bear.

“I don’t believe you mean it,” he said, tapping her lined cheek in a fond way. “You do not seem like the kind of lady who would lash a small boy simply because he was unable to stay motionless. Did you not find staying motionless terribly difficult when you were merely as old as I am?”

“No, I constantly remained motionless whenever I received orders,” Thirza stated, attempting to sound firm, even though she sensed her inner feelings growing gentle beneath the spontaneous affection of Robin.

“Well, I reckon that happened since you used to be a girl,” Robin stated, wriggling returning to where he had been following one more embrace. “I reckon you used to be a girl at one time, even if considering it is terribly strange. Lucy is able to remain seated without moving . . . yet I do not believe there is a lot of enjoyment in that. It appears to me that being a girl has to be dull. Here, Lucy, allow me to make you a little more lively.”
To “liven up” Lucy, Robin’s approach involved clutching her curls with his fingers and pulling them. Lucy let out a shriek and subsequently wept.
“In what way can you act like such a wicked child when your unfortunate mother was placed in her plot only today?” asked Thirza in desperation.

“However, she felt happy to pass away,” Robin whispered in secret. “I am certain of it, since she informed me herself. Sickly for so long, she had grown extremely weary of it. On the evening prior to her passing, we had a lengthy conversation. She mentioned to me that you were planning to care for Lucy and me throughout the winter, and that I must behave myself. I intend to behave, yet is it not possible to behave while racing about just as easily as while remaining seated? Furthermore, she instructed that I must constantly show kindness to Lucy and defend her, and that is my intention.”
“Is yanking her hair what you consider being nice to her?”

“Well, no one else is going to be allowed to pull it by me,” Robin stated, clenching his hands into fists and scowling. “It would be better if they didn't even attempt it. She wasn't hurt much by me . . . her crying was simply because she is a girl. Being a boy makes me glad, though being a twin makes me sorry. Whenever Jimmy Sprott gets contradicted by his sister, his only response is, ‘Because I’m your senior, it follows that I know better,’ which puts an end to her arguments. However, Lucy cannot be told that by me, so she simply continues to hold opinions that differ from mine. Given that I am a man, the gee-gee could be driven by me for a little while.”

On the whole, Thirza felt a sense of gratitude as she entered her personal yard, in which the autumnal night breeze pranced among the brown leaves. Waiting at the gate to greet the arrivals and hoist the twins down was Nell. While Lucy quietly allowed herself to be kissed, Robin returned Nell's greeting by giving her a enthusiastic embrace and merrily declaring, “I’m Mr. Robin Farrow.”
While Lucy conducted herself in the manner of a proper young woman during the evening meal, the behavior of Robin was far from acceptable.

“I am so starved that there is no time for me to eat with manners,” he remarked upon being chided by Thirza. “Lucy is not nearly as starved as me. Consider the vast amount of exercise I got during the trip to this place. The cake is exceptionally delicious and filled with raisins. There has not been any cake at our house for an extremely long time, because mother was excessively ill to bake it and Mrs. Sprott stated that baking our bread for us was the absolute limit of what she could manage. Furthermore, Mrs. Wiggins fails to ever include raisins in her cakes. Not a chance with her! May I get a second slice?”

Although Thirza wished to decline, Nell served a substantial additional piece. Even so, she prompted Robin that he should utter “Thank you” in response to it. Robin simply smiled widely at her and swallowed a massive mouthful. After he completed the piece he remarked,
“I shall express my gratitude if you hand me one more portion.”
“No, you have consumed sufficient cake,” declared Thirza, utilizing an intonation that Nell recognized and Robin would come to realize permitted no debate.

Robin offered a wink to Nell, after which he bent across the board, grabbed the initial portion of cake belonging to Lucy, who had merely had a single delicate small nip of it, directly from her own hands and, parting his jaws as wide as possible, stuffed the entire piece inside. A quiver came to Lucy’s lip and Thirza found herself unable to speak from shock. Nell immediately declared, assuming her finest “schoolma’am” manner,
“Oh, Robin, men of quality would never act in such a manner.”
“I’m aware that they don’t,” Robin uttered, the moment he was able to talk, “yet I’m no gemplum.”
“However, wouldn't you prefer to become one?” inquired a surprised Nell.
“Naturally I do. However, becoming a gemplum is impossible until you are older.”

“Oh, indeed you can,” Nell hastened to say, believing she noticed an opportunity to sow good seed early. “You can start being a gentleman while you are a young boy. And gentlemen never grab things from ladies . . . or neglect to say thank you . . . or yank anyone’s hair.”
“It’s a certainty that they fail to enjoy themselves very much,” Robin stated openly. “I suppose I will hold off on becoming one until I reach adulthood.”

A further slice of cake was sliced for Lucy by a resigned Thirza. Robin was someone she lacked the energy to deal with at that time. Between the funeral service and the extensive journey by car, the day had proven taxing for her. Right then, her outlook on what lay ahead was marked by a gloominess that would have rivaled Eliza Pullen’s own.

Despite both being fair-haired, the twins did not look strikingly similar. The long, sleek curls that Lucy possessed were always perfectly neat. A head of tiny, fuzzy yellow ringlets covered Robin’s round skull. Gentle and mild hazel eyes belonged to Lucy, whereas Robin’s danced with an elfish roguishness. While Lucy had a straight nose, Robin’s was undeniably snubbed; Lucy’s mouth was set in a “prunes and prisms” expression, but Robin’s was perpetually smiling; moreover, a single dimple indented one of his cheeks, giving him a sweet, amusing, uneven appearance whenever he chuckled. Every detail of his small face seemed to harbor joy and playfulness.

“The best option is for them to turn in,” remarked Thirza, believing that this was the simplest manner of dealing with them. “Lucy is going to share my bed, whereas Robin can be accommodated by you in the west gable. Sleeping by yourself doesn't frighten you, does it, Robin?”
“No; however, I am not planning on turning in for a very long time still,” Robin remarked in a relaxed manner.
“Indeed, you are.” The sorely tested Thirza uttered nothing more than those words, yet the quality of her voice silenced Robin himself. Beside Nell, he hurried dutifully up the stairs.
“The moment I become an adult, my absolute highest priority will be remaining awake through an entire night simply to discover how it feels,” he secretly confided to her.

In subsequent years Thirza could not recall that initial week of the twins' stay at Grey Shutters without shivering. It was not that it was actually significantly worse than the weeks that came after; rather, it appeared that way because it was new. Hardly a single conscious minute of any day passed in which Robin was not engaged in mischief or planning it; however, his first remarkable feat took place two days following his arrival, on Sunday morning . . . a lovely, warm day, which was as hazy and gentle as September. While Thirza took care of Lucy, Nell got him ready for church. Initially, Robin resisted forcefully when his face was being washed.

“Thirza did the laundry yesterday . . . and Mrs. Wiggins scrubbed my skin using hard soap on the funeral day. For a single week, that suffices. Being so exceedingly clean seems pointless to me. Staying dirty is far more comfortable.”
“With no need for prompting, Cedric Stanhope cleans his face daily,” observed Nell cleverly.

Robin had resided at Grey Shutters for just a bit more than forty-eight hours; yet his adoration for Nell and his hatred for Cedric Stanhope, whom Nell had been heard praising with great enthusiasm the day following his arrival, were already established. Should Cedric Stanhope wash his face daily, the matter was decided. He, Robin Farrow, would likewise perform the act, even if it proved fatal to him. This very thought persuaded him to yield quietly to the remaining aspects of his grooming, and he truly appeared as an attractive young boy once everything was completed. Nell experienced a feeling of nearly motherly pride regarding him while she escorted him to the ancient Abernethy pew.

Initially, Robin acted rather decently, as he was busy stealing secret looks at every young boy in sight and trying to guess which one might be Cedric Stanhope. Nothing out of the ordinary occurred during the initial pair of hymns or the reading of the Scripture. It was while Mr. Wace was offering a prayer that the stir took place.

Directly ahead of Robin sat Lauretta White, whose head leaned forward a bit while her blonde hair dangled in a pair of lengthy plaits, framing an alluring stretch of pale neck that was enveloped by a relaxed frill of lace. Lauretta was an eight-year-old child, plump and serene in appearance, who had behaved faultlessly during services ever since the initial occasion when her mother brought her to church as a six-month-old baby.

Reaching into his pocket, Robin pulled out . . . a caterpillar, one that was furry and squirming. Thirza caught sight of it and made a grab for him, yet she acted too late. Down Lauretta’s neck, Robin let the caterpillar fall.

A succession of sharp screams shattered the exact center of Mr. Wace’s prayer. Horrified, the minister ceased praying and unclosed his eyes. All the heads throughout the assembly snapped upward. In her pew, Lauretta White was leaping up and down while wildly grabbing at the rear of her dress.

“Ouch . . . mother . . . mother . . . ouch . . . remove it . . . ouch . . . pull it out . . . ouch . . . that naughty child stuffed it inside my collar . . . ouch . . . mother . . . it is slipping deeper down . . . ouch . . . ouch . . . ouch. . . .”

Mrs. White got up and, her countenance resolute, bore the weeping, twisting Lauretta away from the church. As her screams faded into the distance, Mr. Wace continued reading the liturgy. Yet each person sensed that the day's proceedings were ruined. Thirza ignored the sermon for the very first time in her existence, and Nell remained seated, her face flushed red with shame.

After they arrived at their house, Thirza placed Robin in bed, forcing him to remain there through the remainder of the day. Refusing to feed him any dinner, she only permitted him a simple tea consisting of bread and milk. Nell brought this meal up to him and waited sadly beside him as he consumed it with a remorseless delight. Nevertheless, Nell’s sorrowful gaze made him feel uneasy.
“I reckon,” he mused thoughtfully, “that Cedric Stanhope wouldn’t have put a caterpillar down a girl’s neck during a church service, would he?”
“He truly would not,” Nell remarked with sorrow.

“Well, I suppose I regret doing it, in that case,” Robin admitted. “However, the caterpillar was so amazingly large . . . I grabbed him from the church steps right as we entered. Wasting him appeared to be a shame. Also, tell me, was it not amusing listening to that girl scream?”

On Tuesday afternoon, Grey Shutters hosted the gathering of the Aid Society. Nell rushed back from school, aware that Thirza required every bit of help she was able to provide. Lucy, immaculate and genteel in a crisp, starched white dress accented by a black sash, sat among the Aid's attendees inside the parlor, answering modestly whenever addressed, remaining quiet otherwise, and behaving in all respects like an exemplary youth. Robin, delightfully coated in dirt, fashioned mud pies out in the barnyard.

“I said he could,” Thirza remarked with fatigue. “My belief was that it would prevent him from doing something worse. Getting muddy is the only harm there. Before we summon him for his tea, we will finish ours. Lucy is allowed to join us for hers, though I would not have the courage to permit Robin to take a seat at the table while all the Aids are present.”

Going to summon the Aids for tea, Nell discovered that Lucy was missing from the parlor. Mrs. Jasper Bell mentioned that Robin had arrived at the front entrance and asked her to step outside. Following a brief discussion with Thirza in the pantry, they decided that both children should be given their tea together at a later time.

The midway mark of tea had passed when an unhappy shape burst into the dining room. Dismay filled the gazes of Thirza and Nell, while astonishment took hold of the Aids. Might that truly be Lucy . . . that weeping, indistinct person clad in a soaked, trickling dress, her hair shedding streams of water onto Thirza’s new coin-spot rug?
“Lucy, what has happened to you?” exclaimed Nell, glancing guiltily toward Mrs. Jasper Bell, who belonged to what was reputedly the sole family on earth that never suffered accidents.

“Robin forced me to balance on the pigpen fence,” sobbed Lucy. “I refused at first, but he taunted me by calling me a fraid-cat. Then I tumbled down inside the pigpen, which ruined my dress with dirt, and the pig charged straight across me. Even though my dress looked terrible, Robin promised to spray it clean if I stood beneath the pump, so I obeyed him and he drenched me with water, yet my dress remains just as dirty, while my beautiful shoes and sash are completely ruined.”

For the remainder of the dinner, Nell performed the table's duties by herself, during which time Thirza went up to the higher floor and put Lucy back into her previous garments. Robin was captured and dispatched to his room for the night deprived of any evening meal. At dusk, Nell visited his bedchamber and spoke to him in a solemn manner . . . an approach in which she placed immense trust, one that the outcomes did not entirely fail to warrant. She informed him that his behavior made her feel deeply upset.

“Now I feel sorry myself,” Robin conceded, “however the problem is that I am never sorry about doing things until I have done them. Because she was scared of dirtying her clo’es, Lucy refused to assist me in making pies, which made me extremely angry. If Cedric Stanhope had known his sister would fall in, I suppose he would not have forced her to walk a pigpen fence?”
“No, such a thought would never cross his mind. Cedric is an absolute little gentleman.”

Robin squeezed his eyes closed completely and appeared to contemplate the matter briefly. After that, he crept upward and wrapped his arms around Nell’s neck, nestling his warm, small face against her shoulder.
“Nell, isn't there a little bit of affection you have for me, even though I'm not a good boy like Cedric?”

“I certainly do,” Nell stated with genuine feeling. For some reason, she found it impossible not to hold a fond affection for Robin. “Even so, my fondness for you would grow if your mischievous behavior ceased.”

“I . . . performed another action today,” Robin continued, his voice muted. “I regret it at this moment, but I am terribly frightened to inform you. You will not become too angry, will you? And you will not inform Thirza, will you?”

“I’m uncertain, Robin. It might be best if I inform her. However, I believe I can give you my word that I will abstain, provided you give me your word that you will abstain from ever repeating it, no matter what it might be.”
“No, I never will,” I replied, adding, “Anyhow, finding additional ones this year is hardly probable for me, as I discovered this particular one upon the basement stairs.”
“Robin, what have you done?”
“A toad was placed by me in the bed belonging to Thirza. Should you desire to, you may go and remove it. Yet tell me, Nell, wouldn't leaving it in that spot be entertaining?”

“Robin Farrow!” Nell leaped away from the embrace of Robin and rushed through the hall into the room belonging to Thirza. A bit of disorder showed on the bed. With anxious speed, she pulled away the blankets, and beneath a pillow, blinking its eyes at her, sat the toad beyond all doubt.

“In what way am I able to take that terrible creature outside?” Nell groaned, shuddering. She thought of the fire shovel, so she tiptoed downstairs to retrieve it as Thirza was occupied inside the pantry. Nell encountered her own difficulties transporting the toad down the stairs, because it leaped off the shovel on three occasions, and at one point she believed it was lost inside the hall. Upon lastly leaving it within the cherry orchard, a deep sigh of relief escaped her.

“Should Thirza discover this, she would not feel secure entering her bed for the rest of her days. It brings me great joy that the young wrongdoer showed remorse before it was too late. Isolde is making signs to me over from her window. I am pleased . . . I truly require a bit of distraction, because my nerves have suffered almost everything they can tolerate for a single day between Anthony Tulk being at school and Robin Farrow being at home.”

“That old bother Agatha Sowerby dropped by once more today, nagging me to contribute money for purchasing a vestry room carpet,” Mr. Pettifer declared angrily. “My hatred for that woman exceeds my feelings for anyone else I am acquainted with. In merely six words, she is capable of compressing an entire sermon—complete with text, commentary, and application—and launching it at your head as if it were a brick.”

Seated upon the border of the veranda, Nell—who was taking pleasure in the delight of a gentle west breeze sweeping over a recently tilled field during a dim November dusk and whistling an unusual short tune amid the gnarled fir trees beneath the garden—gazed back over her shoulder with her imaginative face.

“The problem stems from you and Mrs. Sowerby not comprehending each other,” she clarified. “Whenever individuals dislike one another, that is invariably the issue. My own initial feelings toward Mrs. Sowerby were not warm; however, learning to appreciate her happened as soon as I grew to comprehend her.”

“Mrs. Sowerby might be a taste that certain people acquire; however, I stopped eating bananas rather than continuing just because I was informed that I would eventually come to enjoy them,” Mr. Pettifer growled. “Furthermore, regarding the matter of comprehending her, I comprehend that she is an inveterate meddler, and I informed her of that fact.”

“Oh, that surely injured her feelings terribly,” Nell stated with reproach. “In what way could you utter a statement like that? A long time ago, I spoke a few terrible words to Mrs. Sowerby, yet it occurred while I was out of temper. Expressing them intentionally is something I could not do.”
“That was what actually happened, and my policy is to speak truthfully to everyone.”

“However, you fail to speak the entire truth,” Nell protested. “The unpleasant portion of the truth is all that you reveal. Indeed, you have informed me twelve times that red was the color of my hair, yet you have not a single time mentioned to me that my nose was pleasant.”
“I imagine you are aware of it without being told,” laughed Mr. Pettifer.
“I am aware that my hair is red as well . . . even though its shade is far deeper than before . . . which means there is no reason to inform me of that as well.”

“Alright, alright, I will attempt to refrain from bringing it up any further if it bothers you so much. You will have to forgive me, Nell. I am accustomed to speaking my mind, so people simply have to tolerate it.”

“Yet they are unable to prevent themselves from caring about it. Nor do I believe that your custom makes it any easier. How would you view someone who walked around poking pins and needles into individuals while declaring, ‘Pardon me, you shouldn't care about it . . . it is merely a habit of mine.’ Wouldn't you consider him insane? Furthermore, regarding Mrs. Sowerby being meddlesome, maybe she indeed is. However, did you inform her that she possessed a most compassionate heart and constantly aided the needy, and never uttered a single word when Timothy Cotton took a crock of butter from her dairy and informed his wife that he had purchased it from her? The next time they encountered each other, Mrs. Cotton reproached her with the fact that it had a turnip flavor, and Mrs. Sowerby merely stated she was regretful it had proved to be so inferior.”

“I imagine there are a few decent traits to her,” Mr. Pettifer admitted reluctantly. “That goes for the majority of people. Even I possess a few, despite how unlikely it may seem to you. Regardless, not a single cent from me will go toward that carpet. It feels like people in this place never stop asking for hand-outs. What is the status of your plan to paint the hall?”

“Excellently. A gathering of the B.V.I.S. took place last Friday evening, during which we discovered that sufficient funds had been pledged not only to paint the hall but also to put new shingles on the roof. The majority of folk contributed most generously, Mr. Pettifer.”
Nell possessed a sweet soul, yet she had the ability to infuse innocent italics with a degree of venom whenever the situation demanded it.
“Which hue will you choose for it?”
“A very pretty green is what we have chosen. Dark red will be used for the roof, naturally. The paint is being fetched from town by Mr. Roger Tulk today.”
“Which person secured the position?”

“Delford’s Mr. Joshua Tulk. The shingling is almost completed by him. The contract had to be awarded to him by us, because all of the Tulks . . . and four families exist, as you are aware . . . declared that not a single cent would be contributed by them if Joshua failed to secure it. A total of twelve dollars had been pledged among them and losing that seemed unwise to us, even though a few folks believe the Tulks shouldn’t have been yielded to by us. It is claimed by Mrs. Sowerby that they attempt to control all things.”
“The primary issue is whether this Joshua performs his duties effectively. Provided he succeeds, his name being Tulk or Pudding seems irrelevant to me.”
“They consider him a skilled worker, although he is reported to be quite an odd individual. He almost never speaks.”

“He’s certainly odd enough,” Mr. Pettifer remarked drily. “At any rate, that’s what the locals will label him. Talking was never really my thing until I arrived in Brierley, where I was forced to start simply to protect myself, otherwise Mrs. Sowerby would have claimed I was mute and launched a fund to get me instructed in sign language. Nell, you aren’t leaving already?”

“I must. This evening I have a bit of sewing to complete for Lucy. On top of that, Robin is likely breaking Thirza’s heart with a new piece of mischief by now. Early today his very first words were, ‘Where does the dark go, Nell? I want to know.’ My answer to him was that it traveled to the opposite side of the earth, yet following breakfast he announced that it did not . . . that it descended into the well. According to Thirza, she found him leaning over the well-box four separate times today, attempting to reach down into the dark.”

“He’s a rascal,” stated Mr. Pettifer. “Prior to my arrival from the barn yesterday, he had come over and plucked half a dozen feathers from the tail of Nutmeg. Ever since then, the poor bird has been drooping. You folks must have a great deal of trouble with those children.”

“Whatever is value-worthy requires a certain degree of effort,” Nell uttered, inwardly deciding to pardon the subsequent misdeed of Robin, regardless of what it could prove to be, because he had taken revenge on Nutmeg for her sake.

That evening, the hall paint was brought home by Mr. Roger Tulk, and the following day, painting was commenced by Mr. Joshua Tulk, who was a taciturn, surly man. Nobody interrupted him while he worked. “The lower road” was the name given to the location of the hall. Because this route was constantly wet and muddy during late autumn, travelers headed to Delford took the “upper” route, which was longer. Fir woods enclosed the hall so tightly that it could not be seen except from close by. In this isolation and self-reliance, which his unsociable nature cherished greatly, Mr. Joshua Tulk kept painting.

On Friday afternoon, having completed his task, he traveled back to his home in Delford. Not long after he left, Mrs. Agatha Sowerby came driving past, having risked the muddy lower road because she was curious about how the hall appeared with its fresh coat of paint. As she came around the spruce curve, the sight met her eyes.

Mrs. Sowerby was strangely moved by what she saw. Releasing the reins, she raised both hands and exclaimed “Gracious Providence!” Her gaze remained fixed as though her vision was deceiving her. After that, her laughter turned nearly hysterical.
“A mistake has surely occurred . . . it must have. I was certain those Tulks would ruin everything.”

Traveling back to her house, Mrs. Sowerby encountered numerous individuals along the route and paused to inform them regarding the hall. The intelligence spread with immense speed. While studying a text book in his residence, Hugh Carrow was told by his father’s hired boy at sunset, whereupon he hurried out of breath to Grey Shutters, with Gideon Duckett joining him along the journey. Beneath the large leafless willows at the yard gate of Grey Shutters, they encountered Isolde Pembroke, Odette Pullen, and Nell Harcourt, who were the very embodiment of despair.
“Hugh cried out, “Is it really not true, Nell?””

“That’s correct,” replied Nell, appearing like the tragedy muse. “Mrs. Sowerby dropped by while traveling from Delford to inform me. Oh, it is just terrible! What point is there in attempting to make anything better?”
“What is terrible?” inquired Oliver Mott, who came up right then carrying a bandbox from town that he had retrieved for Thirza.

“Have you not heard?” Odette asked in anger. “Well, the situation is merely this. . . Joshua Tulk went ahead and chose blue paint for the hall rather than green . . . an intense, vivid blue, the very tint employed for coloring carts and wheelbarrows. And Mrs. Sowerby claims that, particularly when paired with a red roof, it is the most unsightly hue for a structure that she has ever witnessed or pictured. A feather could literally have floored me upon hearing the news. Following all the difficulty we have experienced, it is tragic.”
“In what imaginable way could an error like that have occurred?” cried Isolde.

This merciless catastrophe was ultimately attributed to the Tulks. Morton-Harris paints had been selected by the Improvers, with the Morton-Harris paint tins being assigned digits corresponding to a color chart. A customer picked a preferred tone from the chart and made an order using the corresponding digit. The requested hue of green was Number 147, and after Mr. Roger Tulk conveyed a message to the Improvers through his son, John Andrew, stating that he intended to travel to town and would purchase their paint, the Improvers instructed John Andrew to inform his father to obtain 147. John Andrew forever maintained that this was what he communicated, yet Mr. Roger Tulk asserted just as firmly that John Andrew had specified 157; and that is where the issue remains currently.

Every home in Brierley that housed an Improver was filled with total consternation during that evening. The melancholy present at Grey Shutters was so profound that it subdued even Robin. Unable to be consoled, Nell cried.

“Even if my seventeenth birthday is nearly here, Thirza, I cannot help weeping,” she wept. “This is extremely humiliating. Furthermore, it signals the absolute demise of our social circle. People will just mock us until we cease to exist.”

In reality, much like in dreams, matters frequently turn out in reverse. The residents of Brierley failed to find it amusing; their fury was too great. Because their funds had paid for painting the hall, the error left them feeling deeply wronged. The community directed its wrath toward the Tulks. Responsibility for the blunder lay between Roger Tulk and John Andrew; furthermore, Joshua Tulk had to be a natural idiot to not realize something was amiss upon opening the containers and beholding the paint's hue. When subjected to this criticism, Joshua Tulk countered that Brierley’s preferred shades were not his concern, regardless of his personal views; his employment was to paint the structure, rather than discuss it; and he intended to collect his payment for doing so.
It was with a bitter spirit that the Improvers handed over his payment, having first sought the advice of Mr. Peter Mott, a magistrate.

Peter informed him, “That bill will need to be settled by you.” He added, “Because his statement is that no one ever specified the intended color, but rather he was simply handed the paint and instructed to proceed, he cannot be blamed for the error. Still, it is a terrible disgrace, and without a doubt, that hallway appears terrible.”

The unfortunate Improvers anticipated that Brierley would hold a stronger bias against them than before; nevertheless, the sentiment of the public shifted in their direction. It was believed that the keen, passionate small group who had labored so diligently toward their goal had received unfair treatment. Mrs. Sowerby advised them to persevere and demonstrate to the Tulks that there actually existed individuals in the world capable of accomplishing tasks without creating a mess. Mr. Major Tranter dispatched a message informing them that he would remove every stump alongside his farm's road frontage and sow it with grass at his personal cost; furthermore, Mrs. Hiram Mott visited the school on a certain day and secretly motioned Nell out to the porch to inform her that should the “Sassiety” wish to plant a bed of geraniums at the crossroads when spring arrived, they had no reason to fear her cow, as she would ensure the destructive beast was confined to secure limits. Even Mr. Pettifer, if he laughed inwardly at all, did so in secret, displaying nothing but empathy on the surface.

“Don’t worry about it, Nell. Although a majority of paints grow more hideous as time passes, that blue has already reached maximum ugliness, meaning its fading process can only make it look better. Furthermore, the shingle roof has been properly painted. From now on, people sitting in the hall won't get rained on. Regardless, you have achieved a great deal.”
“Yet from now on, Brierley’s blue hall is going to be a proverb across every adjacent settlement,” Nell remarked with bitterness.
And it must be acknowledged that it was indeed so.

Barbara Shaw had suffered merely a single mishap . . . slopping a water dipper across the floor . . . and Anthony Tulk had been entirely absent from class.

chapter_title: X Robin in Search of a Sensation

However, this year is aging with elegance . . . much like an elegant elderly woman who understands her ability to remain delightful despite her grey hair and lines. Lovely days and delightful dusks have been ours. A profound sense of peace has marked these past two weeks, and Robin himself has been nearly well-mannered. Truly, I believe his behavior is getting much better. The forest is so silent today . . . lacking any sound save for the gentle breeze whispering among the highest branches! That noise resembles ocean waves breaking on a distant coast. These woods are so precious! My splendid trees! Each single one of you is beloved by me as a friend.”

text: “There are a terrible number of actions that one shouldn’t commit,” Robin remarked while sighing. “I had no idea there were that many. I regret that it’s improper to tell whop . . . untruths, because it’s extremely convenient, but because it is bad I won't ever speak another one. How will you punish me for speaking them today? I would like to be told.” Nell turned her gaze pleadingly toward Thirza.

chapter_title: X Robin in Search of a Sensation
text: “I do not wish to judge the youngster excessively,” Thirza remarked. “It is likely that no one actually informed him that lying was improper, and those Sprott youngsters were hardly suitable associates for him. Unfortunate Mary suffered too much illness to instruct him adequately, and I suppose one cannot anticipate a child of six years to understand such matters naturally. It seems we must simply accept that he lacks all correct knowledge and start from the very start. Nevertheless, a penalty is required for his locking Lucy away, though I am unable to conceive a method other than dispatching him to sleep lacking his evening meal, which we have repeated repeatedly. Are you incapable of proposing an alternative, Nell? It seems to me you should possess that capacity, given the imagination you continuously mention.”

chapter_title: X Robin in Search of a Sensation

Clearly he was engaged in some reflection, because upon Nell going to her own chamber shortly afterward, she detected his soft call of her name. Entering his room, she discovered him upright in bed, knees supporting his elbows and hands holding up his chin.

chapter_title: X Robin in Search of a Sensation

His claim was that he failed to perceive any benefit in praying before growing large enough for God to consider him somewhat important. What we will do with that child is unknown to me, Nell. His equal has never been seen by me. Discouragement is completely overwhelming me.”

Lacking any male companions for recreation, his brain requires an outlet for its energy. Lucy’s extreme rigidity and decorum prevent her from being an adequate companion for a young man. Thirza, my genuine opinion is that sending them to school would be preferable.”

While the twins may receive some instruction in the home, they will under no circumstances attend school before turning seven.”

text: “Well, we shall have to attempt to improve Robin in our own house instead,” Nell remarked in a bright manner. “Despite every one of his shortcomings, he truly is a sweet young boy. Loving him is something I am unable to avoid. Thirza, expressing this might be terrible, yet truthfully, Robin appeals to me more than Lucy, even though she is so well-behaved.”

chapter_title: X Robin in Search of a Sensation

text: “Lucy possesses too much goodness,” Nell remarked. “Even without anyone around to direct her actions, her behavior would remain equally flawless. Because her upbringing was complete from the moment she was born, she has no requirement for us; and my belief is,” Nell ended, striking upon a crucial reality, “that those who require us are the ones who always receive our deepest affection. Our help is desperately required by Robin.”

chapter_title: X Robin in Search of a Sensation
text: “He definitely requires something,” concurred Thirza. “A thorough thrashing is what Agatha Sowerby would claim he needed.”

“Educating pupils is actually quite an engaging job,” Nell penned in a letter to a friend from Regent’s Academy. “Odette mentions that she considers it tedious, yet my experience differs. Nearly every day, some humorous event is likely to occur, and the statements from the boys and girls are so entertaining. Odette states that her students receive punishment whenever they utter humorous remarks, a practice that likely explains why she perceives instruction as dull. Earlier today, young Jimmy Pullen attempted to spell ‘speckled’ without success. ‘Well,’ he uttered at last, ‘I can’t spell it but I know what it means.’
“‘Say again?’ I inquired.
“‘The face of St. Clair Trask, miss.’

“St. Clair does have a great deal of freckles, even though I endeavor to stop the rest from making remarks about them . . . because I had freckles at one time and my memory of it is vivid. However, I believe St. Clair is unbothered. The reason St. Clair thrashed Jimmy while returning from school was that Jimmy addressed him as ‘St. Clair’. Word of the thrashing reached me, though not through official channels, which leads me to believe I should ignore the matter.

“I was attempting to instruct Lottie Duckett in adding numbers yesterday. I inquired, ‘If you had three candies in one hand and two in the other, how many would you have altogether?’ Lottie responded, ‘A mouthful.’ Furthermore, during nature study, upon my requesting a valid justification for not destroying toads, Benjie Mott solemnly replied, ‘Because it would rain the next day.’”

“Mabel, refraining from laughter is extremely difficult. All my amusement must be kept inside until I return home, and Thirza claims that hearing unprovoked, wild shrieks of mirth coming from the east gable makes her uneasy. According to her, a man in Welby lost his mind once, and those very sounds marked the start of it.

“Were you aware of the fact that Thomas a Becket was made a saint as a snake? According to Rose Bell, he was . . . and she also claims William Tyndale authored the New Testament. Claude White asserts that a ‘glacier’ means a person who installs window frames!
