“I believe that drawing out the children’s genuine ideas on various subjects is both the hardest and the most fascinating part of instruction. During a tempestuous day this past week, I brought them together around myself at lunchtime and attempted to have them speak with me precisely as though I were their peer. I requested that they share the items they desired above all else. A few of the responses were rather ordinary . . . skates, ponies, and dolls. Other requests were quite unique. Dinah Gammon wished ‘to wear her Sunday dress every day and eat in the sitting room.’ Hannah Bell desired ‘to be good without having to take any trouble about it.’ Marjory White, who is ten years old, wished to be a widow. When I asked her reason, she solemnly remarked that people named you an old maid if you lacked a husband, whereas your husband commanded you if you had one; however, neither hazard existed for a widow. Sally Bell possessed the most extraordinary desire. She desired a ‘honeymoon.’ I inquired whether she understood what that meant, and she replied that she assumed it was a particularly fine sort of bicycle, since her Montreal cousin embarked on a honeymoon upon getting married, and he had invariably owned the newest style of bicycles!

“On a different day, I requested that everyone inform me of the most wicked action they had ever committed. Although I was unable to persuade the older children to comply, the third class responded with complete openness. Eliza Bell had ‘set fire to her aunt’s carded rolls.’ When I questioned whether she intended to accomplish this, she replied, ‘not altogether.’ She merely tested a tiny tip to observe its burning, and the entire package caught fire instantly. Emerson Pettigrew had expended a dime on sweets when he ought to have placed it inside his missionary box. The most severe offense of Annetta Bell was ‘eating some blueberries that grew in the graveyard.’ Willie White had ‘slid down the sheephouse roof a lot of times with his Sunday trousers on.’ ‘But I was punished for it ’cause I had to wear patched pants to Sunday School all summer, and when you’re punished for a thing you don’t have to repent of it,’ Willie asserted.

“How I desire that you might view a few of their writings . . . my longing is such that I intend to forward duplicates of several produced not long ago. The previous week, I instructed the fourth class to compose epistles to me regarding whatever topic they chose, proposing as an idea that they could describe a location they had journeyed to or a fascinating object or individual they had encountered. These communications were to be penned on actual stationery, enclosed within an envelope, and directed to my name, entirely unassisted by anyone else. This past Friday forenoon, a collection of missives awaited me upon my desk, and later that night, I was reminded anew that instruction yields delight alongside its hardships. Those pieces of writing could compensate for a great deal. Below is the one by Ned Clay, with the location, orthography, and syntax preserved precisely as first written.”
“‘Miss schoolmistress ShiRley Green gabels. p.e. Island are birds capable

“‘Dear teacher I believe I shall compose a essay for you regarding birds. birds are extremely helpful creatures. my cat captures birds. He is named William although pa names him tom. he is entirely striped and last winter he had one of his ears froz off. if not for that he would be a handsome cat. My unkle has taken in a cat. it arrived at his house one day and would not leave and unkle states it has forgotten more than the majority of people ever knowed. he allows it to sleep in his rocking chare and my aunt remarks he cares more for it than he does for his children. that is incorrect. we should treat cats kindly and offer them new milk but we should not treat them better than our children. this is oll I am able to think of so nothing further at present from
edward blake ClaY.’”

“St. Clair Trask’s, as per usual, is brief and direct. Words are never wasted by St. Clair. I don't believe that malice aforethought drove his choice of subject or the addition of the postscript. Rather, he simply lacks much tact or imagination.”
“‘Dear Miss Harcourt

“‘We were instructed by you to detail a peculiar thing that we have observed. My description will be of the Brierley Hall. Its doors number two, comprising an inner one alongside an outer one. Six windows are present on it, as well as a chimney. A pair of ends and a pair of sides belong to it. Blue is the color it is painted. That circumstance renders it strange. The lower Delford road is where it is constructed. Among the structures in Brierley, its importance ranks third. The church together with the blacksmith shop constitute the others. Debating clubs, in addition to lectures and concerts, are conducted within it.
“‘Truly yours, “‘Jacob Trask.
“‘P.S. The color of the hall is a most vivid blue.’”

“The length of Annetta Bell’s missive astonished me, because composing compositions is hardly Annetta’s strong suit, and her usual attempts are just as short as St. Clair’s. Although Annetta is a reserved small creature and an exemplar of fine deportment, she possesses not a trace of inventiveness. This is what she wrote.—
“‘Most beloved educator,

“‘I believe I shall compose a missive to you describing the depth of my affection. My love for you encompasses my entire heart, soul, and mind . . . every part of me that is capable of loving . . . and my desire is to be of service to you eternally. To do so would be my greatest honor. This explains my intense effort to behave properly at school and master my lessuns.

“‘You possess such beauty, my teacher. The sound of your voice resembles music, and your eyes look like dew-covered pansies. You bring to mind a tall, majestic queen. Rippling gold is what your hair looks like. Anthony Tulk claims that it is red, but Anthony does not deserve any of your attention.

“‘Although we met merely a handful of months ago, I am unable to conceive that a period existed wherein you were unknown to me . . . before you entered my existence to bestow upon it blessing and sanctity. This year will forever remain in my memory as the most marvelous of my existence, for it delivered you to my side. Furthermore, it marks the time of our relocation to Brierley from Stonebridge. The affection I hold for you has rendered my existence profoundly abundant, shielding me from a great deal of injury and wickedness. Every bit of this is owed to you, my most beloved instructor.

“‘I will always remember how lovely you appeared when I last beheld you wearing that dark gown adorned with blossoms in your hair. That is how I will picture you eternally, even once we have both grown elderly and hoary. To me, my most beloved instructor, you shall perpetually remain youthful and beautiful. My thoughts are constantly filled with you. . . as day breaks, at midday, and during the evening light. My affection for you remains whether you are smiling or lamenting . . . even if your expression appears contemptuous. I have never observed a vexed look on your face, although Anthony Tulk claims that is your perpetual expression, yet I am not surprised you appear vexed toward him because he merits it. My love for you persists in all attire . . . with every additional gown, you appear even more delightful than before.

“‘My most beloved instructor, I wish you a good night. Nightfall has arrived and the stars have begun to gleam . . . stars possessing a brilliance and beauty matching your own eyes. I press my lips to your hands and your face, my darling. May the Almighty guard you and shield you against every danger.
“‘Your afecksionate pupil, “‘Annetta Bell.’”

“I was quite perplexed by this remarkable letter. That Annetta was no more capable of writing it than she was of flying was something I knew. The following day at school, I escorted her to the brook during recess and requested that she share the truth concerning the letter with me. Crying, Annetta readily confessed. She stated that she had not written a letter before, possessed no knowledge of how to do so or what to express, but her mother’s top bureau drawer contained a package of love letters that an old ‘beau’ had sent to her mother.

“‘Father wasn’t the one,’ wept Annetta, ‘a person studying to be a minister was, which meant his letters were written beautifully, yet ma ended up not marrying him. Half the time, she said she had no idea what he meant. However, I found those letters sweet, so I decided to merely transcribe parts of them now and then for my letters to you. Where he had written “lady,” I inserted “teacher,” and whenever an idea came to me, I added my own thoughts, along with changing a few words. Instead of “mood,” I wrote “dress.” What a “mood” actually was eluded me, though I assumed it was an article of clothing. It never occurred to me that you would spot the difference. How you discovered it was not entirely my own work baffles me. Teacher, you have to be extremely clever.’
“I expressed to Annetta that copying someone else’s letter to pretend it was hers was extremely improper. However, I fear that the only thing Annetta regretted was getting caught.”
“‘And I really love you, teacher,’ she cried. ‘Even though the minister wrote it beforehand, it was all true. I love you with my entire heart.’
“Chastising someone effectively becomes extremely hard when you are in a situation like this.
“Barbara Shaw’s letter is right here. The original’s inkblots cannot be reproduced by me.
”‘Beloved instructor,

“‘You mentioned that we could write concerning a visit. I have only ever visited one time. It occurred at my Aunt Mary’s during the previous winter. My Aunt Mary is an extremely particular woman as well as a great housekeeper. On the initial night of my stay, we were having tea. I tipped over a jug and it broke. Aunt Mary stated that she had possessed that jug continuously since her marriage and no one had ever broken it previously. Upon getting up, I trod on her dress and every gather tore away from the skirt. On the following morning, as I rose from bed, I struck the pitcher against the basin, cracking the pair of them, and I spilled a cup of tea onto the tablecloth during breakfast. While I was assisting Aunt Mary with the dishes from dinner, I dropped a china plate and it shattered. That same evening, I tumbled down the stairs and sprained my ankle, forcing me to remain in bed for a week. I overheard Aunt Mary telling Uncle Joseph that it was a blessing, otherwise I would have destroyed every single thing inside the house. By the time I recovered, it was time for me to return home. I do not enjoy visiting very much. I prefer going to school, particularly after I arrived at Brierley.
“‘Respectfully yours, “‘Barbara Shaw.’”
“Willie White’s started,
“‘Respected Miss,

“‘My desire is to inform you regarding my Very Brave Aunt. Ontario is where she resides, and on a particular day, she stepped outside to the barn, noticing a dog present in the yard. Because the dog ought not to have been there, she retrieved a stick, struck him forcefully, forced him inside the barn, and locked him in. Shortly afterward, an individual arrived searching for an inaginary lion’ (Query;—Was Willie referring to a menagerie lion?) ‘which had escaped from a circus. As it transpired, the dog was actually a lion, and my Very Brave Aunt had druv him inside the barn utilizing a stick. That she was not et up was a marvel, yet she possessed great bravery. Emerson Pettigrew claims that provided she believed it was a dog, her bravery was no greater than if it truly were a dog. Emerson, however, feels envy on account of not possessing a Brave Aunt of his own, having merely uncles.’

“‘The finest part has been saved by me for the end. You make fun of me because I believe Cedric to be a genius, yet I am confident his letter will persuade you that he is an exceptionally unusual child. Far down close to the beach, Cedric resides alongside his grandmother, and he lacks companions . . . no true companions. You recall that our professor of School Management informed us that we must refrain from having ‘favorites’ amongst our students, yet I am unable to prevent myself from loving Cedric Stanhope more than any of my others. However, I do not believe it causes any injury, since Cedric is loved by everyone, even Mrs. Sowerby, who claims she never would have thought she could become so attached to a Yankee. He is also liked by the other schoolboys. Nothing about him is weak or girlish, his dreams and fancies notwithstanding. He possesses great manliness and is capable of maintaining his position in every game. Not long ago, he engaged in a fight with St. Clair Trask on account of St. Clair asserting that the Union Jack was far superior to the Stars and Stripes as a flag. An undecided contest and a shared pact to honor one another’s patriotism from that point onward were the outcome. St. Clair remarks that the heaviest blows can be struck by him, but the most frequent ones can be landed by Cedric.’”
“Cedric’s Letter.
“‘My beloved educator,

“‘You informed us that we could send you letters regarding intriguing individuals in our acquaintance. In my opinion, the most fascinating individuals I am acquainted with are my rock people, and I intend to inform you regarding them. Other than grandma and father, I have not ever informed anyone else about them, but I desire to let you know about them since you comprehend things. A large number of people exist who fail to comprehend things, which makes it pointless to inform them.’

“‘By the water's edge reside my stone companions. Prior to winter's arrival, I was accustomed to visiting them nearly every nightfall. At present, I must wait until spring to go, yet they shall remain, because individuals of that nature do not ever alter . . . their unchanging nature is what makes them so wonderful. Nora was the earliest one among them I became friends with, which makes me feel I adore her most of all. Her home is in Pullen’ Cove, and black is the color of her hair and eyes, and she possesses complete knowledge regarding mermaids and water kelpies. She is capable of telling tales you really should listen to. Furthermore, the Twin Sailors exist as well. They lack a fixed residence because they are perpetually at sea, yet they frequently land to converse with me. They represent a couple of merry mariners who have witnessed all things within the world. . . and things beyond what exists in the world. Are you aware of what occurred to the younger Twin Sailor on one occasion? During a voyage, he navigated straight into a moonglade. Teacher, you are aware that a moonglade signifies the path a rising full moon casts across the ocean surface. Now then, the younger Twin Sailor traveled down this moonglade until he arrived directly at the moon itself, where he discovered a small door made of gold set into the moon, which he unlocked before sailing directly inside. Inside the moon he experienced remarkable exploits, but describing them here would render this letter excessively lengthy.’

“‘Furthermore, the cave holds the Golden Lady. A large cavern down by the beach caught my attention one day, so I entered it, discovering the Golden Lady after a bit. Falling all the way to her feet is her golden hair, and her gown shimmers and shines entirely like living gold. Playing all day on a golden harp, she produces music you can catch along the shore whenever you pay close attention, though the majority of folks would assume it was merely the wind passing through the rocks. Nora has never been told about the Golden Lady by me. Fear that it could cause her hurt feelings kept me silent. Talking too much with the Twin Sailors was enough to hurt her feelings.’

“‘My meetings with the Twin Sailors always occurred at the Striped Rocks. A very pleasant disposition belongs to the youngest Twin Sailor, whereas the oldest Twin Sailor is capable of looking terribly ferocious on occasion. Regarding that oldest Twin, I hold my doubts. Should he possess the courage, I think he would become a pirate. Something about him is truly quite enigmatic. Upon one occasion he used a curse word, so I informed him that a second offense would prevent him from coming onto the land to converse with me, since I had given grandmother my word that I would refrain from mingling with anyone who used bad language. You can take my word for it that he was quite frightened, and he stated that he would carry me to the sunset if I agreed to pardon him. Consequently, on the following evening as I sat upon the Striped Rocks, the oldest Twin came navigating across the ocean inside a magical vessel, and I stepped aboard. That vessel possessed a completely pearlescent and iridescent appearance, resembling the interior of mussel shells, while its sail looked like moonlight. Indeed, we navigated straight over to the sunset. Consider that, teacher, I have traveled inside the sunset. What might you imagine it to be? A land consisting entirely of blossoms makes up the sunset. We navigated inside a vast garden, where flowerbeds are formed by the clouds. We navigated inside a vast port, displaying the entire shade of gold, whereupon I walked directly off the vessel onto a large field completely carpeted with buttercups that were as large as roses. My stay there lasted for a very long period. Almost a year seemed to pass, though the Oldest Twin claims it was merely a matter of minutes. As you can tell, duration inside the sunset land lasts considerably longer than it does in this place.’
“‘Your affectionate student, “‘Cedric Stanhope.’
“‘P. S. teacher, naturally this letter is not actually accurate.

The previous evening actually marked the start of it, marked by a fitful, sleepless night of throbbing tooth pain. As Nell got out of bed in the gloomy, biting winter dawn, she was consumed by a sense that existence was dull, weary, and useless.

She was in a far from angelic mood as she went to school. Her face was aching and her cheek had swollen. Because the fire refused to burn, the schoolroom was smoky and cold, and the children were gathered around it in shivering groups. With a tone sharper than any she had used before, Nell sent them to their seats. Anthony Tulk strutted to his with the impertinent swagger he usually had, and she saw him whisper a remark to his seat-mate before looking at her with a grin.

It appeared to Nell that the number of squeaking pencils that morning exceeded anything she had ever experienced; furthermore, as Barbara Shaw approached the desk carrying an arithmetic problem, she stumbled over the coal scuttle with catastrophic consequences. Coal scattered across all areas of the room, her slate shattered into pieces, and upon standing back up, her coal-dust-streaked face caused the boys to burst into loud laughter.
Nell turned away from the class of second readers that she was listening to.

“Honestly, Barbara,” she remarked with coldness, “you should stay in your chair if you are unable to walk without tripping over an object. A young woman of your years acting with such clumsiness is utterly shameful.”

Stumbling back to her desk, poor Barbara saw her tears mix with the coal dust, creating a truly grotesque appearance. Such a tone and manner had never before been used toward her by her cherished, empathetic teacher, leaving Barbara heartbroken. A pang of guilt touched Nell herself, though it merely heightened her inner annoyance, and that particular lesson remains in the memory of the second reader class to this day, alongside the ruthless dose of arithmetic that came after. At the very moment Nell was sharply issuing the sums, St. Clair Trask arrived out of breath.
“St. Clair, you have arrived thirty minutes behind schedule,” Nell informed him with a cold tone. “What caused this?”

“Please, miss, I had to help ma make a pudding for dinner ’cause we’re expecting company and Clarice Almira’s sick,” replied St. Clair, speaking in a completely polite tone that nonetheless amused his classmates immensely.

“Take your seat and work out the six problems on page eighty-four of your arithmetic for punishment,” Nell said. Her tone left St. Clair looking somewhat astonished, yet he proceeded submissively to his desk and pulled out his slate. After that, he surreptitiously handed a tiny package over the aisle to Joe Mott. Spotting him as he did it, Nell arrived at a disastrous assumption regarding the package.

An addition to her meager earnings had recently been sought by old Mrs. Hiram Mott through the baking and vending of “nut cakes.” These confections held a particular appeal for young boys, causing Nell a good deal of difficulty over the preceding few weeks. While traveling to school, the boys were accustomed to spending their extra money at Mrs. Hiram’s shop, carrying the confections to the schoolhouse with them, and, whenever feasible, consuming them and sharing them with their friends throughout the class day. Though Nell had cautioned them that future cakes brought into the schoolhouse would be taken away, St. Clair Trask was nevertheless casually handing over a package of the treats, encased in the blue and white striped paper that Mrs. Hiram employed, directly in front of her.
“Joseph,” Nell said in a low voice, “hand me that package.”

Shaken and embarrassed, Joe complied. That chubby child invariably turned red and stumbled over his words whenever fear struck him. At that instance, no person could have possibly appeared more blameworthy than unfortunate Joe.
“Cast it into the flames,” Nell said.
Joe’s expression became extremely blank.
“M . . . m . . . miss, p . . . p . . . p . . . lease,” he started.
“Follow my instructions, Joseph, and do not speak a word regarding it.”
“B . . . b . . . but m . . . m . . . miss . . . th . . . th . . . those people are . . .” Joe stammered out, completely overwhelmed.
“Joseph, will you do as I command or will you refuse?” inquired Nell.

A boy less daring and confident than Joe Mott would have felt intimidated by her demeanor and the perilous gleam in her eyes. None of her students had previously witnessed this altered version of Nell. Casting a desperate look toward St. Clair, Joe walked over to the stove, pulled open its large, rectangular front door, and tossed the blue and white package inside, moving faster than St. Clair—who had leaped up—could speak. He then leaped backward barely in time.

For a brief time, the frightened inhabitants of Brierley school could not tell if the event was an earthquake or an eruption of a volcano. The harmless-appearing package that Nell had hastily assumed held Mrs. Hiram’s nut cakes actually contained a collection of pinwheels and firecrackers which Warren Mott had requested St. Clair Trask’s father to bring from town the previous day, planning a birthday party for that night. The firecrackers detonated with a booming roar, and the pinwheels, shooting through the doorway, whirled wildly about the space while spluttering and hissing. Nell collapsed onto her seat, pale from shock, and every girl scrambled onto her desk with loud screams. Joe Mott remained frozen like a statue amidst the chaos, while St. Clair, overwhelmed by amusement, swayed back and forth in the aisle. Prillie Rogerson lost consciousness, and Annetta Bell broke into hysterics.

A few minutes passed, though it felt like a lengthy duration, prior to the final pinwheel dying down. Once she regained her composure, Nell rushed to unseal the doors and windows to release the smoke and gas that pervaded the space. Following that, she assisted the girls in transporting the insensible Prillie to the porch, at which point Barbara Shaw, desperate to render aid, dumped a bucket of nearly icy water across Prillie's shoulders and face before anyone had a chance to prevent her.

An entire hour passed before calm returned once more . . . yet it was a stillness that could almost be sensed physically. Everyone understood that the teacher’s mood remained uncleared, despite the outburst. Except for Anthony Tulk, no one ventured to utter a whisper. While solving an arithmetic problem, Ned Clay made his pencil squeak by mistake, met Nell’s gaze, and desired nothing more than for the ground to split apart and consume him. The continent was rushed through by the geography class at a pace that left them reeling. Within an inch of their lives, the grammar class members were parsed and analyzed. When Chester Mott spelled “odoriferous” using a pair of f’s, he was forced to realize that he would never overcome the shame of his error, whether in the present life or the one to follow.

Nell was aware of the absurdity of her actions and that people would jest about the event at numerous tea-tables that evening, yet this awareness merely heightened her fury. Had she been less agitated, she might have laughed the matter off, but such a reaction was currently out of the question; consequently, she paid it no heed with frozen contempt.

Upon Nell’s return to the school following dinner, the pupils were seated as always, each head bowed diligently above a desk with the sole exception of Anthony Tulk’s. From over his book, he stared toward Nell, his dark eyes shimmering with inquisitiveness and derision. Nell yanked the drawer of her desk open to look for chalk, whereupon a energetic mouse jumped from the drawer right beneath her hand, scurried across the desk, and dropped to the floor.
Nell shrieked and leapt backward, as though she had encountered a serpent, while Anthony Tulk burst into open laughter.

After that, a quiet descended . . . an exceedingly eerie, uneasy quiet. Annetta Bell wavered between surrendering to another fit of hysterics or refraining, particularly because she was uncertain about the exact location of the mouse. However, she chose against it. How could anyone derive any solace from hysterics when faced with a teacher whose countenance was so pale and whose eyes burned so intensely?

“Who put that mouse in my desk?” asked Nell. Although she spoke in a rather quiet tone, it sent a tremble along Cedric Stanhope’s backbone. Joe Mott met her gaze and felt guilty from his head down to his feet, yet he babbled out erratically,
“I . . . i . . . isn’t m . . . m . . . my f . . . f . . . fault instructor, i . . . i . . . isn’t m . . . m . . . my f . . . f . . . fault.”
Ignoring the miserable Joseph, Nell directed her gaze toward Anthony Tulk, who returned her look without any shame or embarrassment.
“Anthony, did you do that?”
“Indeed, it was,” Anthony answered in an insolent manner.
Nell removed her long, heavy pointer made of hardwood from her desk.
“Anthony, come here.”

This was by no means the harshest penalty Anthony Tulk had ever experienced. Nell, despite the tempestuous state of her soul right then, was incapable of inflicting cruel punishment on any youngster. Nevertheless, the pointer bit sharp enough that Anthony’s defiance ultimately gave way; he shrank back as tears filled his eyes.

Full of remorse, Nell let go of the pointer and instructed Anthony to return to his place. Ashamed, penitent, and deeply embarrassed, she took her seat at her desk. Now that her swift temper had vanished, she desperately wished she could find comfort through weeping. This was the result of all her bragging . . . she had physically struck a student. Odette was going to gloat so much! Furthermore, Mr. Pettifer was going to laugh heartily! Yet even more painful than those prospects, and the most agonizing realization of all, was that her final opportunity to earn the affection of Anthony Tulk was gone. From this point on, he would never care for her.

Nell, through what has been termed "a Herculaneum effort," held her tears at bay until arriving at her home that evening. At that point, she locked herself inside the east gable room and poured all her shame, remorse, and disappointment into her pillows as she wept . . . weeping for such a duration that Thirza became frightened, entered the room, and demanded to discover the nature of the problem.
“My conscience is bothering me,” weeping, Nell confessed. “Oh, Thirza, today has been an absolute jinx. I feel so embarrassed by my behavior. Anthony Tulk got whipped because I lost my temper.”
“That pleases me,” Thirza declared firmly. “You ought to have taken this action a long time since.”

“Oh, no, no, Thirza. And I fail to understand how I can ever face those children again. It feels as though I have degraded myself completely into the dust. You cannot imagine how irritable and spiteful and terrible I was. The look in Cedric Stanhope’s eyes is something I am unable to forget . . . such surprise and disappointment were on his face. Oh, Thirza, my efforts to remain patient and to gain Anthony’s affection have been so great . . . and now everything has been utterly wasted.”

With an extraordinary gentleness, Thirza ran her rough, labor-calloused hand through the young woman's shiny, disheveled locks. As the weeping of Nell began to subside, she remarked, with a softness unusual for her,

“Nell, you interpret matters far too deeply. Errors are committed by everyone . . . yet folks dismiss them from memory. Furthermore, periods of bad luck happen to each person. Regarding Anthony Tulk, what reason is there for you to mind if he holds a grudge against you? No one else feels that way.”

“It is beyond my control. My desire is for everyone to hold me dear, so whenever someone fails to, it causes me great pain. Now, Anthony certainly never will. Oh, today I simply acted like a fool, Thirza. Every detail will be revealed to you.”
Thirza paid attention to the entire narrative, without Nell ever knowing whether she smiled at particular moments. Once the story had been concluded, she remarked in a brisk tone,

“Oh, don't worry about it. Today is finished, and a fresh day arrives tomorrow that contains no errors as of yet, just as you were accustomed to saying. Simply step down to the lower floor and eat your evening meal. You will discover whether or not a warm mug of tea along with the plum puffs that I baked today will raise your spirits.”
“Plum puffs won’t minister to a mind diseased,” Nell remarked mournfully; Thirza, however, viewed it as a positive indication that her recovery allowed her to modify a quote.

The lively dinner table, featuring the radiant expressions of the twins, along with the peerless plum puffs made by Thirza . . . four of which were consumed by Robin . . . managed to “hearten her up” quite a bit despite everything. Having slept well during the night, she woke up when morning arrived to discover that both she and her surroundings were completely changed. Throughout the dark hours, snow had fallen quietly and heavily, and the lovely white blanket, sparkling under the cold sunlight, appeared to be a cloak of forgiveness draped over every error and embarrassment of yesterday.
“Each morning brings a new start, Each morning the world is created anew,”
“sang Nell, as she dressed.”

Because of the snow, she was forced to take the long way by the road to get to school, and she considered it a truly mischievous twist of fate that Anthony Tulk happened to come trudging past right at the moment she emerged from the Grey Shutters lane. She experienced as much guilt as though they had swapped places; nevertheless, to her immense surprise, Anthony did not merely raise his cap . . . an action he had failed to perform ever before . . . but remarked casually,
“Walking’s a bit rough, isn’t it? Would you like me to carry those books, teacher?”

Nell gave up her volumes and questioned whether she could actually be conscious. Anthony continued walking toward the school without speaking, yet as Nell received her volumes she beamed down at him . . . not the mechanical “kind” beam she had so continuously put on for his sake but an abrupt radiance of genuine fellowship. Anthony beamed . . . no, to be entirely honest, Anthony smirked in return. A smirk is not usually considered to be a polite gesture; nevertheless Nell abruptly sensed that even if she had not yet gained Anthony’s affection she had, one way or another, gained his respect.
This was affirmed by Mrs. Agatha Sowerby when she arrived on the following Saturday.

“Well, Nell, I suppose Anthony Tulk has been won over by you, and that is the truth. He claims he now thinks you have some worth, despite being a girl. He remarks that the beating he received from you was ‘just as good as a man’s.’”

“However, beating him was something I did not anticipate would earn his favor,” Nell remarked with a touch of sadness, sensing that her principles had somehow let her down. “This feels incorrect. My belief in gentle treatment must be correct, I am certain.”
“No, but the Tulks break every established rule, that’s the point,” asserted Mrs. Agatha with certainty.
Upon hearing this, Mr. Pettifer remarked, “Thought you’d come to it,” and Odette emphasized the point in a somewhat pitiless manner.

When Nell was traveling toward Pear Hill, she encountered Isolde, who was going to Grey Shutters, precisely at the place where the brook underneath the Whispering Wood was crossed by the moss-covered ancient log bridge, and the pair took a seat beside the edge of the Nymph’s Well, a spot where small ferns unfolded themselves in the manner of curly-haired green pixy creatures rousing from sleep.
“Saturday is my birthday, and I was coming over right now to ask if you would help me mark the occasion,” said Nell.
“The day you were born? However, in March was when your birthday occurred!”

“That wasn’t my fault,” Nell laughed. “Had my parents consulted me it would never have occurred at that time. Naturally, I should have chosen to be born in spring. Coming into the world alongside the mayflowers and violets must be delightful. One would always feel like their foster sister. Since I didn’t, however, celebrating my birthday in the spring is the next best thing. Saturday, Honora is coming over and Odette will be at home. All four of us will head off to the woods and spend a golden day getting acquainted with the spring. None of us really knows her yet, but back there we’ll meet her in a way we never can anywhere else. Anyhow, I want to explore all those fields and lonely places. I hold a conviction that scores of beautiful nooks exist there that have never truly been seen, even if they may have been looked at. We’ll form friendships with wind and sky and sun, and bring the spring home inside our hearts.”
“It seems terribly pleasant,” Isolde remarked, harboring a degree of secret skepticism regarding Nell’s verbal wizardry. “However, will it not still be extremely wet in certain spots?”

“Oh, we can put on rubbers,” Nell conceded regarding practical matters. “And I need you to arrive early on Saturday morning so you can assist me in making lunch. My plan is to serve the most delicate items I can think of . . . foods that fit the spring season, if you catch my drift . . . small tarts filled with jelly and ladyfingers, alongside drop cookies covered in yellow and pink frosting, as well as buttercup cake. We also need to include sandwiches, even if they lack a certain poetry.”

Saturday turned out to be a perfect day for a picnic . . . a day filled with breeze and blue, warm, sunny, alongside a tiny playful wind sweeping over meadow and orchard. Across each sun-drenched upland and field lay a fragile, flower-starred green.

As he harrowed at the rear of his farm, Mr. Pettifer, who felt a portion of the spring magic despite his sober, middle-aged blood, observed four girls carrying baskets as they lightly stepped over the edge of his field, right where it met a border of fir and birch woods. The sound of their merry laughter and voices reached him from a distance.

“Isn’t it simple to feel joy when a day is like this?” Nell declared, possessing genuine Anneish philosophy. “Girls, let us attempt to turn this day into an exceptionally golden one, an occasion we are forever able to remember with pleasure. We must search for beauty and reject noticing all other things. ‘Begone, dull care!’ Odette, your mind is on a mishap from school yesterday.”
“By what means are you aware?” Odette breathed, filled with wonder.

“Ah, I am familiar with that look . . . my own face has worn it frequently. However, do not dwell on it, sweetheart. It can wait until Monday . . . and if it fails to last that long, all the more preferable. Ah, girls, girls, look at that cluster of violets! It is a treasure for the mind’s art collection. At eighty years of age . . . should I reach that point . . . closing my eyes will allow me to view those violets precisely as they appear to me at this moment. Our day has bestowed its initial wonderful present upon us through them.”
“I believe that if it were possible to see a kiss, its appearance would resemble a violet,” Honora said.
Nell beamed.

“It brings me great joy that you voiced that idea, Honora, rather than merely contemplating it in silence. Life would be vastly more fascinating . . . even though it remains deeply fascinating as it is . . . if individuals openly declared their genuine opinions.”
“Certain people would find it far too scorching to maintain a grip,” wisely repeated Odette.

“I guess that could be true, though they would only have themselves to blame for having unpleasant thoughts. Regardless, we are free to share every single thought today since our minds will hold only lovely ones. Everyone is allowed to speak whatever enters her mind. Conversation is simply that. I have not noticed this small trail until now. Let us go see where it leads.”

The trail meandered, its width so constrained that the young women moved one behind the other, and still the fir branches scraped against their faces. Soft, plush cushions of moss rested beneath the firs, and deeper along the way, in places where the trees grew smaller and sparser, the soil abounded with a diverse assortment of lush green vegetation.
“What an abundance of elephant’s ears,” cried Isolde. “They are so lovely that I shall gather a large bouquet.”
“In what way did such elegant downy creations manage to acquire such a terrible title?” inquired Honora.
“Since the individual who originally gave them a name lacked any imagination or possessed way too much,” Nell remarked, “Oh, girls, check that out!”

“That” referred to a slight forest pond situated in the middle of a tiny grassy clearing where the track terminated. Further along in the season, it would be parched and its location occupied by a luxuriant patch of ferns; however, at present it was a shining quiet expanse, circular like a saucer and transparent as crystal. A circle of thin juvenile birches surrounded it, and small ferns bordered its edge.
“How sweet!” Odette said.
“Let us dance around it like wood-nymphs,” Nell exclaimed, setting down her basket and reaching out her hands.
However, the dance failed to be successful because the earth was marshy and the rubbers belonging to Odette detached.
“If you must wear rubbers, you are unable to be a wood-nymph,” she decided.

“Indeed, a name must be given to this spot prior to our departure,” stated Nell, giving in to the unassailable truth of the situation. “Let each person offer a title, after which we will select one by chance. Isolde?”
“Birch Pool,” Isolde offered without hesitation.
“Crystal Lake,” Odette said.

Positioned in their rear, Nell silently begged Honora through her gaze against committing an additional name like that, causing Honora to handle the situation by offering “Glimmer-glass.” The choice made by Nell was “The Fairies’ Mirror.”

Using a pencil that Schoolma’am Odette took from her pocket, the names were inscribed on pieces of birch bark and deposited inside Nell’s hat. After that, Honora closed her eyes and pulled one out. “Crystal Lake,” announced Odette victoriously. Crystal Lake became the chosen place, and even if Nell believed that fate had dealt the group a poor hand, she kept her thoughts to herself.

Passing through the thicket past that point, the girls stepped into the fresh green privacy of Mr. Silas Mott’s rear field. Traversing it, they discovered the start of a path heading up into the forest and decided to investigate it too. Their exploration paid off with a series of lovely delights. To begin with, running along the edge of Mr. Mott’s field, there appeared a canopy of flowering wild cherry trees. The girls carried their hats by the straps on their arms and decorated their hair using the soft, pale flowers. Next, the path made a square turn and went deep into a forest of spruces that was so dense and dim that they proceeded through a dusk-like darkness, unable to catch even a patch of sky or ray of sun.

“The wicked wood elves live in this place,” Nell murmured softly. “Although they are full of mischief and spite, they are unable to hurt us, since doing evil is forbidden to them during springtime. A single one was spying on us from behind that gnarled ancient fir; furthermore, didn’t you spot a cluster of them atop that large spotted toadstool we recently went by? The sunny spots are where the good fairies constantly reside.”

“I wish fairies actually existed,” Odette remarked. “Would it not be lovely if a person could have three wishes fulfilled . . . or perhaps just one? What wish would you make, girls, if a wish were granted to you? My wish would be for wealth, beauty, and intelligence.”
“I would desire to be slender and tall,” Isolde declared.
“It would be my desire to achieve fame,” Honora expressed. Nell’s mind turned to her companion's hair, though she quickly rejected the notion, considering it unworthy.
“I wish that it could be spring perpetually, within everyone’s heart and throughout all of our lives,” she remarked.
“However, that,” remarked Honora, “would simply be hoping for this world to resemble heaven.”

“Merely as one section of paradise. Summer and autumn would exist in the remaining areas . . . indeed, and a small amount of winter as well. Occasionally, I believe I desire sparkling snow-covered meadows and pale frosts in paradise. Wouldn't you agree, Odette?”

“I . . . I don’t know,” Odette uttered in distress. A decent young woman and a churchgoer, Odette made a diligent effort to abide by her beliefs, accepting without question all the instruction she had received. Nevertheless, she avoided contemplating heaven as much as possible.
“Posy Fay inquired of me recently whether our finest gowns would be worn daily when we are in heaven,” Isolde said with a laugh.
“And weren’t you the one who told her that we would?” inquired Nell.
“Gracious, no! I informed her that we would not be giving any thought to dresses in that place.”

“Oh, I feel that we are going to . . . somewhat,” Nell stated with earnestness. “All eternity will afford us abundant time to do so while still attending to more crucial matters. It is my belief that every one of us will dress in gorgeous gowns . . . or perhaps raiment is a preferable term to use. During the initial few centuries, my desire will be to don pink . . . since I am certain it would require that much time for me to grow weary of it. I am so fond of pink, yet wearing it in this world is never possible for me.”

Beyond the spruces, the lane sloped downward to a bright, small clearing where a brook was crossed by a log bridge; after that appeared the magnificence of a sun-drenched beechwood whose air resembled clear golden wine, with leaves that were green and fresh, and a forest ground that formed a mosaic of flickering sunlight. Next were additional wild cherries, followed by a small valley containing flexible firs, and then a hill of such steepness that the girls became winded while ascending it; yet upon reaching its summit and stepping into the clear, they were met by the most charming surprise of everything.

Further on lay the "back fields" belonging to the farms which extended to the upper Delford road. Immediately preceding them, enclosed by firs and beeches yet facing south, a small corner existed, containing a garden . . . or what used to be one. An dilapidated dyke made of stone, smothered in grass and mosses, encircled it. A line of garden cherry trees, as white as a snowdrift, stretched along the eastern side. Marks of former paths remained visible alongside a double row of rosebushes down the center; however, the remainder of the area formed a expanse of white and yellow narcissi, flowering in their lightest, most abundant, breeze-blown state over the rich green grasses.
“Oh, how perfectly lovely!” exclaimed three of the girls. Nell merely looked on, her quietness speaking volumes.
“How on earth did a garden ever come to exist behind this place?” Honora asked, astonished.

“That has to be Dinah Wren’s garden,” Isolde said. “Mother has talked about it in my hearing, though it is my first time seeing it, and I wouldn’t have thought it was able to still exist. Have you heard the tale, Nell?”
“No, though that name sounds acquainted to me.”

“Ah, you have noticed it in the cemetery. Her grave is situated down in the corner by the poplars. You are familiar with that small brown monument featuring the sculpted opening gates and ‘Sacred to the memory of Dinah Wren, aged twenty-two.’ Beside her lies Jordan Wren, though he lacks a marker. I am surprised Thirza didn't mention it to you, Nell. Of course, thirty years have passed since it occurred, and it has slipped everyone's mind.”

“Well, if a story exists, we need to hear it,” Nell said. “We should sit down immediately in this spot surrounded by the narcissi so Isolde can relate it. Why, girls, hundreds of them are present . . . they have covered the entire area. The garden appears to be carpeted by a mixture of moonshine and sunshine. Making this discovery is truly worthwhile. Just consider that I have resided less than a mile away from this location throughout six years without ever laying eyes on it previously! Now, Isolde.”

“In the past,” Isolde started, “this property was owned by former Mr. David Gray. He resided elsewhere . . . at the location where Silas Mott resides today. A single son was born to him, named Jordan, who traveled to Boston during a particular winter for employment, and during his stay he became enamored with a woman called Dinah Murray. She was employed in a shop, an occupation she despised. Her childhood had been spent in the countryside, and her constant desire was to return there. Upon Jordan requesting her hand in marriage, her condition for agreeing was that he transport her to a peaceful location surrounded solely by fields and trees. Consequently, he conducted her to Brierley. Mrs. Sowerby remarked that his marriage to a Yankee constituted a terrible gamble, and undoubtedly Dinah possessed frail health and lacked housekeeping skills; nevertheless, my mother states she was extremely attractive and charming, and Jordan adored her completely. Eventually, Mr. Gray granted this farm to Jordan, who constructed a small dwelling back here where he and Dinah resided for a four-year period. She rarely ventured forth, and almost no individuals visited her apart from mother and Mrs. Sowerby. Jordan crafted this garden for her, which she adored passionately, occupying the majority of her time within it. Her domestic management was lacking, yet she possessed a talent for plants. Following this, illness struck her. Mother believes that consumption afflicted her prior to her arrival here. She was never fully bedridden, but continuously lost strength. Jordan refused to allow anyone else to attend to her. He performed every task personally, and mother indicates he showed tenderness and gentleness equal to a woman's. On a daily basis, he would enclose her in a shawl, convey her outdoors into the garden, and she would rest on a bench in full contentment. It is reported that she compelled Jordan to bow beside her each evening and dawn to join her in prayer, requesting that her eventual passing occur outside in the garden. This plea was granted. On a certain day, Jordan bore her out to the bench, gathered every blooming rose, and piled them upon her; she merely beamed up toward him . . . shut her eyes . . . and that,” Isolde quietly ended, “marked the finish.”
“Oh, that tale is so precious,” Nell murmured, dabbing her eyes to dry them.
“What happened to Jordan?” Honora inquired.

“Following the death of Dinah, he parted with the farm and returned to Boston. Mr. Jabez Mott purchased the property and relocated the small house to the roadside. Around a decade later, Jordan passed away, and his remains were returned to be interred next to Dinah.”
“I cannot comprehend how she might have desired to reside in this backwater, isolated from the rest of the world,” Odette remarked.

“Oh, I can easily comprehend that,” Nell remarked thoughtfully. “I wouldn’t desire it myself for a permanent arrangement, because, even though I love the woods and fields, I love people as well. However, I can comprehend it in Dinah. She was completely exhausted by the noise of the large city and the masses of individuals constantly arriving and departing and not caring at all about her. She merely wished to flee from everything to a quiet, green, welcoming place where she could find rest. And she received precisely what she desired, which is an achievement very few individuals accomplish, I think. She enjoyed four lovely years prior to her death. . . four years of complete joy, so I believe she should be envied rather than pitied. And then closing your eyes and drifting off to sleep amid roses, while the person you cherished most in the world smiles down upon you . . . oh, I believe it was lovely!”

“Over there, those cherry trees were planted by her,” Isolde remarked. “She mentioned to mother that eating their fruit was something she would not survive to do, yet her desire was to believe that a thing she planted would remain alive and assist in rendering the world lovely once she had passed away.”

“I am very happy that we took this route,” stated Nell, whose eyes were shining. “You are aware that today is the anniversary of my adoption, and the gift it bestowed upon me for my birthday is this garden along with its history. Isolde, did your mother ever describe the appearance of Dinah Wren to you?”
“No . . . merely that she possessed beauty.”

“I am quite pleased about that, since it allows me to picture her appearance without the limitation of reality. It is my belief that she was extremely slender and tiny, possessing gently wavy dark hair alongside large, gentle, shy brown eyes, as well as a small, pensive, fair face.”

The girls deposited their baskets in the garden of Dinah and passed the remainder of the afternoon wandering through the woods and fields encircling it, finding numerous pretty nooks and lanes. As hunger overtook them, they ate lunch in the most delightful spot of all . . . upon the precipitous bank of a murmuring brook where white birches rose from tall, feathery grasses. Sitting down among the roots, the girls did complete justice to the dainties of Nell, with even the unpoetical sandwiches being thoroughly enjoyed by robust, unspoiled appetites heightened by the abundance of fresh air and exercise they had experienced. Nell had supplied glasses and lemonade for her guests, though for her own share she consumed cold brook water out of a cup crafted from birch bark. The cup seeped, and the water possessed a flavor of earth, as brook water frequently does during spring; nevertheless, Nell considered it far more suited to the occasion than lemonade.
“Listen, do you observe that poem?” she asked unexpectedly, gesturing.
“In what place?” Odette and Isolde gazed intently, seeming to anticipate Runic inscriptions appearing upon the birch bark.

“Over there . . . lower in the stream . . . that ancient green, moss-covered log with the current streaming over it in those even ripples that seem like they’ve been brushed, and that one beam of sunlight dropping straight across it, deep down into the water. Oh, it’s the loveliest poem I’ve ever seen.”
“I would describe it more as a picture,” Odette remarked. “Lines and verses make up a poem.”

“Indeed, I am not of that opinion.” Nell gave a firm negative nod of her head, which was crowned with a soft, untamed wreath of wild cherry. “A poem's outward clothing consists merely of its verses and lines, which are no truer representation of it than your own flounces and ruffles are of you, Odette. Within them lies the soul, which is the genuine poem . . . and that lovely fragment constitutes the soul of a poem yet to be composed. One does not behold a soul every day . . . even if it belongs to a poem.”
“I muse upon the appearance of a soul . . . an individual's soul . . .,” Honora remarked in a dreamy manner.

“I would imagine it is similar to that,” Nell replied, indicating a beam of filtered sun rays pouring past a birch tree. “Naturally, it would possess a form and facial details as well. It pleases me to imagine that light forms our souls. Certain ones are completely penetrated by pinkish streaks and flickers . . . while others possess a gentle shimmer, similar to moonbeams upon the ocean . . . and others are faint and see-through, resembling morning fog.”
“I recall reading at some point that souls resembled flowers,” Honora remarked.
“In that case, your soul is a golden narcissus,” Nell said, “while Isolde’s resembles a red, red rose. The soul of Odette is an apple blossom, wholesome and sweet and pink.”
“And yours is a white violet, which has purple streaks at its center,” Honora concluded.
Odette murmured to Isolde that she truly was unable to grasp the subject of their conversation, asking if she could.

Under the glow of a serene, golden sunset, the girls walked home, carrying baskets packed with narcissus flowers from the garden of Dinah, portion of which were taken by Nell to the cemetery the following day and placed on the grave of Dinah. Musical robins whistled within the fir trees while frogs sang throughout the marshes. Topaz and emerald light filled every basin nestled amidst the hills.
“Well, we have enjoyed ourselves tremendously, despite everything,” Isolde remarked, in a manner suggesting she had scarcely anticipated doing so upon her departure.
“A truly golden day it has been,” Honora said.
“I have a truly dreadful fondness for the woods, personally,” Odette remarked.
Nell remained silent. Looking off toward the western sky, she was remembering little Dinah Wren.
Mrs. Sowerby, burdened as always with every concern of church and state, caught up with Nell as she walked back from the post office on a Friday evening.

“I’ve just visited Timothy Cotton’s place to find out if Alice Louise could assist me for a couple of days,” she stated. “I employed her last week, because, even if she moves too sluggishly to halt suddenly, she is preferable to no one. However, she is ill and unable to attend. Timothy is also seated there, coughing and voicing grievances. For ten years he has been in the process of dying, and for another ten years he will continue dying. That sort cannot even perish and complete the matter . . . they are incapable of adhering to anything, including illness, for a sufficient duration to conclude it. They are a dreadfully irresponsible family and I am unaware of what will happen to them, though maybe Providence knows.”
Mrs. Sowerby uttered a sigh, seemingly somewhat skeptical about how much Providence actually knew regarding the matter.
“On Tuesday, Thirza went in concerning her eyes once more, didn't she? How did the specialist assess them?” she went on.

“He was very happy,” Nell remarked cheerfully. “He mentions that they have improved significantly and he believes she is no longer at risk of going entirely blind. However, he notes that she will not ever be capable of reading extensively or performing detailed needlework in the future. In what manner are the arrangements for your bazaar progressing?”
Arrangements for a supper and fair were being made by the Ladies’ Aid Society, with Mrs. Sowerby acting as the leader and driving force behind the project.

“Fairly good . . . which brings something to mind. Mrs. Wace believes it would be lovely to arrange a booth resembling a kitchen from former days and offer a meal consisting of baked beans, doughnuts, pie, and similar items. Old-style decorations are being gathered by us from all over. The braided rugs belonging to her mother will be lent to us by Mrs. Simon Fletcher, a few aged chairs by Mrs. Levi Gammon, and her cupboard featuring glass doors will be lent to us by Aunt Mary Shaw. Thirza will allow us to use her brass candlesticks, I imagine? Furthermore, every piece of old tableware we can obtain is desired by us. Having an authentic blue willow ware platter is something Mrs. Wace particularly insists upon if one can be located by us. Yet one does not appear to be owned by anyone. Are you aware of a place where one might be acquired by us?”
“Miss Lavinia Pembroke possesses one, so I will draft a letter inquiring whether she would be willing to lend it for the event,” Nell remarked.

“Indeed, my hope is that you will. My expectation is that the supper will occur in approximately two weeks. Predictions of rain and tempests around that period are being made by Uncle Zeb Pullen; consequently, fair weather is almost certainly guaranteed for us.”

It could be noted that the aforementioned “Uncle Zeb” resembled other prophets in one respect, as he received little respect among his own people. Indeed, he was regarded as a perpetual laughingstock because his forecasts concerning the weather were rarely accurate. It was the custom of Mr. Elisha Duckett, a man who possessed the mistaken belief that he was a town humorist, to remark that no resident of Brierley ever considered checking the Port Marlow daily papers to learn the weather forecasts. Instead, they simply inquired of Uncle Zeb what conditions to anticipate the next day and anticipated the exact reverse. Undeterred by this, Uncle Zeb continued to issue his predictions.

“We desire to finish the fair prior to the election occurring,” Mrs. Sowerby added, “because the candidates are bound to attend and lavish a great deal of money. The Tories are distributing bribes everywhere, meaning they should be afforded an opportunity to expend their funds honorably for a change.”

Out of faithfulness to the memory of Obed, Nell held fiery Conservative views, yet she remained silent. Getting Mrs. Sowerby onto the topic of politics was something she knew to avoid. From a municipality in British Columbia, she possessed a letter addressed to Thirza, bearing a postmark.
“It likely comes from the uncle of the children,” she declared with excitement upon reaching home. “Oh, Thirza, I am curious about what he writes concerning them.”

“Opening it to look inside could be the finest idea,” Thirza stated abruptly. An attentive spectator might have suspected that she too felt excitement, yet she preferred death over displaying such emotion.
Nell ripped the envelope open and scanned the slightly messy and badly penned text inside.

“He states that taking the children this spring is impossible for him . . . he has been ill for the majority of the winter and his wedding has been postponed. He asks whether we are able to hold onto them until the autumn, at which point he will attempt to take them. We shall, naturally, will we not Thirza?”

“I fail to see any other option open to us,” Thirza remarked with a somewhat stern expression, even as a hidden sense of ease came over her. “In any case, they do not cause as much difficulty as before . . . or perhaps we have simply grown accustomed to them. Robin’s behavior is much better than it was.”
“His behavior has undoubtedly improved,” Nell remarked guardedly, as though she hesitated to offer a similar endorsement regarding his character.

When Nell arrived home from school the evening before, she discovered that Thirza was out attending an Aid meeting, Lucy was sleeping on the sofa in the kitchen, and Robin was inside the sitting room closet, happily consuming what was in a jar of Thirza’s well-known yellow plum preserves . . . “company jam,” as Robin termed it . . . which he was prohibited from touching. A very guilty expression crossed his face as Nell swooped down on him and pulled him quickly from the closet.
“Robin Farrow, do you not realize how terribly wrong it is for you to be consuming that jam, given that you received instructions to never tamper with a single item inside that closet?”

“Indeed, I was aware that it wasn't right,” Robin acknowledged with discomfort, “nevertheless, plum jam tastes terribly good, Nell. My intention was merely to look inside, and its appearance was so inviting that I decided to have only a tiny sample. I dipped my finger inside . . .” Nell uttered a groan . . . “and licked every bit off. Because the taste surpassed my wildest expectations, I grabbed a spoon and simply went to town.”
Nell delivered a sermon so grave regarding the wickedness of taking plum jam that Robin was filled with remorse and swore through penitent kisses that he would not repeat the act.
“At least there is going to be an abundance of preserve in paradise, which provides some consolation,” he remarked contentedly.
Nell suppressed a smile before it could form.
“Maybe there will be . . . should we desire it,” she remarked, “However, why do you believe that?”
“Why, the catechism contains it,” Robin said.
“Oh, no, the catechism contains nothing of that sort, Robin.”

“But I tell you there is,” Robin insisted. “That question Thirza taught me last Sunday had it. ‘Why should we love God?’ The answer is, ‘Because He makes preserves, and redeems us.’ Jam is just called preserves in a holy way.”

“I must get a drink of water,” said Nell hastily. Returning later, she spent considerable effort and time making Robin understand that the meaning of the mentioned catechism question was altered significantly by a particular comma.

“Well, I figured it was just too good to be real,” he finally uttered, giving a sigh filled with let-down certainty. “And what’s more, I couldn’t figure out when He’d get around to making jam if it’s an uninterrupted Sabbath day, like it says in the hymn. I doubt I even desire to go to heaven. Will there never be a single Saturday in heaven, Nell?”

“Yes, Saturdays, and all manner of other lovely days. Furthermore, Robin, each day in heaven will surpass the previous one in beauty,” Nell comforted him, feeling somewhat relieved that Thirza was absent and thus spared from being scandalized. It goes without saying that Thirza was rearing the twins according to traditional religious doctrines and forbade any imaginative theorizing about such matters. Every Sunday, Robin and Lucy were instructed to memorize two verses from the Bible, a catechism query, and a hymn. Lucy absorbed her lessons submissively and repeated them like a small automaton, possessing about the same degree of comprehension or engagement as if she actually were a device. Robin, by contrast, possessed an active inquisitiveness, regularly posing queries that caused Thirza to shudder regarding his ultimate destiny.

“Chester Mott says our sole activity in heaven will be strolling about in white dresses while playing harps; additionally, he expresses a wish to delay going there until he reaches old age, thinking he might find it more appealing at that time. He also believes wearing dresses will be awful, a sentiment I share. What reason prevents male angels from wearing trousers, Nell? Chester Mott pays attention to such matters because he is destined to become a minister. Becoming a minister is mandatory for him since his grandmother bequeathed funds for his college education on the strict condition that he enters the ministry. In her view, having a minister in the family was extremely ‘spectable. Chester remarks that he isn't overly bothered . . . even though he would prefer being a blacksmith . . . yet he is determined to enjoy himself as much as possible prior to entering the ministry, as he anticipates very little enjoyment later. Being a minister is not my plan. My intention is to become a shopkeeper, similar to Mr. Blair, and stock huge quantities of candy and bananas. However, I would quite enjoy attending your version of heaven if I were permitted to play a mouth organ rather than a harp. Do you think they would allow it?”
“Indeed, I believe they’d do so if that were your desire,” was the sole response Nell felt able to utter.

That night, the B.V.I.S. convened at the home of Mr. Gorham Pullen, every member having been urged to come because there was significant business to deliberate upon. The B.V.I.S. was thriving, having achieved remarkable results already. When the spring was young, Mr. Major Tranter had fulfilled his pledge by clearing the stumps, leveling the ground, and sowing grass seed along his entire farm frontage. Inspired either by a resolve not to be outdone by a Tranter or driven to act by Improvers within their own families, twelve other men had duplicated his efforts. Consequently, expansive stretches of fine, soft grass now occupied the places where ugly bushes or thickets had previously grown. In comparison, the untouched farm fronts appeared so terrible that those who owned them were quietly embarrassed into deciding to try their hand at improvements the following spring. Furthermore, the triangular patch of land where the roads intersected had been cleared of debris and sown with grass, and the geranium bed planted by Nell, remaining untouched by any roaming cow, had already been positioned right in the middle.

On the whole, those in the Improvement Society believed their progress was splendid, despite Mr. Levi Gammon, who was discreetly petitioned by a chosen delegation concerning the ancient dwelling on his higher property, flatly informing them that he would not permit them to tamper with it.

During this particular gathering, they planned to draft a petition to the school trustees, respectfully requesting the erection of a fence around the schoolyard; moreover, they were to deliberate a proposal for setting out several decorative trees near the church, provided the society’s money would allow for it . . . because, as Nell remarked, beginning a new subscription was pointless while the hall stayed blue. The members had gathered in the Pullens’ parlor, and Odette was already standing to propose that a committee be named to ascertain and report back regarding the cost of the aforementioned trees, when Tibby Tulk burst in, outfitted in a pompadour and frills to the absolute limit. Tibby was accustomed to arriving late . . . “in order to render her arrival more striking,” malicious individuals claimed. Tibby’s arrival on this occasion was undeniably striking, as she stopped theatricality in the center of the room, raised her hands, rolled her eyes, and cried out, “I’ve just heard something perfectly awful. What do you think? Mr. Judson Tibbs is going to rent all the road fence of his farm to a patent medicine company to paint advertisements on.”
For a single moment in her existence, Tibby Tulk produced the exact stir she wished for. Had she hurled an explosive amidst the self-satisfied Improvers, her impact could scarcely have been greater.
“That is impossible,” Nell uttered expressionlessly.

“When I first heard it, that’s precisely what I uttered, don’t you know,” remarked Tibby, who was deriving immense enjoyment from herself. “I expressed that it wasn't possible for it to be true . . . that Judson Tibbs lacked the heart for such an act, don’t you know. However, father encountered him this afternoon, inquiring about the matter, and he confirmed it WAS true. Imagine that! The Stonebridge road runs side-on to his farm, and viewing advertisements for pills and plasters stretched all along it will appear so completely dreadful, don’t you know?”

The Improvers were indeed fully aware. The most uninspired person in the group was able to visualize the bizarre appearance of a half-mile wooden fence covered in those notices. Any consideration regarding the grounds of the church and school disappeared in the face of this sudden threat. Rules of order and guidelines were discarded, and Nell, feeling hopeless, abandoned her attempt to record the minutes altogether. Everyone spoke simultaneously, creating a terrible uproar.
“Oh, we must remain composed,” begged Nell, despite being the one experiencing the greatest agitation among the group, “and attempt to devise a method to stop him.”

“I fail to see how you will stop him,” Odette declared with bitterness. “Judson Tibbs’s reputation is well known to all. For financial gain, he would commit any act. He possesses no public spirit whatsoever, nor does he have any appreciation for beauty.”

The outlook appeared fairly discouraging. Because Judson Tibbs and his sister constituted the sole Parkers residing in Brierley, family ties offered no possibility of influence. Being a woman of indisputably advanced years, Martha Tibbs looked with disfavor upon youth as a whole and the Improvers especially. As for Judson, he was a cheerful, suave individual whose disposition was so consistently pleasant and mild that his scarcity of comrades seemed astonishing. It was possible that he had emerged victorious from an excessive number of commercial dealings. . . a habit that rarely engenders widespread affection. People considered him to be exceedingly “sharp” and held the prevailing view that he “hadn’t much principle.”
“He will always seize an opportunity to ‘turn an honest penny,’ as he puts it,” Gideon Duckett stated regarding Judson Tibbs.
“Does anyone possess any influence with him?” Nell inquired in despair.
“He pays a visit to Louisa Tranter at Pale Sands,” Carrie Mott put forward. “She might be able to persuade him against letting out his fences.”

“Not that woman,” Hugh stated with force. “Louisa Tranter is someone I am well acquainted with. While Village Improvement Societies aren't something she ‘believes’ in, dollars and cents certainly are. It is far more probable that she would push Judson forward instead of talking him out of it.”

“Appointing a delegation to go to him and object is our sole option,” Julia Bell stated, “and sending girls is necessary, as his politeness toward boys is doubtful . . . yet I refuse to go, meaning any nomination for me is pointless.”
“It would be best for Nell to go by herself,” remarked Oliver Mott. “If anyone is capable of persuading Judson, it’s her.”

Nell made an objection. She was ready to travel and handle the speaking, though she insisted that companions accompany her “for moral support.” Consequently, Isolde and Odette were chosen to offer her moral backing, after which the Improvers disbanded, humming with resentment like furious bees. Nell felt so anxious that she failed to fall asleep until close to dawn, whereupon she envisioned in a dream that the trustees had enclosed the school with a fence and inscribed “Try Purple Pills” across its entire surface.

The following afternoon, Judson Tibbs received a visit from the committee. Nell made an eloquent plea opposing his wicked plan, with Odette and Isolde offering her brave, moral backing. Judson remained smooth, polished, and complimentary; offered them a few compliments as delicate as sunflowers; expressed genuine regret at turning down such delightful young women . . . yet business remained business; he was unable to permit sentiment to interfere during these difficult times.

“However, I am going to share what my actions will be,” he stated, his pale, prominent eyes gleaming with a sparkle. “I am going to instruct the agent to employ exclusively attractive, appealing shades . . . yellow and red and similar ones. I am going to instruct him that under no circumstances is he permitted to paint the advertisements blue.”
The defeated committee withdrew, holding thoughts forbidden to be spoken.
“There is nothing more within our power, so we have to place our faith in Providence for whatever remains,” Odette remarked, mirroring Mrs. Sowerby’s expression and delivery without realizing it.
“I wonder whether Mr. Wace might be able to help,” pondered Isolde.
Nell gave a shake of her head.

“No, troubling Mr. Wace is pointless, particularly at this moment with the baby being this ill. Judson would evade him just as effortlessly as he does us, even though he has commenced attending church rather consistently at present. The sole reason for that is that Louisa Tranter’s father holds the position of elder and is extremely strict regarding those matters.”

“Only Judson Tibbs in all of Brierley would ever think to lease out his fences,” Odette declared, filled with indignation. “As stingy as Levi Gammon or Lorenzo White are, even they would not degrade themselves like that. Public opinion would mean too much to them.”

When the details emerged, popular sentiment undoubtedly turned against Judson Tibbs, yet that provided little relief. Judson laughed inwardly and stood his ground, leaving the Improvers attempting to accept the likely sight of commercial signs ruining the most beautiful section of the Stonebridge road, until Nell calmly stood up at the subsequent Society gathering when the leader requested committee updates, declaring that Mr. Judson Tibbs had directed her to tell the Society he would refrain from leasing his fencing to the Patent Medicine Company.

Odette and Isolde gazed as though they could scarcely trust what they were hearing. Although the normally rigorous rules of parliamentary etiquette within the B.V.I.S. prevented them from immediately expressing their inquisitiveness, Nell was overwhelmed with demands for an explanation once the meeting of the Society came to a close. Nell, however, possessed no explanation that she could offer. Judson Tibbs had caught up to her along the road the previous night, informing her of his choice to indulge the B.V.I.S. regarding its strange bias against advertisements for patent medicine. Then and throughout all the time that followed, that was the extent of what Nell would state, and it was nothing less than the plain truth; nevertheless, as Odette Pullen walked home and shared with Oliver Mott her deep conviction that something further lay beneath the enigmatic shift in Judson Tibbs’s attitude than Nell Harcourt had disclosed, she was likewise speaking the truth.

The previous evening, Nell had visited old Mrs. Stanhope’s along the shore road, returning home via a shortcut that took her across the low shore fields before passing through the beech wood under Robert Dickson’s, following a narrow footpath that emerged onto the main road right above the Lake of Glassy Waters . . . which ordinary people called Pembroke’s pond.

Right where the trail began, a pair of men sat in their buggies, pulled over to the road's edge. Judson Tibbs was one; Tobias Corcoran was the other, a man from Stonebridge against whom nothing dishonorable had ever been proven, as Mrs. Sowerby would have informed you in vivid italics. He sold farm machinery on commission and held a notable position in political affairs. In every political pie that was baked, he had a finger . . . certain folks claimed all his fingers . . .; and since a general election was imminent in Canada, Tobias Corcoran had spent many weeks as a occupied man, traveling through the county to gather support for the candidate of his party. Exactly when Nell stepped out from beneath the overhanging branches of the beech, she caught Corcoran saying, “If you’ll vote for Amesbury, Tibbs . . . well, I’ve a note for that pair of harrows you’ve got in the spring. I suppose you wouldn’t object to having it back, eh?”
“We . . . ll, seeing as you express it like that,” Judson drawled, grinning, “I suppose I may as well comply. In these difficult times, an individual has to safeguard his personal affairs.”

At that exact second, Nell was spotted by the two of them, causing their talk to stop suddenly. Giving a cold bow, Nell continued walking, her chin held just a bit higher than normal. Shortly afterward, she was caught up to by Judson Tibbs.
“Need a ride, Nell?” he asked in a friendly manner.

“I am obliged, but no,” replied Nell courteously, yet her tone possessed a sharp, penetrating scorn that penetrated even the thick skin of Judson Tibbs. His cheeks flushed crimson and he gave his reins an irritated jerk; however, self-preservation halted him in the very next instant. With an anxious gaze, he observed Nell continuing her firm progression, her eyes fixed straight ahead without turning to either side. Was she aware of Corcoran’s explicit proposition and the overly clear manner in which he himself had agreed to it? A curse on Corcoran! Should he fail to express his intentions in safer language, he was bound to find himself in difficulty before long. Furthermore, a curse on red-haired female teachers who possessed a tendency to suddenly appear from beech forests where they had no right to be located. Supposing Nell had overheard, Judson Tibbs—evaluating her character by his own base standards, as the local proverb expressed it, and consequently deceiving himself, as individuals of his sort typically do—was convinced that she would spread the news everywhere. At this point, Judson Tibbs, as previously demonstrated, cared little for the community's judgment; nevertheless, being exposed for taking a bribe would prove disastrous; moreover, should the story ever come to the attention of Isaac Tranter, all prospects of securing Louisa Odette, along with her attractive financial future as the daughter of a prosperous farmer, would be permanently destroyed. Judson Tibbs was aware that Mr. Tranter already viewed him with a degree of suspicion; he was in no position to chance anything.

“Ahem . . . I was hoping to speak with you regarding the small issue we talked about a few days ago, Nell. My decision now is that I will not lease my fences to that firm. An organization whose goal matches yours deserves support.”
Nell unbent to the slightest possible degree.
“I am grateful,” she remarked.
“And . . . and . . . there is no need to speak of that brief chat I had with Tobias.”

“Under no circumstances do I intend to speak of it,” Nell stated coldly, since she would have preferred to behold all the fences in Brierley covered in ads rather than lower herself to strike a deal with a person willing to trade his vote.

“Precisely . . . precisely,” concurred Judson, believing that they held a wonderful mutual understanding. “I did not expect you would. Naturally, I was merely teasing Tobias . . . he believes he is so terribly clever and sharp. I do not intend to vote for Amesbury. I shall vote for Hollis just as I have ever done . . . you will observe that when the election takes place. I simply egged Tobias on to discover if he would declare himself. And regarding the fence, everything is fine . . . you may inform the Improvers of that.”

“A world requires every type of person, according to what I’ve frequently heard, yet I believe a few might be done without,” Nell remarked to her image in the east gable mirror later that evening. “My conscience remains untroubled regarding that matter, as I would not have spoken of the shameful occurrence to anyone regardless. Who or what deserves gratitude for this is beyond my understanding. It was not brought about by any action of mine, and accepting that Providence operates through the sort of politics practiced by men such as Judson Tibbs and Tobias Corcoran is difficult.”

The evening was calm and yellow, with winds murmuring in the spruces encircling the playground and long, idle shadows stretching near the forest’s border, as Nell locked the door of the schoolhouse.
