Contentment marked her sigh when she slipped the key into her pocket. Her teaching year had come to a close, and she had been rehired for the upcoming one amidst numerous compliments. . . . merely Mr. Gorham Pullen advised that she should apply the strap more frequently . . . while two charming months of earned time off called out to her enticingly. Carrying her flower basket down the hill, Nell experienced harmony with both her surroundings and herself. Ever since the first mayflowers bloomed, Nell had faithfully undertaken her weekly trip to the burial place of Obed. Quiet, reserved, insignificant Obed Abernethy had been erased from the minds of all other Brierley residents, Thirza excluded; yet Nell held his memory fresh within her heart, where it would remain forever. She was incapable of forgetting the gentle elder who was the initial person to offer the affection and understanding her deprived youth had yearned for.

Where the hill ended, a boy sat upon the fence within the spruces’ shade . . . a boy possessing large, dreamy eyes alongside a lovely, sensitive countenance. Swinging himself down, he approached Nell with a smile; yet his cheeks bore the marks of tears.

“Since I knew you were headed to the cemetery, teacher, I decided to wait for you,” he said, sliding his hand inside hers. “I’m heading there as well . . . This bouquet of geraniums is being brought by me to place on Grandpa Stanhope’s grave on behalf of grandma. And see, teacher, beside Grandpa’s grave I intend to place this bunch of white roses in memory of my little mother. . . since travelling to her grave to place it there is impossible for me. But don’t you believe she’ll be aware of it all, anyway?”
“Yes, I am sure she will, Cedric.”

“You understand, teacher, it is exactly three years to this day from when my little mother passed away. It is a very, very lengthy duration yet the pain is every bit as strong as always . . . and my longing for her is just as great as ever. At times I feel as though I am simply unable to endure it, the ache is so deep.”
Cedric spoke with a shaking voice, his lip quivering. Hoping his eyes' tears would go unseen by his teacher, he directed his gaze downward toward his roses.
“And even so,” Nell murmured in a very quiet voice, “you would not desire the pain to cease . . . you would not choose to lose the memory of your little mother even were it possible.”

“No, truly, I would not . . . I perceive it in precisely that manner. You possess such a talent for comprehension, teacher. No one else comprehends as effectively . . . not even grandma, even though she treats me with such kindness. Father comprehended fairly well, yet I remained unable to converse with him extensively concerning mother, since it caused him such deep distress. Whenever he placed his hand across his countenance, I was invariably aware that I ought to cease speaking. Poor father, he undoubtedly feels terribly lonely lacking my company; however you see he possesses only a housekeeper at present and he believes housekeepers are unsuitable for raising small boys, particularly when his business requires him to remain away from home so frequently. Grandmothers excel further, second only to mothers. One day, once I am raised, I shall return to father and we shall never suffer separation again.”

Cedric had spoken to Nell regarding his mother and father to such an extent that she felt as though they were already familiar to her. In terms of temperament and disposition, she believed that his mother had likely closely resembled what he was himself; furthermore, it was her impression that Stephen Stanhope was a somewhat reserved individual possessing a deep and tender nature that he meticulously concealed from the public.

“It isn’t very easy to get acquainted with Father,” Cedric had remarked on one occasion. “I didn’t become really acquainted with him until my little mother had died. However, once you do come to know him, he is splendid. I love him most of all in the world, and then Grandma Stanhope, and after that, you, teacher. Were it not my obligation to love Grandma Stanhope next to father on account of everything she is doing for me, I would love you second to him. You understand, teacher. Still, I wish that she would keep the lamp inside my room until I fall asleep. The moment she tucks me in, she takes it straight away, stating that I must not be a coward. Although I am not frightened, I would prefer to have the light. My little mother always used to sit next to me while holding my hand until I fell asleep. I suppose that she spoiled me. You know how mothers do at times.”

No, this was not known to Nell, even if it could be imagined by her. Sooly, she gave thought to her “little mother,” that same mother who had considered her to be so “perfectly beautiful” and who, having passed away so long ago, lay buried next to her boyish husband in a distant, unvisited grave. Because Nell had no memory of her mother, she came close to envying Cedric.

“The coming week brings my birthday,” Cedric mentioned while the pair strolled up the lengthy red hill, enjoying the sunshine of June, “and a letter from father told me he is shipping a present he believes I will prefer above all other possible gifts. My opinion is that it arrived already, because Grandma keeps the drawer of the bookcase locked, which is a novel habit. Also, upon my asking her the reason, she merely appeared enigmatic and remarked that young boys should not possess excessive curiosity. Having a birthday causes great excitement, doesn’t it? Eleven will be my age. Looking at me, you would not suspect it, would you? According to Grandma I am quite tiny for my years, and she blames my insufficient consumption of porridge. Although I try as hard as I can, Grandma serves such large portions . . . Grandma is certainly not stingy, I assure you. From the time you and I discussed prayer on our way back from Sunday School that afternoon, teacher . . . when you advised that we should pray regarding every one of our troubles . . . my nightly prayer has been for God to grant me sufficient grace so I can consume every single scrap of my morning porridge. However, I have not managed it so far, and I truly am unable to determine if the cause is an insufficiency of grace or a surplus of porridge. Grandma states that father was raised on porridge, and the results were certainly excellent for him, since you should observe his broad shoulders. Even so,” Cedric finished, sighing with a thoughtful expression, “I genuinely believe porridge will prove to be my demise.”

Because Cedric’s eyes were turned away, Nell allowed a smile to touch her face. Throughout Brierley, it was common knowledge that ancient Mrs. Stanhope was raising her grandson by adhering to traditional, time-tested principles regarding moral conduct and eating habits.
“Dear, we should wish that won't happen,” she remarked in a bright tone. “What progress are you making with your rock people? Is the senior Twin maintaining his good behavior?”
“It is necessary for him to do so,” Cedric declared with force. “He understands that I will refuse to be seen with him unless he complies. I believe he is truly steeped in evil.”
“And is Nora aware of the Golden Lady by now?”

“No; yet I believe she has an inkling. It is my near certainty that she observed me when I previously visited the cave. Her discovery of it would not bother me . . . my desire for her not to know exists solely on her account . . . to prevent her emotions from being wounded. However, should she be intent on suffering hurt feelings, it is unavoidable.”
“Do you believe that I might also behold your rock people if I went down to the beach with you one evening?”
Cedric solemnly moved his head from side to side.

“No, it doesn't seem to me that my rock people would be visible to you. Only I am able to see them. However, it would be possible for you to view your own rock people. You belong to the type of person who is capable of it. The two of us are both that type. You know, teacher,” he continued, pressing her hand in a friendly way. “Is it not wonderful that we are that type, teacher?”
“Splendid,” agreed Nell, whose shining gray eyes peered down into the shining blue ones. It was known to both Nell and Cedric
“What a beautiful world Imagination reveals to our sight,”

and each was aware of the path leading to that blissful realm. In that place, by valley and brook, the rose of happiness flowered eternally; the bright sky was never shadowed by clouds; melodious bells were never dissonantly out of harmony; and like-minded souls were plentiful. Understanding the location of that country . . . “east o’ the sun, west o’ the moon” . . . constitutes invaluable wisdom, impossible to purchase in any bazaar. The benevolent fairies must bestow it when one is born, and time is unable to spoil or deprive one of it. Possessing it while residing in an attic surpasses being a dweller of mansions lacking it.

The Brierley cemetery remained the overgrown, deserted spot it had ever been. Naturally, the Improvers were paying attention to it, and Honora Hollis had given a presentation regarding graveyards at the previous gathering of the Society. Eventually, the Improvers intended for a tidy wire fence to take the place of the old, crooked board enclosure covered in lichen, as well as for the lawn to be trimmed and the tilting tombstones set upright.

Nell placed the blossoms she had carried for Obed’s grave upon it, and subsequently crossed to the small, poplar-canopied spot where Dinah Wren reposed. Continuously from the date of the spring picnic, Nell had set blossoms upon Dinah’s grave whenever she paid a visit to Obed’s. During the previous evening, she had undertaken a journey back to the small, abandoned forest garden and retrieved a few of Dinah’s personal white roses from that location.
“I believed you would prefer them over all the rest, my love,” she murmured gently.
A shadow covered the grass while Nell remained seated there, and raising her eyes, she saw Mrs. Wace. Side by side, they made their way back home.

The face belonging to Mrs. Wace no longer resembled that of the young bride whom Brierley had seen the minister bring five years earlier. A portion of its youthful roundness and bloom was gone, with delicate, enduring lines appearing around her mouth and eyes. A small grave located in the selfsame cemetery explained a few of those marks; others had newly formed while her young son was lately sick, a trial that had now fortunately passed. Even so, the dimples Mrs. Wace possessed remained just as charming and quick to appear as before, while her eyes stayed every bit as bright, clear, and honest; moreover, any lost maidenly attractiveness was presently far surpassed by an increase in strength and gentleness.
“I assume you are anticipating your break, Nell?” she remarked, while they departed from the cemetery.
Nell gave a nod.

“Yes. . . . I could savor the word like a delicious delicacy beneath my tongue. I believe the summer will be wonderful. To begin with, Mrs. Varley is visiting the Island in July, and Honora will be bringing her here. Just thinking about it gives me one of my familiar ‘thrills.’”
“I wish that you enjoy yourself, Nell. You have labored extremely hard over this previous year and you have achieved success.”
“Oh, I am not sure. In numerous ways, I have fallen very far short. My intentions when I started teaching this past autumn remain unaccomplished. My ideals have not been met by my actions.”

“None of us ever do,” Mrs. Wace said, sighing. “However, Nell, you are aware of Lowell’s words, ‘Not failure but low aim is crime.’ Ideals are necessary, and we must strive to fulfill them, even though complete success eludes us. Without them, life would prove to be a dismal affair. With them, it becomes magnificent and splendid. Keep a firm grip on your ideals, Nell.”

“I will attempt it. However, I must abandon the majority of my ideas,” stated Nell, with a faint laugh. “When I first began working as a teacher, I possessed the finest collection of ideas you could imagine, yet each single one has proved useless to me during various difficult moments.”
“Likewise the doctrine regarding physical discipline,” Mrs. Wace unitized playfully.
However, Nell turned red.
“For giving Anthony a whipping, I will never pardon myself.”

“Foolishness, my love, the punishment was well-merited by him. Furthermore, it did him good. Ever since, he has given you no grief, and he has been persuaded that you are second to none. His affection was earned by your gentleness once the notion that a ‘girl was useless’ had been eradicated from his obstinate brain.”

“Although he might have been deserving of it, that misses the main issue. Had my choice to lash him been made in a calm and considered manner out of a belief that he merited such chastisement, my feelings about the matter would be different. However, the reality, Mrs. Wace, remains that I simply lost my composure and struck him as a result. Considerations of justice or injustice never crossed my mind . . . I would have carried it out regardless of his innocence. My humiliation stems from that fact.”

“Well, we all commit errors, dear, so simply leave it in the past. We ought to feel remorse for our errors and draw lessons from them, yet not bear them ahead into the coming days with us. Yonder travels Hugh Carrow upon his bicycle . . . returning to his house for his holiday as well, I assume. In what manner are you and he progressing in your schoolwork?”
“Fairly well. Our intention is to complete the Virgil this evening . . . merely twenty lines remain. After that, our studies will pause until September.”
“Is it your belief that you will one day attend college?”

“Oh, I don’t know.” Gazing dreamily off toward the horizon colored like an opal, Nell remarked. “Although we feel such gratitude in believing that Thirza’s eyes will fail no further, they are unlikely to ever improve significantly from their current state. Furthermore, regarding the twins . . . I have a feeling their uncle will not actually summon them at any point. College might lie past the turn in the path, yet having not reached that turn myself, I refrain from dwelling on it to avoid becoming dissatisfied.”

“Well, I would be pleased to see you attend college, Nell; however, if you fail to go, do not feel dissatisfied regarding it. In the end, we fashion our own existence no matter where we find ourselves . . . college merely assists us in accomplishing this with greater ease. Our lives become wide or restricted based upon what we invest in them, rather than what we extract. Existing is abundant and complete in this place . . . in all places . . . provided we are able to discover the way to unlock our entire hearts to its abundance and completeness.”

“I believe I grasp your meaning,” Nell remarked contemplatively, “and I am aware that I have a great deal to be grateful for . . . oh, a great deal . . . my employment, alongside Cedric Stanhope, as well as the beloved twins, plus every one of my friends. Are you aware, Mrs. Wace, that I am extremely grateful for friendship? It enhances life to such a degree.”

“A genuinely supportive element is found in authentic friendship,” remarked Mrs. Wace, “and our standards for it ought to be extremely elevated, avoiding any tarnishing caused by a lack of truthfulness and sincerity. It concerns me that the term friendship is frequently lowered to describe a form of closeness that contains no genuine friendship whatsoever.”

“Yes . . . similar to Tibby Tulk’s and Julia Bell’s. They share a close bond and accompany each other everywhere; yet Tibby continually utters unkind remarks about Julia when she is absent, and everyone believes she harbors jealousy toward her since she displays such delight whenever anyone finds fault with Julia. It seems to me a desecration to bestow the name of friendship on such a connection. Should we possess friends, our duty is to search solely for their finest qualities and offer them the finest qualities within ourselves, do you not agree? Were that so, friendship would become the loveliest reality on earth.”
“Amity is truly lovely,” Mrs. Wace grinned, “yet eventually . . .”

Afterward, she stopped suddenly. Beside her, the refined, fair-browed face, possessing frank eyes and expressive features, remained much more that of a child than a woman. Only visions of companionship and aspiration were contained within Nell’s heart at this point, and Mrs. Wace had no desire to spoil the freshness of her gentle innocence. Consequently, she permitted the coming years to complete her thought.

chapter_title: XVI The Substance of Things Hoped For
text: “It’s a bargain,” declared Robin. “I’ll be good, you bet. My intention was to head to Mr. Pettifer’s to shoot peas at Nutmeg using my new popgun, yet another day will work fine. I espect it will resemble Sunday, though having a picnic at the shore will compensate for it.”

During the night, Nell stirred from sleep thrice and journeyed to her window to ensure that the forecast from Uncle Zeb was not being fulfilled. At last, the daybreak arrived, pearl-like and bright within a firmament bursting with argent shimmer and brilliance, marking the arrival of the incredible day.

Isolde showed up shortly following breakfast, carrying a flower basket on one arm and holding her muslin dress over the other . . . since wearing it before finishing all the dinner preparations was out of the question. In the meantime, she was dressed in her afternoon pink print alongside a lawn apron that had fearful and wonderful ruffles and frills; moreover, she looked extremely neat, pretty, and rosy.
“You appear completely charming,” Nell said with admiration.
A sigh escaped Isolde.

“However, all of my dresses have required me to expand them once more. Compared to July, my weight has increased by four pounds. Where is this going to stop, Nell? Tallness and slenderness characterize every heroine created by Mrs. Varley.”

“Well, let’s ignore our problems and consider our blessings,” Nell said cheerfully. “According to Mrs. Wace, every time we recall something that tests us, we ought to likewise recall something pleasant that can balance it out. While you might be a bit too chubby, your dimples are most precious; and though my nose is freckled, its form is perfectly fine. Did the lemon juice help at all, in your opinion?”

“Indeed, I truly believe it achieved that,” Isolde remarked with a critical eye; and, feeling greatly pleased, Nell took the lead toward the garden, an area filled with delicate shadows and flickering beams of gold.

“The parlor will be decorated by us first. Plenty of time is available to us, because Honora stated their arrival would occur around twelve or half past at the latest, which means our dinner will take place at one.”

Somewhere in the United States or Canada, two girls might possibly have been more excited and happier at that instant, though I find it questionable. As peony and rose and bluebell dropped, each snip of the scissors appeared to twitter, “Mrs. Varley is coming today.” Nell was amazed that Mr. Pettifer was able to continue calmly cutting hay in the field over the lane, precisely as though no event was about to occur.

A somewhat austere and somber room was the parlor at Grey Shutters, featuring unyielding horsehair furnishings, rigid lace drapes, and white antimacassars that remained placed at an impeccably precise slant, save for those moments when they attached themselves to the buttons of unlucky individuals. For Thirza refused to allow any changes, meaning that not even Nell had ever succeeded in breathing much elegance into the place. Yet flowers can work amazing transformations provided they are granted an honest opportunity; after Nell and Isolde were done decorating the space, its identity would have been completely lost to you.

An abundance of snowballs spilled over a large blue bowl set upon the buffed table. Roses and ferns were piled high across the gleaming black mantelpiece. A cluster of bluebells rested on each shelf of the what-not; the dismal nooks flanking the grate were illuminated by jars packed with vibrant crimson peonies, while yellow poppies blazed within the grate itself. This entire display of magnificence and shade, combined with sunlight filtering through the window honeysuckle vines to cast a leafy flurry of dancing shadows across the floor and walls, transformed the ordinarily gloomy small space into the genuine “bower” of Nell’s fantasy, and further drew a nod of approval from Thirza, who had entered intending to fault but stayed to admire.

“It is time for us to arrange the table,” declared Nell, adopting the manner of a priestess preparing to carry out a holy ceremony for a deity. “A large vase filled with wild roses will sit at the midpoint, accompanied by a solitary rose placed before each person's plate—along with an exclusive arrangement made solely of rosebuds beside Mrs. Varley’s—which refers to ‘The Rosebud Garden’ as you are aware.”

The sitting room contained the set table, adorned with the highest quality china, glass, silver, and Thirza’s finest linen. You can be entirely sure that each single item put upon it had been scrubbed or buffed until it achieved the utmost achievable peak of shine and sparkle.

After that, the girls hurried out into the kitchen, a room overflowing with delicious scents coming from the oven, inside of which the chickens were already roasting delightfully. Nell took care of the potatoes, whereas Isolde made the peas and beans ready. Next, as Isolde locked herself in the pantry so she could mix the lettuce salad, Nell—her cheeks already starting to turn deep red, as a result of excitement just as much as the warmth from the stove—made the bread sauce intended for the chickens, chopped up her onions to go in the soup, and lastly beat the cream destined for her lemon pies.

And how was Robin faring throughout this period? Was he fulfilling his pledge to behave himself? Indeed, he was doing so. Of course, he maintained that he must stay in the kitchen, because his inquisitive nature demanded that he observe every single thing taking place. Nevertheless, since he remained peacefully in a corner, fully occupied with loosening the knots of a segment of herring net he had carried back from his previous visit to the beach, no person had any objection to it.
By eleven-thirty the lettuce salad had been prepared, whipped cream was piled high on the yellow rounds of the pies, and every item that was supposed to sizzle and bubble was sizzling and bubbling.
“We ought to go and change our clothes now,” Nell said, “because they could arrive by twelve. Dinner needs to be at one precisely, since the soup has to be brought out the moment it is ready.”

Grave indeed were the grooming rituals performed shortly thereafter within the eastern gable. Nell gazed with concern at her nose and felt glad upon observing that its freckles were not particularly noticeable, owing to either the lemon juice or the extraordinary glow upon her cheeks. By the time they were prepared, they appeared just as charming, neat, and youthful as any of “Mrs. Varley’s heroines” ever had.

“I do wish that I can speak occasionally, rather than remain silent like a dummy,” Isolde uttered nervously. “Every heroine created by Mrs. Varley speaks so wonderfully. However, I fear that I will become speech-blocked and foolish. Furthermore, I am certain to utter ‘I seen.’ I have not uttered it frequently since Miss Thorne served as a teacher here; nevertheless, it inevitably escapes during times of agitation. Nell, should I utter ‘I seen’ in front of Mrs. Varley, my shame would kill me. Moreover, remaining completely silent would be nearly as terrible.”
“There are a lot of things that make me anxious,” Nell remarked, “however, I doubt there is much danger of me being at a loss for words.”
And, to be fair to her, there was not.

Nell concealed her muslin finery beneath a large apron and descended to prepare her soup. Thirza, having dressed herself along with the twins, appeared more agitated than anyone had previously seen her. The Waces and Miss Thorne arrived when it was half past twelve. All was proceeding favorably, yet Nell started to experience anxiety. Honora and Mrs. Varley ought to have been there by then. She repeatedly walked to the gate, gazing down the lane with an intensity equal to that of her namesake in the Bluebeard tale watching from the tower window.
“What if they never arrive?” she asked with a pitiful tone.
“Do not assume that. It would be far too low,” stated Isolde, who, nevertheless, was starting to experience uneasy doubts regarding the matter.
“Nell,” said Thirza, emerging from the parlor, “Miss Thorne desires to look at Miss Pembroke’s willowware platter.”

Nell hurried over to the closet in the sitting room so that she could retrieve the platter. Following the pledge she made to Mrs. Sowerby, she had sent a letter to Miss Pembroke of Port Marlow to request borrowing it. As a longtime friend of Nell’s, Miss Pembroke dispatched the platter without delay, along with a note urging Nell to handle it with great caution, since it had cost her twenty dollars. After fulfilling its role during the Aid bazaar, the platter was placed back inside the Grey Shutters closet, because Nell refused to rely on anyone other than herself to carry it back to town.

Holding the platter with care, she brought it to the front entrance where those she was entertaining were taking pleasure in the refreshing air coming from the stream. After it was inspected and praised, a tremendous banging and rattling echoed from the kitchen pantry at the exact moment Nell received it into her hands again. Thirza, Isolde, and Nell rushed out, though the last woman paused just to place the valuable platter hurriedly upon the second stair step.

Upon entering the pantry, a genuinely dreadful sight confronted them . . . a young boy with a guilty expression clambering down from the table, his immaculate print blouse heavily smeared with yellow filling, while atop the table lay the broken ruins of what used to be two splendid, cream-topped lemon pies.

Robin completed untangling his herring net and rolled the cord into a sphere. Next, he walked into the pantry to place it on the ledge above the table, a spot where he maintained around twenty comparable spheres that, as best anyone could tell, fulfilled no practical function other than providing the pleasure of owning them. To accomplish this, Robin was required to step onto the table and stretch toward the ledge at a precarious slope . . . an action that Thirza had instructed him not to perform, given that he had previously met with disaster during such an attempt. His outcome on this occasion proved catastrophic. Robin lost his footing and tumbled heavily right onto the lemon pies. His fresh shirt was destroyed for the moment and the pies were destroyed forever. Nevertheless, it is a bad wind that brings no benefit to anyone, and the pig ultimately profited from Robin’s misfortune.
“Robin Farrow,” Thirza said, while she shook him by the shoulder, “did I not forbid you to climb up on that table again? Did I not?”
“I forgot,” Robin whined. “So many things have been forbidden by you that keeping track of every single one is impossible for me.”

“Indeed, you are to go up to the higher floor and remain there until the evening meal has passed. It may be that you will have them organized properly in your mind before then. No, Nell, do not ever think of pleading on his behalf. My reason for penalizing him is not that he ruined your pies . . . that occurred by chance. My reason for penalizing him is his refusal to obey. Off with you, Robin, I command.”
“Is there no dinner for me?” Robin cried out.
“Once dinner has finished, you may head downstairs and eat your meal in the kitchen.”

“Oh, all right,” said Robin, feeling a bit relieved. “I am sure Nell will keep a few good bones for me, right, Nell? Because you realize that I had no intention of landing on the pies. Listen, Nell, as long as they are ruined, is it okay if I bring a few of the scraps to my room?”
“No, no lemon pie for you, Master Robin,” Thirza said as she shoved him in the direction of the hall.
“What shall we do for dessert?” Nell asked, gazing with regret at the destruction and debris.
“Bring forth a jar of strawberry preserves,” Thirza offered by way of comfort. “The bowl still holds an abundance of whipped cream to go with it.”

When one o’clock arrived, neither Honora nor Mrs. Varley had appeared. Nell experienced intense distress. All the food had been cooked to perfection and the soup was precisely as it ought to be, although it could not be relied upon to stay that way for very long.
“I do not think they are coming after all,” Thirza remarked in an annoyed tone.
Nell and Isolde looked to one another’s eyes for solace.
When it reached half past one, Thirza once more came out of the parlor.
“Girls, we need to eat dinner. Everyone feels hungry, so there is no point in delaying further. It is obvious that Honora and Mrs. Varley will not arrive, and waiting longer makes nothing better.”
Lacking any remaining enthusiasm for the task, Nell and Isolde began to serve the meal.
“I doubt I can swallow even one bite,” Isolde remarked sorrowfully.
“Neither do I. However, for the sakes of Miss Thorne and Mr. and Mrs. Wace, I trust all will turn out well,” Nell remarked without enthusiasm.
As Isolde served the peas, she sampled a bite, causing a most unusual look to pass over her face.
“Nell, was sugar added to these peas by you?”
“Yes,” Nell stated, mashing the potatoes like someone who was expected to perform her duty. “A spoonful of sugar was added by me. It is what we always do. Is it not to your liking?”
“However, a spoon of it was also added by me as I placed them upon the stove,” Isolde stated.
Nell let go of her masher and sampled the peas as well. After that, she pulled a face.

“How terrible! It never occurred to me that you had added sugar, since I was aware that your mother never does so. Miraculously, I happened to remember it . . . it constantly slips my mind . . . which led me to quickly add a spoonful.”

“My guess is that there are simply too many cooks involved,” remarked Thirza, whose face bore a somewhat remorseful look as she took in this conversation. “Since I was absolutely sure you had never kept it in mind in the past, Nell, I didn't expect you to recall the sugar . . . and because of that, I added one spoon.”

Peals of laughter, one following another, reached the guests in the parlor from the kitchen, though the cause of the amusement remained unknown to them. No green peas, nonetheless, appeared on the dinner table that day.

“Well,” Nell remarked, regaining her composure while sighing as she remembered, “at least we possess the salad, and I believe the beans remain undamaged. Let us take the items inside and finish this task.”

It could not be claimed that the meal achieved any great social success. Efforts to rescue the situation were made by the Waces and Miss Thorne, while the usual calmness of Thirza remained without any obvious disturbance. However, owing to a mix of disappointment and the aftermath of their morning excitement, neither Isolde nor Nell was capable of eating or speaking. For the benefit of her visitors, Nell made a heroic attempt to participate in the talk; nevertheless, every bit of her vivacity had been temporarily snuffed out, and, despite her affection for Miss Thorne and the Waces, she was unable to prevent herself from reflecting on how pleasant it would be once all the guests had departed for home, allowing her to hide her fatigue and letdown within the pillows of the east gable.

An ancient adage exists which truly appears to be divinely influenced on occasion . . . “it never rains but it pours.” That day’s capacity for troubles had not yet been reached. Right when Mr. Wace had concluded giving thanks, a peculiar, threatening noise echoed on the staircase, resembling a firm, weighty item tumbling down step after step, culminating in a colossal crash at the base. Everyone rushed out to the hall. Nell uttered a scream of horror.

Down at the foot of the steps, a large pink conch shell was positioned in the middle of the broken pieces of what used to be Miss Pembroke’s platter, while at the head of the steps, a frightened Robin was kneeling, staring below with eyes wide open at the destruction.
“Robin,” Thirza said in a portending manner, “was it your intention to toss that shell down?”

“No, I never did,” Robin whimpered. “I was merely kneeling in this spot, as quietly as could be, so I could look at you people between the bannisters, when my foot hit that old item and knocked it down . . . and I’m so very hungry . . . and I really want you to just whip a boy and get it over with, rather than constantly dispatching him to his room so he loses out on all the enjoyment.”

“Do not hold Robin responsible,” spoken Nell, picking together the pieces using shaking fingers. “The blame rests on me. That platter was placed there by me and completely slipped my mind. My negligence has brought a fitting punishment upon me; yet oh, what is Miss Pembroke going to say?”
“Well, you know it was merely purchased by her, so it lacks the status of a family heirloom,” Isolde said, attempting to offer comfort.

Not long afterward, the guests departed, believing this to be the most considerate course of action, whereupon Nell and Isolde cleaned the dishes while conversing with an unprecedented lack of words. Subsequently, Isolde returned home suffering from a headache, and Nell, plagued by one as well, retreated to the east gable, remaining there until Thirza arrived back from the post office at sunset carrying a letter that Honora had written the previous day. Mrs. Varley had sustained such a serious ankle sprain that she was unable to depart from her room.

“Also, my dear Nell,” Honora expressed in her letter, “it grieves me deeply, yet I fear our trip to Grey Shutters is completely off, because once Aunty’s ankle has healed, returning to Toronto will be necessary for her. Her arrival there is required by a specific day.”

“Well,” sighed Nell, placing the letter onto the red sandstone step of the back porch, the spot where she sat as the dappled sky rained twilight down, “I perpetually considered it too good to be true that Mrs. Varley would actually arrive. Yet there . . . that remark seems as defeatist as Miss Eliza Pullen and I feel disgrace for saying it. When all is said and done, it wasn't too good to be true . . . occurrences equally good and much superior are coming true for me constantly. And I guess today's happenings possess a amusing aspect as well. Maybe once Isolde and I become aged and graying we will find ourselves able to chuckle about them. However I sense that I am unable to anticipate doing so prior to that time, because it has genuinely been a harsh disappointment.”

“You are likely to experience several additional and more severe letdowns than this one prior to finishing life,” remarked Thirza, whose genuine intention was to deliver consoling words. “It appears to me, Nell, as though you will not ever abandon your habit of placing your hopes so intensely on matters and subsequently plunging into hopelessness when you fail to obtain them.”

“I am aware that I have too much of a tendency toward that,” Nell conceded with regret. “Whenever I expect something good to occur, I appear to soar straight up on anticipation’s wings; and subsequently, before I know it, I hit the ground with a bang. However, Thirza, the soaring portion is truly magnificent while it endures . . . it resembles floating across a sunset. I believe it nearly makes up for the bang.”

“Well, perhaps it is so,” Thirza conceded. “I would prefer to proceed at a peaceful pace and forego both the flight and the crash. However, each person possesses her unique manner of existence . . . It was once my belief that a single correct path existed . . . yet my confidence in that has waned since I was tasked with raising you and the twins. How do you intend to handle Miss Pembroke’s platter?”
“Reimburse her the twenty dollars she gave for it, I guess. I am extremely grateful it was not a prized heirloom since no amount of cash would be able to substitute for it then.”
“Perhaps you might discover a similar item in some place and purchase it on her behalf.”

“Regrettably, that is not the case. Platters from that era are extremely rare. For the supper, Mrs. Sowerby was unable to locate one at all. I truly wish I were able to, because Miss Pembroke, naturally, would be just as happy with any platter, provided both shared the same age and authenticity. Thirza, observe that large star above the maple grove belonging to Mr. Pettifer, surrounded by such a sacred stillness of silvery sky. A sensation resembling a prayer comes over me from it. Ultimately, when stars and skies of that nature are visible to us, minor disappointments and mishaps cannot hold so much importance, can they?”
“Where’s Robin?” asked Thirza, casting a casual look toward the star.

“In bed. I’ve pledged that tomorrow I will bring him and Lucy to the beach for an outing. To be sure, he was required to behave well under our initial deal. Nevertheless, he attempted to behave . . . and disappointing him was more than I had the heart to do.”
“Rowing on the pond in that punt will cause your death or the twins’,” Thirza complained. “Sixty years I’ve resided in this place, and not once have I gone out on the pond.”

“Indeed, a situation can always be rectified,” Nell stated playfully. “Imagine joining us on the morrow. Grey Shutters will be locked by us, and we will pass all twenty-four hours on the beach, putting all our cares behind us.”

“No, thank you,” Thirza said, emphasizing her words indignantly. “Wouldn't I look like a fine sight, taking a flat across the pond? I can almost hear Agatha commenting about it. Look at Mr. Pettifer driving off over there. Is there any truth, do you think, to the rumor that Mr. Pettifer intends to visit Isabella Pullen?”

“No, I am certain there is not. He merely dropped by one night to discuss business matters with Mr. Gorham Pullen, and Mrs. Sowerby spotted him, remarking that she was sure he was courting since he was wearing a white collar. I do not think Mr. Pettifer will ever get married. He appears to hold a bias against matrimony.”

“Indeed, predicting the actions of those lifelong bachelors is impossible. Furthermore, provided he wore a white collar, I would concur with Agatha regarding its suspicious appearance, because I am certain nobody ever caught sight of him wearing one previously.”

“I believe the sole reason he wore it was his desire to finalize a business arrangement with Gorham Pullen,” Nell remarked. “I have listened to him state that such an occasion is the single moment a man must pay close attention to his attire, since appearing wealthy makes the second party less inclined to attempt to defraud him. My heart truly goes out to Mr. Pettifer; I doubt he experiences any contentment in his existence. Living with nobody to love besides a parrot has got to be extremely solitary, wouldn't you say? However, I observe that Mr. Pettifer resents being the object of pity. No person enjoys it, I suppose.”
“Hugh is walking up the lane,” Thirza said. “Put on your rubbers and coat if he asks you to row on the pond. Tonight the dew is heavy.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Nell,” declared Robin, who sat upright in his bed while resting his chin upon his hands, “Nell, where is sleep? Every night individuals go to sleep, and naturally I understand that it is the location where I accomplish the actions I dream, yet I desire to learn where it is situated and the way I travel there and return without being aware of anything . . . and wearing my nighty as well. Where is it?”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: At the west gable window, Nell knelt as she observed the evening sky, which resembled a huge blossom featuring crocus-colored petals and a center of burning yellow. Turning her head when Robin questioned her, she replied in a dreamy manner,

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “‘Across the peaks of the moon, Through the vale of the shadow.’”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: Cedric Stanhope would have grasped what this signified, or forged a significance for it on his own, had he not known; yet pragmatic Robin, whom Nell frequently observed with despair possessed no imagination whatsoever, was merely perplexed and repulsed.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Nell, it is my belief that you are merely speaking absurdity.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Naturally, I was, my dear young man. Are you unaware that merely the most senseless people speak reasonably without exception?”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Well, it seems to me that a reasonable query deserves a reasonable reply,” Robin stated, sounding offended.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Oh, you lack the age to comprehend,” Nell remarked. Nevertheless, uttering those words made her feel somewhat humiliated; after all, had she not earnestly promised herself—with sharp memories of numerous comparable rejections suffered during her own childhood—that no child would ever hear her say they were too young to comprehend? Even so, she was now guilty of the exact same thing . . . so vast, on occasion, is the distance dividing principle from action.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Indeed, I am attempting to increase my height as much as I can,” Robin remarked, “yet it is a process that one cannot hasten significantly. Should Thirza prove less frugal regarding her jam, I am convinced my growth would occur much more rapidly.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Robin, Thirza does not lack generosity,” Nell remarked sternly. “Making a statement like that shows a great deal of ungratefulness on your part.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “An alternative term exists with the identical definition that sounds much nicer, though it slips my mind at the moment,” Robin stated, his forehead creasing deeply. “I listened to Thirza state that she was that very thing, herself, a few days ago.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Should you imply thrifty, that is completely distinct from being tightfisted. Being thrifty is a wonderful quality for someone to possess. Had Thirza been tightfisted, she never would have brought in you and Lucy upon the death of your mother. Might you have preferred residing alongside Mrs. Wiggins?”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “I certainly wouldn't!” Robin declared with great emphasis. “And going to Uncle Richard's isn't something I want either. Being here suits me much better, despite Thirza being so stingy with the jam, simply because you are with me, Nell. Tell me, Nell, could you share a tale with me before I drop off? Skip the fairy tales. Girls might like them, I guess, but my preference is for something thrilling . . . packed with slaughter and gunplay, plus a burning home, and similar captivating events.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: It was lucky for Nell that, just then, Thirza shouted from her own chamber.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Nell, Isolde’s signaling very fast, so you ought to check what she wants.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: Nell hurried to the east gable, where she observed bursts of light shining through the dusk from Isolde’s window in clusters of five, signifying, in line with their former childhood signals, “Come over at once for I have something important to reveal.” Placing her white shawl upon her head, Nell rushed across the Whispering Wood and through Mr. Bell’s pasture corner until she reached Pear Hill.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Nell, I have some good news for you,” Isolde said. “Mother and I just returned to the house from Delford, where I ran into Mary Sentner from Tranter vale inside the store belonging to Mr. Blair. According to her, the old Copp girls who live on the Tory Road own a willow-ware platter that she believes is an exact match for the one at our supper. She mentioned that they will probably part with it, since Martha Copp is famous for selling anything she possibly can; however, should they refuse, another platter exists at Wesley Keyson’s place in Tullyvale which she is certain they would sell, though she cannot guarantee it is the precise type that belongs to Aunt Lavinia.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “I will head straight to Tullyvale the following day after it,” Nell stated with determination, “and I need you to accompany me. My mind will be so relieved, because I am required to travel to town the day after that, and in what way am I able to face your Aunt Lavinia if I lack a willow-ware platter? That would prove to be far more terrible than the occasion when I was forced to admit to leaping upon the spare room bed.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: The pair of girls chuckled about the past recollection . . . regarding which, should any among my readers be unaware and inquisitive, I am obliged to direct them toward the former narrative of Nell.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: On the following afternoon, the girls set out on their journey to hunt for platters. Tullyvale was ten miles away, and the weather did not make for a particularly enjoyable trip. Conditions were extremely hot and devoid of wind, while the road was as dusty as one would anticipate following a six-week drought.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Oh, how I long for a prompt rainfall,” Nell lamented. “The drought has dried up everything. My heart goes out to the miserable fields, while the trees appear to reach out with open palms, begging for water. Visiting my garden causes me pain each time I step inside. Yet, I should probably refrain from lamenting a garden while the crops of the farmers are enduring such distress. According to Mr. Pettifer, the dried-out state of his pastures leaves his unfortunate cows with barely a scrap to graze on, making him feel like he is abusing his livestock whenever he looks them in the eye.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: A tireing ride brought the girls to Tullyvale, where they veered onto the “Tory” Road . . . a secluded, verdant thoroughfare whose grassy patches amid the rutted paths testified to a dearth of traffic. For the majority of its length, it was flanked by densely growing juvenile spruces pressing toward the passage, interrupted occasionally by an opening where a rear pasture of a Tullyvale homestead reached the barrier or a stretch of tree-butts blazed with weed-of-fire and goldenrod.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “What is the reason it is named the Tory Road?” Nell inquired.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Mr. Wace claims the rationale resembles naming a location a grove due to its lack of trees,” Isolde stated, “since the only residents along the road are the Copp girls and, at the far end, old Martin Bovyer, a Liberal. When the Tory government held power, they constructed the road merely to demonstrate that they were active.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: The father of Isolde belonged to the Liberal party, an aspect that caused her and Nell to refrain from talking about politics. Conservative views had consistently been held by the people at Grey Shutters.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: At last the young women arrived at the former Copp property . . . an abode possessing such extreme outdoor tidiness that it would have made even Grey Shutters look inferior in comparison. Located upon an incline, the home was of an extremely traditional style, a circumstance that had required a stone cellar to be constructed beneath a single end. A state of dazzling flawlessness was achieved by whitewashing all of the house and outbuildings, while the neat, white-paled kitchen garden displayed not a single visible weed.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Every blind has been drawn,” Isolde remarked with regret. “It seems to me that no one is inside.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: Events unfolded precisely in this manner. A look of confusion passed between the girls.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “I am at a loss,” Nell stated. “Were I certain that the platter was of the correct sort, I wouldn’t care about waiting for their return. However, if it is not, going to Wesley Keyson’s later might be impossible due to the late hour.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: Isolde gazed toward a particular small, square window situated above the basement.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “I feel sure that is the pantry window,” she said, “for this house is an exact match to Uncle Charles’ at Stonebridge, where that window belongs to their pantry. Since the shade is not drawn, climbing onto the roof of that small house would allow us to peer inside the pantry, where we might catch sight of the platter. Do you suppose doing so would cause any harm?”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “No, I don’t think so,” Nell concluded, following careful consideration, “as we are not driven by mere inquisitiveness.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: Once this significant matter of morality had been resolved, Nell got ready to climb onto the previously mentioned “little house,” a lath-built structure featuring a pointed roof that had formerly functioned as a dwelling for ducks. The keeping of ducks had been abandoned by the Copp girls . . . “because they were such untidy birds”. . . meaning the structure had remained unused for several years, except when utilized as a place of punishment for brooding hens. Even though it had been meticulously whitewashed, it was now a bit unstable, causing Nell to feel quite uncertain while she climbed up from the higher position of a keg set atop a box.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “It will collapse under my weight, I fear,” she remarked, cautiously setting foot upon the rooftop.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Rest yourself against the window frame,” Isolde suggested, and Nell proceeded to rest against it. Upon looking through the glass, she observed, to her great happiness, a piece of willow-ware porcelain, precisely like the one she was searching for, sitting upon the ledge directly behind the window. All this was visible to her prior to the disaster. Her happiness caused Nell to become unmindful of how unstable her foothold was; she rashly stopped resting against the window frame and took an excited small jump of delight . . . whereupon she dropped right through the top structure as far as her underarms within a instant, remaining suspended and entirely incapable of pulling herself out. Isolde hurried inside the duck house, where she grabbed the waist of her unlucky companion in an effort to pull her downward.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Ow . . . don’t,” miserable Nell screamed. “Long splinters are thrusting into my skin. Try placing an object beneath my feet . . . and I might be able to pull myself upward.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: Isolde hurriedly pulled the earlier named barrel inside, which Nell discovered was barely tall enough to offer a firm support upon which to rest her feet. Nevertheless, she remained unable to free herself.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “If I went up there, would I be able to haul you out?” Isolde offered.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: Nell gave a hopeless shake of her head.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “No . . . the splinters are giving me too much pain. However, if an axe is available to you, my release might be chopped out by you. Oh dear, the belief that my birth occurred under an unlucky star truly begins to take hold in me.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: Isolde looked diligently, yet she failed to discover any axe.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “I will need to seek assistance,” she stated, walking back toward the captive.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “No, truly, you are not going to,” Nell declared with great force. “Should you do that, word of this incident will spread all over, leaving me too embarrassed to be seen. No, our only option is to wait for the Copp girls to return and make them promise not to tell. They are going to know the location of the axe and free me. Provided I remain completely motionless, I am not in pain . . . physically speaking, that is. I am curious about the price the Copp girls put on this home. The harm I caused will have to be covered by my money, yet that would not bother me if I could just be certain they would comprehend why I peeked into their pantry window. The only thing comforting me is that the dish matches the exact type I desire, and provided Miss Copp agrees to sell it to me, I will accept everything that transpired.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “In the event that the Copp girls fail to return prior to nightfall . . . or perhaps not until the following day, what then?” Isolde inquired.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “In the event that they have not returned when the sun sets, I guess you will be forced to seek alternative help,” Nell stated with hesitation, “however, you must not depart until it becomes absolutely necessary. Oh dear, this situation is a terrible plight. My troubles would not bother me as much if they possessed romance, like the heroines belonging to Mrs. Varley consistently do, yet they are perpetually merely absurd. Imagine the reaction of the Copp girls as they travel into their yard and observe the head and shoulders of a girl protruding from the roof of a building on their property. Hark . . . does that sound like a wagon? No, Isolde, I think that sound is thunder.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: It was unquestionably thunder, and after she completed a hurried tour of the dwelling, Isolde came back with the news that a particularly dark cloud was climbing swiftly in the northwest.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “It looks like a severe thunder-shower is coming,” she cried out with distress, “Oh, Nell, what are we going to do?”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “It is necessary that we get ready for it,” Nell remarked calmly. Compared to the events that had already transpired, a thunderstorm appeared insignificant. “Driving the horse and buggy under that open shed would be a good idea. By good fortune, my parasol remains inside the buggy. Take this . . . bring my hat along with you. Thirza remarked that I was foolish for wearing my finest hat to travel to the Tory Road, and she spoke the truth, just as she invariably does.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: Isolde unfastened the pony and entered the shed, precisely when the initial large raindrops began to fall. Sitting inside, she observed the ensuing deluge, which grew so dense and intense that Nell was barely visible through the curtain of water, valiantly supporting the parasol above her uncovered head. Thunder was not particularly abundant, yet the rain poured down cheerfully for almost an hour. Now and then, Nell tilted her parasol backward to wave a supportive hand toward her companion; however, talking across such a span was entirely impossible. At last, the downpour stopped, the sun emerged, and Isolde braved the yard's puddles to cross over.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Were you soaked terribly?” she inquired with concern.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Oh, no,” Nell cheerfully replied. “The rain only beat through the laths to make my skirt a little damp, while my head and shoulders are entirely dry. Do not feel sorry for me, Isolde, since it hasn't bothered me in the slightest. I continuously reflected on the great benefit of the rain and the joy it brings to my garden, while picturing how the buds and flowers would react as the drops started falling. In my mind, I crafted an exceedingly fascinating conversation involving the sweet peas, the asters, the garden's guardian spirit, and the wild canaries inside the lilac bush. I intend to record it on paper once I arrive back home. It would be wonderful if I possessed paper and a pencil to write it right this second, as I will likely lose the finest details from my memory prior to reaching home.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: A pencil was held by Isolde the faithful, who found a piece of wrapping paper within the buggy's box. After closing her wet parasol and placing her hat upon her head, Nell laid the wrapping paper across a shingle that Isolde passed to her, drafting her garden idyl in an environment that was scarcely suited for literary composition. All the same, the outcome turned out to be rather lovely, leaving Isolde “enraptured” as Nell recited the piece to her.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Oh, Nell, it is delightful . . . simply delightful. You must submit it to the Canadian Woman.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: Nell gave a shake of her head.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Oh, no, it would not be appropriate whatsoever. You see, it lacks any plot. It is merely a sequence of whims. I enjoy composing stuff like that, though obviously nothing like it could ever be published, since editors require plots, or so Honora claims. Oh, Miss Sarah Copp is over there now. Isolde, please step over and clarify.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: Sarah Copp was a diminutive individual, dressed in worn black garments, wearing a headpiece selected not for frivolous decoration but rather for durable attributes. Upon witnessing the unusual sight in her premises, she appeared predictably astonished, yet upon listening to the account provided by Isolde, she became entirely compassionate. Hastily opening the rear entrance, she brought out the hatchet, and via several deft strikes released Nell. Experiencing some fatigue and rigidity, the second girl bent low within her enclosure and gratefully stepped out into freedom again.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Miss Copp,” she declared with sincerity, “you must believe that my sole intention when I glanced through the window of your pantry was to find out whether a willow-ware platter was in your possession; nothing more came to my attention, nor did I seek to observe anything further.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Bless you, that’s all right,” Miss Sarah pleasantly remarked. “There is no need for you to worry—no damage has been done. Thank goodness, the pantries of us Copps are kept presentable continually and we do not mind who looks inside them. Regarding that old duckhouse, its destruction pleases me, because perhaps Martha will consent to its removal now. Before this, she refused every time since she thought it could be useful eventually, forcing me to whitewash it each spring. However, attempting to reason with Martha is like arguing with a post. She traveled to town today—I took her in the carriage to the station. So, you wish to purchase my platter. Well, how much will you offer me for it?”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Twenty dollars,” Nell stated, though she lacked the shrewdness required to contend in business with a Copp, which was evident from her opening with her asking price.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “I suppose I will think about it,” Miss Sarah stated guardedly. “Luckily, that plate belongs to me, otherwise I would not have the courage to dispose of it in Martha's absence. Even so, I reckon she will make a scene. I assure you that Martha controls this house. Being dominated by a different woman is becoming terribly wearying for me. Nevertheless, enter, enter. You are certainly quite exhausted and famished. As for tea, I will prepare whatever I am able to, though I caution you to anticipate merely bread, butter, and a few cowcumbers. Prior to leaving, Martha placed every piece of cake, cheese, and jam under lock and key. It is her constant practice, as she claims that I consume them excessively whenever visitors arrive.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: The girls possessed an appetite great enough to appreciate any meal, and Miss Sarah’s outstanding bread, butter, and “cowcumbers” gave them complete enjoyment. As soon as they finished eating, Miss Sarah said,

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “I am not sure I object to disposing of the platter. However, twenty-five dollars is its value. The platter is extremely old.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: Isolde nudged Nell’s foot softly beneath the table, which signified, “Don’t agree—she’ll let it go for twenty if you hold out.” Nell, however, had no intention of risking the loss of that valuable platter. Without delay, she consented to pay twenty-five, causing Miss Sarah to appear regretful that thirty had not been her asking price.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Well, I suppose it can be yours. Right now, I need to raise every bit of cash I can. The truth of the matter is—” tossing her head with an air of consequence, a glowing, triumphant color touched Miss Sarah’s narrow cheeks—“I am getting married—to Luther Wallace. Two decades back, he desired to marry me. My feelings for him were quite strong, yet his circumstances were poor at the time, so father sent him away. It seems I ought not to have surrendered him so submissively, yet father intimidated me and made me fearful. On top of that, I failed to realize that men were in such short supply.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: As soon as the girls had departed in safety, with Isolde at the wheel and Nell cautiously clutching the treasured platter upon her knees, the verdant, rain-cleansed emptiness of the Tory Road echoed with waves of youthful female laughter.

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “When I travel into town on the next day, I will entertain your Aunt Lavinia with the ‘strange eventful history’ regarding this afternoon. Our experience was somewhat difficult, yet it has come to a close. The platter is in my possession, and the dust has been settled wonderfully by that rain. Consequently, ‘all’s well that ends well.’”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “We haven’t reached home yet,” Isolde remarked with a somewhat pessimistic tone, “and it is impossible to predict what might occur prior to our arrival. Nell, you have a penchant for experiencing adventures.”

chapter_title: XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road
text: “Experiencing adventures happens naturally for certain individuals,” stated Nell placidly. “Either a person possesses a knack for them, or they do not.”

“When it comes down to it,” Nell had formerly remarked to Thirza, “I feel that the most delightful and charming days are not the ones where something exceptionally grand, marvelous, or thrilling takes place, but simply those offering modest small delights, coming softly one after another, akin to pearls sliding from a thread.”

An existence at Grey Shutters consisted of precisely those kinds of days, because the adventures and misadventures of Nell, much like those of everybody else, failed to occur all at the same time, being instead scattered throughout the year with extensive periods of safe, joyful days in between, packed with labor, daydreams, merriment, and schooling. Towards the end of August, one of those days arrived. During the morning, Nell alongside Isolde used a rowboat to take the thrilled twins down the pond toward the sandshore so they could gather “sweet grass” and wade through the surf, above which a ancient song, mastered when the earth was new, was being played by the wind.

During the afternoon, Nell made her way to the old Stanhope place so she could visit Cedric. Beside the dense fir grove offering protection to the north side of the house, she discovered him lying extended on the grassy bank, completely engrossed in a fairy-tale book. Upon catching sight of her, he leaped to his feet with radiant joy.

“Oh, teacher, your arrival makes me so happy,” he said with enthusiasm, “since Grandma is not here. Won't you remain and share tea with me? Having tea completely alone feels so lonely. You understand, teacher. I truly considered requesting that Young Mary Joe join me at the table for her tea, although I anticipate Grandma would not like that. According to her, the French must be kept where they belong. Furthermore, conversing with Young Mary Joe is hard. She simply chuckles and remarks, ‘Well, yous do beat all de kids I ever knowed.’ My notion of conversation is not that.”

“Naturally I will remain for tea,” Nell stated cheerfully. “I was longing for an invitation. Ever since I previously had tea in this place, I have been craving another taste of the mouthwatering shortbread made by your grandma.”
Cedric appeared extremely grave.

“Were it up to my own wishes, teacher,” he remarked, remaining in front of Nell while keeping his hands inside his pockets as an unexpected look of concern clouded his lovely small face, “I would gladly give you shortbread. However, Mary Joe is the one who decides. Before departing, Grandma was overheard by me instructing her that I was not to be allowed any shortcake since it was excessively rich for the stomachs of young boys. Even so, Mary Joe might perhaps slice a portion for you provided I give my word not to consume a bite. We should wish for a favorable outcome.”

“Yes, let us,” concurred Nell, who found this optimistic outlook entirely to her liking, “and if Mary Joe turns out to be ungenerous and refuses to hand over any shortbread it is of no consequence whatsoever, which means you must not feel anxious about it.”
“Are you certain it won’t bother you if she fails to do so?” Cedric asked in an anxious manner.
“Absolutely certain, my love.”

“In that case, I will not be anxious,” Cedric remarked, exhaling deeply in relief, “particularly because I truly believe Mary Joe will hear reason. Naturally, she is not an unreasonable individual, yet experience has taught her that going against Grandma’s commands is a mistake. Grandma is a fine woman, but folks are required to obey her. She felt extremely delighted with me earlier today since I finally contrived to consume my entire plate of porridge. Succeeding required a major exertion. Grandma remarks that she believes she may still turn me into a man. However, teacher, I need to pose a most critical query to you. You are going to give me an honest reply, aren't you?”
“I’ll try,” Nell promised.
“Am I out of my mind, do you believe?” inquired Cedric, as though her response held the weight of his entire life.
“Goodness, no, Cedric,” Nell uttered with surprise. “You definitely are not. Whatever made you think that?”

“Mary Joe . . . however, she was unaware that I overheard her. The hired girl of Mrs. Peter Mott, Veronica, visited Mary Joe yesterday evening, and their conversation in the kitchen reached my ears while I traversed the hall. I overheard Mary Joe remark, ‘Dat Cedric, he is de queeres’ leetle boy. He talks dat queer. I tink dere’s someting wrong in his upper story.’ For a very long time last night, I was unable to sleep because I was pondering her words and questioning whether Mary Joe could be correct. Somehow, I was unable to bring myself to question Grandma regarding the matter, yet I resolved to query you instead. It brings me such joy that you believe the upper story of my mind is completely fine.”

“Naturally you are. Mary Joe is a foolish, uneducated girl, and you must not ever trouble yourself over whatever she tells you,” Nell declared with indignation, privately deciding to subtly suggest to Mrs. Stanhope that it would be wise to curb Mary Joe’s speech.

“Well, that eases my worries,” Cedric remarked. “Thanks to you, teacher, I am completely contented at present. Having a flaw in your head wouldn't be pleasant, would it, teacher? Mary Joe probably thinks I do because I occasionally share my thoughts about things with her, I presume.”
“That is quite a perilous thing to do,” acknowledged Nell, drawing from her personal background.

“Well, eventually I will share with you the ideas I expressed to Mary Joe, and you may judge on your own whether they contain anything strange,” Cedric said, “however, I am going to delay until dusk starts to fall. That happens to be the period when I long to disclose things to others, and whenever no one else is around, I simply must confide in Mary Joe. But following this, I will refrain from doing so if it causes her to think my mind is unbalanced. I will simply suffer the longing in silence.”

“And should the pain become overly severe, you may travel to Grey Shutters to share your ideas with me,” proposed Nell, employing the complete seriousness that made her beloved by youngsters, who truly adore being treated earnestly.

“Yes, I will. However, my wish is that Robin is absent upon my arrival, as he pulls expressions at me. It does not bother me greatly since he is a mere child while I am rather grown-up, yet having expressions pulled at one remains disagreeable. Furthermore, Robin pulls exceptionally dreadful ones. At times, I fear his expression will remain permanently distorted. He pulls them toward me during service, precisely when sacred matters should occupy my thoughts. Lucy enjoys my company, nevertheless, and I enjoy hers, albeit less than prior to her revealing to Posy Fay Pembroke her intention of marrying me upon my reaching adulthood. Although I might wed someone once I am grown, I remain entirely too youthful to contemplate such things presently, wouldn't you agree, teacher?”
“Quite young,” concurred teacher.

“Mentioning marriage brings to my mind a different matter that has been bothering me recently,” Cedric went on. “On a day last week, Mrs. Sowerby came over to have tea alongside Grandma, and Grandma forced me to display the portrait of my little mother to her . . . the picture sent by father as my birthday gift. Showing it to Mrs. Sowerby wasn't something I really wished to do. Mrs. Sowerby is a good, kind woman, yet she lacks the qualities of someone you would choose to see your mother's image. You understand, teacher. Naturally, however, I did as Grandma instructed. Mrs. Sowerby remarked that she was extremely pretty yet appeared rather actressy, and had to be a great deal younger than father. After that, she inquired, ‘Some of these days your pa will be marrying again likely. How will you like to have a new ma, Master Cedric?’ Truly, that thought left me nearly breathless, teacher, yet I refused to allow Mrs. Sowerby to notice it. I simply stared directly into her face . . . in this manner . . . and I replied, ‘Mrs. Sowerby, father made a pretty good job of picking out my first mother and I could trust him to pick out just as good a one the second time.’ And teacher, I truly can trust him. Even so, I desire that, should he ever provide me with a new mother, he will seek my thoughts regarding her prior to it being too late. Mary Joe is approaching to summon us for tea. I am going to talk over the shortbread with her.”

Because of the “consultation,” Mary Joe divided the shortbread and included a dish of preserves on the menu. Nell served the tea, and she and Cedric enjoyed an extremely cheerful meal inside the dark old sitting room with its windows unclosed to the winds from the gulf, and the pair conversed with so much “nonsense” that Mary Joe felt rather shocked and mentioned to Veronica the following night that “de school mees” matched Cedric in being strange. Following tea, Cedric brought Nell to his bedroom so he could display his mother’s portrait, which served as the secret birthday gift Mrs. Stanhope had stored inside the bookcase. Cedric’s small room with its low ceiling formed a gentle swirl of reddish illumination originating from the sun going down over the ocean and moving shadows produced by the fir trees growing near the square, deeply set window. Emerging from this soft radiance and enchantment was a lovely, youthful face possessing gentle mother eyes, which hung upon the wall located at the bed's foot.

“That’s my little mother,” Cedric said, filled with affectionate pride. “I persuaded Grandma to place it right there so it would be the first thing I saw upon waking every morning. Now I do not care at all about being in the dark when going to sleep, for it feels as though my little mother is right beside me. Even though he never inquired, Father understood exactly what I desired for a birthday gift. Isn’t the extent of what fathers know truly remarkable?”
“Cedric, your mother possessed great beauty, and you bear a slight resemblance to her. However, she had hair and eyes of a darker shade than yours.”

“Father’s eyes and mine share the exact same shade,” Cedric mentioned, zipping across the space to stack every cushion he could find upon the window seat, “though gray is the color of father’s hair. It remains thick, yet it has turned gray. Father has almost reached fifty years, you know. Such an advanced age, wouldn't you say? However, his aging is purely external. Internally, he retains a youthfulness equal to anyone else. Now, I ask that you be seated here, teacher; while my spot will be down by your feet. Would you mind if I rest my head against your knee? Sitting together in this manner was the custom for my little mother and me. Oh, I feel this is truly wonderful.”

“Now, I wish to listen to the ideas that Mary Joe deems so strange,” stated Nell, stroking the thick head of ringlets beside her. Cedric required no persuasion whatsoever to share his reflections . . . provided the listeners were like-minded, at any rate.

“I came up with them in the fir grove one evening,” he stated absentmindedly. “I didn’t actually believe them, naturally, yet I thought them. You understand, teacher. Then I desired to share them with someone, and no one else was available except Mary Joe. While Mary Joe was preparing bread in the pantry, I took a seat on the bench next to her and I said, ‘Mary Joe, do you know what I think? I think the evening star is a lighthouse on the land where the fairies dwell.’ To which Mary Joe responded, ‘Well, yous are de queer one. Dare ain’t no such ting as fairies.’ This annoyed me greatly. I was well aware, naturally, that fairies do not exist; nevertheless, that should not stop me from imagining they do. You understand, teacher. Still, I made another attempt with great patience. I said, ‘Well then, Mary Joe, do you know what I think? I think an angel walks over the world after the sun sets . . . a great, tall, white angel, with silvery folded wings . . . and sings the flowers and birds to sleep. Children can hear him if they know how to listen.’ At that point, Mary Joe raised her hands, which were covered in flour, and said, ‘Well, yous are de queer leetle boy. Yous make me feel scare.’ Indeed, she truly appeared frightened. I departed at that moment and breathed the remainder of my ideas to the garden. A small birch tree stood in the garden, and it perished. Grandma claims its death was caused by salt spray; I believe, however, that the dryad attached to it was a silly dryad that roamed off to explore the world and became lost. Consequently, the small tree felt so desolate that a broken heart killed it.”
“And whenever the unfortunate, senseless small dryad grows weary of the world and returns to her tree, it will break her heart,” Nell remarked.

“Indeed; yet should dryads be silly they ought to accept the results, precisely as though they were actual humans,” Cedric remarked solemnly. “Are you aware of my thoughts regarding the new moon, teacher? It strikes me as a tiny golden vessel packed with dreams.”
“And whenever it leans against a cloud, a few of them tumble out, dropping into your dreams.”

“Precisely, teacher. Ah, you truly understand. Furthermore, it is my belief that the violets are small clippings of the heavens that dropped down as the angels excised apertures for the stars to gleam through. Likewise, the buttercups are fashioned from aged sunlight; and I believe that the sweet peas are destined to become butterflies upon reaching heaven. At present, teacher, do you perceive anything exceedingly strange regarding these ideas?”

“No, my darling boy, those ideas are not odd in the least; they are remarkable and lovely reflections for a young lad to hold, which is why individuals who could never imagine anything similar, even given a century to attempt it, consider them odd. However, Cedric, continue to hold these thoughts . . . it is my belief that you will grow up to be a poet eventually.”

Upon arriving home, Nell discovered a completely contrasting kind of boyishness anticipating bedtime. Robin was in a bad mood; after Nell had taken off his clothes, he leaped into bed and hid his face within the pillow.
“Robin, you have neglected to utter your prayers,” Nell said in a tone of rebuke.

“No, I didn’t forget,” Robin stated with defiance, “but saying my prayers isn't something I'll do henceforth. Trying to be good is something I'll abandon, since you’d prefer Cedric Stanhope regardless of how well I behave. Having the enjoyment of being bad makes just as much sense, then.”
“Cedric Stanhope is not someone I like more,” Nell stated with gravity. “My affection for you is every bit as great, merely of another nature.”
“However, I desire for you to care for me in that exact manner,” Robin pouted.
“Different people cannot be liked in identical fashion. Is it true that you fail to like Lucy and me in the same manner?”
Robin sat upright and pondered.
“Na . . . a . . . ay,” he finally confessed, “I’m fond of Lucy on account of her being my sister, yet my fondness for you stems from who you are.”
“And Cedric is dear to me simply for being Cedric, while Robin is dear for being Robin,” Nell remarked lightheartedly.

“Well, I sort of wish I had offered my prayers at that time,” remarked Robin, persuaded by this reasoning. “However, it requires far too much effort to climb out now and speak them. I will recite them two times tomorrow morning, Nell. Will that not serve just as well?”

No, Nell felt certain that it would fail to serve as effectively. Consequently, Robin climbed out and assumed a kneeling position by her knee. Once his prayers were completed, he rocked back upon his small, uncovered, brown heels and raised his eyes toward her.
“Nell, my behavior has improved compared to before.”
“Yes, indeed you are, Robin,” said Nell, who was always quick to acknowledge merit when it was earned.
