“I am aware that I am better,” Robin stated with assurance, “and I will explain to you the way I am sure of it. Thirza provided me with two slices of bread and jam today, intending one for myself and one for Lucy. A particular piece was much larger than the second one, yet Thirza failed to specify which belonged to me. Nevertheless, I handed the larger portion over to Lucy. It was virtuous of me, was it not?”
“Robin, that is very good, and it is also very manly.”

“To be sure,” Robin conceded, “Lucy didn’t have much of an appetite and she ate merely half of her piece before handing the remainder over to me. However, I had no idea she would do such a thing when I handed it to her, which means I was well-behaved, Nell.”

As dusk fell, Nell strolled toward the Nymph’s Well and spotted Hugh Carrow descending through the shadowy Whispering Wood. It abruptly occurred to her that Hugh was not a schoolboy anymore. He appeared so manly—a tall, open-faced guy possessing broad shoulders and eyes that were bright and direct. Hugh struck Nell as an exceptionally good-looking youth, despite failing to resemble her picture of a dream man in any way. A long time back, she and Isolde had chosen the sort of man they held in high regard, and their preferences appeared to be identical. Such a man had to be quite tall and appear refined, featuring eyes that were somber and mysterious, alongside a voice that was tender and full of understanding. Hugh’s face displayed nothing gloomy or secretive, yet naturally that was unimportant where friendship was concerned!

Hugh reclined upon the ferns next to the Bubble, gazing at Nell with admiration. Had anyone requested that Hugh portray his perfect woman, the portrayal would have matched Nell in every detail, including the seven small freckles whose unwelcome existence persisted in bothering her spirit. Hugh remained scarcely more than a youth; nevertheless, a youth possesses his visions just as others do, and within Hugh’s destiny there was constantly a maiden possessing large, clear gray eyes, along with a countenance as refined and fragile as a blossom. Furthermore, he had resolved that his upcoming life ought to be deserving of its divinity. Even within tranquil Brierley, there existed trials that had to be encountered and confronted. The young people of Pale Sands constituted a somewhat “fast” group, and Hugh enjoyed popularity in every place he visited. However, he intended to remain deserving of Nell’s companionship and, possibly on some remote occasion, her affection; thus, he guarded his speech, mind, and actions with as much vigilance as if her transparent eyes would evaluate them. Over him, she exercised the unwitting sway that any maiden, possessing lofty and virtuous principles, exerts upon her companions; an authority that would persist provided she remained true to those principles, and one she would just as surely forfeit should she ever prove disloyal to them. From Hugh’s perspective, Nell’s most appealing quality was that she never descended to the trivial habits of numerous Brierley maidens—the petty envy, the minor dishonesties and competitions, the obvious attempts to gain approval. Nell maintained her distance from all these things, neither deliberately nor by intention, but merely because anything like that was completely alien to her open, spontaneous temperament, which was perfectly transparent in its intentions and desires.

However, Hugh made no effort to express his feelings aloud, because he was already well aware that Nell would coldly and unfeelingly crush any try at romance before it could bloom—or make fun of him, which felt ten times more terrible.
“Under that birch tree, you resemble a genuine dryad,” he remarked in a playful tone.
“I love birch trees,” said Nell, placing her face beside the pale, silky bark of the slender trunk, employing a lovely, tender movement that seemed so effortless for her.

“Then you’ll be pleased to learn that Mr. Major Tranter has made up his mind to plant a line of white birches all across the road front of his farm, in order to promote the B.V.I.S.,” remarked Hugh. “He was speaking with me regarding it today. Major Tranter is the most forward-thinking and civic-minded person in Brierley. And Mr. William Bell plans to plant a spruce hedge down his road front and along his lane. Our Society is doing wonderfully, Nell. It has moved beyond the trial phase and become an established reality. The older people are starting to show interest in it and the folks in Pale Sands are considering forming one as well. Even Elisha Duckett changed his mind after that afternoon the Americans from the hotel held a picnic at the beach. They complimented our roadsides so enthusiastically and declared they were far more attractive than anywhere else on the Island. And when, at the proper time, the rest of the farmers imitate Mr. Tranter’s fine lead and put in decorative trees and hedges along their road fronts Brierley is going to be the loveliest community in the province.”

“The Aids are discussing the idea of renovating the cemetery,” Nell stated, “and I am hoping they do so, since a fundraiser must be organized for it, and attempting it following the hall business would prove useless for the Society. Yet, had the Society not informally suggested it to them, the Aids would not have taken any initiative regarding the issue. The churchyard trees that were planted by us are doing well, while a commitment has been made to me by the trustees to enclose the schoolyard during the upcoming year. Should that occur, an arbor day will be held by me where a tree will be planted by each student; additionally, a garden will be established by us in the roadside corner.”

“Except for having the old Gammon house torn down, we’ve managed nearly every one of our schemes up to now,” Hugh remarked, “and I’ve abandoned that attempt out of hopelessness. Levi refuses to allow its removal merely to annoy us. Every one of the Boulters possesses a stubborn trait, which is heavily marked in him.”
“Although Julia Bell wishes to dispatch a further committee to see him, I believe we would do better by simply leaving him strictly by himself,” Nell advised wisely.

“And put your faith in Providence, as Mrs. Sowerby remarks,” Hugh smiled. “Indeed, no further committees. He is only irritated by them. Julia Bell believes that provided you have a committee to try it, anything can be accomplished. Come next spring, Nell, an agitation for pleasant grounds and lawns must be launched by us. Good seed will be sown by us early this winter. A treatise on lawns and lawnmaking is in my possession here and a paper regarding the topic is going to be prepared by me shortly. Well, it seems to me our vacation has nearly ended. On Monday, school opens. Was the Delford school obtained by Opal Pettigrew?”

“Yes; Honora mentioned in her letter that she was employed at her home school, which led the Delford trustees to assign the position to Opal. Honora’s absence is a disappointment to me, yet because her return is impossible, Opal’s appointment brings me joy. Saturdays will bring her back home, recreating the past as she, Odette, Isolde, and I gather once more.”
As Nell came back to the house, Thirza, who had newly arrived home from Mrs. Sowerby’s, sat upon the step of the back porch.

“Agatha and I are going to take our boat trip into town tomorrow,” she stated. “Because Mr. Sowerby feels improved this week, Agatha desires to travel prior to him experiencing a further bout of illness.”

“Tomorrow morning I plan to rise exceedingly early, because there is so much for me to accomplish,” Nell remarked with virtue. “First, I shall transfer the feathers out of the old tick for my bed and into the new one. This should have been completed ages ago, yet I have continually delayed it . . . the chore is so thoroughly unpleasant. Procrastinating over disagreeable duties is a terrible habit, and I intend never to repeat it, or I will be unable to advise my students against it with a clear conscience. Doing so would lack consistency. Furthermore, I wish to bake a cake intended for Mr. Pettifer, complete the essay about gardens I am preparing for the B.V.I.S., send a letter to Mabel, clean and stiffen my muslin dress with starch, and sew a new apron for Lucy.”
“You will not finish even half,” Thirza remarked gloomily. “I have never once intended to accomplish many tasks without an obstacle arising to stop me.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: Nell got up early the following morning and cheerfully welcomed the new day, as the sunrise unfurled its banners victoriously over the pearl-colored skies. Grey Shutters rested in a sunlit pool, dappled with the moving shadows of willow and poplar. Past the property sat Mr. Pettifer’s wheatfield, a vast, breeze-rippled sheet of light gold. The world possessed such beauty that Nell passed ten joyful minutes leaning lazily across the garden gate taking the charm in.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: When breakfast was finished, Thirza prepared to set out on her trip. Lucy, who had been promised this enjoyment for a long time, was scheduled to accompany her.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “Now, Robin, you attempt to be a well-behaved boy and do not annoy Nell,” she strictly instructed him. “If you behave yourself I will get you a striped candy cane from town.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: For regrettably, Thirza had lowered herself to the wicked practice of paying off individuals so that they would behave well!

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “I won’t be bad intentionally, but what if I’m bad accidentally?” Robin wished to learn.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “You must be careful to avoid mishaps,” cautioned Thirza. “Nell, should Mr. Shearer arrive today, purchase a good roast and a portion of steak. Should he fail to appear, you will need to butcher a bird for tomorrow’s midday meal.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: Nell gave a nod.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “For simply Robin and me today, I won't trouble myself to cook dinner,” she said. “For lunch at noon, that cold ham bone is enough, and once you return home in the evening, I'll fry up some steak for you.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “This morning, I am going to assist Mr. Pettifer in hauling dulse,” declared Robin. “Since he invited me, I expect he will also invite me for dinner. A terribly good man is Mr. Pettifer. He is a truly friendly man. When I am older, I hope to resemble him. That is, act as he does . . . I have no desire to resemble his appearance. However, I suppose that is unlikely, because according to Mrs. Sowerby, I am a quite good-looking youngster. Nell, do you think it will remain that way? I am curious to know?”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “I believe it certainly shall,” Nell remarked solemnly. “Robin, you are an attractive young man,” . . . Thirza’s expression conveyed deep disapprobation . . . “however, you have to match that appearance by acting every bit as polite and well-mannered as you seem.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “And the other day, when Posy Fay Pembroke was crying because somebody called her ugly, you informed her that people wouldn't care about her appearance if she was loving and kind and nice,” Robin remarked unhappily. “It appears to me that, for one reason or another, you simply cannot escape being good in this world. You are forced to behave.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “Do you not wish to be good?” questioned Thirza, a person who had acquired much knowledge but had still to understand how useless it was to ask these things.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “Indeed, my desire is to be good, though not excessively so,” Robin remarked with care. “A person isn't required to be particularly good in order to serve as a Sunday School superintendent. Mr. Bell holds that position, and he is truly a wicked man.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “Most certainly he isn’t,” Marila stated with indignation.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “He is . . . he claims he is himself,” Robin declared. “During his prayer in Sunday School last Sunday, he uttered it. He declared that he was a vile worm, a miserable sinner, and responsible for the blackest ‘niquity. What was the terrible thing he did, Thirza? Did he murder someone? Or did he take the collection pennies? I want to know.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: By good fortune, Mrs. Sowerby drove up the lane just then, prompting Thirza to depart with a sense of having fled the fowler's trap, while earnestly hoping that Mr. Bell would use fewer elaborate figures of speech during his public prayers, particularly when listened to by young boys who were constantly “wanting to know.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: Nell, who had been left alone in her glory, set to work with a will. She swept the floor, made the beds, fed the hens, and washed the muslin dress before hanging it out on the line. After that, Nell made preparations to transfer the feathers. Going up to the garret, she put on the first old dress she happened to find . . . a navy blue cashmere that she used to wear when she was fourteen. It was certainly rather short and just as “skimpy” as the famous wincey Nell had been wearing when she made her debut at Grey Shutters; however, it would not suffer any significant harm from down and feathers. Nell finished dressing by tying over her head a large red and white spotted handkerchief that had once been owned by Obed, and, outfitted in this manner, she went to the kitchen chamber, where Thirza had assisted her in carrying the feather bed prior to her departure.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: Beside the room's window hung a mirror with a crack, and Nell happened to glance inside it at an unfortunate time. Positioned on her nose were those seven freckles, appearing to be even more prominent than before, or at least that was how they looked under the bright illumination streaming from the bare window.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “Oh, I omitted applying that lotion yesterday evening,” it occurred to her. “I ought to hurry to the pantry to put it on right away.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: Nell had undergone numerous ordeals in her efforts to erase those spots. At one point, her nose lost its outer layer of skin entirely, yet the freckles persisted. Only a couple of days before, a magazine provided her with a formula for a freckle-clearing wash, and because the components were accessible to her, she mixed it up immediately, deeply offending Thirza, who believed that if Providence saw fit to put freckles on a person's nose, that person was obligated to keep them there.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: Nell hurried down into the pantry, a room that was perpetually shaded by the large willow tree near the window and had now become nearly pitch-black because the blind was lowered to keep out flies. Grabbing the bottle of lotion off the shelf, Nell generously slathered her nose using a tiny sponge reserved exclusively for that task. Having completed this essential chore, she went back to her labor. Anyone who has undertaken the transfer of feathers between ticks does not require an explanation to understand the spectacle Nell presented upon finishing. Down and fluff turned her dress white, while the front of her hair, which had slipped out from beneath her handkerchief, was decorated with a true ring of feathers. It was during this favorable instance that a knock rang out at the kitchen door.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “Mr. Shearer must be here,” Nell reflected. “My appearance is terribly untidy, yet I must rush downstairs just like this because he is perpetually rushing.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: Down to the kitchen door flew Nell. Should a merciful floor ever split apart to consume an unhappy, plumage-covered maiden, the porch floor of Grey Shutters ought to have swallowed Nell immediately at that instance. Standing upon the doorstep were Honora Hollis, radiant and blonde in silk clothing, a brief, heavy-set, silver-haired woman wearing a tweed suit, and one more woman, lofty, majestic, extraordinarily dressed, possessing a lovely, refined visage and big, dark-lashed violet eyes, who Nell “instinctively felt,” as she might have expressed it during her younger years, was Mrs. Charlotte E. Varley.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: Amid the horror of that instance, a single idea emerged clearly from the turmoil of Nell’s thoughts, and she clutched it like the legendary straw. Every heroine created by Mrs. Varley was famous for “rising to the occasion.” Regardless of their misfortunes, they always rose to the occasion, proving themselves above every hardship of time, space, and quantity. Consequently, Nell believed she had an obligation to rise to the occasion, and she accomplished this so flawlessly that Honora later stated she had never held Nell Harcourt in higher esteem than at that instant. Whatever her offended emotions might have been, she hid them completely. She welcomed Honora and was presented to her friends with as much composure and calmness as though she were dressed in purple and fine linen. Granted, discovering that the woman she had intuitively assumed to be Mrs. Varley was actually a stranger named Mrs. Pendexter, whereas the plump, small, gray-haired lady was Mrs. Varley, came as a bit of a surprise; yet within the larger distress, this smaller one lost its effect. Nell led her visitors to the guest bedroom and then into the parlor, leaving them there while she hurried outside to assist Honora in unharnessing her horse.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “I am sorry to drop in on you so suddenly,” Honora offered as an excuse, “however, it was only yesterday evening that I learned about our trip. Aunt Charlotte leaves on Monday, and she had agreed to pass this day alongside a city friend. Yesterday evening, though, this friend called her on the phone to cancel the visit since scarlet fever had put them under quarantine. Consequently, I proposed that we travel to this place, as I was aware of how much you wished to visit her. After stopping by the Pale Sands Hotel, we picked up Mrs. Pendexter to join us. Being an acquaintance of aunt’s, she resides in New York, and a millionaire is her husband. Our visit must be brief, because Mrs. Pendexter needs to return to the hotel before five o’clock.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: Nell noticed Honora glancing at her secretly and with confusion on multiple occasions as they were stabling the horse.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “There is no reason for her to gaze at me in that manner,” Nell reflected with a slight touch of indignation. “If she lacks firsthand knowledge of turning a feather bed, she could at least picture what it entails.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: After Honora had departed for the parlor, and prior to Nell's ability to flee to the upper floor, Isolde stepped into the kitchen. Grabbing her arm, Nell held her startled friend.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “Isolde Pembroke, who do you imagine is occupying that parlor right now? Mrs. Charlotte E. Varley . . . alongside the wife of a New York millionaire . . . while I am in this state . . . and there is nothing at all to serve for dinner except a cold ham bone, Isolde!”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: At this point Nell realized that Isolde was gazing at her with the exact same confused expression that Honora had shown. It truly exceeded all limits.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “Oh, Isolde, do not regard me in that manner,” she begged. “It ought to be clear to you, above everyone else, that even the most meticulous individual could not transfer feathers between two ticks and stay tidy throughout.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “It . . . it . . . is not the feathers,” Isolde paused. “It’s . . . it’s . . . your nose, Nell.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “My nose? Oh, Isolde, certainly there is nothing amiss with it!”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: Nell hurried toward the small mirror above the sink. A single look confirmed the disastrous reality. Her nose shone a bright red!

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: Nell took a seat upon the sofa, her brave heart finally humbled.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “What is the problem with it?” Isolde inquired, her inquisitiveness surpassing her sense of propriety.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “I believed I was applying my freckle lotion to it, but I must have chosen that red dye Thirza uses to trace the pattern on her rugs,” came the hopeless reply. “What am I to do?”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “Rinse it away,” Isolde stated in a matter-of-fact tone.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “Maybe it will not wash away. Initially I color my hair; after that I color my nose. Thirza sheared my hair away when I colored it but that cure would scarcely be feasible regarding this situation. Ah well, this serves as an additional penalty for vanity and I imagine I merit it . . . even if there is little solace in that thought. It actually is nearly sufficient to render a person a believer in bad luck, even though Mrs. Sowerby claims no such phenomenon exists, since all things are preordained.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: Lucky for her, the dye was removed without difficulty, and Nell, feeling a bit better, retreated to the east gable as Isolde hurried back to her house. Shortly after, Nell returned downstairs, dressed and restored to her senses. Because the muslin dress she had eagerly anticipated wearing was dancing cheerfully on the outdoor clothesline, she had no choice but to settle for her black lawn instead. She had already started the fire and set the tea to steep by the time Isolde came back; the second girl was actually wearing her muslin, and she held a dish with a lid in her hand.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “Your mother has provided this for you,” she stated, raising the lid and exposing a beautifully carved and jointed chicken to the appreciative eyes of Nell.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: To the chicken were added fresh, light bread, fine butter and cheese, fruit cake from Thirza, and a bowl of preserved plums submerged in golden syrup that resembled solidified summer sun. A large basin filled with pink-and-white asters served as an ornament; nevertheless, the meal appeared quite scant when compared to the lavish feast previously made for Mrs. Varley.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: The famished visitors of Nell, nevertheless, appeared to find nothing missing and consumed the basic food with clear pleasure. Yet following the initial moments, Nell ceased considering what her menu did or did not contain. The look of Mrs. Varley could perhaps be rather unsatisfactory, a fact her faithful admirers had been compelled to concede to one another; however, she turned out to be a charming talker. Having journeyed widely, she was a superb raconteur. She had observed many men and women, condensing her observations into humorous short statements and adages that made her audience feel like they were hearing a character from smart literature. Yet beneath her entire radiance existed a deeply perceived baseline of genuine, feminine empathy and benevolence that captured love just as effortlessly as her genius captured esteem. Furthermore, she did not dominate the talk. She possessed the skill to elicit responses from others as adeptly and completely as she was able to speak herself, leading Nell and Isolde to discover that they were conversing with her without restraint. Mrs. Pendexter spoke minimally; she simply offered smiles with her beautiful eyes and lips, and consumed chicken, fruit cake, and preserves with a grace so refined that she gave off the sense of feasting on ambrosia and honeydew. Nevertheless, as Nell remarked to Isolde afterward, a person as heavenly gorgeous as Mrs. Pendexter was not required to speak; existing solely to be looked at was sufficient for her.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: Following dinner, the entire group took a stroll along Linger Lane, Primrose Dell, and the Aspen Path, before returning by way of the Whispering Wood to the Nymph’s Well, at which spot they seated themselves and conversed for an enchanting final thirty minutes. Mrs. Varley inquired about the origin of the Whispering Wood's name, and she wept with laughter upon listening to the tale and Nell’s theatrical description of a particular unforgettable walk taken through it during the magical time of dusk.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “It certainly was an intellectual feast and a soulful exchange, wasn’t it?” Nell remarked once her visitors had left and only she and Isolde remained behind. “I’m unsure what gave me greater pleasure . . . hearing Mrs. Varley speak or looking at Mrs. Pendexter. My feeling is that our time was even more delightful than if their arrival had been anticipated and we had been burdened with preparing a great meal. You have to remain for tea with me, Isolde, so that we can discuss everything.”

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “Honora says that an English earl is married to the sister of Mrs. Pendexter’s husband; and she nevertheless had a second portion of the plum preserves,” Isolde said, as though those two statements were somehow contradictory.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “I reckon that Thirza’s plum preserves wouldn't have been sneezed at even by the English earl himself,” Nell stated with pride.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: That evening, as Nell recounted the events of the day to Thirza, she omitted the calamity that had happened to her nose. She did, however, grab the bottle containing freckle lotion and pour its contents out the window.

chapter_title: XX The Way It Often Happens
text: “I am never going to attempt any beautifying messes again,” she stated, with grim determination. “They might work for people who are cautious and deliberate; however, for someone as completely prone to making errors as I appear to be, it is inviting trouble to mess with them.”

Classes commenced and Nell went back to her job, possessing a lot more experience though significantly fewer theories. Her new students numbered several, six- and seven-year-olds who were merely stepping, wide-eyed, into a marvel-filled world. Robin and Lucy were included in this group. Robin was seated alongside Milty Gammon, a pupil for a year already and thus rather a man of the world. At Sunday School on the preceding Sunday, Lucy had formed an agreement to sit beside Lily Mott; however, because Lily Mott failed to appear on day one, she was provisionally placed with Mirabel Cotton, a ten-year-old who was, from Lucy’s perspective, among the “big girls.”

Upon returning that evening, Robin remarked to Thirza, “School strikes me as wonderful entertainment. It turned out you were right about the difficulty of remaining motionless . . . I've observed that your statements are usually truthful . . . yet shifting your legs beneath the furniture provides considerable relief. Having numerous male companions for games is marvelous. My desk partner is Milty Gammon, who is great. Although he surpasses my height, my breadth exceeds his. The rear seating is preferable, yet occupying those spots requires limbs extended sufficiently to reach the ground. On his slate, Milty rendered a likeness of Nell that looked hideous, prompting my warning that repeating such depictions of Nell would result in my thrashing him during break time. My initial inclination was creating his portrait complete with tail and horns, but concern over damaging his sentiments held me back, since Nell teaches that causing emotional distress is strictly forbidden. Suffering hurt feelings is apparently a terrible ordeal. Should action be required, felling a boy physically is preferable to injuring his feelings. While claiming no fear of me, Milty offered to assign another identity to accommodate me, whereupon he erased the name of Nell and substituted Barbara Shaw's in print beneath the image. His dislike for Barbara stems from her addressing him as a sweet little boy and having once stroked his hair.”

Lucy stated demurely that she enjoyed school; nevertheless, she remained exceedingly silent, even by her own standards; and as dusk fell, upon Thirza instructing her to retire to bed on the upper floor, she paused and started weeping.
“I’m . . . I’m scared,” she wept. “I . . . I don’t wish to ascend to the upper floor by myself in the pitch-black.”
“What idea have you put in your mind now?” Thirza asked. “I know you have retired to bed by yourself throughout the summer and have not been scared until now.”
Nell gathered Lucy up into her arms, gave her a compassionate cuddle, and murmured while she kept weeping,
“Disclose everything to Nell, my love. What is causing you fear?”

“Of . . . of Mirabel Cotton’s uncle,” Lucy wept. “In school today, Mirabel Cotton related everything concerning her family to me. Almost all the people in her family are dead . . . every one of her grandfathers and grandmothers, along with a great many uncles and aunts. According to Mirabel, dying is a habit they have. Mirabel feels terribly proud about possessing such a large number of deceased relatives, and she described to me the cause of death for each one, as well as their final words and their appearance inside their coffins. Furthermore, Mirabel states that after his burial, a certain uncle of hers was spotted roaming about the house. Her mother observed him. The others do not bother me quite as much, but I am unable to stop reflecting on that uncle.”

Nell accompanied Lucy to the upper floor and remained beside her until sleep overtook her. On the following day, Mirabel Cotton was detained during the break and was made to comprehend, “gently but firmly,” that if one happened to be so unlucky as to have an uncle who insisted on wandering through dwellings following a proper burial, discussing that peculiar gentleman with a young classmate sharing one's desk lacked good taste. Mirabel considered this exceedingly severe. The Cottons possessed very little to brag about. In what manner could she maintain her standing with her fellow pupils if she was not allowed to profit from the ghost in her family?
The passing of September led into the gracious gold and crimson of October. Isolde visited one Friday evening.

“I received a letter from Ella Kimball today, Nell, in which she invites us over to tea tomorrow afternoon so we can meet Irene Trent, her cousin from town. However, we are unable to take any of our horses, since they will every one be busy tomorrow, and your pony is lame . . . therefore I guess we will be unable to go.”

“Why can’t we walk?” proposed Nell. “If we return directly through the woods, we will hit the West Welby road close to the Kimball place. I traveled that route last winter, so I am familiar with the road. The distance is at most four miles, and walking all the way home won't be necessary because Oliver Kimball is certain to give us a ride. Having a reason will make him exceedingly happy, as he visits Carrie Mott and people claim that his father rarely permits him to take a horse.”

It was therefore agreed that they would go on foot, and they departed the next afternoon, travelling along Linger Lane toward the rear of the Abernethy farm, where they discovered a path entering the center of expanse upon expanse of shining beech and maple forests, which were completely transformed into a marvelous radiance of fire and gold, resting in a vast violet tranquility and calm.

“Is it not as though the year is bowing in prayer inside a huge cathedral packed with soft, tinted light?” Nell asked wistfully. “Passing through it hastily feels wrong, doesn't it? Sprinting inside a church would be just as disrespectful.”
“Although we have to move quickly,” Isolde remarked, checking the time on her wrist. “Given how little time remains for us now.”

“Well, I’ll step out quickly, but do not request that I speak,” Nell said, moving faster. “My sole desire is to absorb the beauty of the day . . . It seems to me as though it is being offered to my lips like a goblet of light wine, and each step I take will be a sip.”

It might have been due to her being so preoccupied with “drinking it in” that Nell chose the left fork upon reaching a split in the path. Although the right path was the one she ought to have chosen, she subsequently regarded it as the luckiest error she ever made. Eventually, they emerged onto an isolated, grass-covered track, where the only visible objects were rows of young spruce trees.
“Where on earth have we ended up?” asked Isolde, thoroughly confused. “We aren't on the road to West Welby.”

“No, Middle Welby’s base line road is what this is,” Nell stated, feeling quite embarrassed. “At the fork, I surely went the incorrect way. Although our exact location escapes me, Kimballs’ remains a full three miles away at least.”

“Because it is already four thirty,” Isolde remarked, glancing hopeless at her timepiece, “we will not be able to arrive before five. Our arrival will happen once they finish their tea, which means they will face the full nuisance of preparing ours a second time.”
“It would be best for us to head back home,” meekly offered Nell. Isolde, however, thought about it and then rejected the idea.
“No, we might just as well proceed to pass the evening, seeing that we have traveled all this way.”
Advancing another couple of yards, the girls arrived at a spot where the road split once more.
“Which one of these are we taking?” Isolde asked, sounding uncertain.
Nell gave a shake of her head.
“I am uncertain, and making further errors is beyond our means. This gate and path head straight into the forest. On the far end, there has to be a home. Let’s head down and ask.”

“What a romantic old lane this it,” Isolde remarked, while they traversed its winding path. It stretched beneath ancient, majestic fir trees with overhead intertwining limbs, producing an endless darkness where moss alone was able to thrive. Earthy forest beds bordered both sides, traversed now and then by descending shafts of light. Everything felt extraordinarily quiet and distant, as though the earth and its anxieties were miles removed.

“It seems to me that we are strolling in a magical wood,” Nell uttered softly. “Isolde, do you think we will ever manage to return to the actual world? In a moment, I believe we will arrive at a castle containing a bewitched princess.”

Rounding the subsequent bend, there appeared in their view not a grand palace, but a tiny dwelling nearly as astonishing as a palace would have proved in this region of traditional wooden farmhouses, every one so similar in overall traits that they might have sprouted from identical seed. Nell paused abruptly in delight, and Isolde cried out, “Oh, I know where we are now. That is the little stone house where Miss Rosalind Penrose lives . . . Echo Cottage, she calls it, I think. I’ve often heard of it but I’ve never seen it before. Isn’t it a romantic spot?”
“It is the most charming and lovely spot I have ever witnessed or conceived,” Nell expressed with joy. “It appears just like an excerpt from a fairy tale or a vision.”

Constructed from rough, unpolished blocks of red Island sandstone, the building featured low eaves, a small pointed roof pierced by a pair of dormer windows with unusual wooden hoods above them, and two massive chimneys. Richly draped across the entire structure, ivy clung effortlessly to the coarse masonry, its leaves transformed by autumn frosts into stunning shades of bronze and deep wine-red.

An oblong garden, into which opened the lane gate where the girls were standing, was situated before the house. It was bounded on one side by the house; an old stone dyke enclosed it on the three others, being so overgrown with moss and grass and ferns that a high, green bank was what it resembled. Over it, the tall, dark spruces spread their palm-like branches on the right and left; a little meadow, green with clover aftermath, was below it, however, sloping down to the blue loop of the Welby River. In sight was no other house or clearing . . . covered with feathery young firs were nothing but hills and valleys.
“I wonder what kind of individual Miss Penrose might be,” pondered Isolde while they unlatched the garden gate. “It is said that her ways are quite strange.”

“In that case, she will prove interesting,” Nell declared firmly. “Odd individuals invariably manage to be that much, regardless of what other qualities they possess or lack. Didn’t I say to you that our journey would lead to a spellbound castle? I was certain those elves had not spun enchantment across that path without reason.”
“However, Miss Rosalind Penrose can scarcely be considered an enchanted princess,” Isolde chuckled. “She is a spinster . . . I have been told that she is forty-five and her hair is completely gray.”

“Oh, that is merely a fraction of the enchantment,” Nell declared with certainty. “Deep down she remains youthful and lovely . . . and she would emerge glowing and beautiful once more if we just understood the way to break the magic. Yet we lack that knowledge . . . that secret belongs solely and perpetually to the prince . . . and the prince meant for Miss Rosalind has not arrived so far. Maybe he has met with a disastrous misfortune . . . even if such an outcome violates the rules of every fairy tale.”

“I fear his arrival occurred a while back and his departure followed,” stated Isolde. “It is reported that her engagement to Stephen Stanhope . . . the father of Cedric . . . existed during their youth. However, a disagreement arose, causing them to separate.”
“Be quiet,” Nell cautioned. “That door is unclosed.”

In the porch beneath the ivy tendrils, the girls stopped and knocked upon the open door. A patter of footsteps sounded from within, and a somewhat strange small figure appeared . . . a girl near fourteen years old, possessing a face covered in freckles, a nose that was snubbed, a mouth of such width that it appeared to literally reach “from ear to ear,” and a pair of long fair hair braids fastened with a pair of huge blue ribbon bows.
“Is Miss Penrose in?” Isolde inquired.
“Indeed, ma’am. Step inside, ma’am. I shall inform Miss Rosalind of your arrival, ma’am. Her ladyship is on the upper floor, ma’am.”

With those words the diminutive handmaiden darted away, and the girls, remaining by themselves, surveyed their surroundings with joyous eyes. Inside, this marvelous small house proved every bit as captivating as it appeared from the outside.

Low-ceilinged, the room possessed a pair of square windows with small panes, which muslin-frilled curtains draped. Aged as all the furniture was, its maintenance was so fine and neat that it produced a delightful impression. However, one must honestly concede that the item possessing the greatest appeal to a couple of robust girls after walking four miles in the autumn breeze was a table, which held a spread of delicacies on light blue china, whereas small golden ferns strewn across the tablecloth imparted to it what Nell would have called “a festal air.”

“Company for tea must be expected by Miss Rosalind,” she murmured. “Six places have been laid. However, what a strange little child she possesses. A messenger from pixy land is what she resembled. The way could likely have been given to us by her, I assume, yet seeing Miss Rosalind was my desire. S . . . s . . . sh, coming is she.”

And with that Miss Rosalind Penrose appeared in the doorway. The girls were taken so unawares that good manners were forgotten, and they just stared. Without realizing it, they had been anticipating the conventional sort of aged spinster from their past experience . . . an inclined-to-be bony individual, possessing neat gray hair and glasses. Something less resembling Miss Rosalind could not conceivably be pictured.

She was a tiny woman possessing snow-white hair that was lovely, wavy, and thick, thoughtfully set in flattering puffs and coils. An almost youthful face appeared below it, having rosy cheeks, sweet lips, large gentle brown eyes, and dimples . . . truly dimples. Her dress was a particularly delicate cream muslin adorned with light-colored roses . . . an attire that would have appeared absurdly young on the majority of women her age, yet it fitted Miss Rosalind so flawlessly that it never crossed your mind.
“Belinda the Fourth mentioned that you wanted to speak with me,” she stated, employing a voice that suited her look.

“We intended to inquire about the correct route to West Welby,” Isolde said. “Mr. Kimball invited us to tea, however, taking the incorrect track while traveling through the woods brought us out to the base line rather than the West Welby road. Should we turn right or left when we reach your gate?”
“On the left,” stated Miss Rosalind, casting a doubtful look toward the table where her tea was set. Subsequently, she gave a cry, as though propelled by a brief, unexpected wave of determination,

“However, oh, will you not remain and partake of tea with me? I beg of you, do. The tea at Mr. Kimball’s will be finished prior to your arrival there. Furthermore, Belinda the Fourth and I shall be exceedingly happy to host you.”
Isolde offered Nell a silent, questioning glance.

“We’d like to stay,” Nell stated without delay, having resolved that she wished to learn further details about this astonishing Miss Rosalind, “provided it doesn't put you out. However, you are anticipating additional visitors, aren’t you?”
Miss Rosalind cast another glance toward her tea table, her cheeks turning red.

“I am aware you will consider me terribly silly,” she stated. “I am silly . . . and I feel humiliated about it whenever I am caught, but only when I am caught. I am not awaiting anyone . . . I was merely imagining that I was. You understand, I felt very isolated. I adore society . . . meaning, the proper sort of society . . . but hardly any individuals ever visit this place since it is extremely remote. Belinda the Fourth felt isolated as well. Consequently, I simply imagined I was about to host a tea party. I prepared food for it . . . and adorned the table for it . . . and arranged it using my mother’s wedding china . . . and I put on fine clothes for it.”

In Isolde’s private opinion, Miss Rosalind was just as odd as rumor had described her to be. Imagine a forty-five-year-old woman pretending to host a tea party, exactly like a young girl would! Nell, however, with her glowing eyes, cried out in delight,
“Ah, is imagining things something you do as well?”
Hearing “too” made Miss Rosalind recognize someone who shared her own feelings.

“Yes, I do,” she admitted with courage. “Naturally it is foolish for a person of my age. However, why be an unattached elderly woman if one cannot act foolishly whenever desired, provided no one is harmed? One requires certain rewards. Occasionally, I doubt I could survive without imagining things. Usually I am not discovered doing it, and Belinda the Fourth remains silent. Nonetheless, I am pleased to be discovered this afternoon, because you are actually here and I have prepared tea for you. Would you like to ascend to the guest bedroom to remove your hats? You will find it behind the white door at the top of the staircase. I have to hurry into the kitchen to ensure Belinda the Fourth does not allow the tea to boil. Although Belinda the Fourth is an excellent girl, she tends to let the tea boil.”

Miss Rosalind hurried away toward the kitchen, her mind set on hospitality, while the girls made their path upstairs to the spare room, a space every bit as white as its own door, illuminated through the ivy-draped dormer window and appearing, as Nell said, “like the place where happy dreams grew.”
“This is a real adventure, don’t you think?” Isolde asked. “And isn’t Miss Rosalind delightful, even though she is slightly peculiar? She does not look at all like an old maid.”
“In my opinion, her appearance resembles the way music sounds,” Nell replied.
As they descended, Miss Rosalind entered with the teapot, followed by Belinda the Fourth, who appeared thoroughly delighted as she held a dish of warm biscuits.

“At present, I need you to give me your names,” Miss Rosalind said. “It makes me very happy that you are young girls. Young girls are dear to me. Pretending to be a girl myself comes so naturally when I am in their company. I really despise” . . . making a slight face . . . “accepting that I am advanced in years. Now, which one is which . . . simply for the sake of convenience? Isolde Pembroke? And Nell Harcourt? Is it all right if I act as though our acquaintance goes back a century and address you as Nell and Isolde from this moment on?”
“You, may” both the girls said at the same time.

“Then let us merely sit down comfortably and consume all of it,” Miss Rosalind remarked with joy. “Belinda, take your seat at the bottom and assist with the chicken. Having prepared the sponge cake and doughnuts is such a stroke of luck. Naturally, making them for non-existent visitors was silly . . . I am aware Belinda the Fourth held that opinion, wasn't that your thought, Belinda? Yet you observe how favorably the situation developed. Naturally they would not have gone to waste, since Belinda the Fourth and I were capable of consuming them as time passed. However, sponge cake does not become better over time.”
It was a joyful and unforgettable feast; and upon its conclusion, everyone walked out into the garden, which rested in the enchantment of dusk.
“I really believe you possess the most beautiful spot right here,” Isolde remarked, gazing about herself with admiration.
“For what reason is it named Echo Cottage?” inquired Nell.
“Belinda,” Miss Rosalind said, “walk inside the house and fetch the small tin horn hanging above the shelf with the clock.”
Belinda the Fourth bounded away and came back bringing the horn.
“Puff on it, Belinda,” Miss Rosalind ordered.

Belinda therefore sounded the horn, producing a somewhat harsh and grating note. A brief quiet followed . . . before a host of enchanted echoes rang out from the forest across the water, soft, fleeting, and clear, resembling the collective sounding of every "horn of elfland" in the fading light. Nell and Isolde cried out with pleasure.
“Laugh at present, Belinda . . . giggle with great volume.”

Belinda, who likely would have complied had Miss Rosalind instructed her to stand on her head, got up onto the stone bench and chuckled in a loud, hearty manner. The echoes returned, appearing like a crowd of pixy folk mimicking her chuckling within the purple woods and beside the fir-bordered points.

“Individuals continuously hold my echoes in great esteem,” declared Miss Rosalind, as though she owned those echoes herself. “I adore them personally. They serve as excellent companions . . . provided one uses a bit of imagination. When the evenings are peaceful, Belinda the Fourth and I frequently remain outside here to entertain ourselves using them. Belinda, retrieve the horn and hang it attentively where it belongs.”
“Why is she named Belinda the Fourth by you?” inquired Isolde, whose curiosity regarding this matter was about to overflow.

“Simply so I do not confuse her with the different Charlottas in my mind,” Miss Rosalind remarked solemnly. “Because they appear so similar, distinguishing them is impossible. Actually, her name is not Belinda whatsoever. It is . . . let me think . . . what could it be? My belief is that it is Leonora . . . indeed, Leonora is correct. You see, the situation is like this. A decade ago, when my mother passed away, remaining here by myself was impossible . . . and covering the pay for an adult girl was beyond my means. Therefore, I arranged for young Belinda Bowman to live with me in exchange for room, board, and garments. Belinda was genuinely her name . . . she represented Belinda the First. Thirteen was her exact age. She remained in my home until reaching sixteen, at which point she departed for Boston, as superior opportunities awaited her there. At that time, her sister arrived to reside with me. Julietta was her name . . . it seems to me Mrs. Bowman possessed a fondness for extravagant names . .. yet her appearance mirrored Belinda’s to such an extent that I continually addressed her by that name . . . and it caused her no distress. Consequently, I simply ceased attempting to recall her actual name. She became Belinda the Second, and following her departure, Evelina arrived as Belinda the Third. Currently, Belinda the Fourth is with me; however, upon turning sixteen . . . her current age being fourteen . . . she will likewise desire to leave for Boston, and what my course of action will be at that point is truly unknown to me. Among the Bowman daughters, Belinda the Fourth is the final one, as well as the finest. The alternate Charlottas consistently made it clear they considered my imaginative pretending foolish, whereas Belinda the Fourth refrains from doing so, regardless of her actual opinions. Whatever opinions people hold regarding me causes me no concern, provided they refrain from making it apparent to me.”
“Well,” Isolde stated while gazing mournfully at the sinking sun. “I guess we ought to depart if getting to Mr. Kimball’s prior to nightfall is our goal. Our time here was delightful, Miss Penrose.”
“Will you not visit me once more?” Miss Rosalind begged.
Tall Nell wrapped her arm around the small lady.

“Truly we will,” she pledged. “Because we have found you, our visits will become overly frequent. Yes, it is time for us to depart . . . ‘we must wrench ourselves away,’ to quote Cedric Stanhope each time he visits Grey Shutters.”
“Cedric Stanhope?” Miss Rosalind’s tone shifted slightly. “What is his identity? I was under the impression that no person with that name resided in Brierley.”
Annoyance at her own carelessness washed over Nell. At the moment Cedric’s name escaped her lips, she had failed to remember the past love affair of Miss Rosalind.

“He is a young student whom I teach,” she clarified in a unhurried manner. “He arrived from Boston during the previous year so that he could reside beside his grandmother, Mrs. Stanhope, who lives on the shore road.”
“Does Stephen Stanhope claim him as a son?” inquired Miss Rosalind, leaning down toward the flowerbed that shared her name in order to conceal her countenance.
“Yes.”

“Each of you girls will get a cluster of lavender from me,” Miss Rosalind remarked cheerfully, acting as though the reply to her query had gone unheard. “Don’t you find it remarkably sweet? It was always a favorite of Mother’s. Many years back, she established these borders. Because he cherished it so much, Father chose Rosalind for my name. His introduction to mother occurred when her brother brought him to see her family in East Welby. It was love at first sight for him; moreover, when they placed him in the guest room bed for the night, the lavender-perfumed sheets kept him awake through the dark hours thinking about her. From that point on, he adored lavender’s fragrance . . . which explains his choice for my name. Make sure you return before long, my dear girls. Belinda the Fourth and I will be eagerly awaiting your arrival.”

She unlatched the entryway beneath the fir trees so that they could go by. In an instant, she appeared aged and fatigued; the bright luminosity had vanished from her features; her final smile remained as delightfully youthful as it had always been, yet as the girls turned to look back from the initial bend of the path, they observed her resting upon the ancient stone seat beneath the silver poplar at the center of the garden, her head resting heavily upon her hand.
“It is true that she seems lonely,” Isolde remarked in a quiet voice. “We ought to visit her frequently.”

“My belief is that her mother and father assigned her the sole correct and appropriate name she could ever have received,” Nell remarked. “Had they lacked the vision to call her Elizabeth, Nellie, or Muriel, she would still have needed to be named Rosalind regardless, in my opinion. It brings to mind sweetness, ancient elegance, and ‘silk attire.’ On the other hand, my own name merely tastes of bread and butter, patchwork, and domestic tasks.”

“Oh, I disagree,” Isolde remarked. “To my mind, Nell appears truly dignified and regal. However, Kerrenhappuch would appeal to me if you occurred to be named that. It seems to me that individuals render their names pleasant or unpleasant solely through their own character. Names such as Flossie or Tibby are insufferable to me at present, though prior to meeting the Tulk girls, I considered them quite charming.”

“Isolde, that is a wonderful thought,” Nell remarked with great enthusiasm. “Existing in a way that adorns your name, even though it lacked beauty initially . . . causing it to represent a concept so charming and agreeable in human minds that they fail to consider it on its own. I appreciate it, Isolde.”

“Did you have tea with Rosalind Penrose at the stone house?” Thirza inquired while sitting at the breakfast table the following morning. “How does she appear these days? More than fifteen years have elapsed since our last meeting . . . that occurred on a Sunday inside Welby church. I imagine she is quite different now. Robin Farrow, whenever an item is out of your reach, request someone to hand it to you instead of stretching across the table like that. Did Cedric Stanhope ever behave in such a manner when he ate his meals with us?”

“However, Cedric’s arms possess greater length than mine,” grumbled Robin. “They have enjoyed eleven years of growth, whereas mine have merely had seven. Furthermore, I actually did make a request, but you and Nell were engaged in such deep conversation that you failed to pay any attention. Furthermore, Cedric has not ever been present here for any meal save for tea, and exercising politeness is simpler during tea than during breakfast. Your hunger is not nearly as great. An immense amount of time passes between supper and breakfast. At present, Nell, that spoonful is not a bit larger than it was a year ago, yet my size is significantly greater.”

“Naturally, I am unaware of how Miss Rosalind appeared in the past, yet I somehow doubt she has altered very much,” Nell remarked, following her assistance in serving Robin maple syrup, handing him two spoonfuls to quiet him down. “Her hair may be as white as snow, but her complexion remains bright and nearly like a young girl's, featuring the most delightful brown eyes . . . a lovely tone of wood-brown filled with tiny flecks of gold . . . while her voice recalls white satin, splashing water, and fairy bells all blended together.”

“In her youth, people considered her a major beauty,” Thirza remarked. “Although I was not acquainted with her intimately, she pleased me to the extent that I was familiar with her. Even in those days, certain individuals viewed her as odd. Robin, if I ever discover you engaging in that sort of prank another time, you will be forced to delay your dining until all the others have finished, in the manner of the French.”

The majority of talks that occurred between Nell and Thirza while in the company of the twins were broken up by these admonitions directed at Robin. On this occasion, Robin, it grieves one to say, failed to scrape together the final drops of his syrup using his spoon, so he resolved the problem by raising his plate with his two hands and licking it with his tiny pink tongue. Nell stared at him using eyes so filled with horror that the young offender blushed and uttered, partly embarrassed, partly boldly,
“No part is ruined when done like that.”

“Individuals who diverge from the norm are consistently labeled peculiar,” Nell remarked. “Miss Rosalind is undoubtedly distinct, even if pinpointing the exact nature of that dissimilarity proves difficult. Her status as a person who never ages might account for it.”

“A person may just as well age along with the rest of their peers,” remarked Thirza, paying little heed to her grammatical choices. “Failing to do so leaves you without a place anywhere. From what I am able to gather, Rosalind Penrose has simply withdrawn from all social life. By residing in that isolated spot, she has caused everyone to forget her existence. That dwelling made of stone stands as one of the Island’s most ancient structures. Eight decades in the past, after arriving from England, old Mr. Penrose constructed it. Robin, quit bumping Lucy’s arm. Oh, my eyes were on you! There is no point in attempting to appear blameless. Whatever is causing your misconduct like this today?”

“Perhaps I rose from the incorrect side of my bed,” Robin proposed. “Milty Gammon claims that doing so ensures your whole day will turn out badly. That came from his grandmother. But how do you tell which side is correct? Also, how can you manage if the wall is right up against your bed? I am looking for answers.”

“I’ve always pondered what occurred to ruin things between Stephen Stanhope and Rosalind Penrose,” Thirza went on, paying no attention to Robin. “They were undeniably betrothed twenty-five years back, and then, without warning, it ended. I am unaware of what the issue was, yet it had to be a dreadful thing, because he departed for the States and has not returned home ever since.”

“It might not have been anything so terrible, when all is said. In my view, minor occurrences in existence frequently cause greater difficulty than major ones,” Nell remarked, displaying a moment of understanding that no amount of living could have improved upon. “Thirza, I beg you not to mention to Mrs. Sowerby that I was at Miss Rosalind’s. She would certainly pose endless inquiries, and somehow I would prefer it not to happen . . . and I am certain Miss Rosalind would not care for it either, were she aware.”

“I suppose Agatha might be interested,” Thirza conceded, “even if she lacks the leisure she once enjoyed to attend to the business of others. Thomas’s condition keeps her bound to the house these days; moreover, her spirits are quite low, as I believe she is starting to give up on his recovery. Should he pass away, Agatha will find herself rather isolated, considering that every one of her offspring has relocated out west, barring Eliza who resides in town; and she holds no affection for her son-in-law.”
Thirza’s choice of words brought dishonor upon Eliza, whose devotion to her spouse was deep.

“Agatha claims he would recover if he would merely pull himself together and use his willpower. However, why ask a jellyfish to sit upright?” Thirza went on. “Thomas Sowerby has never possessed any willpower to use. His mother commanded him until his marriage, and Agatha took over after that. It is surprising he ventured to fall ill without obtaining her approval. Still, I ought not to speak in this manner. Agatha has proven to be a devoted wife to him. Without her, he surely would have come to nothing. He was created to be commanded; and fortunately, he ended up in the care of a smart, competent director like Agatha. Her methods did not bother him. They spared him the trouble of ever deciding anything for himself. Robin, please cease wriggling like an eel.”
“There is nothing else for me to do,” Robin objected. “I am unable to eat another bite, and seeing you and Nell eating is not enjoyable.”
“Well, you and Lucy step outside and feed the wheat to the hens,” Thirza said. “And also do not attempt to yank any further feathers from the white rooster’s tail.”

“I wished for a few feathers to make an Injun headpiece,” Robin uttered sullenly. “Milty Gammon possesses a fine one, fashioned from the feathers his mother provided to him after she slaughtered their elderly white gobbler. You could allow me to take a few. That rooster possesses far more than he requires.”
“The old feather duster in the garret is yours,” said Nell, “and for you, I’ll dye them yellow and red and green.”

“That boy is spoiled dreadfully by you,” Thirza remarked, after Robin, his countenance glowing, had gone out behind proper Lucy. Over the previous six years, Thirza had made immense progress in her education; nevertheless, she still could not free herself from the belief that gratifying a child’s desires too frequently was extremely harmful to it.

“Robin wishes for an Indian headdress because every other boy in his class possesses one,” Nell stated. “I understand that emotion . . . my desire for puffed sleeves back when every other girl wore them is something I will always remember. Furthermore, Robin is not being ruined. His behavior gets better with each passing day. Consider how much he has changed from the time he arrived here one year ago.”

“Since he started attending school, his involvement in trouble has definitely decreased,” Thirza conceded. “I imagine he exhausts that inclination alongside his peers. Still, I find it surprising that Richard Farrow hasn't contacted us prior to now. There hasn't been a single message since previous May.”

“I’ll be terrified to get news from him,” sighed Nell, starting to pack up the dishes. “In the event that a letter arrives, I’d be frightened to open it, because it might instruct us to ship the twins to his place.”

One month afterward, a missive arrived indeed. However, it had not been sent by Richard Farrow. An acquaintance of his had written to inform us that Richard Farrow had passed away from consumption two weeks prior. The author of the missive served as the executor of his testament, and through that testament, the amount of two thousand dollars was bequeathed to Miss Thirza Abernethy held in trust for David and Lucy Farrow until their adulthood or marriage. During the intervening period, the generated interest was to be applied toward their care.
“It feels terrible to feel happy about anything related to someone dying,” Nell remarked thoughtfully. “My heart goes out to poor Mr. Farrow; however, I am pleased that the twins can remain with us.”

“The money is a very fortunate matter,” Thirza remarked pragmatically. “My desire was to retain them, yet I truly failed to perceive how I might manage the expense, particularly as they advanced in age. What the farm yields in rent merely maintains the residence, and I was resolved that not a single penny of your funds would be expended upon them. Indeed, your contributions to them are already excessive. That new hat you purchased for Lucy was as unnecessary to her as two tails would be to a cat. However, the path has now opened up, and their future is secured.”

Robin and Lucy felt immense joy upon learning that Grey Shutters would be their home "for good." The passing of an uncle they had never met was completely insignificant to them when weighed against such news. Nevertheless, a single doubt troubled Lucy.
“Did they bury Uncle Richard?” she asked Nell in a whisper.
“Certainly, my love, naturally.”
“Is he . . . is he . . . anything like Mirabel Cotton’s uncle?” she asked in a whisper that was even more troubled. “He won’t roam around homes once he’s been put in the ground, will he, Nell?”
“This December Friday afternoon, I believe I will stroll over to Echo Cottage,” Nell stated.
“Snow appears to be on the way,” Thirza remarked with uncertainty.

“I will arrive prior to the arrival of the snow, and my intention is to remain the entire night. Isolde is unable to attend due to having guests, and I am certain that Miss Rosalind will expect my presence this evening. Two full weeks have elapsed since my last visit.”

Since that day in October, Nell had frequently visited Echo Cottage. At times, she and Isolde took the road around in their drive; at other times, their path went through the woods on foot. Nell proceeded by herself whenever Isolde was unable to accompany her. A intense, beneficial bond had formed between her and Miss Rosalind, the sort that can only occur between a woman whose heart and soul retain the vigor of youth, and a girl whose lack of experience is compensated by her intuition and imagination. Nell had finally found a genuine “kindred spirit,” whereas Nell and Isolde entered the little lady’s isolated, solitary existence of dreams carrying the healthy delight and vigor of the outside world—a world Miss Rosalind, “the world forgetting, by the world forgot,” had given up participating in long ago; to the small stone dwelling, they imparted an aura of youth and actuality. Belinda the Fourth invariably welcomed them with her broadest possible grin . . . and the smiles of Belinda were terribly broad . . . holding them dear for their own merits as well as for the sake of her cherished mistress. Never had the small stone house hosted such “high jinks” as those taking place during that lovely, lingering late autumn, a time when November appeared to repeat October, and even December imitated the summer's hazes and sunlit warmth.

However, on this specific day, December appeared to recall its winter duty, abruptly becoming gloomy and somber with a windless stillness that forecasted approaching snow. Even so, Nell derived great pleasure from her stroll across the vast, gray labyrinth of the beechlands; she was by herself, yet she never considered it solitary; her mind filled her trail with cheerful friends, and she engaged with them in a lively, imaginary dialogue that proved more clever and enchanting than actual conversations tend to be, since individuals in reality occasionally fall disastrously short of expectations. Within an imagined gathering of select souls, every person utters precisely what you desire her to utter, thereby granting you the opportunity to state exactly what you desire to state. Accompanied by this unseeable group, Nell made her way through the forest and reached the fir lane at the exact moment large, downy flakes started floating down gently.

Upon reaching the initial curve, she discovered Miss Rosalind, who was positioned beneath a large fir with wide branches. A dress of vibrant, deep red was clad upon her, while a silk shawl of shimmering gray enveloped her head and shoulders.
“You resemble the queen of the fir tree fairies,” Nell shouted cheerfully.

“I believed you would arrive this evening, Nell,” Miss Rosalind said, rushing toward her. “And my happiness is doubled, because Belinda the Fourth has gone. She was forced to return to her house until tomorrow because her mother is ill. Had you not arrived, I would have felt exceedingly solitary . . . not even my echoes and dreams could have provided sufficient fellowship. Oh, Nell, you are so lovely,” she remarked abruptly, gazing upward at the slender, tall girl whose face bore a gentle pink glow from her walk. “So lovely and so youthful! Being seventeen is truly wonderful, is it not? I am quite jealous of you,” Miss Rosalind admitted frankly.
“However, seventeen is all you are in your soul,” Nell said with a smile.

“No, I’m advanced in years . . . or more accurately in my middle years, a condition considerably more terrible,” Miss Rosalind uttered with a sigh. “On occasion I am able to feign that I am not, yet on different occasions it becomes clear to me. And I am unable to accept it the way the majority of women appear to do. My defiance remains identical to how it was upon finding my initial gray hair. Currently, Nell, cease making a face as though you were attempting to comprehend. A person of seventeen is incapable of understanding. Immediately I shall act as if I am seventeen as well, an act I am capable of performing, now that you have arrived. In your palm you invariably carry youth similar to a present. A splendid evening lies ahead for us. Starting with tea . . . what is your desire for tea? Whatever meets your approval shall be served to us. Pray conceive of something pleasant and hard to digest.”

Noises of revelry and amusement echoed through the small stone cottage on that evening. Between the culinary efforts, the banquet, the confectionery making, the laughter, and the "pretending," Miss Rosalind and Nell indeed behaved in a manner completely inappropriate for a forty-five-year-old unmarried woman and a solemn schoolmistress. Afterwards, once exhaustion set in, they placed themselves upon the floor mat in front of the parlor hearth, which was illuminated solely by the gentle glow of the flames and fragranced wonderfully by the uncovered rose-jar belonging to Miss Rosalind atop the mantle. Outside, the breeze had grown stronger, moaning and lamenting about the roof edges while snow struck the windowpanes with quiet thuds, resembling a multitude of storm imps knocking to be let in.

“Nell, having you with me brings me such joy,” Miss Rosalind remarked, taking small bites of her sweet. “Without your presence, my mood would be low . . . terribly low . . . nearly as dark as navy. Fancies and imaginings suffice perfectly well during daylight hours and under bright skies, yet they fall short of comforting us once nightfall and tempest arrive. Authentic matters are required at such times. You remain unaware of this truth, however . . . youth at seventeen is always ignorant of it. For a seventeen-year-old, fantasies ARE enough, as you believe that actualities lie in store for you down the road. Back when I was seventeen, Nell, it never occurred to me that reaching forty-five would see me transformed into a silver-haired, tiny elderly spinster possessing merely visions to occupy my existence.”
“However, you are no old maid,” Nell remarked, offering a smile toward the yearning, woodbrown eyes of Miss Rosalind. “Old maids are created at birth . . . they do not develop later.”
“With playful humor, Miss Rosalind offered a parody, stating, “A few women are old maids from birth, others attain the status of an old maid, and still others find old maidenhood forced on them.””
“Then you are numbered among those who have managed it,” Nell said with a laugh, “and your success is so lovely that were all old maids similar to you, I believe they would become quite fashionable.”

“I always prefer to execute things as thoroughly as I can,” Miss Rosalind remarked thoughtfully, “and because it was my fate to become an old maid, I resolved that I would be an exceptionally pleasant one. I am considered strange by some; however, that is merely because I pursue my personal manner of being an old maid instead of imitating the conventional model. Nell, has anybody ever mentioned a single thing to you regarding Stephen Stanhope and myself?”
“Yes,” Nell admitted frankly, “it has come to my attention that you and he used to be engaged.”

“So we were . . . a quarter of a century back . . . a whole lifetime back. And our marriage was supposed to take place the following spring. I had prepared my wedding gown, even though no one except mother and Stephen was ever aware of that. One could say we had been engaged in some manner nearly our entire lives. During Stephen's childhood, his mother used to accompany him to this place whenever she visited my mother; and on his very second visit . . . he was nine years old and I was six . . . he informed me in the garden that he was nearly certain he would marry me upon growing up. I recall replying ‘Thank you’; and after his departure, I informed mother with great seriousness that a heavy burden had been lifted from my thoughts, since I no longer feared becoming an old maid. How poor mother laughed!”
“And what failed?” Nell gasped out.

“We merely had an absurd, foolish, ordinary fight. It was so ordinary that, if you can believe it, I cannot even recall precisely what started it. I am barely sure which of us was more at fault. Stephen actually started it, though I imagine I goaded him through some folly of my own. You see, he had a couple of rivals. I was conceited and flirting, and I enjoyed teasing him slightly. He was an extremely nervous, easily hurt guy. Anyway, both of us left in an angry mood. However, I assumed everything would be resolved; and it would have been had Stephen not returned prematurely. Nell, my dear, I regret to tell you” . . . Miss Rosalind lowered her tone as though she were on the verge of admitting a desire to kill folks, “that I am an awfully moody individual. Oh, there is no need to grin, . . . it is all too factual. I do brood; and Stephen returned before my brooding was done. I refused to hear him out and I refused to pardon him; and therefore he left permanently. He possessed too much pride to return a second time. And after that I brooded because he failed to return. Perhaps I could have summoned him, yet I was unable to demean myself to act like that. My pride matched his own . . . pride together with moodiness form a terrible mixture, Nell. However, I could never feel affection for anyone else, nor did I desire to. I was certain I would prefer being an unmarried woman for ten centuries over marrying anyone who was not Stephen Stanhope. Well, it all feels like a fantasy at present, naturally. You appear so understanding, Nell . . . as understanding as only a person of seventeen can appear. Yet do not exaggerate it. I am actually a quite cheerful, satisfied small person despite my fractured heart. My heart certainly shattered, if a heart ever did, once I understood that Stephen Stanhope was never returning. Yet, Nell, a fractured heart in actual life is not nearly as terrible as it appears in novels. It resembles a decayed tooth quite a bit . . . although you will not consider that a particularly poetic comparison. It suffers fits of pain and grants you an occasional restless night, but in the intervals it allows you to take pleasure in existence and fantasies and reverberations and peanut brittle as though nothing were wrong with it. And now you appear let down. You do not consider me nearly as fascinating an individual as you considered me five minutes prior when you thought I was constantly suffering from a sorrowful remembrance courageously concealed under outward grins. That is the most awful . . . or the finest . . . aspect of actual life, Nell. It refuses to allow you to suffer. It continues attempting to render you cozy . . . and accomplishing it...even when you are resolved to be sad and poetic. Is this sweet not delicious? I have consumed much more than is healthy for me by now, but I intend to carry on recklessly.”
Following a brief pause, Miss Rosalind remarked suddenly,

“When you arrived here on that initial day, Nell, learning of Stephen’s boy startled me. Though I have been unable to bring him up to you from that moment on, I have longed to hear everything concerning him. How would you describe the boy?”
“Miss Rosalind, he is the sweetest, dearest child I have ever known . . . and just like you and me, he pretends things as well.”

“I would like to view him,” Miss Rosalind remarked in a quiet voice, seemingly addressing only herself. “I am curious whether he resembles in any way the small dream-boy residing in this place alongside me . . . my tiny dream-boy.”
“I’ll have Cedric come over with me one day, if you’d care to meet him,” Nell said.

“It would please me . . . yet not immediately. I wish to become accustomed to the idea. It could bring greater sorrow than joy . . . should his resemblance to Stephen be too strong . . . or if he failed to resemble him sufficiently. You have my permission to present him in a month.”

Thus, one month afterward, Nell and Cedric traversed the forest toward the dwelling made of stone, encountering Miss Rosalind upon the path. Because she was not anticipating their arrival at that moment, her face lost its color.

“Thus this is the son of Stephen,” she uttered softly, grasping the hand of Cedric and gazing upon him while he remained standing, handsome and youthful, clad in his elegant small fur cap and coat. “He . . . he closely resembles his father.”
“Everyone claims that I am a chip off the old block,” Cedric observed, feeling totally comfortable.

Nell, having observed the brief occurrence, let out a breath of relief. It was evident to her that Miss Rosalind and Cedric had become fond of one another, ensuring an absence of awkwardness or formality. Despite her inclination toward romance and dreams, Miss Rosalind proved to be a most practical individual, hiding her emotions away following that initial slight slip, and she amused Cedric with as much brightness and ease as though he were the child of anyone else visiting her. A delightful afternoon was shared by everyone, followed by a lavish evening meal that would have caused old Mrs. Stanhope to raise her hands in dismay, convinced that Cedric’s stomach would be permanently damaged.
“Pay us another visit, my boy,” said Miss Rosalind, gripping his hand as they said goodbye.
“If it pleases you, you are permitted to kiss me,” Cedric stated solemnly.
Miss Rosalind leaned down and gave him a kiss.
“In what way did you realize that I wished to?” she murmured.

“Because the way you gazed at me was identical to how my little mother looked whenever she desired to kiss me. Generally, being kissed is not something I enjoy. Boys feel that way. Miss Penrose, you are aware of this. However, I believe I quite enjoy being kissed by you. And naturally, I will visit you another time. Provided you have no objections, I think I would enjoy having you as a special friend of mine.”

“I . . . I believe I won't have any objection,” Miss Rosalind said. Turning around, she went inside extremely fast; however, shortly afterward, she was at the window, smiling and waving a cheerful farewell to them.

While they strolled among the beech trees, Cedric declared, “Miss Rosalind pleases me. Her manner of looking at me was nice, her stone dwelling is nice, and Belinda the Fourth is nice too. It would be better if Grandma Stanhope kept a Belinda the Fourth rather than a Mary Joe. It seems certain to me that Belinda the Fourth would not consider me crazy if I shared my thoughts with her. Didn’t we enjoy a magnificent tea, teacher? According to Grandma, a boy ought not to focus on his food, yet resisting it proves difficult on occasions when he feels truly ravenous. You understand, teacher. My belief is that Miss Rosalind would not force a boy to consume breakfast porridge against his preference. She would provide him with foods he enjoyed instead. Even so” . . . Cedric possessed a great sense of fairness . . . “that could prove unhealthy for him. Still, it makes a lovely treat, teacher. You understand.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: A certain day in May brought a slight flutter of excitement to the people of Brierley on account of some “Brierley Notes” bearing the signature “Observer,” which were published in the Port Marlow Daily Enterprise. Local rumors credited Wilfred Mott with writing them, owing in part to the fact that the aforementioned Wilfred had penned comparable pieces of writing in the past, and owing in part to the appearance of a mockery directed at Hugh Carrow in one of the items.
