The youth of Brierley continued to view Hugh Carrow and Wilfred Mott as competitors seeking the favor of a particular young lady who possessed gray eyes and an imaginative mind.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: Rumors, as was typically the case, were incorrect. The messages were authored by Hugh Carrow, who was helped and encouraged by Nell, and he included the message regarding himself to mislead everyone. Merely two among the notes possess any relevance to this account:

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Word is going around that a marriage is set to take place in our village before the daisies bloom. An inhabitant who is both new and greatly esteemed will escort one of our most well-liked women to the nuptial altar.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Our famous forecaster of the weather, Uncle Zeb, forecasts that a severe tempest with lightning and thunder will occur on the night of May twenty-third, commencing precisely at seven o’clock. Most of the Province will be included in the region affected by the storm. Individuals who are journeying during that evening would be wise to bring along mackintoshes and umbrellas.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “A storm for some point this spring has indeed been foretold by Uncle Zeb,” Hugh remarked, “yet do you believe that Isabella Pullen is truly visited by Mr. Pettifer?”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “No,” Nell said with a laugh, “I am certain his sole purpose is playing checkers alongside Mr. Pettifer Pullen, yet according to Mrs. Sowerby, she is positive Isabella Pullen is bound to wed soon, given how cheerful she has been throughout this spring.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: The notes made poor old Uncle Zeb feel somewhat indignant. That “Observer” was mocking him was his suspicion. Although he furiously repudiated having set a specific date for his storm, he was believed by nobody.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: Existence in Brierley proceeded along its calm and uniform course. The "planting" was accomplished; an Arbor Day was observed by the Improvers. Every single Improver planted, or arranged to have planted, five decorative trees. Because the organization currently comprised forty members, a grand total of two hundred saplings resulted from this. The red fields turned green with early oats; great blossoming branches were wrapped around the farmhouses by apple orchards, and the Frost Maiden beautified itself like a bride preparing for her groom. Nell preferred sleeping with an open window so that the aroma of cherries could drift across her face throughout the night. It struck her as extremely poetical. Thirza believed her life was being put at risk.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Thanksgiving ought to be kept in the springtime,” Nell remarked to Thirza one night, while the two of them were sitting on the front door steps and listening to the frogs’ silver-sweet chorus. “It seems to me it would be so much preferable to holding it in November, when all things are deceased or dormant. At that time you are forced to recollect to be thankful; whereas in May a person just cannot prevent being thankful . . . because they are living, if for no other reason. My feelings are precisely what Eve’s must have been in the garden of Eden prior to the trouble starting. Does that grass in the hollow look green or golden? Thirza, it strikes me that a gem of a day such as this, with the blossoms open and the winds unsure which direction to blow from next out of pure wild joy, must be almost as wonderful as heaven.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: Thirza appeared shocked and cast an anxious look about her to ensure that the twins were out of hearing range. At that precise moment, they rounded the corner of the dwelling.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Ain’t it an awful nice-smelling evening?” Robin inquired, inhaling with joy while wielding a hoe with dirty hands. He had been laboring in his plot. During that spring, Thirza, hoping to direct Robin’s love of playing with clay and mud toward productive ends, had provided a tiny patch of land to him and Lucy to serve as a garden. Each child had enthusiastically begun working in a distinct manner. Lucy executed her planting, weeding, and watering with care, system, and a lack of emotion. Consequently, neat, organized small lines of annuals and vegetables made her plot green already. On the other hand, Robin labored with greater enthusiasm than judgment; his digging, hoeing, raking, watering, and transplanting were done so vigorously that the seeds he planted were denied any opportunity to survive.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “In what manner is your plot of land progressing, Robin-boy?” inquired Nell.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Rather sluggish,” Robin uttered, sighing. “The reason these things fail to thrive more escapes me. Milty Gammon claims the entire problem stems from me planting them during the moon's dark phase. According to him, sowing seeds, slaughtering pigs, trimming hair, or performing any crucial task during an incorrect lunar phase is something you must never do. Does truth lie in that, Nell? Knowledge of this is what I seek.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Perhaps if you refrained from yanking your plants out by their roots every couple of days just to check their progress ‘at the other end,’ they might thrive,” Thirza remarked sarcastically.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “I merely yanked up six of them,” Robin objected. “I wished to check for grubs at the roots. Milty Gammon stated that if the fault did not lie with the moon, grubs were responsible. However, I discovered merely a single grub. It was a huge, moist, bent grub. Placing him on a rock, I retrieved a second rock and crushed him completely. I am telling you, he produced a splendid sqush. I felt regretful that they were not more numerous. The planting of Lucy’s garden occurred at the same time as mine, yet her plants are developing properly. The moon cannot be to blame,” Robin decided thoughtfully.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Thirza, glance over at that apple tree,” Nell remarked. “Why, it resembles a person. Extending its lengthy arms, it delicately gathers its own pink skirts to entice our praise.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Those Yellow Duchess trees never fail to yield a good crop,” Thirza remarked with satisfaction. “There will be a heavy load on that tree this year. I am truly pleased. . . they make excellent pies.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: Yet neither Thirza nor Nell nor anyone at all was destined to bake pies from Yellow Duchess apples during that year.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: May twenty-third arrived . . . it was a day that was abnormally hot, a fact no one understood more sharply than Nell together with her tiny cluster of students, who were sweating through syntax and fractions inside the schoolroom at Brierley. Throughout the entire morning, a warm wind gusted; however, following the lunch hour, it vanished into a thick quietness. Nell caught the faint sound of rolling thunder at three-thirty. She immediately let the pupils out of school right then, in order for the youngsters to reach home prior to the arrival of the tempest.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: While they walked out toward the playground, Nell noticed that a particular darkness and somberness hung over the world, even though the sun continued to shine brilliantly. Annetta Bell anxiously grabbed her hand.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Oh, instructor, observe that terrible cloud!”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: Nell stared and uttered a cry of distress. A collection of clouds, unlike any she had ever seen in her entire existence, was swiftly rising in the northwest. It was completely black, except where its twisted and feathered margins displayed an eerie, deathly white. As it loomed in the unclouded blue sky, there was an indefinable threat to it; every so often a flash of lightning darted across it, which was succeeded by a fierce rumble. Descending so close to the earth, it appeared nearly to brush the summits of the forest-covered hills.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: Mr. Gorham Pullen arrived noisily up the slope aboard his truck wagon, driving his pair of grays as fast as they could go. Right across from the school, he brought the horses to a stop.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Nell, it looks like Uncle Zeb was actually right this single time,” he yelled out. “That storm of his is arriving a small bit early. Have you ever set eyes on a cloud like that one? Come on, every one of you kids who is traveling in my direction, hop inside, while those of you who aren’t must run quickly to the post office should you have farther than a quarter of a mile left to walk, and remain in that place until the rain passes.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: Grabbing Robin and Lucy by their hands, Nell raced down the incline, traversed the Aspen Path, and hurried past Primrose Dell and Reedmere at the maximum speed the twins' chubby legs could manage. Arriving at Grey Shutters just in time, they met Thirza at the entrance, who had been hurriedly driving her chickens and ducks to cover. The moment they burst into the kitchen, the light appeared to disappear, like a giant breath had extinguished it; the terrifying cloud swept across the sun, casting a darkness akin to late twilight over the land. Simultaneously, accompanied by a thunderous crash and an intense flash of lightning, the hail descended fiercely, erasing the surrounding scenery in a single blanket of white rage.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: Amidst the whole din of the tempest arrived the impact of severed boughs hitting the home alongside the harsh snapping of shattering glass. Within three minutes all the panes within the western and northern windows were shattered and the hail streamed inside via the gaps burying the floor in stones, with the tiniest among them being equal in size to an egg of a hen. For forty-five minutes the tempest stormed without lessening and not a single person who endured it ever erased it from memory. Thirza, driven out of her calmness for a single time in her existence by pure fright, was kneeling beside her rocking chair within a kitchen corner, panting and weeping in the intervals of the blaring thunder claps. Nell, pale like paper, had pulled the couch from the window and was sitting upon it flanked by a twin on each side. Robin during the initial impact had cried, “Nell, Nell, is it the Judgment Day? Nell, Nell, I never meant to be naughty,” before burying his face against Nell’s lap and maintaining it in place, his small frame shaking. Lucy, rather pale yet entirely calm, was sitting while holding hands with Nell, silent and still. It remains questionable whether an earthquake could have unsettled Lucy.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: Then, nearly as abruptly as it had started, the tempest died down. The hail ceased, the thunder rumbled and growled off toward the east, and the sun broke through bright and cheerful upon an earth so altered that believing a mere forty-five minutes could have wrought such a change felt ridiculous.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: Rising from her knees in a feeble and shaking state, Thirza collapsed onto her rocking chair. She possessed a drawn face and appeared a decade older.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Is everyone out of there with their lives?” she inquired gravely.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “We certainly have,” Robin chimed in bright spirits, having fully recovered himself. “And I wasn’t frightened in the least . . . except right at the start. It struck a guy so abruptly. In the blink of an eye, I decided against fighting Teddy Mott Monday like I’d agreed to; but perhaps I’ll do it after all now. Tell me, Lucy, did you feel afraid?”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Indeed, I felt somewhat frightened,” Lucy remarked in a proper manner, “yet I gripped Nell’s hand firmly and continuously recited my prayers.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Indeed, I would have uttered my prayers as well had it crossed my mind,” Robin stated; “however,” he appended with a victorious air, “you can see that I survived precisely as unharmed as you despite not having uttered them.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: Nell fetched a glass of her strong currant wine for Thirza . . . Nell had known all too well, during her younger years, just how strong it was . . . and after that, the two of them walked over to the doorway so they could gaze out at the unusual sight.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: A knee-deep, white carpet of hailstones stretched far and wide; beneath the eaves and upon the steps, drifts of them had piled high. Those hailstones thawed three or four days afterward, whereupon the devastation they had caused became clearly visible, because all green plants growing within the garden or field were severed. The apple trees lost not only every single blossom, but also huge branches and boughs that were ripped off. Furthermore, out of the two hundred trees planted by the Improvers, the vast majority were shredded or broken in two.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Is there any way this is still the identical world from an hour before?” Nell inquired, in a daze. “Playing this much havoc must have required more time.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Nothing like this has ever occurred on St. Brendan’s Island,” Thirza remarked, “ever. A severe storm took place when I was a young girl, as I recall, though it could not compare to this one. You can be certain that we will learn of dreadful ruin.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “I do hope none of the children were caught out in it,” Nell anxiously murmured. As was found out afterwards, not a single child had been, because every one who had some way to travel had followed Mr. Pullen’ excellent advice and taken shelter in the post office.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “John Henry Carter is arriving,” Thirza stated.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: John Henry approached, striding through the hail with an expression that was frightened yet smiling.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Oh, isn’t this terrible, Miss Abernethy? I was sent over by Mr. Pettifer to check whether yous had emerged unscathed.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Not one of us has been killed,” Thirza stated with a grim expression, “and not a single building was hit. It is my hope that you fared just as well.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Yas’m. A bit worse, ma’am. Our place got hit. The lightning brought down the kitchen chimbly, traveled through the flue, overturned Nutmeg’s cage, ripped a hole through the floor, and entered the sullar. Yas’m.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Did Nutmeg sustain any injuries?” Nell asked.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Yas’m. He was hurt pretty bad. He was killed.” Afterward, Nell crossed over to offer comfort to Mr. Pettifer. She discovered him seated beside the table, a shaking hand caressing the bright, lifeless form of Nutmeg.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Nutmeg won’t be calling you names again, Nell, poor thing,” he uttered sorrowfully.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: It had never occurred to Nell that Nutmeg could make her weep, yet tears welled up in her eyes.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Nell, he was the only companion I possessed . . . and now he has passed away. Oh well, caring this deeply just proves I am a foolish old man. I will pretend that it doesn't bother me. I am aware you intend to offer words of comfort the moment I grow quiet . . . but please refrain. Should you say anything, I would weep like an infant. Wasn't the tempest dreadful? It seems unlikely that people will mock the forecasts of Uncle Zeb in the future. It appears that every single storm he foretold throughout his existence that failed to materialize arrived simultaneously. Isn't it extraordinary how he hit upon the precise date, nevertheless? Observe the disaster surrounding us. I need to hurry about and locate a few planks to repair the opening in the flooring.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: The following day was spent by Brierley folks solely in visiting one another to assess their losses. Because hailstones made the roads impossible for wheeled vehicles, travel was done on foot or on horses. Disastrous news from every corner of the province arrived with the delayed mail. Lightning had struck houses, leaving people dead and hurt; total disruption had hit the telephone and telegraph networks, while countless young farm animals left out in the pastures had died.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: Early in the morning, Uncle Zeb waded out to the blacksmith’s forge, where he remained for the entire day. This was Uncle Zeb’s moment of victory, and he took complete pleasure in it. Saying Uncle Zeb felt happy about the storm's occurrence would be an injustice to him; however, given that it was destined to occur, he felt immense joy at having forecasted it . . . precisely to the day, as well. Uncle Zeb lost all recollection of ever having disclaimed fixing the date. Regarding the minor difference in the time, it was of no consequence.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: It was evening when Hugh reached Grey Shutters, where he discovered Thirza and Nell hard at work as they nailed pieces of oilcloth to cover the shattered windowpanes.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Heaven alone can tell the time we will receive glass to fit them,” stated Thirza. “Although Mr. Pembroke travelled across to Delford earlier today, he was unable to secure even one pane regardless of what he offered. By ten o’clock, the residents of Delford had completely emptied Lawson and Blair. Did you experience a severe storm over at Pale Sands, Hugh?”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “I certainly would. Having been trapped inside the school alongside every child, I believed a few might be driven insane by terror. Three children lost consciousness, while a pair of girls suffered hysterical fits, and Tommy Scobie endlessly screamed as loudly as he could throughout the entire ordeal.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “A single squeal was all I uttered,” Robin declared with pride. “Everything in my garden had been flattened,” he went on sadly, “though Lucy’s suffered the exact same fate,” he remarked with an attitude showing that Gilead still possessed its balm.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: Sprinting down from the west gable, Nell approached.

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Oh, Hugh, have you received word? The former residence of Mr. Levi Gammon was hit and completely consumed by fire. I feel as though I am terribly sinful for being pleased about it, considering how much harm occurred. According to Mr. Gammon, he thinks the B.V.I.S. conjured that tempest intentionally.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Indeed, a single fact cannot be denied,” Hugh uttered with a laugh, “‘Observer’ has established the renown of Uncle Zeb as a forecaster of conditions. In the annals of this area, ‘Uncle Zeb’s storm’ shall be remembered. That its arrival coincided precisely with the date chosen by us is a truly remarkable event. A sense of slight culpability genuinely affects me, as though the tempest was summoned by my own sorcery. Since the destruction of our young trees leaves little cause for celebration, we might as well take pleasure in the destruction of the former residence. Under ten of those saplings remain standing.”

chapter_title: XXIV A Prophet in His Own Country
text: “Oh, indeed, we are simply required to sow them once more when the coming spring arrives,” Nell observed with resignation. “Such is a single positive aspect regarding our existence . . . we can perpetually count on further springs to come.”
On a cheerful June morning, two weeks following the storm of Uncle Zeb, Nell emerged lazily from the garden into the Grey Shutters yard, holding a pair of withered white narcissus stems in her hands.

“Look, Thirza,” she uttered mournfully, raising the blossoms in front of the gaze of a stern woman, whose hair was covered by a green gingham apron, as she made her way indoors carrying a featherless chicken, “these represent the sole buds unharmed by the tempest . . . and even those are damaged. I’m so sorry . . . I wished for a few for Obed’s grave. He was forever so fond of June lilies.”
“To tell the truth, I miss them too,” Thirza conceded, “even if grieving for them feels wrong after such greater disasters. . . the destruction of all the crops in addition to the fruit.”

“However, folks have re-sown their oats,” Nell remarked reassuringly, “and Mr. Pettifer mentions that in his opinion provided there is a favorable summer they will turn out fine albeit belatedly. Moreover, my annuals are all sprouting anew . . . yet alas, no substitute exists for the June lilies. Unfortunate little Dinah Wren will be without any as well. I traveled the entire distance back to her garden yesterday evening, yet not a single one remained. I feel certain she will feel their loss.”

“I truly do not believe you should make those kinds of statements, Nell,” Thirza remarked sternly. “Thirty years have passed since Dinah Wren died, and her soul resides in heaven . . . at least, I trust it does.”

“Yes, but my belief is that she remains fond of and still recalls her garden in this place,” Nell stated. “I am certain that regardless of my length of stay in heaven, I would want to gaze below and observe a person placing blossoms upon my burial site. Had a garden such as Dinah Wren’s belonged to me here, a period exceeding thirty years, even within heaven, would be required before I ceased feeling longings for home at times.”
“Well, do not allow the twins to listen to you speaking in that manner,” Thirza protested weakly, carrying her chicken inside the house as she did so.

Attaching her narcissi to her hair, Nell proceeded to the lane gate, where she remained briefly basking in the June radiance prior to heading inside to take care of her chores for Saturday morning. Beauty was returning to the world; ancient Mother Nature was exerting every effort to erase the storm's marks, and even if full success would elude her for numerous moons, she was truly performing miracles.

“It would be wonderful if I could simply do nothing for the rest of the day,” Nell remarked to a bluebird that was warbling and swaying upon a willow branch, “however, a schoolma’am who likewise assists in raising twins is forbidden from giving in to idleness, birdie. Your song is so lovely, little bird. You are expressing the emotions in my soul through your music far superior to anything I could manage on my own. Oh, who is approaching?”

A delivery cart came rattling along the path, carrying a pair of passengers in the front and a large chest in the rear. As the vehicle approached, Nell identified the man driving as the child of the station master at Alder River; however, the person beside him was unfamiliar . . . a tiny female who leapt agilely to the ground by the entrance even before the horse fully stopped. This individual was a most attractive small lady, clearly closer to fifty than forty years of age, yet possessing blushing cheeks, gleaming dark eyes, and glossy dark locks, topped with a remarkable hat adorned with flowers and feathers. Although she had traveled eight miles along a dirty highway, her appearance was as immaculate as though she had newly emerged from the well-known bandbox.
“Does Mr. James A. Pettifer reside in this place?” she asked in a prompt manner.
“No, Mr. Pettifer resides in that direction,” said Nell, entirely consumed by surprise.

“Indeed, it struck me that this residence appeared excessively neat . . . far too neat for James A. to be residing in, provided he has not altered significantly since the time I was acquainted with him,” trilled the small woman. “Is it accurate that James A. intends to wed a certain woman who resides within this village?”

“Oh no, no,” Nell exclaimed, her face turning red with such an expression of guilt that the unfamiliar woman gazed at her inquisitively, almost as though she harbored a suspicion that Nell entertained plans to marry Mr. Pettifer.

“Yet I read it within an Island newspaper,” maintained the Fair Unknown. “I received a marked edition from a friend . . . acquaintances show such constant eagerness for those actions. Over ‘new citizen,’ James A.‘s name had been inscribed.”
“Oh, that letter was just supposed to be a gag,” Nell panted. “Mr. Pettifer does not plan to take anyone as a wife. I promise you he doesn’t.”

“Hearing that gives me great joy,” stated the woman with the rosy complexion, as she agilely ascended to her place in the wagon once more, “for it so occurs that he is currently wed. His spouse is me. Ah, you have good reason to appear astonished. It seems to me he has been posing as an unmarried man while shattering hearts everywhere. Oh dear, James A.,” she said, bobbing her head forcefully across the countryside toward the lengthy white dwelling, “the time for your amusement has passed. Here I am . . . yet I would not have troubled myself to arrive had I not suspected you were engaging in some wrongdoing. Is that bird of his,” she inquired, facing Nell, “still as full of foul language as before?”
“His parrot . . . has died . . . it seems to me,” breathed unfortunate Nell, for whom even her own name was uncertain at that exact second.
“Deceased! That means everything will turn out fine,” the rosy lady exclaimed with joy. “With that bird gone, James A. will be easy for me to handle.”
After making that enigmatic statement, she proceeded happily on her path, prompting Nell to rush over to the kitchen entrance in order to greet Thirza.
“Nell, who was that woman?”
“Thirza,” Nell said, her eyes sparkling even as her manner remained serious, “is there anything about my appearance that suggests insanity?”
“No extra amount than normally,” Thirza uttered, intending no sarcasm whatsoever.
“Well then, do you suppose that I am awake?”
“Nell, what absurd idea has taken hold of you? I demand to know, who was that woman?”

“Thirza, unless I have lost my mind or am dreaming, it is impossible for her to be the mere material of dreams . . . she has to be actual. Regardless, I am certain a bonnet like that is beyond my imagination. She claims to be the wife of Mr. Pettifer, Thirza.”
Thirza likewise directed her gaze back.
“His spouse! Nell Harcourt! Why, then, has he been pretending to be single?”

“I really don’t imagine he did,” Nell remarked, attempting to remain fair. “He didn’t ever state that he was unmarried. Everyone just assumed it. Oh Thirza, how is Mrs. Sowerby going to react to this?”

They discovered the news from Mrs. Sowerby upon her arrival later that night. Mrs. Sowerby experienced no astonishment whatsoever! Mrs. Sowerby had perpetually anticipated an event of this nature! Mrs. Sowerby had constantly recognized that Mr. Pettifer possessed a peculiar quality!

“To imagine him abandoning his wife!” she exclaimed with indignation. “It resembles a story you would come across in the States, yet who would anticipate something like this occurring right here in Brierley?”

“However, we are not certain that she was abandoned by him,” Nell objected, resolute in considering her friend guiltless until guilt had been demonstrated. “We are entirely ignorant of the truth behind the matter.”

“Indeed, it won't be long before we do. I intend to head right across to that place,” declared Mrs. Sowerby, a woman who was entirely ignorant of the concept of delicacy. “Officially, her coming is unknown to me, but Mr. Pettifer was scheduled to fetch a prescription for Thomas from Delford this afternoon, which provides a suitable pretext. Once I uncover every detail, I will stop by to inform you as I return.”

Mrs. Sowerby hurried into the situation that Nell was too afraid to enter. No persuasion could have forced Nell to cross over to the Pettifer residence; nonetheless, possessing her fair and rightful portion of inquisitiveness, she was privately pleased that Mrs. Sowerby intended to unravel the secret. She and Thirza eagerly anticipated the return of that worthy woman, yet their waiting proved useless. Mrs. Sowerby failed to return to Grey Shutters that evening. Upon coming home at nine o’clock from the Gammon place, Robin provided the reason.

“I ran into Mrs. Sowerby along with a woman I didn’t know in the Hollow,” he stated, “and goodness, the two of them were chatting simultaneously! Mrs. Sowerby asked me to pass along her apologies that it was too late to visit this evening. Nell, I’m terribly hungry. Milty’s was where we took tea at four o’clock, and I feel Mrs. Gammon is truly stingy. She provided us with no preserves or cake . . . and there was barely any bread, either.”
“Robin, whenever you pay a visit, you ought not to ever find fault with any food offered to you,” Nell remarked with gravity. “Such behavior shows extremely poor etiquette.”
“Very well . . . I will merely think it,” Robin stated happily. “Nell, please grant a guy some dinner.”
Nell turned her gaze toward Thirza, who came behind her into the pantry and carefully closed the door.
“You may spread a bit of jam upon his bread, for I am aware of the usual nature of tea at Levi Gammon’s.”
With a sigh, Robin accepted his piece of bread and jam.

“When all is said and done, it’s a rather disappointing world,” he observed. “Milty owns a cat that suffers from fits . . . every single day for three weeks, she’s had a fit. Milty claims watching her is tremendous fun. I made a trip down today specifically to catch her having a fit, yet the miserable old thing refused to suffer one and simply remained completely healthy, even though Milty and I lingered about the entire afternoon and waited. But it doesn't matter” . . . Robin cheered up as the subtle solace of the plum jam seeped into his spirit . . . “perhaps I'll still get to see her in one sometime. Since she’s been so accustomed to it, it doesn’t seem probable that she’d cease having them all of a sudden, does it? This jam is extremely delicious.”
Robin was free of any griefs that plum jam was unable to heal.

Because Sunday turned out to be exceedingly wet, no one could venture outside; nevertheless, all persons had learned a variation of the Pettifer account by Monday. The school hummed with the news, and Robin returned to the house, packed with details.

“Thirza, Mr. Pettifer possesses a different wife . . . well, not precisely different, yet according to Milty they have ceased being wed for a considerable duration. My assumption was always that folks were required to remain wedded once they started, but Milty claims otherwise, stating methods exist to cease if agreement is impossible. Milty states a single method involves simply departing from your wife, which is the action Mr. Pettifer took. Milty claims Mr. Pettifer departed from his wife owing to her hurling items toward him . . . solid items . . . whereas Arty Mott claims the reason was her refusal to permit his smoking, and Ned Clay claims the reason was her constant scolding toward him. My own wife would not be left by ME over such matters. My choice would be simply planting my foot and stating, ‘Mrs. Robin, you’ve just got to do what’ll please me ’cause I’m a man.’ My guess is that would resolve her rather fast. Conversely, Annetta Clay claims the departure was hers on account of his refusal to clean his boots by the entrance, and she holds no fault against her. I am heading straight across to Mr. Pettifer’s at this very moment to observe her nature.”
Before long, Robin came back, looking a bit dispirited.

“Mrs. Pettifer was absent . . . she has traveled to Delford alongside Mrs. Agatha Sowerby in order to purchase fresh wallpaper for the parlor. Also, Mr. Pettifer instructed that Nell be told to visit him over there since he desires to speak with her. Furthermore, the floor has been scrubbed, and Mr. Pettifer has shaved, even though no preaching took place yesterday.”

To Nell, the appearance of the Pettifer kitchen seemed extremely unusual. Indeed, the floor had been washed to a remarkable degree of cleanliness, as had every piece of furniture present; the stove was shined to such an extent that it reflected her face; the walls had been given a coat of whitewash, and the window glass glistened under the sun. Beside the table, Mr. Pettifer was seated in his work garments, which had possessed various rips and tears on Friday, yet were currently tidily mended and swept. He had been cleanly shaven, and the small amount of hair remaining on his head had been attentively cut.

“Take a seat, Nell, take a seat,” Mr. Pettifer urged, speaking in a voice almost identical to the one residents of Brierley employed during funeral services. “Emily has headed to Delford alongside Agatha Sowerby . . . already, she has formed an enduring bond of friendship with Agatha Sowerby. The sheer perversity of women surpasses everything. Ah, Nell, my days of comfort have come to an end . . . completely ended. I imagine it will be order and cleanliness for me throughout my remaining days.”
Although Mr. Pettifer attempted to sound sorrowful, he was given away by an uncontrollable glimmer in his eye.
“Mr. Pettifer, you are pleased that your wife has returned,” Nell exclaimed, pointing her finger toward him. “There is no need to act as though you are not, since it is obvious to me.”
A sheepish smile spread across Mr. Pettifer’s face as he relaxed.

“Well . . . well . . . it is becoming familiar to me,” he acknowledged. “Seeing Emily was not something I regretted, I must admit. In a town of this nature, a man truly requires a degree of defense, since he cannot engage in a checkers match with a neighbor without people alleging he desires to wed the sister of that neighbor and publishing the claim in the newspaper.”
“If you had not acted as though you were single, no one would have believed you had gone to visit Isabella Pullen,” Nell remarked sternly.

“I never claimed to be. Had anyone inquired whether I was a married man, I would have answered that I was. Everyone simply assumed it, however. I had no desire to discuss the subject . . . my feelings about it were still far too tender. Mrs. Agatha Sowerby would have been utterly delighted to learn that my wife had deserted me, would she not?”
“Yet certain individuals claim that you abandoned her.”

“Nell, she was the one who started it; it was her. I shall recount the entire tale to you, because I wish for you not to hold a poorer opinion of me than what I am due . . . or of Emily either. However, let us step out onto the porch. The sheer, frightening tidiness in this place somehow gives me a feeling of homesickness. It is likely that I will become accustomed to it in time, yet gazing at the yard brings me relief. Emily has not found the time to straighten it out as of now.”
The moment they had settled themselves comfortably on the veranda, Mr. Pettifer started to recount his tale of woe.

“Prior to arriving at this place, Nell, my home was in Scottsford, New Brunswick. The housekeeping was handled by my sister, who satisfied me completely; her neatness was merely sensible, and she gave me my space while indulging me . . . according to Emily. However, her death occurred three years back. As her end approached, my future welfare caused her great anxiety, until she ultimately obtained my word that I would wed. Her counsel was for me to choose Emily Scott, owing to Emily possessing her own funds and being a model of domestic management. Says I, ‘Emily Scott wouldn’t look at me.’ My sister says, ‘You ask her and see;’ and simply to comfort her, I gave my word that I would . . . and I followed through. Whereupon Emily accepted my proposal. I was never more astonished in my life, Nell . . . a clever, attractive small woman such as her and a man of my advanced years. I assure you that initially I believed I was fortunate. Anyhow, our wedding took place, followed by a brief two-week honeymoon in St. John, after which we returned to our residence. Upon our arrival home at ten o’clock in the evening, I assure you on my honor, Nell, that within thirty minutes that woman had begun housecleaning. Ah, I realize you think my dwelling required it . . . your facial expression is highly telling, Nell; what you think appears upon it as clearly as type . . . yet it was not in such terrible shape. Granted, things had grown rather disarranged while I maintained a bachelor's residence, but prior to my marriage I had hired a woman to clean it thoroughly, and a great deal of painting and repairing had been completed. I assure you that if Emily were brought into a newly constructed white marble palace, she would start scrubbing the moment she could change into old clothes. Well, her housecleaning persisted until one o’clock that night, and by four o’clock she had risen to resume the task. And she continued in that manner . . . so far as I could tell, she never ceased. It was perpetual scouring, sweeping, and dusting, bar Sundays, though even then she eagerly anticipated the arrival of Monday to restart. Still, that was her chosen pastime, and I could have accepted it had she not bothered me. Yet she refused to refrain. She resolved to reform my character, but she had not acquired me at a sufficiently tender age. Permission to enter the dwelling was denied to me unless I swapped my boots for slippers right at the threshold. Upon my life, I dared not smoke a pipe unless I retreated to the barn. Furthermore, my grammar was insufficiently proper. In her younger days, Emily had served as a schoolteacher, a trait she had never outgrown. Additionally, she despised observing me eat using my knife. Well, that was the situation: ceaseless fault-finding and nagging. Yet I suppose, Nell, to remain impartial, I was also cross. I made no effort to better myself as I could have done . . . I merely became ill-tempered and unpleasant whenever she criticized me. I remarked to her one day that she had raised no objections to my grammar when I asked her to marry me. Saying that was hardly diplomatic. A woman would sooner pardon a husband for physically striking her than for implying she was overly delighted to secure him. At any rate, we continued squabbling in that fashion, which was hardly enjoyable, yet in time we might have adapted to one another had Nutmeg not interfered. Nutmeg proved to be the final point of contention that separated us. Emily disliked parrots and was unable to endure Nutmeg’s habit of using foul language. I felt an affection for the bird on account of my brother the sailor. As young children, my brother the sailor had been a favorite of mine, and he had dispatched Nutmeg to me during his final illness. I perceived no reason to become upset over the bird's cursing. Nothing is more repulsive to me than bad language from a person, but regarding a parrot, which merely echoes what it has overheard without comprehending it any more than I would comprehend Chinese, concessions should be granted. Emily, however, was incapable of viewing it from that perspective. Logic is lacking in women. She attempted to cure Nutmeg of cursing, yet she met with no greater triumph than when she attempted to stop me from uttering ‘I seen’ and ‘them things.’ It appeared that the harder she tried, the worse Nutmeg behaved, precisely like myself.

“Well, matters continued in this manner, with both of us becoming increasingly irritated, until the final breaking point arrived. Emily asked our minister and his wife over for tea, along with a guest minister and his wife who were staying with them. I had given my word to stow Nutmeg away in a secure location where he could not be heard . . . Emily refused to touch his cage with a ten-foot pole . . . and I fully intended to do so, because I had no desire for the ministers to overhear anything disagreeable in my home. However, I forgot all about it . . . Emily was troubling me to such an extent regarding clean collars and proper grammar that it was hardly surprising . . . and that poor parrot never crossed my mind until we were seated for tea. Exactly while minister number one was right in the middle of offering the blessing, Nutmeg, who was perched on the veranda beyond the dining room window, began to shout. The gobbler had appeared in the yard, and seeing a gobbler constantly produced a bad reaction in Nutmeg. On that occasion, he outdid himself. You are welcome to smile, Nell, and I admit I have laughed about it a bit myself since then, but during the moment I experienced nearly as much embarrassment as Emily. I stepped outside and hauled Nutmeg off to the barn. I cannot claim that I found the meal pleasant. I gathered from Emily's expression that a storm was gathering for Nutmeg and James A. Once the guests departed, I headed toward the cow pasture, doing some deep reflecting along the way. I pitied Emily and somewhat believed I had not been as considerate of her as I could have been; furthermore, I questioned whether the ministers would suspect that Nutmeg had acquired his words from me. To make a long story short, I reached the conclusion that Nutmeg must be humanely done away with, and after I had driven the cows back home, I went inside to inform Emily of this. Yet Emily was nowhere to be found, and a letter was sitting on the table . . . exactly as it happens in fiction books. Emily had written that a choice must be made by me between her and Nutmeg; she had returned to her personal home, and she intended to remain there until I visited to inform her that I had disposed of the parrot.

“My temper got the better of me, Nell, so I declared she could remain until judgment day if she was waiting for that, and I didn't back down. I gathered her things and had them forwarded to her. It caused a tremendous amount of rumor . . . Scottsford almost rivaled Brierley when it came to gossip . . . and all the townspeople took Emily's side. The whole affair left me perpetually ill-tempered and irritable, making me realize I needed to leave if I ever wanted tranquility. I made up my mind to relocate to the Island. I had visited during my childhood and enjoyed it; however, Emily had consistently claimed she refused to reside in a location where people were terrified to take evening strolls lest they tumble off the brim. Therefore, simply to be stubborn, I relocated to this side. And that covers the entire matter. I had not received any news concerning Emily until I returned from the rear pasture Saturday and discovered her washing the floor, though a initial proper meal I had tasted since her departure was already set upon the table. She instructed me to consume it before we discussed anything . . . which made me gather that Emily had absorbed a few truths regarding coexisting with a husband. Consequently, she has arrived and plans to remain . . . considering that Nutmeg has passed away and the Island proves somewhat larger than she imagined. That is Mrs. Sowerby alongside her at this moment. No, remain where you are, Nell. Stick around and become familiar with Emily. She developed quite a liking for you Saturday . . . inquiring about the identity of that attractive red-headed young lady residing next door.”
Nell was received with a radiant welcome by Mrs. Pettifer, who urged that she remain for tea.

“James A. was just informing me about everything regarding you, as well as how good-natured you have been by baking cakes and other items for his benefit,” she remarked. “It is my desire to become familiar with every one of my new neighbors at the earliest opportunity. Mrs. Sowerby is a wonderful person, would you not agree? Extremely welcoming.”
As Nell returned to her house during the pleasant June evening, Mrs. Pettifer accompanied her through the meadows, where fireflies lit their starry lanterns.
“I assume,” Mrs. Pettifer mentioned in confidence, “that James A. disclosed our history to you?”
“Yes.”

“So there is no requirement for me to relate it, because James A. is an upright person and he’ll speak truthfully. He was by no means the only one at fault. Now I am able to recognize that. Before I had been home for even sixty minutes, I regretted my impatience, yet I refused to yield. At present, I realize my expectations for a man were excessive. Furthermore, taking offense at his poor grammar was truly silly of me. A husband's poor grammar is irrelevant provided he supplies well for the home and refrains from snooping in the pantry to check your weekly sugar consumption. My sense is that James A. and I will enjoy true happiness from now on. If only I were aware of ‘Observer’’s identity to express my thanks to him. My obligation to him for this favor is very great.”

Nell maintained her silence, leaving Mrs. Pettifer unaware that her thankfulness reached the person for whom it was intended. The wide-ranging repercussions of those senseless “notes” left Nell feeling somewhat confused. A husband and his wife had been reunited by them, and they had established a prophet's fame.
Inside the kitchen at Grey Shutters, Mrs. Sowerby was located. To Thirza, she had been recounting the entire tale.
“So, what is your opinion of Mrs. Pettifer?” she inquired of Nell.
“Extremely so. In my opinion, she’s a truly sweet small lady.”

“That is precisely what she is,” Mrs. Agatha stated emphatically, “and just as I was telling Thirza, it is my belief that we should all ignore Mr. Pettifer’s quirks on her account and endeavor to help her feel welcome here, indeed. Now, I have to return. Thomas will be missing me. Although I manage to leave the house a bit now that Eliza has arrived and he has appeared much improved over the last few days, I still dislike being gone from him for extended periods. I understand Hugh Carrow has stepped down from Pale Sands. I imagine he will be leaving for college this autumn.”

Mrs. Agatha cast a keen glance toward Nell, yet Nell was leaning down toward a drowsy Robin who was dozing on the couch, leaving her features impossible to decipher. She bore Robin off, pressing her rounded youthfulness of cheek against his bright ringlets. While they mounted the steps, Robin wrapped a weary arm around the neck of Nell, bestowing upon her an affectionate embrace and a tacky kiss.
“You’re extremely kind, Nell. On his slate today, Milty Gammon wrote a message and displayed it to Jennie Mott,
“‘Sugar is sweet, and you are too; vi’lets are blue, and roses red”
and those words convey my sentiments toward you precisely, Nell.”

The passing of Thomas Sowerby occurred as silently and modestly as the way he had conducted his existence. A compassionate, forbearing, and tireless caregiver was found in his wife. On occasion, Agatha had treated her Thomas with a degree of sharpness during his well days, whenever his lack of speed or submissiveness had irritated her; yet once sickness befell him, not a single voice proved quieter, no touch was more softly adept, and no watchfulness was borne with less grievance.

“Agatha, to me you have been a good wife,” he quietly remarked on one occasion, as she sat beside him in the twilight, cradling his pale, slender, aged hand within her own coarsened by labor. “A good wife. It grieves me that I do not leave you in a finer financial state; yet our offspring will care for you. Every one of them is an intelligent, competent child, taking right after their mother. A good mother . . . a good woman . . . .”

His slumber came upon him after that, and when the pale daylight began edging over the sharp-topped fir trees down in the hollow the following morning, Thirza stepped quietly into the east gable to rouse Nell.
“Nell, Thomas Sowerby has passed away . . . the news was just delivered by their hired boy. I am heading down to Agatha immediately.”

The day following the burial of Thomas Sowerby, Thirza moved around Grey Shutters looking curiously distracted. At times she gazed at Nell, appearing as if she were about to speak, but she would then shake her head and press her lips together tightly. Following tea, she walked down to visit Mrs. Agatha; upon coming back, she made her way to the east gable, the place where Nell was marking school papers.
“In what condition is Mrs. Sowerby this evening?” inquired the second person.

“She is acting more peaceful and collected,” Thirza replied, taking a seat on Nell’s bed . . . an action that signified a rare state of emotional agitation, since according to Thirza’s set of domestic rules, resting on a bed once it had been prepared was an unforgivable breach of conduct. “However, she feels extremely solitary. Eliza was obliged to return home today . . . her boy is sick, so she believed she was unable to remain here any more.”

“After I complete these exercises, I am going to run downstairs and have a talk with Mrs. Sowerby for a bit,” Nell stated. “Tonight I had planned on studying a bit of Latin composition, although that is able to wait.”
“I guess Hugh Carrow will be attending college this autumn,” Thirza stated unevenly. “What would you think about going as well, Nell?”
Nell raised her eyes, filled with surprise.
“Thirza, I would certainly enjoy that, yet it cannot be done.”
“I suppose we can arrange it. It has always been my belief that you ought to depart. My conscience was never at peace believing that my presence forced you to surrender everything.”
“However Thirza, not once have I regretted my decision to remain at home. My happiness has been complete . . . Oh, this two-year period that just passed was simply wonderful.”

“Oh, yes, I know you’ve been happy enough. But that isn't precisely the point. You should continue your schooling. You've set aside a sufficient amount to cover a single year at Wexcombe and the funds from the stock sale will manage a second year . . . and there are scholarships and similar awards you could earn.”
“Indeed, but my going is impossible, Thirza. It is true that your eyes have improved; nevertheless, I am unable to desert you with the twins. So much care is required by them.”

“I will not be by myself with them. That is the topic I intended to talk about with you. I spoke for a long time with Agatha this evening. Nell, she feels terribly upset regarding numerous matters. She is not left in a good financial state. Apparently, eight years back, they took out a mortgage on the farm to provide the youngest boy with a beginning when he moved west; and from that time on, they have barely managed to pay off anything beyond the interest. On top of that, Thomas’ illness has obviously been quite expensive, in various ways. Selling the farm will be necessary, and Agatha believes almost nothing will remain once the debts are paid. She states that residing with Eliza will be her only option, and the prospect of departing from Brierley is breaking her heart. Making new friends and finding new interests is not easy for a woman who is her age. And, Nell, while she was speaking of it, I had the idea that I might invite her to move in and reside with me, though I felt I should discuss it with you beforehand prior to mentioning it to her. If Agatha were residing alongside me, attending college would be possible for you. What is your reaction to this?”

“It seems to me . . . almost . . . like . . . I’ve been given . . . the moon . . . without knowing . . . precisely . . . how to handle . . . it,” Nell uttered, bewildered. “However, regarding an invitation for Mrs. Sowerby to visit this place, Thirza, the choice rests with you. Is it your opinion . . . do you feel certain . . . that this would please you? A fine person and a helpful neighbor though Mrs. Sowerby is, . . . still . . .”

“However, you are implying that she has her flaws? Naturally, she does; yet my preference would be to tolerate much greater defects instead of witnessing Agatha leave Brierley. Her absence would be missed by me terribly. Here, she is my sole intimate companion, and I would be at a loss in her absence. For forty-five years, our status has been that of neighbors without a single disagreement . . . albeit we approached one closely on the occasion when you attacked Mrs. Agatha because she referred to you as plain-looking and red-headed. Is that within your memory, Nell?”
“I am certain that I do,” Nell remarked regretfully. “Individuals fail to erase such memories. At that instant, my hatred for poor Mrs. Agatha was immense!”

“And furthermore, the ‘apology’ you offered to her. Indeed, Nell, you were quite difficult to deal with, in all honesty. Managing you left me feeling completely perplexed and confused. Obed had a superior understanding of you.”
“Obed grasped all of it,” Nell uttered quietly, in her habitual manner of speaking about him.

“Indeed, my view is that we might arrange things to prevent any friction whatsoever between Agatha and me. In my estimation, the conflict between two women living under one roof stems entirely from their attempts to use a single kitchen and stepping on one another's toes. Should Agatha move in, the north gable could serve as her sleeping quarters, and the spare room might just as easily become her kitchen, given that a spare room is totally unnecessary for us. Installing her stove and whatever furnishings she wishes to retain in that space would make her truly cozy and self-reliant. Naturally, her financial needs will be met...her children will take care of that...meaning my contribution is limited solely to shelter. Yes, Nell, speaking for myself, I am quite in favor of it.”
“Ask her, in that case,” Nell said without hesitation. “I personally would be extremely grieved if Mrs. Agatha were to depart.”

“And provided that she arrives,” Thirza went on, “it will be perfectly easy for you to attend college. I will have her for companionship, and she can handle the things for the twins that are beyond my ability, meaning there is absolutely no justification for you not going.”

That night, Nell engaged in a lengthy period of contemplation while seated at her window. Within her breast, happiness and sorrow contended with one another. Eventually . . . abruptly and without warning . . . she had arrived at the turn in the path; and beyond it lay college, accompanied by a century of iridescent expectations and dreams; yet Nell also understood that rounding this bend required her to abandon numerous precious delights. . . every small, humble responsibility and pastime that had become so cherished by her over the previous two years, which she had elevated into magnificence and joy through the passion she brought to them. Her school would have to be relinquished . . . and she possessed affection for each of her students, including those who were dull or misbehaved. Simply contemplating Cedric Stanhope caused her to question whether Wexcombe was truly such a magical name to evoke when all was said and done.

“Over these past two years, I’ve grown a great number of tiny roots,” Nell said to the moon, “and pulling them out will cause me a lot of pain. Even so, I believe leaving is the right choice, and, just as Thirza remarks, no valid reason exists for me to stay. I need to take out all my ambitions and give them a dusting.”

Nell submitted her notice of resignation twenty-four hours later; and Mrs. Agatha, following a candid conversation with Thirza, gladly agreed to the proposal of making her home at Grey Shutters. Nevertheless, she chose to stay in her personal residence during the summer season; because the farm would not be put up for sale until autumn and a great number of plans needed to be finalized.

“Living as distant from the thoroughfare as Grey Shutters was definitely something I had never considered,” Mrs. Agatha quietly uttered to herself. “However, Grey Shutters honestly appears less isolated than it once did . . . Nell receives plenty of visitors, while the twins keep things quite energetic. Regardless, I would prefer dwelling deep within a well to departing from Brierley.”

As these two choices became widely known, they quickly displaced the arrival of Mrs. Pettifer from local chatter. Wise individuals shook their heads regarding Thirza Abernethy’s reckless move to invite Mrs. Agatha to reside with her. Folks expressed the opinion that they would fail to coexist peacefully. Each was “too fond of their own way,” resulting in numerous gloomy forecasts, not one of which bothered the involved individuals in the slightest. Having reached an explicit and definite agreement regarding the duties and rights inherent to their updated living situation, they intended to adhere to them.

“I will not interfere with you, and you will not interfere with me,” Mrs. Agatha had stated firmly, “and regarding the twins, I will happily assist them as much as possible; however, I refuse to guarantee to respond to Robin’s inquiries, and that is final. I am no encyclopedia, and I am not a Philadelphia lawyer either. You will long for Nell because of that.”

“At times the replies Nell gave were nearly as strange as the inquiries Robin made,” Thirza remarked drily. “There is no doubt the twins are going to miss her; however, her prospects must not be given up for the sake of Robin’s desire to know things. Whenever he poses queries I am unable to reply to, I will simply inform him that young ones ought to be looked at rather than listened to. That is the manner in which I was raised, and I am not so sure but that it was quite as fine a method as every one of these modern ideas regarding child-rearing.”
“Well, the way Nell does things appears to have succeeded reasonably well where Robin is concerned,” Mrs. Sowerby remarked with a smile. “That’s what he is, a changed person.”

“He isn’t a bad little soul,” admitted Thirza. “I never thought I would become as attached to those children as I have. Robin wins you over somehow . . . and Lucy is a lovely child, even if she is . . . sort of . . . well, sort of . . .”

“Unvarying? Precisely,” Mrs. Agatha offered. “Similar to a volume in which all pages are identical, it is precisely that. Lucy is going to become an amiable, dependable woman, yet she is never going to achieve anything extraordinary. Oh, that variety of people is pleasant to be around, although they are not quite as captivating as the alternative type.”

Hugh Carrow was likely the sole individual who experienced complete joy at the revelation that Nell had resigned. Her students, conversely, viewed the event as an absolute disaster. Going home, Annetta Bell fell into hysterics. To vent his emotions, Anthony Tulk engaged in two deliberate, unprovoked fights against fellow boys. All night long, Barbara Shaw wept. Cedric Stanhope boldly informed his grandmother that she should not count on him eating a single bowl of porridge over the coming week.

“Grandma, I can’t do it,” he said. “I’m really not sure if I’m able to eat a thing. It feels like a terrible lump is stuck in my throat. Had Jake Trask not been observing me, I’d have wept on my way back from school. I think I’m going to weep once I’m in bed. My eyes wouldn’t reveal it by tomorrow, would they? And I’d feel so much better. Regardless, eating porridge is impossible for me. Grandma, enduring this is going to require every bit of my mental fortitude, leaving me with none to tackle porridge. Oh Grandma, what I am going to do when my lovely teacher departs is beyond me. Milty Gammon wagers that Odette Pullen will be awarded the school. Miss Pullen is likely very pleasant, I imagine. Even so, I am certain her understanding of things won't match Miss Harcourt’s.”
Isolde held a similarly bleak perspective on the situation.

“The coming winter will be terribly lonely in this place,” she grieved, during an evening dusk as the moonlight poured down “airy silver” via the branches of the cherry tree and bathed the east gable in a gentle, ethereal glow where both girls sat conversing, Nell occupying her low rocking chair near the window, Isolde positioned cross-legged upon the bed. “Hugh and you will have departed . . . alongside the Waces. Port Marlow intends to issue a call to Mr. Wace, which he will naturally agree to. It is so unfair. I expect our pulpit will remain empty the entire winter, forcing us to endure an endless succession of candidating ministers . . . and a good portion of them will be useless.”

“I certainly trust they do not invite Mr. Baxter to come here from East Welby,” Nell stated with conviction. “Although he desires the position, his sermons are extremely somber. According to Mr. Bell, he belongs to the old school of clergy, yet Mrs. Sowerby claims that his sole issue is indigestion. Apparently, his spouse is not a particularly skilled cook, and Mrs. Sowerby remarks that whenever a gentleman is forced to consume sour bread two out of every three weeks, his religious views are certain to become warped. Mrs. Wace is deeply sorrowful regarding her departure. She mentions that everyone has shown her such warmth since her arrival as a newlywed that departing feels like parting from friends she has known her whole life. Furthermore, there is the matter of the infant's burial plot. She explains that she cannot imagine departing and abandoning it . . . it was such an exceptionally tiny creature and merely three months of age, and she expresses fear that it might yearn for its mother, even though she recognizes the folly of that thought and would never utter such a thing to Mr. Wace. She reveals that she has crept through the birch woods behind the parsonage almost every evening to reach the cemetery and sing a quiet lullaby to it. She disclosed all of this to me yesterday evening while I was up there placing a few of those early wild roses upon Obed’s grave. I assured her that for as long as I remain in Brierley I will place blossoms upon the infant's grave and whenever I am elsewhere I felt confident that . . .”
“I promised to undertake it,” Isolde offered with enthusiasm. “I certainly shall. Furthermore, I shall place them upon Obed’s grave as well, on your account, Nell.”

“Oh, I appreciate that. I intended to request that you do so. And also regarding little Dinah Wren’s? Kindly remember hers as well. You see, my thoughts and dreams have dwelt on little Dinah Wren to such an extent that she feels remarkably actual to me. My mind envisions her, over there within her tiny garden inside that refreshing, quiet, verdant nook; and I entertain a notion that were I able to slip back to that place on a certain spring evening, right at the magical moment between daylight and nightfall, and walk on tiptoe so gently up the hill of beeches that my treads would not startle her, I might discover the garden exactly as it used to exist, completely fragrant with lilies of June and early-blooming roses, with the small dwelling past it entirely covered in vines; and little Dinah Wren would be present, possessing her gentle eyes, with her dark hair ruffled by the breeze, walking around, placing her fingertips beneath the chins of the lilies and sharing secrets in whispers with the roses; and I would advance, oh, extremely quietly, and extend my hands and speak to her, ‘Little Dinah Wren, won’t you let me be your playmate, for I love the roses too?’ And the two of us would sit on the ancient bench and converse a bit and daydream a bit, or simply remain wonderfully quiet alongside one another. And after that the moon would ascend and I would survey my surroundings . . . and neither Dinah Wren nor the small vine-draped home nor any roses would be present . . . merely a neglected former garden dotted with June lilies among the wild grass, alongside the breeze lamenting, oh, so mournfully among the cherry trees. And I would be unable to tell if it was genuine or whether I had merely envisioned everything.” Isolde crept upward and positioned her back against the bed's headboard. Whenever the person sharing your dusk hour uttered such eerie statements, it was preferable to prevent yourself from imagining that something was lurking behind you.
“I fear the Improvement Society will collapse once you and Hugh have both left,” she observed mournfully.

“There isn’t any danger of that,” Nell rejoined with vigor, returning to real-world matters from her reveries. “It has been built on too solid a foundation to fail, particularly as the elderly folk are getting so excited over it. Consider the work they are putting into their yards and pathways during these summer months. Furthermore, I intend to keep an eye out for ideas while at Wexcombe, and during the coming winter I am going to compose an essay about it to mail across. Stop looking at the world so pessimistically, Isolde. Nor should you resent this brief moment of joy and triumph that I am experiencing right now. At a future time, when my departure arrives, my mood will be far from joyful.”
“It is fine for you to feel happy . . . you are heading to college where you will enjoy yourself and form plenty of wonderful new friendships.”

“I trust that I will form new friendships,” Nell remarked with contemplation. “The prospects of creating fresh acquaintances assist in rendering life exceedingly intriguing. However, regardless of the quantity of companions I acquire, they will not ever hold the same fondness for me as my former ones . . . particularly a particular female possessing dark eyes and facial indentations. Are you able to deduce her identity, Isolde?”

“However, Wexcombe will have a great number of smart girls,” Isolde sighed, “whereas I am merely an unintelligent little girl from the country who occasionally says ‘I seen’. . . even if I actually am aware of the correct phrasing whenever I pause to consider it. Oh well, naturally the previous two years were truly far too enjoyable to endure forever. I am aware of a person who is pleased that you will be attending Wexcombe regardless. Nell, I shall pose a query to you . . . a grave query. Do not become angry and please give a grave reply. Is Hugh of any importance to you?”
“Just like a friend and not at all how you imply,” Nell stated with composure and firmness, genuinely believing in her own truthfulness as she spoke.
Isolde let out a sigh. Somehow, she desired that Nell’s response had been different.
“Are you never going to get married, Nell?”
“Maybe . . . eventually . . . whenever the ideal person comes along,” Nell uttered, looking up into the moonlight with a dreamy smile.
“Yet by what means can you be certain when the correct individual is actually encountered by you?” Isolde continued to press.
“Oh, he would be recognized by me . . . I would be alerted by an inner feeling. The nature of my ideal is known to you, Isolde.”
“However, a person's values occasionally undergo a transformation.”
“My own will not change. Furthermore, it would be impossible for me to feel affection for a man who failed to satisfy it.”
“What if you never meet him?”
“In that case, I will pass away as an old maid,” she replied in a spirited manner. “I am inclined to think it is far from being the most difficult way to die.”

“Oh, I guess dying would not be very difficult; living as an old maid is what I would dismally dislike,” Isolde remarked, without meaning to be funny. “Even though being an old maid would not bother me greatly if I could resemble Miss Rosalind. However, I could never manage that. By the time I reach forty-five, I will be terribly stout. And whereas a slender old maid might possess some romance, a stout one could not possibly have any. Oh, listen to this, Nelson Atkins asked Opal Pettigrew to marry him three weeks back. Opal related the whole story to me. She claims she had no plan whatsoever to accept him, since whoever marries him must reside with his parents; yet Opal claims his proposal was so completely lovely and romantic that it totally overwhelmed her. Nevertheless, not wishing to act hastily, she requested a week for deliberation; and a couple of days afterward, she attended a Sewing Circle gathering at his mother's house, where a volume titled ‘The Complete Guide to Etiquette’ was situated on the parlor table. Opal stated that she just could not express what she felt when she discovered, within a chapter labeled ‘The Deportment of Courtship and Marriage,’ the exact proposal Nelson had delivered, verbatim. She returned home and composed a thoroughly blistering rejection to him; and she claims his father and mother have taken turns guarding him continuously since then because they dread he will drown himself in the river; however, Opal claims there is no need for their fear; because the Deportment of Courtship and Marriage explained the proper conduct for a turned-down suitor, and drowning is not mentioned there. Furthermore, she claims Wilbur Blair is truly wasting away on account of her, but she is utterly powerless in the situation.”
Nell shifted with a gesture of impatience.

“I am reluctant to admit it . . . it feels terribly disloyal . . . but, really, I no longer care for Opal Pettigrew. I was fond of her during our time at school and Regent’s together . . . although certainly not as much as you and Odette. However, throughout this past year at Delford she appears so changed . . . so . . . so . . .”

“I know,” Isolde nodded. “It’s the Pettigrew in her coming out . . . she cannot help it. Mrs. Sowerby claims that if a Pettigrew girl ever contemplated anything other than the boys, it was never evident in her walk and conversation. She speaks of nothing except boys and the compliments they give her, as well as how mad they all are for her at Delford. And the odd part is, they really are, too . . .” This was admitted somewhat resentfully by Isolde. “When I observed her in Mr. Blair’s store last night, she whispered to me that she had just secured a new ‘mash.’ Because I knew she was eager to be asked, I wouldn’t ask her who he was. Well, I suppose it is what Opal always desired. You recall how even as a little girl she constantly stated she intended to possess dozens of beaus when she reached adulthood and enjoy the very gayest time possible prior to settling down. She is so unlike Odette, isn’t she? Odette is a girl who is so nice, sensible, and lady-like.”

“Sweet old Odette is a treasure,” concurred Nell, “however,” she continued, bending toward the fleshy, pitted small hand suspended above her cushion to give it a affectionate stroke, “no one can truly compare to my very own Isolde. Can you recall that night of our initial encounter, Isolde, when we ‘pledged’ undying companionship within your garden? I believe we have honored that ‘vow’ . . . not a single disagreement or even a chilly distance has ever come between us. The surge of excitement that swept through me on the day you confessed your affection for me will remain with me forever. Throughout my youth, my heart was so desolate and deprived. Only now am I starting to understand the true extent of that deprivation and solitude. No one had any regard for me or wished to be burdened by my presence. Had it not been for my peculiar little world of fantasy, in which I pictured all the companions and devotion I desired, I would have been wretched. Yet arriving at Grey Shutters altered every single thing. Following that, I encountered you. The significance of your comradeship to me is beyond your knowing. Right at this moment, my dear, I wish to express my gratitude for the steadfast and genuine fondness you have constantly bestowed upon me.”

“And forever, forever I will,” weeping, Isolde uttered. “I will not ever care for any person . . . any girl . . . even half so much as I care for you. And should I actually wed and give birth to a small daughter of my own, I intend to call her Nell.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Nell, where are you headed, so finely clad?” Robin inquired. “That dress makes you look stunning.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: Nell had descended to the evening meal wearing a fresh gown of faint green muslin . . . the initial hue she had adopted following Obed’s passing. It suited her flawlessly, accentuating every fragile, blossom-like tone of her complexion along with the luster and sheen of her locks.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Robin, I have repeatedly instructed you to avoid using that word,” she admonished. “Echo Cottage is where I am heading.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Take me with you,” Robin begged.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “If I were traveling by car, I would bring you. However, I plan to go on foot, a distance too great for legs belonging to an eight-year-old. Furthermore, Cedric will accompany me, and I suspect his presence does not bring you pleasure.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Oh, my liking for Cedric has grown considerably,” Robin stated, commencing a fierce assault upon his dessert. “His superior virtue isn't as bothersome to me now that my own has improved quite a bit. Provided I maintain my progress, I will eventually equal him, in legs as well as in virtue. Furthermore, Cedric treats us second-primer schoolboys very kindly. He prevents the remaining older pupils from bothering us, and he teaches us numerous games.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Why did Cedric drop into the stream at lunchtime yesterday?” Nell inquired. “Upon seeing him on the playground, he was so soaked that I dispatched him straight home to get dressed before I could learn the reason.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Indeed, it happened partly by zacksident,” Robin clarified. “Though he intentionally dipped his head, the remainder of his body tumbled in zacksidentally. All of us were gathered by the brook, and Prillie Rogerson grew angry with Cedric over some matter . . . she possesses a really mean and terrible nature regardless, even if she IS attractive . . . and claimed his hair was wrapped in curl rags by his grandmother each evening. I suppose Cedric would not have cared about her remark, except Gracie Pullen giggled, which caused Cedric to turn extremely red, since Gracie is his sweetheart, as you are aware. He is completely smitten with her . . . presenting her with blooms and transporting her schoolbooks all the way to the shore road. Turning as crimson as a beet, he declared that his grandmother performed no such act and that he possessed natural curls from birth. Following that, he reclined upon the edge and plunged his head straight into the spring so they could see. Oh, it failed to be the drinking spring we use . . .” noticing a expression of horror across Thirza’s face . . . “it was the smaller one further down the stream. However, the edge is extremely slick, causing Cedric to slide completely inside. I assure you he generated a grand splash. Oh, Nell, Nell, I failed to intend to speak those words . . . they merely escaped me prior to my thinking. He created a magnificent splash. Nevertheless, he appeared utterly comical as he dragged himself out, entirely drenched and covered in mud. The female children giggled even harder, yet Gracie refrained from laughing. She appeared regretful. Gracie is a lovely female child, though she possesses a turned-up nose. Once I grow sufficiently old to possess a sweetheart, I shall refuse to choose one featuring a turned-up nose . . . I shall select one possessing an attractive nose like yours, Nell.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “A youth who gets pudding syrup so thoroughly scrambled across his features during mealtime is sure to be ignored by every young woman,” Thirza declared strictly.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “However, I will clean my face prior to going courting,” Robin argued, attempting to make things better as he dragged the back of his hand across the smudges. “Furthermore, I will clean behind my ears as well, even if nobody tells me. Thirza, I remembered to do it this morning. My forgetting happens not nearly as frequently as it used to. Nevertheless . . .” Robin then gave a sigh . . . “a person has such a great number of corners that keeping track of every single one is terribly difficult. Oh well, provided I am unable to visit Miss Rosalind’s, I will head over to visit Mrs. Pettifer instead. I am telling you, Mrs. Pettifer is a tremendously pleasant woman. Inside her pantry, she maintains a cookie jar specifically for young boys, and whenever she has prepared a plum cake, she invariably presents me with the remnants scraped from the pan. As you can understand, a large quantity of plums remain attached to the sides. Mr. Pettifer was invariably a pleasant man, yet his pleasantness has doubled ever since he remarried. It seems to me that marrying causes people to become kinder. Thirza, for what reason do you not get married? I am curious to learn.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: Being unwed had not ever proved to be a tender subject for Thirza, hence she replied pleasantly, trading a meaningful glance with Nell, saying that she presumed no one desired to marry her.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “However, perhaps you didn't ever request that anyone take you,” Robin objected.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Oh, Robin,” Lucy said with primness, startled into making a remark without prior address, “the asking has to be done by the men.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “I can’t understand why they must continually act this way,” muttered Robin. “It appears to me that the men bear the entire burden in this life. May I take another portion of pudding, Thirza?”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “As much as was beneficial for you has been served,” Thirza remarked; nevertheless, she provided him with an average additional portion.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “I would be glad if individuals were able to subsist on pudding. What prevents them, Thirza? It is something I desire to understand.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “For the reason that they would before long grow weary of it.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “I want to test that on my own,” stated doubting Robin. “However, I suppose getting pudding exclusively on fish and visitor days surpasses having it never. At Milty Gammon’s, they do not ever get any. Milty remarks that whenever visitors arrive, his mother serves them cheese and divides it personally . . . a single small portion per person and an extra one for politeness.”
