chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “If Milty Gammon speaks about his mother in such a manner, you certainly do not need to echo his words,” Thirza said sternly.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Bless my soul,” . . . Robin had learned this phrase from Mr. Pettifer and employed it with enormous enthusiasm . . . “Milty intended it to be a compelment. He’s terrible proud of his mother, because people claim she could eke out a living on a rock.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “I . . . I imagine those troublesome hens have gotten into my pansy bed once more,” remarked Thirza, standing up and exiting in a rush.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: The maligned chickens were not anywhere close to the patch of pansies, a spot Thirza failed to so much as look toward. Rather than looking there, she took a seat upon the cellar door, laughing continuously to the point that she felt embarrassed by her own behavior.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: Upon arriving at the stone house that afternoon, Nell and Cedric discovered Miss Rosalind and Belinda the Fourth working in the garden, where they were weeding, raking, clipping, and trimming with desperate intensity. Miss Rosalind herself, looking joyful and lovely amid the frills and laces she cherished, set down her shears and rushed with delight to greet her visitors, as Belinda the Fourth offered a cheerful grin.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Greetings, Nell. It occurred to me that today would bring your arrival. It delivered you because the afternoon is where you belong. Items that are meant for one another inevitably unite. If folks were simply aware of that fact, how much effort it would spare them. They remain ignorant, however . . . and consequently expend precious vitality upending everything to unite items that are mismatched. As for you, Cedric . . . well, you have gotten bigger! Since your previous visit, your height has increased by half a head.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Yes, I’ve started growing like pigweed overnight, just as Mrs. Sowerby remarks,” Cedric stated, completely charmed by the situation. “Grandma believes the porridge is finally doing its work. Maybe that's true. Goodness knows . . .” Cedric let out a profound sigh . . . “the amount I’ve consumed is sufficient to cause anyone to grow. Now that I’ve started, I really hope to continue until my height equals father’s. He stands at six feet, as you are aware, Miss Rosalind.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: Indeed, Miss Rosalind was aware; the color on her lovely cheeks grew slightly darker; holding Cedric’s hand in one of hers and Nell’s in the other, she proceeded toward the house without speaking.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Is it a good day for the echoes, Miss Rosalind?” Cedric asked in an anxious manner. Because the day of his initial visit had possessed too much wind for echoes, Cedric had experienced great disappointment.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Indeed, it is simply the finest sort of day,” replied Miss Rosalind, coming out of her thoughts. “However, everyone will partake in some food beforehand. You two individuals surely became famished during your long trek back through those beechwood trees, whereas Belinda the Fourth and I possess the ability to dine at any given time . . . our appetites are delightfully accommodating. Thus, we shall simply plunder the larder. By good fortune, it is wonderfully stocked. A hunch told me that visitors would arrive today, so Belinda the Fourth and I made ready.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “It seems to me that you are among those who keep delightful treats stocked in their pantry,” Cedric stated. “Grandma is similar in that way. However, having snacks outside of mealtimes is something she disapproves of. I am pondering,” he continued in a thoughtful tone, “whether I should consume them when I am not at home, knowing full well she disapproves.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Oh, after a long walk, I doubt she would mind. That alters things,” stated Miss Rosalind, who shared entertained looks with Nell across the brown curls of Cedric. “I imagine that light bites are terribly bad for one's health. That explains our frequent consumption of them at Echo Cottage. Belinda the Fourth and I live by flouting every established rule regarding food. Daytime or nighttime, whenever the mood strikes, we consume all manner of heavy foods; yet we thrive like green bay trees. Reforming our ways is our constant intention. Should we come across a newspaper piece cautioning about a treat we enjoy, we snip it out and attach it to the kitchen wall for memory's sake. Somehow, though, we never manage to . . . until that exact food has already been consumed. We have not been slain by anything so far; nevertheless, following pre-bedtime helpings of doughnuts, mince pie, and fruit cake, Belinda the Fourth has been observed experiencing nightmares.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Grandma permits me to drink a glass of milk and eat a piece of bread and butter prior to going to sleep; and when it is Sunday night she spreads jam on the bread,” Cedric said. “Therefore I am consistently pleased when Sunday night arrives . . . owing to several reasons. Sunday passes as a very lengthy day on the shore road. Grandma states that it feels far too brief for her and that father did not ever consider Sundays tedious when he was a small boy. It would not appear quite as long if I was able to converse with my rock people, yet I do not ever do that since Grandma disapproves of it on Sundays. I do a lot of thinking; however, I fear that my thoughts prove worldly. Grandma states that we ought to solely think religious thoughts on Sundays. However, teacher here mentioned one time that all truly lovely thoughts were religious, regardless of what they concerned, or which day they occurred to us on. However, I am certain Grandma believes that sermons and Sunday School lessons represent the sole matters concerning which a person can think genuinely religious thoughts. And whenever a disagreement in opinion occurs between Grandma and teacher, I am uncertain how to act. Within my heart” . . . Cedric placed his hand upon his chest and lifted exceptionally earnest blue eyes toward Miss Rosalind’s instantly understanding face . . . “I side with teacher. Yet then, as you observe, Grandma raised father according to her method and turned him into a brilliant success; whereas teacher has not raised anyone up to this point, although she assists regarding Robin and Lucy. Still, one is unable to know how those two will develop until they reach adulthood. Thus at times I sense that following Grandma’s views might be safer.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “It would, in my opinion,” Nell gravely concurred. “Regardless, I venture that should your Grandma and I both get to the core of our actual meaning, despite our distinct manners of articulating it, we would discover that we both intended virtually identical things. You ought to follow her manner of articulating it, as experience has produced it. Until we witness the ultimate outcome of the twins, we must hold off on confirming whether my manner is just as effective.” Following their noon meal, their return to the garden occurred, where Cedric was introduced to the echoes, experiencing awe and pleasure, whereas Nell and Miss Rosalind took seats upon the stone bench beneath the poplar tree to converse.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “So you are going away in the fall?” Miss Rosalind inquired with sadness. “For your sake, Nell, I ought to be glad . . . but I am dreadfully and selfishly grieved. I will miss you terribly. Oh, at times, it seems to me that making friends serves no purpose. After a bit, they merely depart from your life, leaving behind an ache that exceeds the void existing before their arrival.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Miss Eliza Pullen might utter such a remark, but Miss Rosalind certainly would not,” Nell remarked. “Emptiness is the absolute worst thing . . . and my departure from your existence is not happening. Letters and vacations do exist, after all. My dear, you appear somewhat pale and exhausted, I fear.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Oh . . . hoo . . . hoo . . . hoo,” proceeded Cedric upon the embankment, where he had been persistently producing sounds . . . not every one of them harmonious as they were produced, but all of them returning converted into the actual gold and silver of acoustics by the sprite enchanters across the stream. Miss Rosalind performed an irritated gesture using her attractive hands.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Everything has simply made me weary . . . even the reverberations. My existence contains nothing except reverberations . . . reverberations of vanished expectations, visions, and delights. Mocking as they are, they remain lovely. Oh Nell, speaking in this manner while hosting a visitor is dreadful on my part. The problem is merely my advancing age, which does not suit me. Reaching sixty will surely find me terribly ill-tempered. A series of blue pills, however, might be the sole remedy I require.” Right then, Belinda the Fourth, who was nowhere to be seen following the midday meal, came back and declared that early strawberries turned the northeast section of Mr. John Kimball’s field red, asking whether Miss Harcourt would care to gather a few.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Strawberries early for tea!” cried Miss Rosalind. “Oh, my age isn't what I believed . . . and I do not require one blue pill! Girls, after returning with your strawberries we will take tea in this spot beneath the silver poplar. It will be fully prepared by me for you with cream grown at home.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: Nell and Belinda the Fourth consequently made their way back to the pasture belonging to Mr. Kimball, a verdant, secluded spot where the air possessed a velvet-like softness, a fragrance resembling a bed of violets, and an amber goldenness.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Oh, is it not fresh and sweet in this back area?” Nell whispered. “It simply feels to me like I am absorbing the sunlight.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Yes, ma’am, so do I. That’s just exactly how I feel too, ma’am,” concurred Belinda the Fourth, who would have uttered the selfsame words had Nell observed that she felt similar to a pelican of the wilderness. Continual upon Nell's visits to Echo Cottage, Belinda the Fourth ascended to her small chamber above the kitchen and attempted in front of her mirror to converse and appear and walk in the manner of Nell. Belinda was never able to convince herself that she fully accomplished it; nevertheless, practice makes perfect, just as Belinda had been taught at school, and she tenderly trusted that eventually she could acquire the art of that delicate raising of chin, that swift, starry beaming of eyes, that manner of strolling as though one were a branch bending in the breeze. Observing Nell made it appear quite simple. Belinda the Fourth held Nell in total admiration. This was not because she considered her so extremely good-looking. Isolde Pembroke’s attractiveness of red cheek and dark ringlets suited Belinda the Fourth’s preference far better than Nell’s moonlight appeal of radiant gray eyes and the fair, constantly shifting roses of her cheeks.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “However, I would prefer looking like you to being attractive,” she expressed to Nell in all honesty.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: Nell chuckled, drank in the sweetness of the praise, and discarded its sharp bite. Mixed compliments were something she had grown accustomed to receiving. Concerning Nell’s appearance, the general consensus was always divided. Individuals who expected a handsome woman upon meeting her felt let down. Individuals who expected an unattractive woman saw her and questioned the vision of others. As for Nell herself, she would not ever accept that she possessed any beauty whatsoever. Gazing into the mirror, the only thing she noticed was a small, white face bearing seven freckles upon its nose. The glass failed to show her the subtle, constantly shifting emotion that passed across her countenance such as a pinkish, glowing light, or the alluring mix of reverie and amusement that shifted within her large eyes.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: Although Nell lacked beauty according to any rigid definition of the term, she had an elusive grace and notable air that granted observers a delightful feeling of contentment when viewing her gently curved youth, which was filled with deeply sensed capacities. People who were most familiar with Nell experienced, despite not consciously recognizing it, a sense that her most compelling feature was the vibe of potentiality that enveloped her. . . the capacity for upcoming growth contained within her. It appeared as though she moved within an aura of events on the verge of occurring.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: While they gathered, Belinda the Fourth shared with Nell her anxieties concerning Miss Rosalind. The compassionate young servant was genuinely troubled about the state of her cherished mistress.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Miss Rosalind is sick, Miss Harcourt, ma’am. Though she keeps it to herself, I am certain of it. For a great while now, she has been acting strangely, ma’am . . . ever since the previous time that Cedric and you visited here as one. That evening, I am positive she took a chill, ma’am. Following the departure of him and you, she stepped outside and strolled around the garden well past nightfall, wearing merely a small shawl. Snow lay thick upon the paths, and I am convinced she caught a cold, ma’am. From that moment onward, I have seen her looking weary and lonely. Nothing appears to hold her attention, ma’am. She does not play at having guests, nor does she dress up for them, nor any such thing, ma’am. Only upon your arrival does she appear to brighten up slightly. And indicating the most terrible omen, Miss Harcourt, ma’am . . .” Belinda the Fourth dropped her tone to a whisper, as though she intended to reveal a truly bizarre and horrific condition . . . “when I shatter items now, she fails to grow angry. Why, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, I shattered her green and yaller bowl yesterday, the one that continuously rested atop the bookcase. It was brought over from England by her grandmother, and Miss Rosalind treasured it immensely. As I was wiping it with utmost caution, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, it slipped right out, in that manner, before my hands could catch it, and smashed into roughly forty millyun fragments. I swear I felt terribly grieved and frightened. It was my expectation that Miss Rosalind would reprimand me terribly, ma’am; and I would have preferred a scolding over her actual reaction. Coming into the room, she barely glanced at the mess and remarked, ‘It doesn’t matter, Belinda. Gather the fragments and discard them.’ Spoken precisely like that, Miss Harcourt, ma’am . . . ‘gather the fragments and discard them,’ precisely as though it lacked value as her grandmother’s bowl from England. Oh, her health is failing, and it makes me feel terrible. Except for me, there is no one else to care for her.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: Tears filled Belinda the Fourth’s eyes. Comfortingly, Nell stroked the small brown paw that was grasping the damaged pink cup.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Belinda, it seems to me that Miss Rosalind requires a change of scenery. Her time spent here in solitude is far too great. Is there no way we can persuade her to take a short journey?”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: Belinda, wearing a headpiece filled with wild ribbons, shook her head in a crestfallen manner.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “I do not believe that is the case, Miss Harcourt, ma’am. Visiting is something Miss Rosalind detests. Three relatives are all she ever pays visits to, and according to her, those calls are made strictly out of family duty. Upon her return after the most recent occasion, she declared that she would no longer go on visits due to family duty. ‘Belinda, I’ve returned home enamored with solitude,’ she tells me, ‘and my wish is to never wander away from my own vine and fig tree again. An effort is made so earnestly by my relatives to turn me into an old woman, and it impacts me poorly.’ Precisely in those words, Miss Harcourt, ma’am. ‘It impacts me very poorly.’ Therefore, I doubt that encouraging her to go on a visit would accomplish anything.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “We have to discover what is possible,” declared Nell firmly, while placing the final berry she could fit into her pink cup. “The moment my vacation begins, I will travel over to stay an entire week alongside you. Every day we will enjoy a picnic, imagine various engaging scenarios, and try to brighten Miss Rosalind's spirits.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “That will be the very thing, Miss Harcourt, ma’am,” Belinda the Fourth uttered delightedly. For Miss Rosalind’s benefit, as well as her own, she felt happy. Having an entire week to observe Nell continuously, she would certainly manage to discover how to carry herself and act just like her.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: Upon the girls' return to Echo Cottage, Miss Rosalind and Cedric had already moved the small, square kitchen table into the garden and prepared the complete spread for tea. Under an expansive blue sky layered with soft, white clouds, and amid the elongated shadows of the rustling, murmuring forest, no meal had ever seemed more delectable than those strawberries and cream. Once tea concluded, Nell assisted Belinda with the dishwashing inside the kitchen, whereas Miss Rosalind took a seat on the stone bench beside Cedric to learn everything concerning his rock people. This gentle Miss Rosalind listened attentively, yet right at the very end, Cedric noticed that her attention regarding the Twin Sailors had abruptly vanished.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Miss Rosalind, what makes you gaze upon me in such a manner?” he inquired with seriousness.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Cedric, how do I look?”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “As though your gaze passes right through my form to a person I bring to your memory,” remarked Cedric, whose periodic bursts of eerie perception rendered the keeping of confidences somewhat risky whenever he was around.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Indeed, you remind me of an acquaintance from my past,” Miss Rosalind said in a dreamy tone.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Back in your youth?”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Indeed, back in my youth. Is it your impression that I am quite aged, Cedric?”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “To tell you the truth, I am unable to decide regarding that matter,” Cedric admitted in confidence. “Your hair appears elderly . . . a youthful individual possessing white hair is something I have never encountered. Conversely, the moment you laugh, your eyes possess the exact same youthfulness as those of my lovely instructor. I will share a thought with you, Miss Rosalind” . . . the expression and tone of Cedric matched the gravity of a judge . . . “in my opinion, you possess the qualities to be a magnificent mother. The expression within your eyes is precisely correct . . . it is the very look that was constantly present in my own dear mother’s eyes. It seems unfortunate to me that you do not possess any sons of your own.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Cedric, I harbor a small dream boy.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “Oh, is that truly so? What is his age?”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “I believe he is roughly your age. Since my dreams of him began well before your birth, he should logically be your senior. However, I will refuse to allow his age to exceed eleven or twelve, for if I permitted that, he could eventually become a full adult, causing me to lose him.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “I know,” Cedric nodded. “The wonderful thing about dream-people is that . . . they remain whatever age you desire them to be. The only individuals in existence that I am aware of who possess dream-people are you, my gorgeous teacher, and I. Is it not peculiar and pleasant that we all happen to be acquainted? However, I suppose those sorts of folks invariably discover one another. Dream-people are something Grandma never possesses, and Mary Joe believes my mind is touched due to my having them. Yet having them seems marvelous to me. You understand, Miss Rosalind. Relate to me everything concerning your small dream-boy.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “His eyes are blue and his hair is curly. Every morning, he sneaks in to wake me with a kiss. After that, he spends the whole day playing here in the garden . . . and I join in his play. The games we play are wonderful. We race each other and converse with the echoes; and I recount stories to him. And as twilight approaches . . .”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “I know,” Cedric eagerly cut in. “He arrives and places himself next to you . . . like this . . . since naturally at twelve years old he would be overly large for sitting in your lap . . . and rests his head against your shoulder . . . like this . . . and your arms encircle him to grasp him very, very closely, resting your cheek upon his head . . . yes, it happens precisely like that. Oh, you certainly understand, Miss Rosalind.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: When Nell emerged from the stone house, she discovered the pair of them in that spot, and an expression on Miss Rosalind’s face caused her to feel reluctant to interrupt them.

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “We ought to leave, Cedric, if our goal is to reach home prior to nightfall, I fear. Miss Rosalind, I plan to self-invite to Echo Cottage for an entire week in the near future.”

chapter_title: XXVII An Afternoon at the Stone House
text: “I will retain you for a fortnight if you visit for seven days,” warned Miss Rosalind.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: School’s final day arrived and passed. An impressive “semi-annual examination” took place, and the students of Nell performed exceptionally well. When it ended, they presented her with a presentation speech and a writing desk. Every girl and woman in attendance wept, and several boys were teased about crying as well in the time that followed, even though they constantly disputed it.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: In each other's company, Mrs. Gorham Pullen, Mrs. Peter Mott, and Mrs. William Bell made their way back to their houses while discussing the matter.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Since the youngsters appear to be so fond of Nell, her departure strikes me as an absolute shame,” uttered Mrs. Peter Mott with a sigh, given her inclination to sigh about all matters and to conclude even her humorous remarks in that manner. “Of course,” she quickly put in, “it is known to us all that our teacher for the upcoming year will likewise be a fine one.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “I have no doubt that Odette will perform her duty,” Mrs. Pullen stated with a degree of stiffness. “She probably will not share quite as many fairy stories with the children or devote such a large amount of time to wandering through the woods beside them. Nevertheless, her name appears on the Inspector’s Roll of Honor, and the individuals from Stonebridge are deeply upset about her departure.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Nell going to college makes me real glad,” Mrs. Bell stated. “It is something she has always wished for, and for her, it will be a splendid thing.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Indeed, I am uncertain,” stated Mrs. Pullen, who had made up her mind not to concur entirely with anyone on that occasion. “It appears to me that additional schooling is unnecessary for Nell. Provided his fascination with her persists until his graduation, she is likely to wed Hugh Carrow, which makes me wonder how Latin and Greek will benefit her at that point. Should higher education instruct a person in the handling of a husband, her attendance could perhaps be justified.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: According to the rumors in Brierley, Mrs. Gorham Pullen had failed to figure out how to handle her “man,” which meant that the Pullen home could hardly be called a pattern of marital bliss.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “I notice that the Presbytery is considering the Port Marlow call to Mr. Wace,” Mrs. Bell stated. “I guess that implies he will be leaving us shortly.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “It won’t be prior to September that they depart,” Mrs. Mott remarked. “Their absence will be deeply felt by everyone . . . even if I constantly held the opinion that Mrs. Wace’s attire was somewhat overly showy for the spouse of a clergyman. However, every single one of us has flaws. Did you observe Mr. Pettifer’s tidy and comfortable appearance today? Never have I witnessed a person so completely transformed. Every Sunday sees him attending church, and he has contributed to the minister’s pay.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Is that not Cedric Stanhope who has become such a large boy?” inquired Mrs. Pullen. “He was so small for his years upon his arrival here. Truly, I scarcely recognized him today. He is starting to resemble his father quite a bit.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “That boy is intelligent,” Mrs. Bell stated.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “He possesses sufficient intelligence, yet” . . . Mrs. Pullen dropped her tone . . . “I think he recounts odd tales. Gracie returned from school a day during last week carrying the most absurd nonsense he had shared with her regarding folks residing down at the beach . . . tales wherein not a single statement could possibly be true, as you are aware. I instructed Gracie to disbelieve them, whereupon she stated that Cedric had no intention for her to do so. However, if that was not his purpose, why did he relate them to her?”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Nell thinks Cedric is exceptionally clever,” Mrs. Mott said.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “He might be. They Americans are completely unpredictable,” Mrs. Pullen stated. Mrs. Pullen’s sole familiarity with the term “genius” originated from the informal habit of labeling any peculiar person “a queer genius.” She likely believed, along with Mary Joe, that it signified someone who was mentally unbalanced.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: Returning to the classroom, Nell sat by herself at her desk, just like she had sat when school started for the first time two years earlier, resting her face against her hand while her tearful eyes gazed longingly through the window toward the Lake of Glassy Waters. Because her heart was aching so deeply from saying goodbye to her students, college briefly seemed to have forfeited all its appeal. She could still sense Annetta Bell’s arms wrapped around her neck and hear the girl’s young cry, “I’ll never love any teacher as much as you, Miss Harcourt, never, never.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: Over a period of two years, her labor had been diligent and devoted as she committed numerous errors and gained wisdom through them. A recompense had come to her. Something had been imparted by her to her students, yet her own feeling was that a far greater amount had been imparted by them to her . . . insights into affection, emotional restraint, blameless intelligence, knowledge of young minds. It might be that she had failed in “inspiring” her students with any extraordinary aspirations, but through the influence of her lovely disposition rather than through her diligent instructions, she had shown them that as they faced the upcoming years, it was proper and essential to exist with nobility and elegance, clinging tightly to honesty, politeness, and benevolence, while steering clear of everything possessing a hint of untruthfulness, petty behavior, and crudeness. It was possible they had no awareness of acquiring those principles; nevertheless, those concepts would be recalled and applied by them a great deal of time after the capital of Afghanistan and the dates of the Wars of the Roses had faded from their minds.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “A further part of my existence has come to an end,” Nell uttered out loud, while securing her writing table. The situation made her feel truly sorrowful; nevertheless, she found a small amount of solace in the romantic notion of that “closed chapter.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: During the beginning of her break, Nell passed two weeks at Echo Cottage, which brought enjoyment to all involved.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: She accompanied Miss Rosalind on a shopping trip to town and convinced her to purchase a new organdy dress; afterwards, they experienced the thrill of cutting and sewing it as a team, with the joyful Belinda the Fourth basting and sweeping up scraps. Miss Rosalind had stated that she was unable to feel much enthusiasm for anything, yet the glimmer returned to her eyes concerning her lovely garment.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “How silly and light-headed I have to be,” she uttered with a sigh. “It makes me thoroughly embarrassed that an untested gown . . . even one made of forget-me-not organdy . . . can thrill me in this way, whereas a clean conscience plus an increased donation to Foreign Missions failed to accomplish it.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: Halfway through her stay, Nell returned to Grey Shutters for one day so that she could repair the stockings belonging to the twins and answer the collection of questions Robin had saved up. During the evening, she walked toward the shore road for the purpose of visiting Cedric Stanhope. When she went past the square, low window belonging to the Stanhope sitting room, she caught sight of Cedric sitting upon the lap of someone; however, immediately afterward he rushed out through the hall.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Oh, Miss Harcourt,” he exclaimed with excitement, “you can’t imagine what took place! Something truly wonderful. Father has arrived . . . only imagine that! Father has arrived! Step right inside. Father, this is my lovely teacher. You understand, father.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: Smiling, Stephen Stanhope stepped ahead to greet Nell. With iron-gray hair, sunken dark blue eyes, and a powerful, sorrowful countenance remarkably shaped around the brow and chin, he was a well-favored, tall man of middle age. Nell felt a wave of deep contentment as she reflected that his face was precisely right for a romantic hero. Discovering that a person who should be a hero was stooped or bald, or in some other manner devoid of masculine attractiveness, was exceedingly disheartening. Had the subject of Miss Rosalind’s romance failed to look his role, Nell would have deemed it terrible.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Thus, here is the ‘beautiful teacher’ belonging to my small boy, about whom so many things have reached my ears,” Mr. Stanhope uttered, shaking my hand warmly. “Because Cedric’s missives have contained so much about you, Miss Harcourt, my feeling is that our acquaintance is already quite well established. My wish is to express my gratitude for your efforts on Cedric's behalf. It seems to me that the effect you had on him was precisely the thing he required. While Mother ranks among the finest, most beloved women, her sturdy, pragmatic Scottish practicality was not perpetually capable of comprehending a nature such as my little boy possesses. Whatever she lacked, you provided. Through the efforts of you both, I believe that the instruction Cedric received over this previous two-year period reached a state as close to perfection as possible for a youngster lacking a mother.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: Everyone enjoys receiving appreciation. Beneath the compliments of Mr. Stanhope, the face of Nell “burst flower like into rosy bloom,” and as he observed her, the occupied, tired worldling believed no girlhood slip had ever appeared fairer or sweeter to him than this small “down east” educator possessing red hair and magnificent eyes.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: Cedric was positioned in the middle of the two of them, filled with pure joy.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “It never entered my mind that father was on his way,” he stated with a beaming face. “Not even Grandma was aware of it. It proved to be a major shock. Usually . . .” Cedric solemnly moved his brown curls from side to side . . . “being surprised isn't to my liking. The entire joy of looking forward to events is stripped away when a surprise happens. However, for an occasion such as this, it works out fine. Father arrived yesterday evening once I was already asleep. Then, when Grandma and Mary Joe were no longer shocked, he and Grandma went to the upper floor to check on me, intending to leave me asleep until daytime. I awoke immediately, though, and spotted father. Believe me, I simply launched myself into his arms.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “With an embrace similar to a bear’s,” Mr. Stanhope said, placing his arms around the shoulder of Cedric with a smile. “I scarcely recognized my boy, because he had become so large and tan and strong.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “I am not sure whether Grandma or I felt more delighted upon seeing father,” Cedric went on. “Grandma spent the whole day inside the kitchen preparing the food father enjoys eating. She stated that she would not rely on Mary Joe to cook them. Demonstrating joy is done that way by her. Sitting and chatting with father is what I enjoy most. However, provided you will pardon me, I am going to step away from you briefly at present. The cows need to be brought by me for Mary Joe. Doing that counts among my everyday chores.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: As Cedric scampered off to perform his “daily duty,” Mr. Stanhope conversed with Nell about different subjects. Nell, however, sensed that beneath it all, he was preoccupied with another thought the entire time. Before long, it emerged.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “In his final letter, Cedric mentioned traveling alongside you to see a former . . . friend of mine . . . Miss Penrose residing in the stone house located in Welby. Are you well acquainted with her?”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Yes, indeed, she is a very dear friend of mine,” Nell answered demurely, betraying nothing of the abrupt sensation that shivered through her whole body upon hearing Mr. Stanhope’s inquiry. Nell “felt instinctively” that a sense of romance was peeking out at her from behind a corner.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: Getting up and walking over to the window, Mr. Stanhope gazed out at a vast, golden, rolling ocean where a fierce wind played like a harp. A quiet spell fell over the small room with its dark walls for a brief period. He then turned around, a expression that was partly playful and partly affectionate forming a smile as he looked down at Nell’s understanding face.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “I am curious about the extent of your knowledge,” he said.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “It is all known to me,” Nell answered right away. “The reason being,” she hurried to clarify, “that Miss Rosalind and I share a deep intimacy. Things of so sacred a character would not be disclosed by her to just anyone. Our spirits are kindred.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Yes, it seems to me that you are. Now, I shall request a service from you. Should she permit it, I desire to visit Miss Rosalind. Would you inquire whether she will allow my visit?”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: Was she unwilling? Ah, she certainly was not! Indeed, this was true romance, the genuine article itself, possessing every bit of the enchantment found in verse, tales, and reveries. It might have arrived somewhat late, akin to a blossom opening its petals in October rather than June; yet it remained a rose all the same, overflowing with sweet perfume, its center shining with gold. On her trek through the beech forest to Welby the following day, Nell’s legs had never carried her to a task she desired more. She discovered Miss Rosalind outdoors in the garden. Nell felt terribly worked up. Her fingers turned frigid, and her tone wavered.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “I have a piece of news for you, Miss Rosalind . . . a matter of great significance. Are you able to deduce what it might be?”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: It was never expected by Nell that Miss Rosalind might divine it; yet the face of Miss Rosalind turned extremely white, and Miss Rosalind spoke in a calm, hushed tone, out of which had drained all the vibrancy and brilliance that the voice of Miss Rosalind typically brought to mind.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Has Stephen Stanhope returned?”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “In what manner did you discover this? By whom were you informed?” exclaimed Nell with disappointment, irritated that the major news she had to share was already known.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “No one. From your manner of speaking alone, I was certain that had to be the case.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “He wishes to visit you,” Nell stated. “Am I permitted to inform him that he can?”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Indeed, certainly,” Miss Rosalind fussed nervously. “Nothing prevents him from doing so. His visit is simply that of any former acquaintance.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: Nell held her own view on the matter while she hurried indoors so as to compose a letter at the desk belonging to Miss Rosalind.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Ah, residing within a tale is truly wonderful,” her cheerful mind reflected. “Naturally, everything is going to end well . . . it has to . . . plus Cedric is going to get a mother just as he desires, bringing joy to everyone. However, Miss Rosalind will be carried off by Mr. Stanhope . . . while the fate of the small stone dwelling remains entirely uncertain . . . which proves that this situation possesses two aspects, just as every single thing in this life appears to have.” After the crucial letter had been composed, Nell personally took it over to the post office in Welby, intercepting the mail carrier there to request that he deliver the message to the office in Brierley.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “It’s so very important,” Nell anxiously told him. A messenger of Cupid was hardly reflected in the appearance of the mail carrier, who was quite a crabby old figure; furthermore, Nell felt doubtful about the reliability of his memory. Nevertheless, he promised to make every effort to keep it in mind, leaving her no choice but to be satisfied with his answer.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: It seemed to Belinda the Fourth that an air of secrecy hung over the stone house that afternoon . . . an enigma that shut her out. Miss Rosalind wandered around the garden in an agitated manner. Nell was likewise overtaken by a spirit of disquiet, pacing back and forth and climbing up and down. Belinda the Fourth put up with this until her endurance reached its limit; at that point, she stood in Nell’s path during the third purposeless journey that fanciful youth made through the kitchen.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Please, Miss Harcourt, ma’am,” said Belinda the Fourth, jerking her extremely blue bows in indignation, “it can easily be noticed that a secret exists between you and Miss Rosalind, and I believe, asking for your forgiveness if I am being overly bold, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, that withholding it from me is truly unkind, considering how close we have all been as friends.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “My dear Belinda, were this my own mystery, I would have revealed everything to you . . . yet it belongs to Miss Rosalind, as you understand. Even so, I shall disclose this small amount . . . and provided it leads to nothing, you are required to keep it completely hidden from every single person forever. The reality is that Prince Charming will arrive this evening. Though he appeared in times past, a lapse in judgment caused him to depart and roam in distant places, losing all memory of the hidden route that leads back to the spellbound fortress, the place where the princess kept crying with a loyal heart for his return. At long last, the recollection returned to him, and the princess continues to wait even now . . . for the simple reason that no one except her beloved prince was capable of rescuing her.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Oh, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, what does that mean in plain language?” the bewildered Belinda gasped.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: A laugh came from Nell.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Stated plainly, a longtime acquaintance of Miss Rosalind’s is visiting her this evening.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Are you referring to a former suitor of hers?” asked the matter-of-fact Belinda.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “In prose . . . that is likely what I intend,” Nell replied solemnly. “Cedric’s father . . . Stephen Stanhope, is the one. And what shall arise from it, goodness only knows, but Belinda, let us anticipate the best outcome.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “It’s my hope he weds Miss Rosalind,” Belinda answered without hesitation. “Certain women are meant to be spinsters right from the beginning, and I fear I belong to that group, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, on account of having precious little tolerance for men. Miss Rosalind, however, never was meant for that. I’ve been dreadfully anxious, pondering whatever would become of her once I grew so large that I must depart for Boston. No other girls remain in our family, and heaven only knows what would happen to her if she hired a stranger who could mock her imaginative play, leave items scattered out of place, and refuse to accept the name Belinda the Fifth. She could find a person who wouldn’t prove as unfortunate as I am at smashing crockery, but she’ll never find a single person who’d cherish her more.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: And with a sniff, the devoted little handmaiden hurried over to the door of the oven.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: That evening at Echo Cottage, they performed the routine of taking tea, yet not a soul actually consumed any food. Once tea had ended, Miss Rosalind retired to her chamber and dressed in her fresh forget-me-not organdy dress, as Nell styled her hair. Though both were consumed by intense excitement, Miss Rosalind feigned complete composure and apathy.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Tomorrow I am going to have to fix that tear in the drape,” she remarked nervously, examining it as though nothing else mattered at that moment. “For what I spent on them, those drapes ought to have lasted longer. Goodness, Belinda neglected to wipe down the banister once more. I am certainly going to have to address that with her.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: Stephen Stanhope was walking down the lane and going across the garden while Nell sat on the steps of the porch.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “This is the single spot where time stops,” he remarked, sweeping his enchanted gaze over his surroundings. “Not a single detail of this residence or garden has altered from the time I visited a quarter of a century in the past. It restores my youth.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “You are aware that time continuously stops inside a magic castle,” Nell remarked gravely. “Things only start occurring once the prince arrives.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: Mr. Stanhope offered a slightly sorrowful smile down at her upturned face, which shone brightly with youth and potential.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “The prince comes too late on occasion,” he stated. He made no request for Nell to render her statement into plain language. Similar to every soulmate, he was one who “understood.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Oh, no, provided he is the genuine prince arriving to see the true princess,” stated Nell, giving her red head a firm shake while opening the door to the parlor. After he entered, she closed it firmly behind him, whereupon she turned to face Belinda the Fourth, who stood in the hallway, entirely composed of “nods and becks and wreathed smiles.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Oh, Miss Harcourt, ma’am,” she gasped, “I stole a glance through the kitchen window . . . and he is remarkably handsome . . . and precisely the proper age for Miss Rosalind. And oh, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, do you suppose there would be any great harm in eavesdropping at the door?”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Belinda, it would be awful,” Nell stated decisively, “so you must simply leave with me to escape the lure of temptation.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “There is nothing I can do, and remaining here merely waiting is terrible,” Belinda sighed. “What if he fails to propose in the end, Miss Harcourt, ma’am? One can never feel certain about those men. The first Belinda, who is my elder sister, believed she was betrothed to a man at one time. However, it transpired that he held a contrasting view, and she declares she will never place her trust in any of them again. Furthermore, I learned about a different instance in which a man believed he desired one girl terribly much when his true desire was actually her sister the entire time. If a man remains ignorant of his own intentions, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, how can a helpless woman possibly feel certain about them?”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “To the kitchen we’ll go so we can polish the silver spoons,” Nell said. “Fortunately, that is a job that won’t need a great deal of thought . . . because tonight I couldn’t manage to think. Also, it will help time pass.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: An hour went by. Following that, at the exact moment Nell set the final gleaming spoon down, the closing of the front door reached their ears. Frightened, each looked to the other’s eyes for reassurance.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Oh, Miss Harcourt, ma’am,” Belinda gasped, “if he’s going away this early there’s nothing into it and never will be.” To the window they flew. Going away was not Mr. Stanhope’s intention at all. Down the middle path toward the stone bench, he and Miss Rosalind were strolling slowly.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Oh, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, his arm is wrapped around her waist,” Belinda the Fourth whispered with delight. “She wouldn't ever permit it unless he has proposed to her.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: Grabbing Belinda the Fourth around her round waist, Nell spun her about the kitchen until neither of them could breathe.

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Oh, Belinda,” she exclaimed with glee, “I am not a prophetess, nor am I the daughter of one, yet I will offer a prophecy. A wedding will occur within this old stone house prior to the reddening of the maple leaves. Would you like a prose translation of that, Belinda?”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Indeed, that makes sense to me,” Belinda remarked. “There is no poetry in a wedding. My goodness, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, tears are falling from your eyes! For what reason?”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Oh, since it is entirely so gorgeous . . . and like a fairy tale . . . and full of romance . . . and sorrowful,” remarked Nell, blinking away the tears from her eyes. “Everything is completely wonderful . . . yet a bit of grief is blended into it as well, in some way.”

chapter_title: XXVIII The Prince Comes Back to the Enchanted Palace
text: “Oh, naturally taking anyone as a husband carries a risk,” admitted Belinda the Fourth, “yet, taking everything into account, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, plenty of things are far worse than being married.”

During the following month, Nell resided in a state that, by Brierley's standards, could be considered a whirlwind of activity. Preparing her own simple wardrobe for Wexcombe took a back seat. Miss Rosalind was preparing for her wedding, making the stone residence the hub of perpetual deliberations, arrangements, and debates, while Belinda the Fourth lingered nearby in flustered joy and amazement. Afterwards, the seamstress arrived, bringing the delight and misery associated with selecting styles and undergoing fittings. Nell and Isolde passed half of their time at Echo Cottage, and on certain nights, Nell lay awake worrying if she had given proper counsel when she suggested that Miss Rosalind pick brown instead of navy blue for her going-away attire, and choose a princess style for her gray silk.

All who were involved in the tale of Miss Rosalind experienced great happiness. As soon as he learned the news from his father, Cedric Stanhope hurried over to Grey Shutters so that he and Nell could discuss it together.

“I was sure father could be relied upon to choose a lovely little second mother for me,” he stated with pride. “Teacher, it is wonderful to possess a father you can rely on. Miss Rosalind has earned my absolute love. Grandma feels happy as well. She remarks that she is truly relieved father refrained from choosing an American as his second spouse, since, even if matters worked out well on the initial occasion, a similar outcome would probably not occur a second time. Mrs. Sowerby mentions that the union has her complete approval, and she considers it probable that Miss Rosalind will abandon her odd ideas and resemble ordinary folks, now that her marriage is approaching. However, teacher, my wish is that she keeps her odd ideas, since I enjoy them. Furthermore, I do not desire her to resemble ordinary folks. As things stand, there are far too many ordinary folks about. Teacher, you understand.”
Belinda the Fourth represented an additional person who was radiant.

“Oh, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, everything has ended up so wonderful. As soon as Mr. Stanhope and Miss Rosalind return from their tower, I am permitted to travel to Boston and reside alongside them . . . even though I am merely fifteen, whereas the remaining girls did not leave until reaching sixteen. Isn't Mr. Stanhope magnificent? He simply adores the very earth she walks upon, and observing the expression in his eyes while he looks at her gives me such a strange feeling at times. It is beyond words, Miss Harcourt, ma’am. I am terribly grateful that they care for one another so deeply. When everything is considered, it is the finest manner to be, even if certain people are able to manage without it. I have an aunt who was wedded three separate times and claims that her first marriage was for love while the final two were purely for business, and she experienced happiness with every one of them except during the funerals. However, I believe she ran a resk, Miss Harcourt, ma’am.”

“Oh, it’s all so romantic,” Nell whispered to Thirza later that evening. “If I hadn’t chosen the incorrect route the day we traveled to Mr. Kimball’s, I would never have become acquainted with Miss Rosalind; and if I hadn’t encountered her, I would never have brought Cedric there . . . and he would never have sent a letter to his father regarding a visit to Miss Rosalind at the exact moment Mr. Stanhope was departing for San Francisco. Mr. Stanhope mentions that as soon as he received that correspondence, he decided to dispatch his associate to San Francisco and travel to this place rather than going himself. He had not received any news concerning Miss Rosalind in fifteen years. At that time, someone had informed him that she was going to wed, so he assumed she had and refrained from making inquiries about her to anyone. And now all of it has turned out properly. And I played a role in causing it to happen. Maybe, just as Mrs. Sowerby claims, all things are predetermined and it was destined to occur regardless. Even if that is true, though, it feels pleasant to consider that one served as an agent employed by destiny. Yes indeed, it’s very romantic.”

“I don’t see how it’s so terribly romantic in any way,” Thirza remarked quite sharply. It was Thirza’s opinion that Nell was overly excited regarding the matter and possessed more than enough tasks preparing for college, rather than “traipsing” over to Echo Cottage two out of every three days to assist Miss Rosalind. “To begin with, a pair of young fools argue and act sullen; next, Steve Stanhope departs for the States and following a period of time marries over there, living completely happily according to every report. Subsequently his spouse passes away, and following an appropriate gap of time, he decides to return home to discover whether his initial crush will accept him. In the meantime, she has remained unmarried, likely due to no one sufficiently pleasant coming around to desire her, and the two meet and concur to wed in the end. So, what part of all that contains romance?”

“Oh, if you state it like that, there is no reason,” Nell sputtered, sounding almost as though she had been splashed with icy water. “I imagine it appears that way in prose. However, viewing it by way of poetry makes it quite different . . . and I believe it is far better . . .” Nell pulled herself together as her eyes sparkled and her face turned red . . . “viewing it by way of poetry.”

Thirza looked toward the glowing young visage and held back additional sharp remarks. It may be that she somewhat understood it was preferable, in the end, to possess, as Nell did, “the vision and the faculty divine” . . . that present which cannot be granted or stripped away by the world, of viewing existence by way of a transfiguring . . . or unmasking? . . . lens, through which all appeared dressed in heavenly radiance, carrying a brilliance and a novelty unseen by individuals who, such as herself and Belinda the Fourth, saw reality solely through prose.
“When is the wedding scheduled to take place?” she inquired following a brief silence.

“They will wed on the final Wednesday of August beneath the garden's honeysuckle trellis . . . precisely where Mr. Stanhope asked her to marry him a quarter of a century earlier. Thirza, even written down, that possesses romance. The only people present will be Mrs. Stanhope, Cedric, Hugh, Isolde, myself, and the cousins of Miss Rosalind. Following that, they are departing on the train at six o’clock for a journey to the Pacific coast. Upon returning in the autumn, Cedric along with Belinda the Fourth will move to Boston to reside alongside them. However, Echo Cottage will remain exactly as it stands. . . except naturally they will dispose of the cow and hens, shutter the windows . . . and each summer they intend to return and inhabit it. This makes me so happy. During the upcoming winter at Wexcombe, it would have pained me terribly to imagine that beloved stone home stripped bare and abandoned, filled with vacant rooms . . . or even more terrible, inhabited by strangers. Instead, I am able to envision it as I have always known it, patiently and joyfully awaiting the return of life and laughter with the coming summer.”

Greater romance existed in the world than the portion that had been granted to the middle-aged lovers residing in the stone house. Nell unexpectedly came across it one evening as she crossed over to Pear Hill through the wood cut and emerged into the Pembroke garden. Isolde Pembroke and Gideon Duckett were positioned beside one another beneath the large willow. Isolde was resting against the gray trunk, her eyelashes lowered over extremely crimson cheeks. A single hand was gripped by Gideon, who stood with his face turned down toward her, stammering a message in quiet, serious tones. No other individuals existed in the world besides the two of them during that enchanting moment; thus, neither one observed Nell, who, following a single stunned look of understanding, turned around and ran silently back through the spruce wood, refusing to halt until she reached her own gable room, where she sat out of breath by her window and attempted to gather her fragmented thoughts.
“Gideon and Isolde share a mutual love,” she breathed heavily. “Oh, it appears extremely . . . extremely . . . extremely mature.”

Lately, Nell had entertained certain doubts that Isolde was being unfaithful to the somber Byronic protagonist of her former reveries. However, because “things seen are mightier than things heard,” or surmised, the actual manifestation of this truth struck her with a force nearly resembling absolute astonishment. Following this, a strange, faint sense of isolation took hold . . . as though Isolde had somehow advanced into a fresh realm, closing a portal in her wake, and abandoning Nell on the exterior.

“Events are transforming with such speed that I am nearly terrified,” was the slightly sorrowful reflection of Nell. “Moreover, I fear that our relationship, Isolde's and mine, will inevitably be altered by this. My certainty is complete that I will be unable to share every one of my confidences with her following these events . . . she could reveal them to Gideon. Furthermore, what attraction does Gideon hold for her? Although he is quite pleasant and cheerful . . . his identity remains merely Gideon Duckett.”

The query of what one person perceives in another remains an enduringly perplexing mystery. Nevertheless, it is truly advantageous that human perspectives differ, because if all minds were in agreement, then, to quote the old Indian, “Everybody would want my squaw.” Regardless of how blinded Nell's vision was, Isolde undoubtedly discerned a special quality in Gideon Duckett. Arriving at Grey Shutters on the following night as a contemplative and timid maiden, Isolde shared the entire narrative with Nell within the shadowed privacy of the east gable. Tears were shed, kisses exchanged, and laughter shared by the two young women.
“I’m so happy,” Isolde said, “yet the idea of my engagement feels completely absurd.”
“How does it truly feel to be engaged?” Nell inquired with curiosity.

“Well, that relies entirely upon the person you’re engaged to,” Isolde replied, adopting that infuriating demeanor of higher intelligence ever exhibited by engaged individuals toward those who are single. “Being engaged to Gideon is absolutely wonderful . . . however, being engaged to anybody else would be downright terrible, in my opinion.”
“Seeing as Gideon is the only one, the rest of us cannot take much solace in that,” Nell chuckled.
“Oh, Nell, you fail to comprehend,” Isolde stated with annoyance. “I was not implying that . . . expressing it is quite difficult. Forget it, you will comprehend eventually, once it happens to you.”
“God bless you, most beloved Isolde, I comprehend at present. What purpose does a capacity for fantasy serve if it fails to permit one to glimpse existence using the sight of others?”
“You have to serve as my bridesmaid, Nell, you know. Make me a promise regarding that . . . no matter where you happen to be at the time of my marriage.”
“If required, I will travel from the furthest reaches of the globe,” Nell declared in a earnest manner.

“Naturally, it will not happen for a very long time,” Isolde stated, her cheeks turning red. “At minimum, three years . . . because my age is just eighteen and my mother declares that a daughter of hers will not wed until reaching twenty-one. Furthermore, Gideon’s father intends to purchase the Abraham Fletcher farm on his behalf, and he asserts that two thirds of the cost must be settled before he transfers the title to him. However, three years is hardly excessive for preparing a home, since I possess no handmade decorations whatsoever so far. Even so, I will start making crocheted doilies tomorrow. Myra Pettigrew possessed thirty-seven doilies upon her marriage, and I am set on having an equal number to hers.”
“I imagine that managing a home with a mere thirty-six doilies would be completely out of the question,” agreed Nell, her expression grave even as her eyes gleamed with mischief.
Isolde looked hurt.
“I expected you wouldn't mock me, Nell,” she remarked with disappointment.

“Dearest, I wasn’t making fun of you,” Nell exclaimed with regret. “I was merely teasing you a little. I believe you’ll be the sweetest tiny housekeeper anywhere. And I find it absolutely wonderful that you are already making plans for your home o’dreams.”

As soon as Nell had spoken the words, “home o’dreams,” her imagination was caught, and she at once started building one for herself. Naturally, it was inhabited by a perfect master who was dark, proud, and gloomy; yet strangely, Hugh Carrow continued to linger around as well, aiding her with hanging pictures, planning gardens, and completing various other chores that a proud and gloomy hero clearly felt were below him. Nell attempted to drive Hugh’s likeness away from her castle in Spain, but somehow he remained present, so Nell, feeling rushed, abandoned the effort and continued her imaginary construction so successfully that her “home o’dreams” stood erected and decorated before Isolde uttered another word.

“Nell, it must seem amusing to you, I imagine, that Gideon appeals to me so much when he is so unlike the sort of husband I always claimed I’d choose . . . the lean, towering type? Yet somehow, I’d prefer Gideon not to be lean and towering . . . since, you see, that would make him someone other than Gideon. To be sure,” Isolde continued with a somewhat mournful tone, “our pair will be terribly plump. Still, that beats a combination where one partner is squat and heavy while the other is towering and thin, similar to Varley Mott and his spouse. Mrs. Sowerby claims that seeing the two of them side by side perpetually reminds her of the long and short of it.”

"Well," Nell remarked inwardly during that evening, while combing her hair in front of her gilt framed glass, "Isolde's great joy and contentment make me glad. However, should my own moment arrive . . . assuming it ever will . . . I truly wish it will involve a bit more excitement. Then again, Isolde used to feel the same way. On numerous occasions, I have listened to her declare that she would refuse to become betrothed in any dull, ordinary manner . . . her suitor would need to perform a magnificent deed to gain her hand. Yet her mindset shifted. It is possible that my own views will shift as well. Still, I refuse to . . . and my resolve is firm that I will not. Oh, experiencing these betrothals among your close companions is, I believe, terribly disquieting."

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: The final week of August arrived. It was the period set for Miss Rosalind's wedding. Nell and Hugh were departing for Wexcombe College two weeks after that. Within a week, Mrs. Agatha Sowerby planned to relocate to Grey Shutters and establish her lares and penates inside the former spare room, a space that was prepared for her arrival already. Having disposed of every bit of her excess household furniture through an auction, she was currently delighting in the agreeable task of assisting the Waces with their packing. The following Sunday was when Mr. Wace was scheduled to deliver his final sermon. As Nell perceived with a faint sorrow woven through all of her anticipation and joy, the old order was swiftly transforming to make way for the new.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “Modifications are not entirely agreeable, yet they are wonderful affairs,” Mr. Pettifer remarked with philosophy. “A couple of years is roughly sufficient time for circumstances to remain completely unchanged. Should they remain stationary for any greater duration, they could become covered in moss.”

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: Mr. Pettifer engaged in smoking upon his veranda. A willingness had been expressed by his wife, out of self-sacrifice, allowing him to smoke within the house provided he was attentive to sit near an open window. Mr. Pettifer repaid this compromise by stepping outside entirely for his smoking during pleasant weather, thereby maintaining a spirit of mutual goodwill.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: Nell had arrived to request a few of her yellow dahlias from Mrs. Pettifer. That night, she and Isolde were heading to Echo Cottage so they could assist Miss Rosalind and Belinda the Fourth in making their last preparations for the wedding the next day. Miss Rosalind herself did not ever keep dahlias; she disliked them, nor would they have fitted the refined seclusion of her old-style garden. However, owing to Uncle Zeb’s storm, blooms of any sort were somewhat rare that summer in Brierley and the surrounding areas; thus Nell and Isolde believed a particular old cream-colored stone jug, which was normally reserved for doughnuts, filled to the top with yellow dahlias, would serve perfectly placed in a dark corner of the stone house staircase, set against the deep backdrop of red wallpaper in the hall.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “I guess you’ll be leaving for college in two weeks?” Mr. Pettifer went on. “Indeed, Emily and I are going to miss you terribly. Of course, Mrs. Sowerby will be across there instead of you. Nobody except a replacement can be found for those people.”

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: Paper cannot convey the sheer irony that marked Mr. Pettifer’s tone. Regardless of how close his wife was to Mrs. Sowerby, an armed neutrality remained the highest standard achievable for the connection between her and Mr. Pettifer, even after the new regime began.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “Indeed, I am leaving,” Nell remarked. “My mind feels quite pleased . . . while my heart feels deeply saddened.”

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “I guess you will be gathering every single honor that happens to be available at Wexcombe.”

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “I might attempt to win a couple of those,” Nell admitted, “however, such achievements hold less value for me than they did a pair of years in the past. My objective for my time at college is acquiring an understanding of how to live in the finest manner and make the absolute most of it. My desire is to gain the ability to comprehend and assist both myself and others.”

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: Mr. Pettifer nodded.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “Precisely so. Colleges should exist for that purpose, rather than for producing numerous B.A.‘s who are so packed with academic knowledge and self-conceit that nothing else can fit inside them. You are fine. I suppose college will not manage to damage you very much.”

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: Following tea, Isolde and Nell traveled to Echo Cottage, bringing along every bit of floral plunder acquired from a series of raiding trips through their own and nearby gardens. Upon arrival, they discovered that the stone residence was buzzing with activity. Belinda the Fourth was darting about with immense energy and speed, making her blue bows appear capable of existing in all places simultaneously. Much like the helmet of Navarre, the blue bows belonging to Belinda fluttered perpetually in the midst of the wildest commotion.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “Thank goodness you arrived,” she remarked piously, “since a multitude of chores remains . . . and the icing on that cake refuses to set . . . and every bit of silver still requires polishing . . . and the horsehair trunk needs packing . . . and the roosters destined for the chicken salad are still strutting past the henhouse over there, crowing, Miss Harcourt, ma’am. Moreover, Miss Rosalind cannot be relied upon to perform a single task. I felt relieved when Mr. Stanhope arrived a short while back and escorted her away for a stroll through the forest. Romance is fine where it belongs, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, but combining it with culinary work and cleaning ruins the whole affair. That is how I see it, Miss Harcourt, ma’am.”

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: So diligently did Nell and Isolde labor that Belinda the Fourth found nothing to complain about by the time ten o’clock arrived. Plaiting her hair into countless braids, she retired to bed with her exhausted small frame.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “However, I am certain I will not sleep a single moment, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, because I am afraid that an issue will arise right at the end . . . the cream will fail to whip . . . or Mr. Stanhope will suffer a stroke, preventing him from attending.”

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “Is he accustomed to suffering strokes?” inquired Isolde, as the dimpled edges of her mouth quivered. In the eyes of Isolde, Belinda the Fourth was a perpetual joy, even if she was not precisely a beautiful sight.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “These are not events that follow routine,” Belinda the Fourth stated with composure. “They simply occur . . . and then it is done. A stroke can happen to anyone. It does not require practice. Mr. Stanhope bears a strong resemblance to a relative of mine who suffered one right as he was sitting down to eat dinner a while back. However, perhaps things will turn out fine. While living in this world, a person must merely wish for the best, get ready for the worst, and accept whatever comes from God.”

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “My sole concern is that the weather will not be good tomorrow,” Isolde stated. “Rain was forecasted for midweek by Uncle Zeb, and I have been unable to avoid thinking Uncle Zeb’s words carry significant weight ever since that major storm.”

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: Because Nell understood far more clearly than Isolde the precise extent of Uncle Zeb's involvement in the tempest, this did not cause her much distress. She enjoyed the deep slumber reserved for those who are righteous and exhausted, until Belinda the Fourth awakened her at a extraordinarily early hour.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “Oh, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, it’s awful to call you so early,” wailed through the keyhole, “but there’s so much to do yet . . . and oh, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, I’m skeered it’s going to rain and I wish you’d get up and tell me you think it ain’t.” Hoping desperately that Belinda the Fourth uttered this just to wake her up completely, Nell rushed over to the window. However, the morning appeared dismal, unfortunately. Miss Rosalind’s garden below her window was dark and still when it ought to have shone with bright early daylight; furthermore, sullen clouds darkened the sky above the fir trees.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “Is it not excessively unkind!” Isolde remarked.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “Our hope must be for the best outcome,” Nell said with determination. “Provided it refrains from genuinely raining, an overcast, cool, pearly gray day such as this one will actually prove more pleasant than scorching sun.”

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “Yet rain is coming,” grieved Belinda, entering the room stealthily, looking absurd with her head encircled by numerous plaits whose tips, bound with white cotton, projected every which way. “Rain will be delayed until the ultimate second and then fall in torrents. Subsequently, everyone will become drenched . . . and bring mud into every corner of the dwelling . . . and holding the wedding beneath the honeysuckle will be impossible . . . and a bride deprived of sunshine suffers terrible misfortune, whatever you might claim, Miss Harcourt, ma’am. My intuition warned me that our good fortune was too great to endure.”

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: Belinda the Fourth appeared without doubt to have taken a page from the book of Miss Eliza Pullen.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: Precipitation never fell, even if the sky continually appeared ready to deliver it. The chambers had been embellished and the table exquisitely arranged when midday arrived; meanwhile on the upper floor, a bride was expecting her groom, “adorned for her husband.”

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “You really do appear sweet,” Nell remarked enthusiastically.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “Lovely,” Isolde repeated.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “Everything’s ready, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, and nothing dreadful has happened yet,” declared a cheerful Belinda before she went into her small back room to get dressed. Undoing all her braids, she took the wild crinkles that remained, plaited them into two pigtails, and fastened them using four brand-new, vivid blue ribbon bows instead of just two. Sprouting from Belinda’s neck, the pair of top bows looked remarkably like oversized wings, much like those on Raphael’s cherubs. Nevertheless, they were considered extremely lovely by Belinda the Fourth, who, having rustled into a white dress starched so heavily it was capable of standing on its own, looked at her reflection in the mirror with immense pride . . . a pride that endured right up to the moment she stepped into the hallway and saw, through the open spare room door, a tall girl wearing a softly draped dress, who was placing white, star-like blossoms into the sleek waves of her reddish hair.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “Oh, I shall not ever manage to resemble Miss Harcourt,” poor Belinda reflected in desperation. “A person simply must be created that way, I suppose . . . it does not appear as though any degree of training could grant a person that carriage.”

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: The visitors had arrived by one o’clock, among them Mr. and Mrs. Wace, because Mr. Wace was scheduled to conduct the service while the Welby minister was away on vacation. The wedding lacked any ceremony. Miss Rosalind descended the steps to join her groom at the bottom, and when he grabbed her hand she raised her large brown eyes to his with an expression that caused Belinda the Fourth, who caught the glance, to feel more peculiar than before. They walked outside to the honeysuckle arbor, the place where Mr. Wace was expecting them. The visitors arranged themselves in whatever manner they preferred. Nell and Isolde stood near the ancient stone bench, having Belinda the Fourth positioned between them while she frantically held onto their hands with her icy, shaking small paws.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: When Mr. Wace unclasped his blue book, the ritual began. At the exact moment that Miss Rosalind and Stephen Stanhope were declared husband and wife, an exceptionally lovely and meaningful event occurred. Without warning, the sun broke past the gloom and showered an abundance of light upon the joyful bride. Immediately, the garden became filled with moving shadows and shimmering rays.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
text: “What a lovely omen,” Nell thought while she hurried over to kiss the bride. Afterwards, leaving the remaining guests behind as they laughed around the newlyweds, the three girls sped inside the house to ensure that everything was prepared for the feast.

chapter_title: XXX A Wedding at the Stone House
